P62E-COP-BR-017.feedback: Marginal cost helps define willingness to accept.

P62E-COP-BR-018.q: Producer surplus differs from accounting profit partly because:
options: Producer surplus is tied to variable or marginal costs, while accounting profit also subtracts fixed costs
P62E-COP-BR-018.feedback: The measures use different cost concepts.

P62E-COP-BR-019.q: A monopoly and a competitive firm may use the same cost schedule. What differs later?
options: Their revenue and demand conditions, not the cost identities
P62E-COP-BR-019.feedback: Cost machinery is shared even when revenue conditions differ.

P62E-COP-BR-020.q: Why is marginal cost relevant to a competitive firm’s supply decision?
options: It measures the additional resource cost of another unit
It is fixed at every output
P62E-COP-BR-020.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional production cost of another unit and therefore helps determine whether expanding output is worthwhile at a given market price.

PMC-COP-BR-011.q: How does the general idea of opportunity cost carry into a firm’s production-cost analysis?
options: Opportunity cost is replaced by accounting profit
A firm counts only costs that change with output
Resources supplied by the owner are valued by the best alternative return sacrificed
Only purchased inputs have opportunity cost
PMC-COP-BR-011.feedback: The same next-best-alternative principle applies to labor, capital, land, and other resources used by a firm.

PMC-COP-BR-027.q: How does opportunity cost explain the difference between accounting profit and economic profit?
options: The two measures differ only when fixed cost changes
Economic profit subtracts the forgone returns of owner-supplied resources
Accounting profit subtracts more opportunity costs than economic profit
PMC-COP-BR-027.feedback: Economic profit extends accounting profit by charging the firm for owner resources at their next-best use.

PMC-COP-BR-028.q: Why is normal profit connected to the idea of opportunity cost?
options: It is identical to producer surplus
It compensates entrepreneurial resources for what they could earn in their next-best use
It is a tax on accounting profit
It measures consumer willingness to pay
PMC-COP-BR-028.feedback: Normal profit is the implicit opportunity cost required to keep entrepreneurial resources in the firm.

PMC-COP-BR-029.q: How does marginal decision-making differ from comparing total economic profit?
options: Marginal analysis focuses on changes from one more action, while economic profit compares total revenue with all opportunity costs
Marginal analysis compares total revenue with total explicit costs, while economic profit isolates the value of the next unit
Economic profit evaluates the next incremental action, while marginal analysis measures the return on the entire project
Both methods compare total revenue and total cost, but marginal analysis reports the result per unit of output
PMC-COP-BR-029.feedback: The two tools answer different questions: one about incremental choices and one about overall return after opportunity costs.

PMC-COP-BR-030.q: How does marginal product connect the production function to marginal cost when the wage is unchanged?
options: A higher marginal product necessarily raises marginal cost
Marginal cost and marginal product move together in the same direction
A higher marginal product generally means a lower marginal cost of additional output
PMC-COP-BR-030.feedback: When each worker adds more output for the same wage, the labor cost per additional unit falls.

PMC-COP-BR-031.q: Why does diminishing marginal product help explain the upward-sloping portion of short-run marginal cost?
options: Total product must fall as soon as diminishing returns begin
Additional variable input eventually adds less output, so each extra unit of output becomes more costly
Fixed cost rises with every worker
PMC-COP-BR-031.feedback: With a fixed input, falling marginal product raises the variable-input cost of producing additional output.

PMC-COP-BR-032.q: How does average product connect to average variable cost when labor is the only variable input and the wage is constant?
options: Average product equals total fixed cost per worker
Higher average product tends to imply lower average variable cost
Higher average product raises average fixed cost
Average product and average variable cost are unrelated
PMC-COP-BR-032.feedback: More output per worker spreads the wage cost across more units of output.

PMC-COP-BR-033.q: Why does the short-run/long-run distinction matter when interpreting cost curves?
options: Some inputs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs can vary in the long run
All costs are variable in both horizons
The long run is always exactly one year
Fixed costs rise only in the long run
PMC-COP-BR-033.feedback: Short-run cost curves reflect at least one fixed input; long-run cost analysis allows plant size and all other inputs to change.

PMC-COP-BR-034.q: How does the marginal-versus-average rule connect product curves to cost curves?
options: Marginal and average values always move in opposite directions
A marginal below an average always raises the average
The rule applies to product but never to cost
A marginal value above an average pulls the average up; a marginal cost below an average cost pulls that average down
PMC-COP-BR-034.feedback: The same arithmetic relationship governs MP versus AP and MC versus AVC or ATC.

PMC-COP-BR-035.q: How does identifying fixed and variable inputs help classify short-run costs?
options: Variable inputs determine accounting profit but not cost
Payments tied to fixed inputs generate fixed cost, while costs of variable inputs change with output
Every input creates only variable cost
PMC-COP-BR-035.feedback: Input flexibility is the production-side basis for distinguishing fixed and variable cost.

PMC-COP-BR-047.q: How does a fixed input in the production model connect to fixed cost?
options: Fixed inputs determine revenue rather than cost
A fixed input makes marginal cost zero
A payment associated with an input that cannot be changed in the short run contributes to fixed cost
Every fixed input creates variable cost only
PMC-COP-BR-047.feedback: The production distinction between fixed and variable inputs carries directly into short-run cost classification.

PMC-COP-BR-048.q: How does hiring additional labor connect production decisions to variable cost?
options: Variable cost falls automatically whenever workers are added
If labor is variable, more labor raises total variable cost
Hiring labor changes total fixed cost only
Labor cost is sunk by definition
PMC-COP-BR-048.feedback: Payments to adjustable inputs are part of total variable cost.

PMC-COP-BR-049.q: Why is the vertical distance between TC and TVC constant in a standard short-run total-cost graph?
options: The distance equals TFC, which does not vary with output
The distance equals MC, which is constant
TVC and TC have different output units
PMC-COP-BR-049.feedback: Because TC = TFC + TVC, the fixed-cost amount separates the two curves at every output.

PMC-COP-BR-050.q: How does a cost schedule support marginal analysis?
options: A cost schedule eliminates the need to compare changes
Only TFC is needed to calculate marginal cost
Marginal cost is found by adding TC and TVC
Changes in TC or TVC between output levels can be used to calculate marginal cost
PMC-COP-BR-050.feedback: Cost schedules provide the change in cost associated with a change in output.

PMC-COP-BR-051.q: How does TC = TFC + TVC relate to average total cost?
options: It implies ATC equals TFC at every output
It makes AVC independent of variable cost
Dividing each component by output gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by output gives MC = AFC + AVC
PMC-COP-BR-051.feedback: The total-cost identity becomes the average-cost identity after dividing by quantity.

PMC-COP-BR-052.q: Why does a pure increase in TFC leave the change in total cost between two output levels unchanged?
options: The increase reduces TVC by the same amount
The same fixed amount is added to TC at both output levels
TFC becomes variable after the increase
MC is defined as total fixed cost per unit
PMC-COP-BR-052.feedback: Marginal cost depends on cost differences across output, so a constant fixed-cost addition cancels out.

PMC-COP-BR-070.q: How does the fixed-cost concept connect to the downward slope of AFC?
options: TFC falls automatically as output rises
Variable cost is spread across fewer units
AFC is determined by marginal product only
The same TFC is spread across more units as output rises
PMC-COP-BR-070.feedback: AFC falls because the numerator stays fixed while the denominator grows.

PMC-COP-BR-071.q: How can rising average product of labor affect AVC when the wage is constant?
options: It tends to raise AVC because a worker producing more output increases total wage cost faster than output
It leaves AVC unchanged because a constant wage fixes variable cost per unit regardless of worker productivity
It tends to lower AVC because each worker produces more output per dollar of wage cost
It lowers average fixed cost rather than AVC because labor productivity affects the spreading of fixed cost
PMC-COP-BR-071.feedback: Higher output per worker reduces variable labor cost per unit.

PMC-COP-BR-072.q: How does the identity TC = TFC + TVC connect to ATC?
options: Dividing by Q gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by Q gives ATC = MC + AVC
PMC-COP-BR-072.feedback: The average-cost identity follows directly from the total-cost identity.

PMC-COP-BR-073.q: Why can ATC fall even when AVC is flat?
options: Falling AFC can pull ATC downward
PMC-COP-BR-073.feedback: Because ATC = AVC + AFC, a declining fixed-cost component can reduce ATC.

PMC-COP-BR-074.q: Why is AVC often more relevant than AFC for understanding the cost of current production activity?
options: AFC determines how much extra output one worker adds
AFC changes directly with every unit produced
AVC reflects variable resources used to produce the current output
PMC-COP-BR-074.feedback: Variable cost is tied to inputs adjusted as production changes.

PMC-COP-BR-075.q: How does a below-average marginal cost affect ATC?
options: It leaves ATC unchanged by definition
PMC-COP-BR-075.feedback: The marginal-versus-average rule applies to costs just as it does to other averages.

PMC-COP-BR-120.q: How does the sunk-cost rule connect to marginal analysis?
options: Both rules say fixed costs are always irrelevant
Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
Marginal analysis requires adding all past costs
Sunk cost is another term for marginal cost
PMC-COP-BR-120.feedback: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision.

PMC-COP-BR-121.q: How can a cost be fixed with respect to current output but still relevant to a future decision?
options: It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
Every fixed cost is permanently sunk
Fixed costs always change one-for-one with output
Future fixed costs are excluded from economic cost
PMC-COP-BR-121.feedback: Cost behavior with output and recoverability across decisions are different classifications.

PMC-COP-BR-122.q: Why is “recovering what we already spent” a poor reason by itself to continue a project?
options: Continuing can convert past spending into a relevant marginal benefit if enough future revenue is earned
Past spending should be added to expected future benefits because the project needs to recover its historical cost
A project should continue when accounting profit remains positive, even if future incremental costs exceed benefits
Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
PMC-COP-BR-122.feedback: The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment.

PMC-COP-BR-145.q: How does specialization connect to economies of scale?
options: A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
Specialization always creates diminishing marginal product
Specialization raises fixed cost per unit forever
PMC-COP-BR-145.feedback: Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range.

PMC-COP-BR-146.q: How do coordination problems connect organizational size to diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination problems reduce all input prices
They guarantee constant returns to scale
They turn fixed cost into sunk cost
Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
PMC-COP-BR-146.feedback: Very large scale can create managerial inefficiencies that push LRAC upward.

PMC-COP-BR-147.q: How does the short-run/long-run distinction connect SRATC curves to LRAC?
options: SRATC includes implicit cost but LRAC does not
The curves differ only because of revenue
Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
LRAC fixes plant size while SRATC changes every input
PMC-COP-BR-147.feedback: Long-run flexibility over plant size is what lets LRAC trace the least-cost envelope.

PMC-COP-BR-148.q: How is economies of scale different from spreading a fixed short-run cost over more units?
options: Falling AFC is a long-run scale effect only
Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
Economies of scale requires one input to remain fixed
PMC-COP-BR-148.feedback: Both can lower average cost, but they arise from different mechanisms and horizons.

PMC-COP-BR-149.q: How can productivity improvements affect long-run average cost?
options: If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
Productivity affects revenue but never cost
PMC-COP-BR-149.feedback: More output from a given bundle of resources can lower the cost required per unit.

PMC-COP-BR-164.q: How does MES build on the idea of economies of scale?
options: MES is the largest feasible plant regardless of cost
MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
MES is where diseconomies first begin at zero output
PMC-COP-BR-164.feedback: Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached.

PMC-COP-BR-165.q: How does constant returns to scale differ from short-run diminishing marginal product?
options: Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
Constant returns requires a fixed plant
Diminishing marginal product requires all inputs to change proportionally
PMC-COP-BR-165.feedback: The concepts apply to different production experiments and time horizons.

PMC-COP-BR-166.q: Why can MES matter when comparing efficient firm scale with the size of a market?
options: It fixes the market price by law
It measures accounting profit rather than cost
It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
PMC-COP-BR-166.feedback: MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.

P62F-PC-E-001.q: Which condition is most consistent with perfect competition?
options: Many small firms sell an identical product
One firm controls a unique product
Each seller offers a heavily differentiated brand
P62F-PC-E-001.feedback: Perfect competition has many small sellers and a standardized product.

P62F-PC-E-002.q: A perfectly competitive firm is called a price taker because:
options: It is legally forbidden to change output
Its individual output is too small to affect the market price
It sets the price for all firms
P62F-PC-E-002.feedback: The market determines price; one small firm cannot move it.

P62F-PC-E-003.q: Which decision remains for a price-taking firm?
P62F-PC-E-003.feedback: The firm accepts price but chooses quantity.

P62F-PC-E-004.q: The demand curve facing an individual competitive firm is:
options: The same downward-sloping curve as market demand
P62F-PC-E-004.feedback: The firm can sell its feasible output at the given price.

P62F-PC-E-005.q: Market demand differs from the individual firm’s demand because market demand is:
options: Downward sloping while firm demand is horizontal
Horizontal while firm demand slopes downward
Vertical while firm demand is horizontal
P62F-PC-E-005.feedback: The market determines price; the small firm takes it.

P62F-PC-E-006.q: For a competitive firm, average revenue equals:

P62F-PC-E-007.q: For a competitive firm, marginal revenue equals:
P62F-PC-E-007.feedback: Each additional unit sells at the constant market price.

P62F-PC-E-008.q: If price is $12 and the firm sells 20 units, total revenue is:

P62F-PC-E-009.q: Which relationship holds for a price-taking firm?
options: P = ATC = AFC at every output
MR falls below price as output rises
P62F-PC-E-009.feedback: Constant price makes average and marginal revenue equal to price.

P62F-PC-E-010.q: For a competitive firm, economic profit is calculated as:
options: Total revenue minus total economic cost
Total revenue minus variable cost only
P62F-PC-E-010.feedback: Economic profit subtracts all explicit and implicit costs.

P62F-PC-E-011.q: If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost for the next unit, the firm should:
P62F-PC-E-011.feedback: The unit adds more revenue than cost.

P62F-PC-E-012.q: For the next unit of output, marginal cost is greater than marginal revenue. Producing that unit would:
P62F-PC-E-012.feedback: The unit adds more cost than revenue.

P62F-PC-E-013.q: The standard output rule for a competitive firm is to produce where:
options: MR equals MC on the rising portion of MC
Price equals ATC at every output
P62F-PC-E-013.feedback: The relevant MR=MC crossing lies on rising MC.

P62F-PC-E-014.q: Why is the rising-MC condition important?
options: A falling-MC crossing need not be a profit maximum
P62F-PC-E-014.feedback: Profit is maximized at the crossing where MC rises through MR.

P62F-PC-E-015.q: If price exceeds ATC at the chosen output, the firm earns:
P62F-PC-E-015.feedback: P>ATC creates positive profit per unit.

P62F-PC-E-016.q: If price equals ATC at the chosen output, the firm earns:
options: A loss equal to fixed cost

P62F-PC-E-017.q: If price is below ATC but above AVC at the chosen output, the firm should generally:
options: Produce in the short run while earning a loss
Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
Exit immediately and erase fixed cost
P62F-PC-E-017.feedback: Covering AVC and some fixed cost reduces the short-run loss.

P62F-PC-E-018.q: The short-run shutdown rule compares price with:
P62F-PC-E-018.feedback: Variable cost is avoidable in the short run.

P62F-PC-E-019.q: The shutdown price is the minimum of:
P62F-PC-E-019.feedback: The minimum AVC is the threshold for short-run operation.

P62F-PC-E-020.q: If a firm shuts down in the short run, its fixed cost:
P62F-PC-E-020.feedback: Short-run fixed cost is unavoidable even at zero output.

P62F-PC-E-021.q: Short-run shutdown differs from long-run exit because exit:
options: Removes the firm from the industry and avoids all future costs
Occurs whenever P is below ATC for one day
Means the firm produces at minimum AVC
P62F-PC-E-021.feedback: Exit is the long-run industry decision.

P62F-PC-E-022.q: The competitive firm’s short-run supply curve is:
options: The portion of MC at or above AVC
The portion of MC below AVC
P62F-PC-E-022.feedback: Below AVC the firm shuts down rather than supplies along MC.

P62F-PC-E-023.q: Market supply in a competitive industry is found by:
options: Horizontally summing firms’ quantities supplied at each price
P62F-PC-E-023.feedback: At each price, add quantities across firms.

P62F-PC-E-024.q: Short-run economic profit tends to attract:
P62F-PC-E-024.feedback: Entry expands market supply and erodes profit.

P62F-PC-E-025.q: Persistent economic losses tend to cause:
options: A permanent fall in supply price with more firms
P62F-PC-E-025.feedback: Exit contracts market supply and helps remove losses.

P62F-PC-E-026.q: In long-run competitive equilibrium, firms earn:
options: A loss equal to fixed cost
P62F-PC-E-026.feedback: Entry and exit eliminate economic profit and loss.

P62F-PC-E-027.q: Zero economic profit means the firm covers:
options: All explicit and implicit opportunity costs
P62F-PC-E-027.feedback: Normal profit is included among implicit costs.

P62F-PC-E-028.q: Productive efficiency occurs when a firm produces at:
P62F-PC-E-028.feedback: Minimum ATC is the lowest feasible per-unit cost.

P62F-PC-E-029.feedback: P reflects marginal benefit and MC reflects marginal cost.

P62F-PC-E-030.q: Perfect competition is best understood as:
options: A literal description of every farm or stock market
A benchmark model for studying price taking and efficiency
A model in which firms never choose output
P62F-PC-E-030.feedback: The model is an analytical benchmark with strong assumptions.

P62F-PC-E-031.q: Refer to the graph. What market price does the competitive firm take as given?
P62F-PC-E-031.feedback: The horizontal P = MR = AR line is at $30.

P62F-PC-E-032.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the $30 MR line meet rising MC, identifying the profit-maximizing quantity?
P62F-PC-E-032.feedback: The relevant rising MC curve meets P = MR at Q = 50.

P62F-PC-E-033.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, what is average total cost?
P62F-PC-E-033.feedback: At Q = 50, the ATC guide is $20.

P62F-PC-E-034.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does the firm operate?
P62F-PC-E-034.feedback: P = MR intersects rising MC at Q = 50.

P62F-PC-E-035.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, what relationship holds between price and ATC?
P62F-PC-E-035.feedback: The price line passes through ATC at $25.

P62F-PC-E-036.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the $30 MR line meet rising MC, identifying the firm’s output in the loss-but-operate case?
P62F-PC-E-036.feedback: The horizontal price line meets rising MC at Q = 30.

P62F-PC-E-037.q: Refer to the graph. What market price does the firm face?
P62F-PC-E-037.feedback: The P = MR = AR line is at $30.

P62F-PC-E-038.q: Refer to the graph. What price is shown by the horizontal P = MR = AR line?
P62F-PC-E-038.feedback: The horizontal price line is at $10.

P62F-PC-E-039.q: Refer to the graph. Which labeled point marks the minimum of AVC?
P62F-PC-E-039.feedback: MC crosses AVC at its minimum at point A.

P62F-PC-E-040.q: Refer to the graph. Given the price, what is the firm’s short-run output?
P62F-PC-E-040.feedback: The $10 price lies below minimum AVC, so the firm shuts down and supplies zero.

P62F-PC-E-041.q: Refer to the graph. What market-clearing price is determined by the intersection of market supply and demand?
P62F-PC-E-041.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at a price of $40.

P62F-PC-E-042.q: Refer to the graph. The market panel settles at $40. Reading across to the firm panel, which quantity is selected where MR meets rising MC?
P62F-PC-E-042.feedback: On the firm panel, P = MR = $40 meets rising MC at Q = 90.

P62F-PC-E-043.q: Refer to the graph. In the paired loss case, what price is transmitted from the market equilibrium to the representative firm?
P62F-PC-E-043.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at $15.

P62F-PC-E-044.q: Refer to the graph. With the market equilibrium price at $15, where does the firm panel place the MR–MC output choice?
P62F-PC-E-044.feedback: The firm’s P = MR line meets rising MC at Q = 50.

P62F-PC-E-045.q: Refer to the graph. In the market panel where equilibrium quantity is 100, what equilibrium price is shown?
P62F-PC-E-045.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at $25.

P62F-PC-E-046.q: Refer to the graph. At the long-run market price of $25, which firm quantity lies at the rising-MC intersection?
P62F-PC-E-046.feedback: The firm’s horizontal MR line meets MC at Q = 50.

PM5-PC-E-022.q: A competitive firm has price $18 and ATC $15 at its chosen output. Economic profit per unit is:
PM5-PC-E-022.feedback: Profit per unit equals price minus average total cost.

PM5-PC-E-023.q: A firm sells 40 units at $12 and has ATC of $9. Total economic profit is:

PM5-PC-E-024.q: At a competitive firm’s chosen output, price equals ATC. The firm is:
options: Earning a loss equal to fixed cost
Breaking even with zero economic profit
PM5-PC-E-024.feedback: When P = ATC, total revenue equals total economic cost.

PM5-PC-E-025.q: A firm has price $14 and ATC $17 at its chosen output. Its economic loss per unit is:
PM5-PC-E-025.feedback: Loss per unit is ATC minus price when ATC exceeds price.

PM5-PC-E-026.q: A firm produces 25 units, receives $10 per unit, and has ATC of $12. Total economic loss is:

PM5-PC-E-027.q: Which statement is true when a competitive firm earns zero economic profit?
options: Accounting profit must also be zero because economic and accounting costs are identical in competition
The firm must leave the industry immediately
Economic cost already includes normal profit to owner-supplied resources
The owner receives no return of any kind
PM5-PC-E-027.feedback: Zero economic profit means revenues cover explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit.

PM5-PC-E-037.q: A competitive firm should shut down in the short run when price is:
options: Below minimum ATC but above AVC
PM5-PC-E-037.feedback: If price cannot cover variable cost, producing makes the short-run loss larger than shutting down.

PM5-PC-E-038.q: A firm has P = $14, AVC = $10, and ATC = $18 at its best positive output. In the short run it should:
options: Shut down because P is below ATC
Produce even though it has an economic loss
PM5-PC-E-038.feedback: Price covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost, so producing minimizes the short-run loss.

PM5-PC-E-039.q: Which statement best distinguishes shutdown from exit?
options: Shutdown occurs only when economic profit is positive
Exit refers only to reducing one unit of output
Shutdown is a short-run zero-output decision; exit is a long-run decision to leave the industry
Shutdown and exit are identical because both set output to zero and permanently remove the firm from the market
PM5-PC-E-039.feedback: A firm can temporarily shut down while fixed commitments remain, whereas exit changes long-run industry participation.

PM5-PC-E-050.q: For a competitive firm, the short-run supply curve is the portion of:
options: ATC at and above minimum AVC
MC at and above minimum AVC
PM5-PC-E-050.feedback: The firm follows rising MC when operating and supplies zero below the shutdown price.

PM5-PC-E-051.q: If market price rises and the competitive firm remains open, the firm typically moves:
options: Along a horizontal MC curve by assumption
To zero output because price changed
Up along its rising MC curve to a larger quantity
Down its ATC curve with no output change
PM5-PC-E-051.feedback: Since P = MR, a higher price intersects rising MC at a larger output.

PM5-PC-E-052.q: A rise in a firm’s fixed property tax, with variable costs unchanged, does what to its short-run supply curve?
options: Shifts it left because MC rises
Shifts it right because AVC falls
PM5-PC-E-052.feedback: Fixed cost does not change MC or AVC, so the firm’s short-run supply schedule is unchanged.

PM5-PC-E-053.q: A wage increase raises the variable cost of producing each unit. Other things equal, the firm’s short-run supply tends to:
options: Shift right because fixed cost is spread out
Stay unchanged because wages are not marginal costs
PM5-PC-E-053.feedback: Higher variable input costs raise MC and reduce quantity supplied at each price.

PM5-PC-E-054.q: To construct market supply from individual competitive firms, economists:
options: Vertically adding each firm’s prices at one quantity
Using the output of the largest firm only
Adding market demand to one firm’s MC curve
Add the quantities each firm supplies at the same price
PM5-PC-E-054.feedback: Industry quantity supplied is the sum of firm quantities at the same market price.

PM5-PC-E-055.q: Below the firm’s shutdown price, its short-run quantity supplied is:
PM5-PC-E-055.feedback: Below minimum AVC, the firm minimizes loss by shutting down.

PM5-PC-E-056.q: At a price of $20, each of 50 identical firms supplies 8 units. Market quantity supplied is:
PM5-PC-E-056.feedback: Market supply adds the 8 units supplied by each of 50 firms: 50 × 8 = 400.

PM5-PC-E-057.q: Which change is most likely to leave a competitive firm’s short-run supply unchanged?
options: A higher fixed annual permit fee
A higher price for raw materials
PM5-PC-E-057.feedback: Fixed-cost changes do not alter the firm’s MC or AVC schedule.

PM5-PC-E-073.q: Persistent positive economic profit in a competitive industry tends to encourage:
options: A permanent price increase with no supply response
PM5-PC-E-073.feedback: Positive economic profit attracts resources and firms when entry is available.

PM5-PC-E-074.q: Persistent economic losses in a competitive industry tend to encourage:
PM5-PC-E-074.feedback: Long-run losses push resources toward better alternatives.

PM5-PC-E-075.q: In the standard long-run competitive equilibrium, economic profit is:
PM5-PC-E-075.feedback: Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.

PM5-PC-E-076.q: Zero economic profit means the firm is earning:
options: A normal return included in economic cost
No accounting profit and no return to the owner
A loss equal to fixed cost
PM5-PC-E-076.feedback: Normal profit compensates owner resources for their opportunity cost and is included in economic cost.

PM5-PC-E-077.q: When firms enter a competitive industry, market supply generally:
options: Equals market demand at every price
PM5-PC-E-077.feedback: More firms contribute output at each price, shifting market supply right.

PM5-PC-E-078.q: Several firms permanently leave a competitive industry. Holding the remaining firms’ cost schedules fixed, market supply:
PM5-PC-E-078.feedback: Fewer firms supply the market, shifting industry supply left.

PM5-PC-E-091.q: In a constant-cost competitive industry, industry expansion leaves input prices and firms’ cost curves essentially unchanged. The long-run industry supply curve is typically:
PM5-PC-E-091.feedback: If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.

PM5-PC-E-092.q: If industry expansion bids up specialized input prices, the industry is best described as:
PM5-PC-E-092.feedback: Higher input prices raise firms’ costs as the industry expands.

PM5-PC-E-093.q: If industry expansion leads to cheaper specialized suppliers and lower unit costs, the industry may be:
PM5-PC-E-093.feedback: Industry growth can lower firm costs when external economies develop.

PM5-PC-E-094.q: A permanent demand increase in a competitive industry usually creates what first?
options: Immediate zero economic profit with no price change
A short-run price and profit increase before entry completes
PM5-PC-E-094.feedback: Demand changes first affect the existing set of firms; entry is a long-run response.

PM5-PC-E-095.q: Which condition best supports a constant-cost industry?
options: Industry growth creates supplier efficiencies that lower costs
Firms are legally prevented from entering
The industry can expand without materially changing the prices of its inputs
Every new firm makes a key input scarcer and more expensive
PM5-PC-E-095.feedback: Constant-cost means industry size does not materially shift representative firms’ cost curves.

PM5-PC-E-105.q: Allocative efficiency in the competitive benchmark is associated with:
PM5-PC-E-105.feedback: Price reflects marginal willingness to pay while MC reflects marginal opportunity cost.

PM5-PC-E-106.q: Productive efficiency for a competitive firm is associated with producing at:
PM5-PC-E-106.feedback: Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.

P62F-PC-M-001.q: A competitive firm faces price $18. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $6, $9, $12, $16, $20, $25. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
P62F-PC-M-001.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

P62F-PC-M-002.q: At price $18, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $16. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
P62F-PC-M-002.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

P62F-PC-M-003.q: A competitive firm faces price $24. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $8, $13, $17, $21, $26, $32. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
P62F-PC-M-003.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

P62F-PC-M-004.q: At price $24, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $21. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
P62F-PC-M-004.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

P62F-PC-M-005.q: A competitive firm faces price $30. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $10, $16, $22, $28, $35, $43. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
P62F-PC-M-005.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

P62F-PC-M-006.q: At price $30, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $28. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
P62F-PC-M-006.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

P62F-PC-M-007.q: A competitive firm faces price $15. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $4, $8, $11, $14, $18, $23. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
P62F-PC-M-007.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

P62F-PC-M-008.q: At price $15, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $14. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
P62F-PC-M-008.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

P62F-PC-M-009.q: A competitive firm faces price $27. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $9, $14, $19, $25, $31, $38. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
P62F-PC-M-009.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

P62F-PC-M-010.q: At price $27, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $25. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
P62F-PC-M-010.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

P62F-PC-M-011.q: At its MR=MC output of 50 units, a competitive firm has P=$40, ATC=$32, and AVC=$22. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
P62F-PC-M-011.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

P62F-PC-M-012.q: A competitive firm produces 50 units at price $40. ATC at that output is $32. What is profit per unit?

P62F-PC-M-013.q: At its MR=MC output of 60 units, a competitive firm has P=$28, ATC=$34, and AVC=$20. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down and eliminate all costs
Produce and incur a loss of $360
P62F-PC-M-013.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

P62F-PC-M-014.q: A competitive firm produces 60 units at price $28. ATC at that output is $34. What is profit per unit?

P62F-PC-M-015.q: At its MR=MC output of 45 units, a competitive firm has P=$24, ATC=$24, and AVC=$17. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
P62F-PC-M-015.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

P62F-PC-M-016.q: A competitive firm produces 45 units at price $24. ATC at that output is $24. What is profit per unit?

P62F-PC-M-017.q: At its MR=MC output of 55 units, a competitive firm has P=$19, ATC=$28, and AVC=$16. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down and eliminate all costs
Produce and incur a loss of $495
P62F-PC-M-017.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

P62F-PC-M-018.q: A competitive firm produces 55 units at price $19. ATC at that output is $28. What is profit per unit?

P62F-PC-M-019.q: At its MR=MC output of 40 units, a competitive firm has P=$14, ATC=$26, and AVC=$18. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down in the short run
P62F-PC-M-019.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

P62F-PC-M-020.q: A competitive firm produces 40 units at price $14. ATC at that output is $26. What is profit per unit?

P62F-PC-M-021.q: Competitive firms are earning positive economic profit. What happens as entry occurs?
options: Market supply falls and price rises
Market supply increases and market price falls
P62F-PC-M-021.feedback: Entry shifts market supply right and erodes profit.

P62F-PC-M-022.q: Competitive firms are earning economic losses. What happens as firms exit?
options: Market supply increases and price falls
Market supply decreases and market price rises
P62F-PC-M-022.feedback: Exit shifts market supply left and reduces remaining firms’ losses.

P62F-PC-M-023.q: In a constant-cost industry, demand rises permanently. After long-run adjustment, price typically:
options: Equals minimum AVC but not ATC
P62F-PC-M-023.feedback: Entry expands output without changing input prices or cost curves.

P62F-PC-M-024.q: In an increasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price typically ends:
options: Above the original price but below the short-run price
At zero economic profit only if price is zero
P62F-PC-M-024.feedback: Industry expansion raises input costs, so long-run price rises.

P62F-PC-M-025.q: In a decreasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price can end:
options: At the original price by definition
P62F-PC-M-025.feedback: External economies can lower firms’ costs as the industry expands.

P62F-PC-M-026.q: At long-run competitive equilibrium, which pair holds?
options: P = MC and P = minimum ATC
P62F-PC-M-026.feedback: Long-run competition combines allocative and productive efficiency.

P62F-PC-M-027.q: A fixed annual license fee rises for every competitive firm. In the short run, each firm’s output at a given price is:
options: Unchanged because MC and AVC are unchanged
P62F-PC-M-027.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change shifts ATC, not MC or AVC.

P62F-PC-M-028.q: A per-unit production tax is imposed. For a competitive firm, the tax directly shifts:
P62F-PC-M-028.feedback: A per-unit tax is a variable and marginal cost.

P62F-PC-M-029.q: A technology improvement lowers marginal cost. At the same market price, the firm generally chooses:
options: The same output because price is fixed
P62F-PC-M-029.feedback: Lower MC moves the P=MC output to a larger quantity.

P62F-PC-M-030.q: A competitive outcome has P=MC but the firm is not at minimum ATC. The outcome is:
options: Productively efficient but not allocatively efficient
Allocatively efficient but not productively efficient
P62F-PC-M-030.feedback: P=MC is allocative efficiency; minimum ATC is productive efficiency.

P62F-PC-M-031.feedback: The AVC guide at Q = 50 is $10.

P62F-PC-M-032.q: Refer to the graph. At the 50-unit output, what vertical price–ATC gap represents profit on each unit?
P62F-PC-M-032.feedback: Profit per unit is P − ATC = $30 − $20 = $10.

P62F-PC-M-033.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at the profit-maximizing output?

P62F-PC-M-034.q: Refer to the graph. What economic profit does the firm earn at the output?
P62F-PC-M-034.feedback: Because P equals ATC at Q = 50, economic profit is zero.

P62F-PC-M-035.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s total revenue at the break-even price and output shown?

P62F-PC-M-036.q: Refer to the graph. The blue ATC guide at the chosen 30-unit output lands on which dollar value?
P62F-PC-M-036.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 30 is $40.

P62F-PC-M-037.q: Refer to the graph. The green AVC marker at Q = 30 gives what variable cost per unit?
P62F-PC-M-037.feedback: The AVC guide at Q = 30 is $20.

P62F-PC-M-038.q: Refer to the graph. At the firm’s chosen output in the loss graph, what is the loss per unit?
P62F-PC-M-038.feedback: Loss per unit is ATC − P = $40 − $30 = $10.

P62F-PC-M-039.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s shutdown price?
P62F-PC-M-039.feedback: Minimum AVC is $20 at point A.

P62F-PC-M-040.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the firm’s short-run supply curve begin?
options: At the left end of the entire MC curve
At point C and then along ATC
At point A and then along rising MC
Along the AVC curve below A
P62F-PC-M-040.feedback: Short-run supply is rising MC at and above minimum AVC.

P62F-PC-M-041.q: Refer to the graph. At the 90-unit output in the paired profit graph, what vertical price–ATC gap represents profit per unit?
P62F-PC-M-041.feedback: Price is $40 and ATC is $20, so profit per unit is $20.

P62F-PC-M-042.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit for the representative firm?

P62F-PC-M-043.q: Refer to the graph. How does the market-panel equilibrium price enter the representative firm’s decision?
options: It becomes the firm’s ATC curve, determining average cost at every possible output level
It becomes the firm’s quantity of 75, so market quantity and individual output are identical
It becomes the firm’s horizontal P = MR = AR line used to choose output along MC
It shifts the firm’s MC curve upward, changing production cost without changing marginal revenue
P62F-PC-M-043.feedback: A price-taking firm accepts the market price as its marginal and average revenue.

P62F-PC-M-044.q: Refer to the graph. Use the price and ATC at the representative firm’s chosen output. What is the loss per unit?
P62F-PC-M-044.feedback: ATC is $18 and price is $15, so loss per unit is $3.

P62F-PC-M-045.q: Refer to the graph. What is the representative firm’s total economic loss?

P62F-PC-M-046.q: Refer to the graph. Use price and AVC at the chosen output. Why does the representative firm continue producing in the short run?
options: P = $15 exceeds AVC = $10 at Q = 50, so revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost
P = $15 exceeds ATC = $18 at Q = 50, so the firm is earning positive economic profit
The competitive firm can raise its own price above $15, so it avoids the loss shown by ATC
Producing at Q = 50 eliminates fixed cost, so any price above AVC guarantees zero economic loss
P62F-PC-M-046.feedback: The firm covers variable cost and part of fixed cost because P > AVC.

P62F-PC-M-047.q: Refer to the graph. What economic profit does the representative firm earn at the long-run equilibrium?
P62F-PC-M-047.feedback: Price equals ATC at the selected output, so economic profit is zero.

P62F-PC-M-048.q: Refer to the graph. Which pair of conditions holds at the representative firm’s selected output?
options: P < AVC and MC < ATC for the displayed firm
P = MC and P = minimum ATC
P62F-PC-M-048.feedback: Long-run competitive equilibrium has P = MC and P at minimum ATC.

PM5-PC-M-001.q: A competitive wheat farm doubles its own output while every other seller and market demand are unchanged. Why is the market price essentially unaffected?
options: The farm is too small relative to the market to influence price
The farm can force buyers to accept any price
Its average total cost determines the market price for all sellers
Doubling output makes its demand curve downward sloping
PM5-PC-M-001.feedback: A price-taking firm is individually too small to move the market price.

PM5-PC-M-002.q: The market price of soybeans is $12 per bushel. Which statement best describes the demand curve facing one competitive soybean farm?
options: It slopes downward because the farm must cut price to sell more
It is vertical at the farm’s current quantity
It coincides with the entire market demand curve
It is horizontal at $12 over the farm’s feasible output range
PM5-PC-M-002.feedback: A competitive firm can sell feasible output at the prevailing market price, so its firm-level demand is horizontal.

PM5-PC-M-003.q: A competitive firm sells its first 25 units at $18 each. If it can also sell the 26th unit at $18, marginal revenue from the 26th unit is:
PM5-PC-M-003.feedback: For a price-taking firm, each additional unit adds the unchanged market price to total revenue.

PM5-PC-M-004.q: A price-taking firm has total revenue of $1,260 from selling 70 units. Its average revenue is:
PM5-PC-M-004.feedback: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price for a competitive firm.

PM5-PC-M-005.q: If the competitive market price falls from $24 to $20, what happens to the individual firm’s P, AR, and MR?
options: Price becomes $20 while AR and MR stay $24
MR falls to $20 but AR stays $24
Only total revenue changes; P, AR, and MR do not
PM5-PC-M-005.feedback: For a price-taking firm, price, average revenue, and marginal revenue all equal the market price.

PM5-PC-M-006.q: A competitive firm faces a constant market price of $15. Which total-revenue pattern is consistent with price taking?
options: Total revenue rises by a smaller amount with each additional unit
Total revenue is fixed because the firm cannot change price
Total revenue falls whenever output rises
Each additional unit raises total revenue by $15
PM5-PC-M-006.feedback: With constant price, total revenue increases linearly and each unit adds the same amount.

PM5-PC-M-007.q: Which pair correctly contrasts market demand with the demand facing one perfectly competitive firm?
options: Market demand is horizontal; firm demand slopes downward
Both curves slope downward because every seller faces the same market demand
Market demand slopes downward; the individual firm faces a horizontal line at market price
Both curves are horizontal because all firms are price takers
PM5-PC-M-007.feedback: Industry demand determines market price with supply, while an individual competitive firm takes that price as given.

PM5-PC-M-008.q: A market has many sellers, standardized output, and easy entry. Which additional implication is most consistent with the competitive model?
options: Brand loyalty gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve
No single seller has meaningful control over market price
Each firm chooses a unique profit-maximizing price
Firms must coordinate output to avoid price wars
PM5-PC-M-008.feedback: The competitive assumptions make individual firms price takers.

PM5-PC-M-009.q: A competitive firm sells 40 units at $9 and then 45 units at the same price. By how much does total revenue increase?
PM5-PC-M-009.feedback: Five additional units at $9 each add $45 to total revenue.

PM5-PC-M-040.q: A competitive firm faces P = $11. At the output where MR = MC, AVC = $8 and ATC = $15. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Exit immediately because fixed cost is positive
Produce in the short run and incur a loss
Shut down because price is below ATC
PM5-PC-M-040.feedback: Price covers AVC but not ATC, so the firm produces and uses revenue to cover variable cost plus part of fixed cost.

PM5-PC-M-041.q: At the best positive output, a firm faces P = $7, AVC = $9, and ATC = $13. What should it do in the short run?
options: Shut down because revenue cannot cover variable cost
Produce because price is below ATC
Raise output until ATC falls to $7
PM5-PC-M-041.feedback: When P < AVC, producing fails to cover avoidable variable cost.

PM5-PC-M-042.q: A competitive firm has already paid a nonrefundable annual license fee. The fee increases while market price, MC, and AVC are unchanged. What happens to the short-run output decision?
options: Output falls because every fixed-cost increase shifts MC upward
The firm must shut down immediately
Output rises to spread the fee across more units
The profit-maximizing positive output is unchanged, though profit is lower
PM5-PC-M-042.feedback: A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.

PM5-PC-M-058.q: A firm’s MC for units 1–5 is $6, $9, $13, $18, and $24. Assume AVC is covered. If price rises from $14 to $20, output changes from:
PM5-PC-M-058.feedback: The firm produces through the last unit whose MC does not exceed price on rising MC.

PM5-PC-M-059.q: At price $16, 30 identical firms each supply 5 units. At price $22, each supplies 8 units. What is the industry response?
options: Market quantity supplied falls from 240 to 150 units
Market quantity supplied stays at 30 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 150 to 240 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 35 to 38 units
PM5-PC-M-059.feedback: Horizontal aggregation multiplies each firm’s quantity by the number of identical firms.

PM5-PC-M-060.q: A fixed insurance premium increases by $4,000 for every firm in a competitive industry. Market demand and variable costs are unchanged. In the immediate short run, what happens to each operating firm’s supply curve?
options: It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It does not shift because MC and AVC are unchanged
It shifts left because ATC rises
It shifts right because firms need more output
PM5-PC-M-060.feedback: Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.

PM5-PC-M-061.q: A per-unit fee raises MC and AVC by $2 at every positive output. Which supply effect is most consistent?
options: The firm requires a higher market price to supply a given quantity
The supply curve is unchanged because the fee is fixed
The firm supplies more at every price
Only ATC changes, so shutdown price cannot change
PM5-PC-M-061.feedback: A per-unit cost raises marginal and variable cost, shifting the operating supply schedule upward.

PM5-PC-M-062.q: A firm has minimum AVC of $9. At P = $8, its quantity supplied is zero; at P = $12, it supplies where P = MC. What does this illustrate?
options: The entire MC curve is supply even below AVC
ATC alone determines the firm’s supply
Market demand is the firm’s supply curve
The supply curve includes rising MC only above the shutdown threshold
PM5-PC-M-062.feedback: The shutdown threshold determines where the rising MC curve becomes the firm’s short-run supply.

PM5-PC-M-063.q: Ten firms each increase quantity supplied by 3 units when price rises. If no firms enter or exit, industry quantity supplied increases by:
PM5-PC-M-063.feedback: Industry supply sums the individual output responses: 10 × 3 = 30.

PM5-PC-M-064.q: Market demand increases in a competitive industry. Before entry occurs, the market price rises. How does one firm respond if its costs are unchanged?
options: It cuts price below the new market price to expand sales
Its P = MR line rises and it moves to a larger quantity on MC
Its ATC becomes the market supply curve
PM5-PC-M-064.feedback: The market price change is transmitted to the firm as a change in MR, producing movement along its supply curve.

PM5-PC-M-079.q: A competitive industry earns positive economic profit. What long-run sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Entry decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
Firms keep the profit permanently because they are price takers
Entry increases market supply, price falls, and economic profit is pushed toward zero
Exit decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
PM5-PC-M-079.feedback: Free entry expands industry supply and erodes positive economic profit.

PM5-PC-M-080.q: Firms in a competitive industry are sustaining economic losses. What long-run sequence is most likely?
options: Firms shut down for one day and long-run equilibrium is restored automatically
Exit reduces market supply, price rises, and losses are pushed toward zero
Entry raises supply, price falls, and losses deepen indefinitely
Exit raises supply and lowers price
PM5-PC-M-080.feedback: Long-run exit contracts industry supply and raises the market price relative to the loss-making situation.

PM5-PC-M-081.q: A firm has positive accounting profit but zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium. How can both be true?
options: Accounting profit can cover the owner’s implicit opportunity costs that economists count as costs
Accounting profit must always equal zero when economic profit is zero
The firm receives a subsidy equal to normal profit
PM5-PC-M-081.feedback: Economic cost includes owner-supplied resources, so accounting and economic profit need not be equal.

PM5-PC-M-082.q: A firm temporarily produces zero because price is below AVC, but managers expect conditions to improve next season. This is best described as:
options: Short-run shutdown rather than long-run exit
PM5-PC-M-082.feedback: A temporary zero-output choice can occur while the firm remains in the industry.

PM5-PC-M-083.q: For a representative firm in the standard constant-cost competitive benchmark, which condition is associated with long-run equilibrium?
options: P is below AVC while the firm continues forever
MR is zero at the profit-maximizing output
P = MR = MC and P equals minimum ATC
PM5-PC-M-083.feedback: At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.

PM5-PC-M-096.q: A competitive industry expands after demand rises. The larger industry raises land rents and skilled-worker wages, shifting firms’ ATC upward. Compared with the original long-run equilibrium, the new long-run price is most likely:
PM5-PC-M-096.feedback: In an increasing-cost industry, expansion raises input costs, so a higher price is required for zero-profit long-run equilibrium.

PM5-PC-M-097.q: Demand for an industry rises permanently. As firms enter, specialized suppliers expand and input costs fall. What long-run outcome is consistent with a decreasing-cost industry?
options: Industry output rises and the long-run equilibrium price can fall below its original level
Industry output falls and price must rise
The long-run supply curve must be vertical
PM5-PC-M-097.feedback: External cost reductions can shift firms’ costs down as the industry grows.

PM5-PC-M-107.q: Why is P = MC important for competitive allocative efficiency?
options: It means every firm earns positive economic profit
It makes all fixed costs disappear
The value buyers place on the last unit matches the opportunity cost of producing it
It guarantees equal incomes across consumers
PM5-PC-M-107.feedback: At P = MC, the marginal benefit reflected by price equals marginal resource cost.

PM5-PC-M-108.q: A representative competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium at the minimum point of ATC. What efficiency idea does that condition illustrate most directly?
PM5-PC-M-108.feedback: Producing at minimum ATC uses the least-cost scale available to the firm in the benchmark.

PM5-PC-M-109.q: Which observation is a limitation of using perfect competition as a literal description of many real markets?
options: Products may be differentiated and firms may have some control over price
All real markets contain many tiny firms selling identical products
Entry is always costless and instantaneous
Consumers never care about product differences
PM5-PC-M-109.feedback: The competitive model is a benchmark; many real markets relax one or more of its assumptions.

PM5-PC-M-110.q: A competitive allocation maximizes total surplus under the benchmark assumptions, but one household receives very little income. What does this illustrate?
options: The allocation cannot be efficient because incomes differ
Efficiency does not by itself guarantee an equitable distribution
PM5-PC-M-110.feedback: Total-surplus efficiency and distributional equity are separate evaluative questions.

P62F-PC-H-001.q: Aurora Grain is a price-taking firm. Price is $22, fixed cost is $180, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $5, $9, $14, $20, $27, $35. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 3 units with economic loss of $142
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $145
Produce 4 units with economic loss of $140
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-H-001.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-002.q: Cedar Components is a price-taking firm. Price is $25, fixed cost is $200, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $6, $10, $15, $21, $28, $36. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 3 units with economic loss of $156
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $155
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
Produce 4 units with economic loss of $152
P62F-PC-H-002.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-003.q: Delta Berries is a price-taking firm. Price is $28, fixed cost is $220, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $7, $11, $16, $22, $29, $37. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 4 units with economic loss of $164
Produce 3 units with economic loss of $170
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $165
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-H-003.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-004.q: Harbor Salt is a price-taking firm. Price is $31, fixed cost is $240, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $5, $12, $17, $23, $30, $38. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 4 units with economic loss of $173
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $172
Produce 6 units with economic loss of $179
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-H-004.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-005.q: Juniper Paper is a price-taking firm. Price is $34, fixed cost is $260, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $6, $9, $18, $20, $31, $39. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 4 units with economic loss of $177
Produce 6 units with economic loss of $179
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $174
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-H-005.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-006.q: Keystone Tiles is a price-taking firm. Price is $22, fixed cost is $280, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $7, $10, $14, $21, $27, $40. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 3 units with economic loss of $245
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $249
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
Produce 4 units with economic loss of $244
P62F-PC-H-006.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-007.q: Lumen Glass is a price-taking firm. Price is $25, fixed cost is $300, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $5, $11, $15, $22, $28, $35. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 4 units with economic loss of $253
Produce 3 units with economic loss of $256
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $256
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-H-007.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-008.q: Mesa Beans is a price-taking firm. Price is $28, fixed cost is $320, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $6, $12, $16, $23, $29, $36. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 3 units with economic loss of $270
Produce 4 units with economic loss of $265
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $266
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-H-008.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-009.q: Northline Steel is a price-taking firm. Price is $31, fixed cost is $340, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $7, $9, $17, $20, $30, $37. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 4 units with economic loss of $269
Produce 6 units with economic loss of $274
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $268
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-H-009.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-010.q: Orchard Fiber is a price-taking firm. Price is $34, fixed cost is $360, and marginal costs for units 1–6 are $5, $10, $18, $21, $31, $38. Which statement correctly combines output and economic profit?
options: Produce 4 units with economic loss of $278
Produce 6 units with economic loss of $279
Shut down solely because fixed cost is positive
Produce 5 units with economic loss of $275
P62F-PC-H-010.feedback: Choose output from MR and MC, then calculate TR−TC at that output.

P62F-PC-H-011.q: A firm graph shows the price line above ATC at the rising-MC intersection. Which sequence is correct?
options: Choose the intersection output, then measure a rectangular economic profit
Choose minimum ATC regardless of price
Shut down because MC is rising
Use the area below AVC as profit
P62F-PC-H-011.feedback: Output comes from P=MC; profit comes from P−ATC.

P62F-PC-H-012.q: A firm graph shows price below ATC but above AVC at the rising-MC intersection. What should the firm do?
options: Shut down because price is below ATC
Produce in the short run and incur a loss
Earn positive profit because price exceeds AVC
Exit instantly and erase fixed cost
P62F-PC-H-012.feedback: Price covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

P62F-PC-H-013.q: A firm graph shows price below minimum AVC. What is the correct short-run response?
options: Exit with zero fixed cost immediately
Shut down and bear fixed cost
P62F-PC-H-013.feedback: Price does not cover avoidable variable cost.

P62F-PC-H-014.q: On a competitive firm graph, price is tangent to minimum ATC and intersects rising MC there. The firm earns:
options: Positive economic profit while producing below the minimum point of average total cost
An economic loss while producing above the minimum point of average total cost
Zero accounting profit while producing where price exceeds marginal cost
Zero economic profit and produces productively efficiently
P62F-PC-H-014.feedback: P=min ATC and P=MC characterize long-run competitive equilibrium.

P62F-PC-H-015.q: A market-and-firm diagram shows market price rising. On the firm panel, the horizontal MR line rises. What happens to the firm’s chosen output?
options: It rises along the firm’s MC curve above AVC
It falls because firm demand slopes downward
It remains fixed because the firm is a price taker
P62F-PC-H-015.feedback: A higher market price raises MR and the P=MC output.

P62F-PC-H-016.q: A competitive firm’s MC curve crosses the price line twice. Which crossing is relevant?
options: Neither because output is chosen at minimum ATC
P62F-PC-H-016.feedback: The second-order condition requires MC to rise through MR.

P62F-PC-H-017.q: A graph shows MC below AVC for low quantities. Why is that MC segment not part of short-run supply?
options: Prices on that segment exceed the profit-maximizing threshold for every firm
Prices on that segment equal average total cost but remain below marginal cost
Prices on that segment are below the shutdown threshold
Prices on that segment allow production because they exceed average variable cost
P62F-PC-H-017.feedback: The firm shuts down when price is below minimum AVC.

P62F-PC-H-018.q: After entry, the market supply curve shifts right and the firm price line falls. Why does entry stop?
options: Economic profit is driven to zero
P62F-PC-H-018.feedback: Entry continues while positive economic profit remains.

P62F-PC-H-019.q: After exit, market supply shifts left and the remaining firm’s price line rises. Why does exit stop?
P62F-PC-H-019.feedback: Exit continues until firms cover all economic costs.

P62F-PC-H-020.q: A long-run supply curve is upward sloping. Which industry condition does it represent?
P62F-PC-H-020.feedback: Industry expansion raises input prices and long-run cost.

P62F-PC-H-021.q: A competitive firm receives a lump-sum subsidy unrelated to output. In the short run, what changes?
options: ATC falls, but MC and the chosen output at a given price do not change
The firm sets a higher price
P62F-PC-H-021.feedback: A lump-sum change affects fixed cost, not marginal cost.

P62F-PC-H-022.q: A per-unit tax raises MC and AVC. If the market price does not change, which outcome is possible?
options: The firm reduces output or shuts down
P62F-PC-H-022.feedback: A per-unit tax changes the relevant marginal and shutdown comparisons.

P62F-PC-H-023.q: Demand rises in a constant-cost competitive industry. Which sequence is correct?
options: Price and profit rise in the short run; entry returns price and profit to their original long-run levels
Profit remains zero at every moment
P62F-PC-H-023.feedback: Short-run profit induces entry; constant input costs let price return.

P62F-PC-H-024.q: Demand falls in an increasing-cost competitive industry. As firms exit, input prices may fall. Long-run price can end:
options: Above the original price by definition
At the short-run loss price permanently
At zero because all firms leave
P62F-PC-H-024.feedback: Industry contraction can lower input costs in an increasing-cost industry.

P62F-PC-H-025.q: A firm is earning zero economic profit. An owner says, “We should exit because there is no profit.” What is wrong?
options: Zero economic profit includes normal return on owner resources
P62F-PC-H-025.feedback: All opportunity costs are covered at zero economic profit.

P62F-PC-H-026.q: At the chosen output, P=MC and P>minimum ATC. Which efficiency statement is correct?
options: The firm is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient
The output is allocatively efficient, but the firm is not at the productive-efficiency point
P62F-PC-H-026.feedback: P=MC gives allocative efficiency; min ATC gives productive efficiency.

P62F-PC-H-027.q: A pollution externality exists in an otherwise competitive industry. Why may P=private MC fail to be socially efficient?
options: Competitive firms are no longer price takers
P62F-PC-H-027.feedback: The competitive benchmark needs private and social marginal costs to coincide.

P62F-PC-H-028.q: Consumers cannot distinguish product quality, but firms know it. Which assumption behind the benchmark is weakened?
P62F-PC-H-028.feedback: Information problems can break the standard efficiency result.

P62F-PC-H-029.q: A market has many sellers but substantial product differentiation. Why is perfect competition an imperfect model?
options: Individual firms may face downward-sloping demand
P62F-PC-H-029.feedback: Differentiation gives firms some price discretion.

P62F-PC-H-030.q: A constant-cost long-run supply curve is horizontal. What does the horizontal shape mean?
options: Industry output can expand without changing firms’ long-run cost curves
P62F-PC-H-030.feedback: Input prices and cost curves remain unchanged as the industry expands.

P62F-PC-H-031.q: Refer to the graph. What is total revenue at the profit-maximizing output and market price shown?

P62F-PC-H-032.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s total cost at the profit-maximizing output?

P62F-PC-H-033.q: Refer to the graph. What is total variable cost at the chosen output?

P62F-PC-H-034.q: Refer to the graph. What total fixed cost is implied by the ATC and AVC values at Q = 50?

P62F-PC-H-035.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s total economic loss at the selected output?

P62F-PC-H-036.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s total revenue in the loss case?

P62F-PC-H-037.q: Refer to the graph. Use the vertical gap between ATC and AVC at the chosen output to calculate total fixed cost.

P62F-PC-H-038.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose market price rose to the price level represented by point B. Which output rule would apply?
options: Continue producing zero because the original $10 price permanently determines the firm’s short-run output
Produce at point A because minimum AVC fixes the firm’s output whenever market price changes
Choose point C because minimum ATC determines output even when marginal revenue intersects MC elsewhere
Produce at point B because its rising-MC value equals the new price and lies above the shutdown threshold
P62F-PC-H-038.feedback: Once price is above minimum AVC, the firm chooses the rising-MC intersection.

P62F-PC-H-039.q: Refer to the graph. What economic role does point C play on the graph?
options: Point C is minimum ATC, where the rising MC curve crosses the ATC curve
Point C is minimum AVC, where rising MC first enters the firm’s short-run supply curve
Point C is the current market price, where the horizontal P = MR line crosses MC
Point C is the shutdown point, where price exactly equals the minimum of average variable cost
P62F-PC-H-039.feedback: MC crosses ATC at ATC’s minimum at point C.

P62F-PC-H-040.q: Refer to the graph. What is the representative firm’s total revenue in the paired profit case?

P62F-PC-H-041.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 90, use the ATC to calculate the representative firm’s total cost.

P62F-PC-H-042.q: Refer to the graph. The firm panel shows positive economic profit. If that condition persists, which market adjustment follows?
options: Persistent profit induces exit, shifting market supply left and pushing the equilibrium price upward for the displayed firm
Persistent profit induces entry, shifting market supply right and pushing the equilibrium price downward
The representative firm raises its own price, so market supply stays fixed while profit disappears
Market demand becomes horizontal, so entry changes firm output without affecting the market price
P62F-PC-H-042.feedback: Positive economic profit attracts entry, increasing market supply.

P62F-PC-H-043.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50 in the loss-making firm panel, use price to calculate total revenue.

P62F-PC-H-044.q: Refer to the graph. From the ATC–AVC separation in the loss panel, determine the firm’s total fixed cost.

P62F-PC-H-045.q: Refer to the graph. The firm panel shows an economic loss. If that loss persists, which market adjustment follows?
options: Persistent losses induce entry, shifting market supply right and lowering the market price further
The representative firm raises its own price, leaving market supply and the number of firms unchanged
Market demand becomes horizontal, allowing every remaining firm to choose a higher price independently
Persistent losses induce exit, shifting market supply left and raising the market price for survivors
P62F-PC-H-045.feedback: Persistent losses induce firms to exit, reducing market supply.

P62F-PC-H-046.q: Refer to the graph. At the selected output, which efficiency condition is illustrated by the equality of price and marginal cost?
P62F-PC-H-046.feedback: P = MC is the competitive allocative-efficiency condition.

P62F-PC-H-047.q: Refer to the graph. At the selected output, which efficiency condition is illustrated by production at the minimum of ATC?
P62F-PC-H-047.feedback: Producing at minimum ATC is productive efficiency.

P62F-PC-H-048.q: Refer to the graph. If demand and cost conditions remain unchanged, what entry-or-exit pressure exists at the equilibrium?
P62F-PC-H-048.feedback: Zero economic profit removes the incentive for net entry or exit.

PM5-PC-H-010.q: A competitive firm initially faces a market price of $30 and sells 80 units. A market-wide demand decrease lowers the price to $26. Holding the firm’s output at 80 units only for comparison, which statement is correct?
options: Only MR falls by $4 because average revenue stays at the old price when output is held fixed
AR stays at $30 because the firm is a price taker
The firm can keep charging $30 if its costs have not changed
The firm’s AR and MR both fall by $4, and total revenue falls by $320
PM5-PC-H-010.feedback: Price taking implies P = AR = MR. At 80 units, the $4 price decline reduces total revenue by $320.

PM5-PC-H-011.q: A competitive firm is currently producing where its own cost conditions make 50 units optimal. Industry entry then lowers the market price. Which change occurs before the firm chooses a new output?
options: The firm keeps its old horizontal demand line because entry changes only the number of sellers, not its price
The firm sets a new price based on its minimum ATC
The firm’s horizontal demand and MR lines shift downward to the new market price
The firm rotates its demand curve downward while MR stays fixed
PM5-PC-H-011.feedback: A market-price change shifts the price-taking firm’s horizontal P = AR = MR line; output is then re-optimized against MC.

PM5-PC-H-065.q: A competitive industry has 40 identical firms. At P = $25, each firm supplies 12 units. A variable-input cost increase reduces each firm’s quantity supplied at $25 to 9 units. With no entry or exit, what happens to market quantity supplied at that price?
options: It stays at 480 because the number of firms is unchanged
PM5-PC-H-065.feedback: Industry supply horizontally aggregates firm quantities, so the per-firm decline of 3 units reduces market quantity by 40 × 3 = 120.

PM5-PC-H-066.q: Two policies hit identical competitive firms. Policy A adds a $1,000 annual license fee. Policy B adds a $2 fee to every unit produced. Which short-run comparison is correct?
options: Both policies shift MC by the same amount
Policy A shifts supply but Policy B affects only fixed cost
Neither policy can affect the firm because it is a price taker
Policy B shifts MC and supply; Policy A lowers profit but leaves MC-based supply unchanged
PM5-PC-H-066.feedback: Per-unit costs are marginal/variable; lump-sum fixed costs are not.

PM5-PC-H-084.q: A competitive industry begins in long-run equilibrium. A permanent demand increase raises price and creates economic profit in the short run. Ignoring industry-cost-condition complications, what completes the long-run adjustment?
options: The market price stays permanently above average total cost because firms are price takers
Entry shifts industry supply right until price and economic profit fall toward their long-run levels
Existing firms cut supply until price rises further
Exit shifts supply left until profits become larger
PM5-PC-H-084.feedback: Short-run profit attracts entry; added industry supply then erodes the profit signal.

PM5-PC-H-085.q: A competitive industry begins with firms earning losses but price remains above AVC, so firms continue operating in the short run. What long-run force can eliminate the losses?
options: Some firms exit, reducing market supply and raising price for those that remain
All firms expand output until ATC rises
New firms enter and reduce price further
PM5-PC-H-085.feedback: Short-run operation can coexist with losses, but persistent losses induce long-run exit.

PM5-PC-H-098.q: Two competitive industries experience the same permanent demand increase. Industry A is constant-cost; Industry B is increasing-cost. After entry is complete, which comparison is most consistent?
options: Both must return to the original price regardless of input markets
A must have a higher long-run price than B
B must settle at a lower price because entry always lowers costs
A can return to its original long-run price, while B settles at a higher long-run price
PM5-PC-H-098.feedback: The long-run price response depends on how industry expansion affects input costs.

P62F-PC-EL-001.q: Atlas Wire faces price $26. Output can rise in 10-unit blocks; MC per unit for the six blocks is $8, $14, $21, $29, $38, $48. Fixed cost is $300. What is the best integrated conclusion?

Produce 40 units with economic profit of $20
Shut down because fixed cost is positive

options: Produce 30 units with economic profit of $245
Produce 50 units with economic profit of $275
Shut down because fixed cost is positive
Produce 40 units with economic profit of $305
P62F-PC-EL-004.feedback: Use MC per unit to choose blocks, then subtract total cost from total revenue.

P62F-PC-EL-005.q: Evergreen Resin faces price $42. Output can rise in 10-unit blocks; MC per unit for the six blocks is $9, $14, $25, $33, $42, $52. Fixed cost is $440. What is the best integrated conclusion?
options: Produce 50 units with economic profit of $430
Produce 40 units with economic profit of $430

Shut down because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-EL-005.feedback: Use MC per unit to choose blocks, then subtract total cost from total revenue.

P62F-PC-EL-006.q: Falcon Wool faces price $26. Output can rise in 10-unit blocks; MC per unit for the six blocks is $10, $15, $21, $34, $38, $53. Fixed cost is $475. What is the best integrated conclusion?
options: Produce 20 units with economic loss of $205
Produce 30 units with economic loss of $155
Produce 40 units with economic loss of $235
Shut down because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-EL-006.feedback: Use MC per unit to choose blocks, then subtract total cost from total revenue.

P62F-PC-EL-007.q: Granite Soap faces price $30. Output can rise in 10-unit blocks; MC per unit for the six blocks is $8, $16, $22, $29, $39, $48. Fixed cost is $510. What is the best integrated conclusion?
options: Produce 30 units with economic loss of $70
Produce 50 units with economic loss of $150
