P62F-PC-EL-008.q: Helix Corn faces price $34. Output can rise in 10-unit blocks; MC per unit for the six blocks is $9, $17, $23, $30, $40, $49. Fixed cost is $545. What is the best integrated conclusion?
options: Produce 30 units with economic loss of $15
Produce 50 units with economic loss of $35
Shut down because fixed cost is positive
Produce 40 units with economic profit of $25
P62F-PC-EL-008.feedback: Use MC per unit to choose blocks, then subtract total cost from total revenue.

P62F-PC-EL-009.q: Ion Copper faces price $38. Output can rise in 10-unit blocks; MC per unit for the six blocks is $10, $14, $24, $31, $41, $50. Fixed cost is $580. What is the best integrated conclusion?
options: Produce 40 units with economic profit of $150
Produce 30 units with economic profit of $80
Produce 50 units with economic profit of $120
Shut down because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-EL-009.feedback: Use MC per unit to choose blocks, then subtract total cost from total revenue.

P62F-PC-EL-010.q: Jasper Milk faces price $42. Output can rise in 10-unit blocks; MC per unit for the six blocks is $8, $15, $25, $32, $42, $51. Fixed cost is $615. What is the best integrated conclusion?
options: Produce 40 units with economic profit of $265
Produce 50 units with economic profit of $265
Produce 60 units with economic profit of $175
Shut down because fixed cost is positive
P62F-PC-EL-010.feedback: Use MC per unit to choose blocks, then subtract total cost from total revenue.

P62F-PC-EL-011.q: A firm initially earns profit. A fixed annual fee raises ATC above price but leaves price above AVC. What happens in the short run and long run?
options: It shuts down immediately because P<ATC
Output rises because fixed cost rose
The firm keeps producing in the short run but may exit in the long run
The market price is set by the firm
P62F-PC-EL-011.feedback: Fixed cost does not change short-run output, but persistent loss can cause exit.

P62F-PC-EL-012.q: A per-unit tax shifts MC and AVC upward enough that price falls below minimum AVC. What is the short-run outcome?
options: The firm produces at the old output
Only profit changes because taxes are fixed
Entry restores the old firm output immediately
P62F-PC-EL-012.feedback: The tax changes avoidable cost and the shutdown threshold.

P62F-PC-EL-013.q: A technology improvement lowers MC and AVC but not market price. Which sequence is correct?
options: Firm output rises, profit tends to rise, and later entry can lower market price
Firm output falls and exit occurs
Market price rises because supply falls
P62F-PC-EL-013.feedback: Lower costs raise firm supply and profit, inviting entry.

P62F-PC-EL-014.q: An industry demand increase creates short-run profit. Entry raises an input price used by every firm. What industry type is this?

P62F-PC-EL-015.q: An industry expands and suppliers develop specialized infrastructure that lowers every firm’s cost. What industry type is this?
P62F-PC-EL-015.feedback: External economies lower costs as industry output expands.

P62F-PC-EL-016.q: A firm’s price line is below ATC but above AVC. Fixed cost doubles. What happens to the short-run output choice?
options: It is unchanged because MC and AVC are unchanged
P62F-PC-EL-016.feedback: Short-run output and shutdown use MC and AVC, not fixed cost.

P62F-PC-EL-017.q: A competitive firm is producing where P=MC, but MC is falling. What should an analyst conclude?
options: The displayed crossing is not the profit-maximizing crossing
The firm is necessarily at long-run equilibrium
The firm must be shut down
P62F-PC-EL-017.feedback: The relevant crossing is where MC rises through MR.

P62F-PC-EL-018.q: The market price rises, but a firm’s cost curves are unchanged. Which elements change on the firm graph?
options: The horizontal P=MR line and the selected output
The firm demand curve becomes downward sloping
P62F-PC-EL-018.feedback: The price line moves; output changes along MC.

P62F-PC-EL-019.q: A firm operates at a loss of $5 per unit on 100 units, while fixed cost is $900. What does producing save relative to shutdown?
P62F-PC-EL-019.feedback: Operating loss is $500 versus $900 fixed-cost loss after shutdown, so production saves $400.

P62F-PC-EL-020.q: At the shutdown price, a firm produces at minimum AVC. Which loss does it incur whether it produces or shuts down?
P62F-PC-EL-020.feedback: At P=min AVC, revenue exactly covers variable cost, leaving fixed cost.

P62F-PC-EL-021.q: A demand increase in a constant-cost industry raises the short-run price from $30 to $44. After entry, what is the long-run price and firm economic profit?
P62F-PC-EL-021.feedback: Entry returns price to unchanged minimum long-run cost.

P62F-PC-EL-022.q: Demand rises in an increasing-cost industry. Which ordering is most plausible?
options: Short-run price < original price < long-run price
Original price < new long-run price < short-run price
New long-run price < original price < short-run price
All three prices must be identical
P62F-PC-EL-022.feedback: Entry reduces the short-run price, but higher input costs keep the new long-run price above the original.

P62F-PC-EL-023.q: Demand rises in a decreasing-cost industry. Which ordering is possible?
options: Original price < short-run price < new long-run price
Short-run price < new long-run price < original price
New long-run price < original price < short-run price
P62F-PC-EL-023.feedback: External economies can push the final price below the original.

P62F-PC-EL-024.q: A competitive firm earns positive profit while producing where P=MC. What market adjustment preserves allocative logic but removes profit?
options: Exit shifts supply left and lowers P
The firm raises its own price
Entry shifts market supply right and lowers P
P62F-PC-EL-024.feedback: Entry lowers market price until economic profit disappears.

P62F-PC-EL-025.q: A competitive firm suffers loss while P remains above AVC. What market adjustment can restore long-run equilibrium?
options: Exit shifts market supply left and raises P
Entry shifts supply right and raises P
The firm shuts down and fixed cost vanishes
P62F-PC-EL-025.feedback: Exit raises the price received by remaining firms.

P62F-PC-EL-026.q: A competitive market achieves P=MC, but production creates an unpriced external cost. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The market is productively inefficient by definition
The market is privately allocatively efficient but may be socially inefficient
Zero economic profit guarantees social efficiency
P62F-PC-EL-026.feedback: The benchmark uses private MC unless external costs are included.

P62F-PC-EL-027.q: Firms in a competitive industry earn zero economic profit at outputs above minimum ATC because a regulation fixes plant size. Which benchmark condition fails?
P62F-PC-EL-027.feedback: Zero profit alone does not guarantee production at minimum ATC.

P62F-PC-EL-028.q: A market is allocatively efficient at P=MC, but firms produce at different ATCs due to poor management. What can be said?
options: P=MC guarantees every firm has minimum ATC
Allocative efficiency can coexist with firm-level productive inefficiency
P62F-PC-EL-028.feedback: The two efficiency criteria are distinct.

P62F-PC-EL-029.q: Entry is legally free, but a scarce input price rises sharply as firms enter. Why may long-run supply slope upward?

P62F-PC-EL-030.q: The product is standardized and firms are small, but buyers have severe information problems. Which judgment is best?
options: The price-taking model may describe firm behavior while the welfare benchmark is weakened
P62F-PC-EL-030.feedback: Some assumptions can fit while others fail.

P62F-PC-EL-031.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, what total fixed cost is implied by ATC and AVC?

P62F-PC-EL-032.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose fixed cost rises by $200 while the price and profit-maximizing output initially remain unchanged. Relative to the graph, total economic profit becomes:
P62F-PC-EL-032.feedback: The graph implies initial profit of $500; a $200 fixed-cost increase reduces it to $300.

P62F-PC-EL-033.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the firm not at its shutdown point?
options: P lies below minimum AVC, so the firm cannot cover variable cost at the selected output
The firm sets P equal to ATC itself, so the market shutdown rule does not apply here
P equals ATC and remains above AVC, so the firm covers all economic costs rather than shutting down
Zero economic profit always triggers shutdown, even when price remains above average variable cost for the displayed firm
P62F-PC-EL-033.feedback: Zero economic profit is break-even, not shutdown; price remains above AVC.

P62F-PC-EL-034.q: Refer to the graph. Why does operating at Q = 30 reduce the firm’s short-run loss relative to shutting down?
options: Revenue falls below total variable cost, so operating increases the loss relative to shutdown
Producing eliminates the firm’s fixed cost, so its remaining loss consists only of variable cost
Revenue covers all variable cost and contributes $300 toward the firm’s fixed cost

P62F-PC-L-096.q: Refer to the graph. If price were exactly $20 at point A, which statement would be correct?

options: MC and AVC fall, output and profit can rise, and entry can follow

P62F-PC-LB-028.q: The wage rises across the industry. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?

P62F-PC-LB-028.feedback: Classify the cost or market failure and trace the short-run and long-run implications.

P62F-PC-LB-029.q: A lump-sum subsidy is introduced. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?

options: The firm is both allocatively and productively efficient because P=MC is enough to satisfy both efficiency conditions

options: The firm is allocatively efficient because producing at minimum ATC also implies that P=MC at this output

options: The private competitive output is likely above the social optimum

P62F-PC-LB-035.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

options: Price-taking may fit while the welfare benchmark fails
P62F-PC-LB-036.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

P62F-PC-R-001.q: A student says a competitive firm chooses both price and quantity. What is the correction?
options: The firm sets price but not quantity

P62F-PC-R-002.q: Why does a competitive firm not cut price below the market price?
options: It can sell its feasible output at the market price
P62F-PC-R-002.feedback: A price taker gains nothing by charging less.

P62F-PC-R-003.q: Which curve slopes downward in the standard model?
P62F-PC-R-003.feedback: The individual firm faces horizontal demand at market price.

P62F-PC-R-004.q: A graph labels the horizontal firm line “D=AR=MR.” What does it represent?
options: Market demand for the entire industry
The market price faced by the individual firm
P62F-PC-R-004.feedback: The horizontal line is the firm’s demand and revenue line.

options: The firm raises price each time

P62F-PC-R-010.feedback: Multiply the per-unit gap by quantity.

P62F-PC-R-011.q: For a competitive firm, earning zero economic profit means:
options: All explicit and implicit costs are covered
P62F-PC-R-011.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost.

P62F-PC-R-012.q: Why can accounting profit be positive at zero economic profit?
options: Accounting profit does not subtract implicit costs
P62F-PC-R-012.feedback: Implicit costs account for the difference.

P62F-PC-R-013.q: P is below ATC but above AVC. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
P62F-PC-R-013.feedback: Operating covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

P62F-PC-R-014.q: P is below minimum AVC. What should the firm do?
options: Exit and erase fixed cost immediately
P62F-PC-R-014.feedback: Revenue does not cover avoidable variable cost.

P62F-PC-R-015.q: Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?
options: MC at and above minimum AVC
P62F-PC-R-015.feedback: The firm supplies along MC only when operating.

P62F-PC-R-016.q: At a price below minimum AVC, a firm’s quantity supplied is:
P62F-PC-R-016.feedback: The firm shuts down below the threshold.

P62F-PC-R-017.q: Positive economic profit causes entry. What does entry do to market supply and price?

P62F-PC-R-018.q: Economic loss causes exit. What does exit do to market supply and price?

P62F-PC-R-020.feedback: Price reflects marginal benefit and MC reflects marginal resource cost.

PM5-PC-R-016.q: A learner says a competitive firm should keep expanding whenever MR is above ATC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Stop whenever total revenue exceeds total cost
Compare MR with MC for the next unit, not MR with ATC
Compare price only with fixed cost because fixed cost determines whether the next unit should be produced
Expand until ATC is as large as possible
PM5-PC-R-016.feedback: The output rule is marginal: add units while MR is at least as large as rising MC.

PM5-PC-R-017.q: A learner finds an output where MR = MC but MC is falling at that point and declares it profit maximizing. What condition is missing?
options: MC should be rising through MR for the usual maximum
ATC must equal zero so the firm has no cost burden at the point where MR and MC meet
Market demand must be horizontal at zero
PM5-PC-R-017.feedback: The standard profit maximum occurs where rising MC crosses MR from below.

PM5-PC-R-018.q: A learner sees MR = $20, the next unit’s MC = $18, and stops production at the current output. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Stop because any positive marginal cost reduces profit even when marginal revenue is larger
Raise price to $22 before adding output
Shut down because MR exceeds MC
Add the next unit because it adds $20 of revenue and only $18 of cost
PM5-PC-R-018.feedback: A unit with MR greater than MC increases profit or reduces loss.

PM5-PC-R-019.q: A learner chooses the output with the lowest ATC as the profit-maximizing quantity. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Choose output where AFC is minimized
Choose output where total revenue is smallest
Choose output using MR and MC; minimum ATC answers a different question
Choose the largest feasible output instead because spreading fixed cost always maximizes profit
PM5-PC-R-019.feedback: Productive efficiency and profit maximization are distinct decisions.

PM5-PC-R-028.q: A learner computes profit per unit as ATC − P when P exceeds ATC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Use P − ATC for profit per unit
Use P − AVC for economic profit per unit
Use TR − TC without dividing by quantity and call it per-unit profit
PM5-PC-R-028.feedback: When price exceeds ATC, the vertical gap P − ATC is profit per unit.

PM5-PC-R-029.q: A learner reports $5 of total profit because P − ATC = $5 and the firm sells 60 units. What is missing?
options: Multiply the $5 per-unit profit by 60 units
Subtract fixed cost a second time
Use only the last unit’s marginal cost
PM5-PC-R-029.feedback: The price-ATC gap is per unit; total profit requires multiplying by quantity.

PM5-PC-R-030.q: A learner says P = ATC means the firm has no accounting profit and no return to the owner. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: P = ATC means the firm is shutting down because covering total cost leaves no reason to produce
P = ATC means marginal revenue is zero
P = ATC guarantees an accounting loss
P = ATC means zero economic profit; normal profit is included in economic cost
PM5-PC-R-030.feedback: Economic cost includes implicit opportunity costs, including the normal return needed to keep owner resources in the firm.

PM5-PC-R-031.q: A learner sees P < ATC and concludes the firm must shut down. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Shutdown depends on P versus AFC
Losses matter only in the long run
P < ATC establishes an economic loss, but shutdown depends on P versus AVC
Any economic loss requires immediate shutdown even when the market price still covers variable cost
PM5-PC-R-031.feedback: Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons.

PM5-PC-R-043.q: A learner uses P < ATC as the shutdown rule. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Compare MR with total fixed cost
Compare price with AVC for shutdown; ATC determines profit or loss
Compare price with AFC for shutdown
PM5-PC-R-043.feedback: The firm may rationally produce at a loss if price covers variable cost.

PM5-PC-R-044.q: A learner says producing at a loss is irrational under any circumstances. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Fixed cost is avoidable whenever profit is negative
In the short run, producing can reduce the loss when price covers AVC and contributes to fixed cost
A firm should produce whenever price is positive
Losses disappear if output rises enough
PM5-PC-R-044.feedback: The relevant comparison is the loss from producing versus the fixed-cost loss from shutting down.

PM5-PC-R-045.q: A learner says shutting down eliminates all costs immediately. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Short-run fixed costs remain even when output is zero
Shutdown makes fixed cost become variable
The firm earns zero economic profit when shut down
Shutdown raises average fixed cost to zero
PM5-PC-R-045.feedback: Shutdown avoids variable production cost but does not erase fixed commitments in the short run.

PM5-PC-R-046.q: A learner treats a one-month shutdown as permanent industry exit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Exit is the short-run version of shutdown
A shut-down firm has no fixed cost
Shutdown can be temporary; exit means leaving the industry in the long run
PM5-PC-R-046.feedback: Time horizon separates the temporary operating decision from long-run participation.

PM5-PC-R-067.q: A learner labels the entire MC curve as the firm’s short-run supply curve. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Use MC only below minimum AVC
Use average fixed cost above its minimum
Use only the rising MC portion at and above minimum AVC
Use the entire ATC curve instead
PM5-PC-R-067.feedback: Below minimum AVC the firm shuts down rather than supplying the MC-indicated positive quantity.

PM5-PC-R-068.q: A learner shifts short-run supply left after a fixed-cost increase. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Supply shifts right because firms spread the cost
Fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MC or AVC, so short-run supply does not shift
Any cost increase must shift MC
PM5-PC-R-068.feedback: The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.

PM5-PC-R-069.q: A learner adds firms’ supply prices vertically to build market supply. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: At each price, add the quantities supplied across firms horizontally
At each quantity, add firms’ fixed costs
Use only the median firm’s output
Add market demand to firm supply
PM5-PC-R-069.feedback: Market supply sums how much all firms supply at a common market price.

PM5-PC-R-070.q: A learner says a higher wage cannot shift supply because the firm is a price taker. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Price-taking means the market price is given, so input-cost changes affect profit but not the firm's marginal cost curve
A higher wage changes average fixed cost because labor payments become fixed after the firm hires its workers
A wage increase changes the firm's demand curve by raising the price required to cover its labor costs
Price taking fixes the output price, not the firm’s costs; a wage increase can raise MC and shift supply
PM5-PC-R-070.feedback: Competitive firms take price as given but still respond to changes in production costs.

PM5-PC-R-086.q: A learner says positive economic profit causes existing firms to raise the market price. What is the long-run repair?
options: Profit causes exit, which raises price
Each firm can raise price independently because profit is positive
Economic profit has no effect on industry size
Profit attracts entry, which increases market supply and tends to lower price
PM5-PC-R-086.feedback: In competition, the adjustment occurs through entry and market supply, not unilateral price setting.

PM5-PC-R-087.q: A learner says loss-making competitive firms can remain forever with no industry adjustment. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Long-run fixed costs prevent any firm from leaving
Persistent losses encourage exit when firms can leave in the long run
PM5-PC-R-087.feedback: Long-run mobility lets resources leave industries that do not cover opportunity cost.

PM5-PC-R-099.q: A learner says every competitive industry has a horizontal long-run supply curve. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Long-run supply depends only on market demand
A horizontal curve requires monopoly power
Horizontal long-run supply is the constant-cost case; other cost conditions can slope up or down
Competition always makes long-run supply vertical
PM5-PC-R-099.feedback: The slope depends on how industry expansion affects input costs and firms’ cost curves.

PM5-PC-R-100.q: A learner says entry can never raise production costs because each firm is a price taker. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Competitive firms do not buy inputs
Industry expansion can bid up shared input prices even though firms take output price as given
Price-taking firms also take every input price as permanently fixed
Entry always creates economies that lower cost
PM5-PC-R-100.feedback: Output-market price taking does not prevent industry growth from affecting input markets.

PM5-PC-R-101.q: A learner interprets a downward-sloping long-run industry supply curve as a violation of competition. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: It can arise when industry expansion lowers firms’ costs through external economies
It means demand is perfectly elastic
It means firms are operating below AVC
PM5-PC-R-101.feedback: A decreasing-cost industry can remain competitive while industry growth reduces input or supplier costs.

PM5-PC-R-111.q: A learner says productive efficiency and allocative efficiency are the same condition. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Allocative efficiency means every firm earns positive profit
Productive efficiency concerns minimum ATC; allocative efficiency concerns P = MC
PM5-PC-R-111.feedback: The two efficiency concepts answer different questions: least-cost production versus whether marginal value equals marginal cost.

P62F-PC-BR-001.q: A competitive firm uses which cost curve to decide whether another unit should be produced?
P62F-PC-BR-001.feedback: The incremental output decision compares MR with MC.

P62F-PC-BR-002.q: Which average cost determines profit per unit after output is chosen?

P62F-PC-BR-003.q: Which average cost determines the short-run shutdown threshold?
P62F-PC-BR-003.feedback: AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run.

P62F-PC-BR-004.q: Why does a fixed-cost increase not change short-run competitive output?
options: It does not change MC or AVC
P62F-PC-BR-004.feedback: Output and shutdown depend on marginal and variable costs.

P62F-PC-BR-005.q: Zero economic profit includes which owner return?
P62F-PC-BR-005.feedback: Normal profit covers entrepreneurial opportunity cost.

P62F-PC-BR-006.q: How is a competitive firm’s supply response connected to cost?
options: It follows rising MC above AVC
P62F-PC-BR-006.feedback: MC gives the additional cost of supply.

P62F-PC-BR-007.q: What converts individual competitive firm supplies into market supply?
P62F-PC-BR-007.feedback: Add firm quantities supplied at each price.

options: Moving upward along the same supply curve
P62F-PC-BR-008.feedback: More firms supply more total output at each price.

P62F-PC-BR-009.feedback: Fewer firms reduce total quantity supplied.

P62F-PC-BR-010.q: A competitive firm should expand output while:
P62F-PC-BR-010.feedback: Marginal benefit to the firm exceeds marginal cost.

P62F-PC-BR-011.q: The last profitable unit in a discrete table is the last unit with:
options: MR at least as large as MC
P62F-PC-BR-011.feedback: The next unit would reduce profit once MC exceeds MR.

P62F-PC-BR-012.q: Why is the rising-MC crossing used?
options: It is the crossing where moving beyond the output makes MC exceed MR
P62F-PC-BR-012.feedback: The local profit maximum occurs where MC rises through MR.

P62F-PC-BR-013.q: Why is P=MC associated with allocative efficiency?
options: The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal unit’s cost
P62F-PC-BR-013.feedback: The last unit’s marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

P62F-PC-BR-014.q: What does entry after profit tend to do to consumer surplus?
options: Raise price and lower consumer surplus
Lower price tends to increase consumer surplus
P62F-PC-BR-014.feedback: Entry expands supply and lowers price.

P62F-PC-BR-015.q: A per-unit tax on competitive output directly raises:
P62F-PC-BR-015.feedback: The tax is tied to each unit produced.

P62F-PC-BR-016.q: A lump-sum annual tax on a competitive firm directly raises:
options: Average total cost but not marginal cost
P62F-PC-BR-016.feedback: A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost.

P62F-PC-BR-017.q: A higher wage shifts a competitive firm’s cost curves because labor is:
options: A variable input in the standard short-run model
P62F-PC-BR-017.feedback: Higher variable input cost raises AVC and MC.

P62F-PC-BR-018.q: Compared with a price-taking firm, a firm with market power generally faces:
options: A horizontal demand curve at all outputs
P62F-PC-BR-018.feedback: Market power changes the firm’s revenue conditions; the competitive firm takes price.

P62F-PC-BR-019.q: Why can a perfectly competitive outcome fail to maximize social surplus?
options: Private marginal cost may omit external costs
P62F-PC-BR-019.feedback: The benchmark requires private and social marginal costs to align.

P62F-PC-BR-020.q: A small competitive firm selling a traded good takes which price as given in the open-market model?
options: The relevant market or world price
P62F-PC-BR-020.feedback: Competitive firms respond to the price established in the wider market.

PM5-PC-BR-012.q: How does the competitive firm’s price-taking assumption connect market equilibrium to the firm’s decision problem?
options: Market demand determines the firm’s fixed cost
Market supply and demand determine price; the firm then chooses quantity at that price
The firm chooses price first from its cost curves and then the market determines how much buyers take
The firm’s ATC determines the market equilibrium price directly
PM5-PC-BR-012.feedback: The market establishes the price signal, and the individual firm responds by selecting output.

PM5-PC-BR-013.q: How does P = AR = MR connect the competitive revenue model to marginal analysis?
options: The market price is both revenue per unit and the added revenue from one more unit
Average revenue equals fixed cost while marginal revenue equals price
Marginal revenue falls below price because selling more requires the firm to cut price on all earlier units
Price equals marginal cost at every possible output
PM5-PC-BR-013.feedback: With price fixed, each additional unit adds the same amount to total revenue, so marginal revenue equals price. The firm then compares that marginal revenue with marginal cost when choosing output.

PM5-PC-BR-014.q: How does a horizontal firm demand curve connect to the shape of the competitive firm’s total-revenue function?
options: A horizontal demand curve makes total revenue constant even when the firm sells additional units
A constant price makes total revenue fall as quantity rises
The total-revenue function must be U-shaped
A constant price makes total revenue rise proportionally with quantity
PM5-PC-BR-014.feedback: With price fixed, TR = P × Q rises by the same dollar amount for each additional unit.

PM5-PC-BR-015.q: What prior market concept helps explain why the individual competitive firm can face a horizontal demand line even though market demand slopes downward?
options: The firm owns the market supply curve
The firm faces no scarcity in its inputs
The firm is a tiny participant taking the equilibrium price generated by the whole market
The law of demand stops applying at the firm level because competitive sellers can choose any price they want
PM5-PC-BR-015.feedback: Firm-level price taking is consistent with a downward-sloping market demand curve because the individual seller is negligible relative to the market.

PM5-PC-BR-020.q: How does the competitive firm’s MR = MC rule connect to the broader marginal-analysis principle?
options: Maximize output whenever average benefit is positive
Expand an activity while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost and stop near equality
Choose the activity with the largest total cost because total cost identifies the strongest marginal gain
Ignore incremental effects once fixed cost exists
PM5-PC-BR-020.feedback: For the firm, marginal revenue is the marginal benefit of another unit and MC is its marginal cost.

PM5-PC-BR-021.q: How does a market-price increase reach a competitive firm’s profit-maximizing output decision?
options: The higher price raises the firm’s MR line, so the firm moves along rising MC to a larger output
The higher price shifts the firm’s MC curve left automatically while leaving its marginal revenue line unchanged
The higher price lowers MR and therefore output
The firm ignores market price once its plant is built
PM5-PC-BR-021.feedback: Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.

PM5-PC-BR-032.q: How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?
options: ATC is irrelevant once output is chosen
The vertical gap P − ATC measures profit per unit when positive and loss per unit when negative
The gap P − AVC always equals total profit because fixed cost is irrelevant once the firm chooses output
PM5-PC-BR-032.feedback: Average total cost converts the firm’s chosen price and quantity into a per-unit economic-profit measure.

PM5-PC-BR-033.q: How does total economic profit connect the revenue and cost frameworks?
options: Profit equals total revenue minus total economic cost
Profit equals total revenue minus variable cost only
Profit equals price minus marginal cost on the last unit only
Profit equals accounting revenue plus implicit cost
PM5-PC-BR-033.feedback: The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit.

PM5-PC-BR-034.q: Why can a firm remain in long-run competitive equilibrium when economic profit is zero?
options: The firm has no opportunity costs
Zero economic profit means total revenue is zero
Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
PM5-PC-BR-034.feedback: Normal profit is part of economic cost, so zero economic profit can still keep resources in their current use.

PM5-PC-BR-035.q: How does break-even connect the firm’s revenue line to its average-cost curve?
options: MR equals zero at minimum ATC
At the chosen output, price equals ATC so total revenue equals total cost
Price equals AVC so fixed cost disappears
PM5-PC-BR-035.feedback: Break-even is the point where the per-unit revenue and total-cost averages match.

PM5-PC-BR-036.q: How should a measured short-run economic loss connect to the next decision?
options: The firm should compare price with AFC instead
After measuring the loss, separately compare price with AVC to decide produce versus shut down
Any loss automatically implies exit today because a competitive firm should never operate while ATC exceeds price
A loss means the firm should maximize quantity
PM5-PC-BR-036.feedback: Loss measurement uses ATC; the short-run operating decision uses AVC.

PM5-PC-BR-047.q: How does the shutdown rule connect to the distinction between fixed and variable costs?
options: Variable cost is sunk in the short run
Price must cover variable cost because fixed cost is unavoidable in the short run
Price must cover fixed cost before variable cost matters
PM5-PC-BR-047.feedback: The shutdown test asks whether operating revenue covers the costs that can be avoided by not producing.

PM5-PC-BR-048.q: How does producing at a loss connect to incremental decision making?
options: Use average fixed cost as the marginal benefit of output
Produce if operating adds more revenue than avoidable variable cost, even if total profit is negative
Produce only if accounting profit is positive
Ignore revenue because fixed cost is already paid
PM5-PC-BR-048.feedback: Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.

PM5-PC-BR-049.q: How does the shutdown-versus-exit distinction connect to the short-run/long-run distinction in cost theory?
options: Some inputs and costs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs are adjustable in the long run
All costs are variable in the short run and fixed in the long run
Exit changes only marginal cost, not industry participation
Shutdown requires the firm to sell all fixed inputs immediately
PM5-PC-BR-049.feedback: Temporary shutdown occurs with short-run fixed commitments; exit becomes possible when those commitments can be changed.

PM5-PC-BR-071.q: How does the firm’s short-run supply curve connect the MR = MC rule to market supply?
options: The firm supplies where ATC equals AFC
The firm’s supply is its horizontal demand curve
At each price above shutdown, P = MR identifies the quantity on rising MC that the firm supplies
Market supply is unrelated to the firm’s marginal choice
PM5-PC-BR-071.feedback: The output rule becomes a price-to-quantity supply schedule when repeated across possible market prices.

PM5-PC-BR-072.q: How does individual-firm supply become the competitive industry supply curve?
options: Use the market demand curve instead
Add firms’ quantities supplied at each common price
Add firms’ prices at each quantity
PM5-PC-BR-072.feedback: Horizontal aggregation connects firm-level marginal-cost decisions to the market supply schedule.

PM5-PC-BR-088.q: How does entry connect firm-level profit to a market-level supply response?
options: Positive economic profit attracts firms, and additional firms increase industry supply
Positive profit shifts market demand left
Entry makes each incumbent’s MC automatically fall
PM5-PC-BR-088.feedback: The profit signal changes the number of firms, linking firm outcomes to market supply.

PM5-PC-BR-089.q: How does exit connect economic loss to long-run resource allocation?
options: Resources leave uses that fail to cover opportunity cost and move toward better alternatives
Exit increases the number of firms in the industry
Economic loss means variable cost is always zero
PM5-PC-BR-089.feedback: Long-run exit is an opportunity-cost response: resources seek higher-valued uses.

PM5-PC-BR-090.q: How does normal profit connect long-run competitive equilibrium to economic cost?
options: Normal profit is a monopoly markup above economic cost
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
Normal profit exists only when P exceeds ATC
Normal profit is the implicit return required to keep owner resources in the industry
PM5-PC-BR-090.feedback: Zero economic profit can be sustainable because normal profit is already included among opportunity costs.

PM5-PC-BR-102.q: How does a constant-cost industry connect entry/exit to the long-run supply curve?
options: Entry permanently raises every firm’s ATC
The number of firms cannot change
Entry changes industry quantity without permanently shifting representative firms’ cost curves, producing horizontal long-run supply
PM5-PC-BR-102.feedback: Stable input costs let entry absorb demand changes while long-run price returns to the original cost level.

PM5-PC-BR-103.q: How does an increasing-cost industry connect output-market expansion to input markets?
options: Input prices cannot matter in perfect competition
Higher input prices shift market demand rather than supply
Industry growth raises demand for scarce inputs, which can raise input prices and firm costs
Industry growth reduces input demand automatically
PM5-PC-BR-103.feedback: The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets.

PM5-PC-BR-104.q: How does a demand increase connect short-run profit to the eventual long-run industry response?
options: Long-run price is always the short-run peak price
Higher short-run price can create profit, attracting entry; final price depends on the industry’s cost condition
Demand changes cause immediate exit before price changes
Profit has no connection to entry
PM5-PC-BR-104.feedback: Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.

P62G-MON-E-001.q: Which feature most directly distinguishes a monopoly from perfect competition?
options: A single seller is protected by substantial barriers to entry
Many sellers offer an identical product
Each firm faces a horizontal demand curve
P62G-MON-E-001.feedback: A monopoly is sustained by one seller and barriers that prevent competitive entry.

P62G-MON-E-002.q: A firm has market power when it can:
options: Choose any price and quantity without losing customers
Influence the price of its product within the limits imposed by demand
Force every consumer to buy the product
P62G-MON-E-002.feedback: Market power permits price influence, but demand still constrains the firm.

P62G-MON-E-003.q: Which is a legal barrier to entry?
options: A patent that grants temporary exclusive production rights
A competitive firm earning normal profit

P62G-MON-E-004.q: Control of the only commercially useful deposit of a critical mineral is an example of:
P62G-MON-E-004.feedback: Exclusive control of a necessary input can block entry.

P62G-MON-E-005.q: A network effect can strengthen monopoly power when:
options: The product becomes more valuable as more people use the same network
Average fixed cost rises with output
Consumers can resell the product freely
New firms face no coordination problem
P62G-MON-E-005.feedback: Network value can make switching and entry difficult.

P62G-MON-E-006.q: A natural monopoly usually exists because:
options: Marginal revenue equals price at every output
Average total cost falls over the relevant range of market demand
The firm owns a patent forever
P62G-MON-E-006.feedback: Large scale economies can make one supplier less costly than several.

P62G-MON-E-007.q: The demand curve facing a single-price monopolist is:
P62G-MON-E-007.feedback: With one seller, firm demand and market demand are the same.

P62G-MON-E-008.q: For a monopolist, average revenue equals:
options: Price and therefore the demand curve
P62G-MON-E-008.feedback: AR=TR/Q=P, so average revenue lies on demand.

P62G-MON-E-009.q: Why is marginal revenue below price for a single-price monopolist?
options: Selling another unit requires a lower price that also applies to earlier units
Marginal cost always exceeds average cost
The firm pays a tax on every unit
Fixed cost rises when output expands
P62G-MON-E-009.feedback: The price effect on previous units makes MR less than the new price.

P62G-MON-E-010.q: The output effect of selling one more unit is:
options: Revenue lost because all earlier units sell for less
Revenue gained from selling the additional unit
The decline in average total cost
P62G-MON-E-010.feedback: The added unit contributes its sale price to revenue.

P62G-MON-E-011.q: The price effect of selling one more unit is:
options: Revenue gained from the new unit
Revenue lost because the lower price applies to units already being sold
P62G-MON-E-011.feedback: A single-price monopolist must lower price on all units.

P62G-MON-E-012.q: When marginal revenue is positive, total revenue is:
P62G-MON-E-012.feedback: Positive MR means another unit adds to total revenue.

P62G-MON-E-013.q: For a downward-sloping linear demand curve, the marginal-revenue curve has:
options: The same price intercept and twice the slope
The same slope and half the price intercept
A horizontal shape at market price
A higher quantity intercept than demand
P62G-MON-E-013.feedback: Linear MR shares demand’s vertical intercept and is twice as steep.

P62G-MON-E-014.q: A single-price monopolist with nonnegative marginal cost will choose output on:
options: Only the unit-elastic point regardless of cost
P62G-MON-E-014.feedback: MR is positive on elastic demand; on inelastic demand, reducing output raises revenue and lowers cost.

P62G-MON-E-015.q: The standard monopoly output rule is to produce where:
options: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost on rising MC
Total revenue is highest regardless of cost

P62G-MON-E-016.q: After finding the monopoly quantity, the monopolist determines price by:
options: Reading the marginal-revenue curve at that quantity
Setting price equal to marginal cost
Reading the demand curve at that quantity
P62G-MON-E-016.feedback: Demand gives the highest price consumers will pay for the chosen quantity.

P62G-MON-E-017.q: If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost for the next unit, the monopolist should:
P62G-MON-E-017.feedback: That unit adds more revenue than cost.

P62G-MON-E-018.q: If marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue for the next unit, producing it would:
P62G-MON-E-018.feedback: The unit adds more cost than revenue.

options: Marginal revenue minus average variable cost
P62G-MON-E-019.feedback: ATC includes all economic cost per unit.

P62G-MON-E-020.q: A monopoly can earn an economic loss because:
options: A monopoly is required to charge marginal cost
Barriers to entry force price below AVC
Its demand may be too weak relative to its costs
P62G-MON-E-020.feedback: Market power does not guarantee profitable demand and cost conditions.

P62G-MON-E-021.q: A loss-making monopolist should shut down in the short run when:
options: Price at its best output is below average variable cost
Price is below average total cost but above AVC
P62G-MON-E-021.feedback: The short-run shutdown rule still compares price with AVC.

P62G-MON-E-022.q: Why can monopoly economic profit persist in the long run?
options: Barriers prevent entry from expanding supply and eroding profit
P62G-MON-E-022.feedback: Barriers block the entry mechanism that removes competitive profit.

P62G-MON-E-023.q: Compared with perfect competition, a single-price monopoly generally charges:
options: A lower price and produces a higher quantity
A higher price and produces a lower quantity
A price equal to minimum ATC
P62G-MON-E-023.feedback: The monopoly restricts output where MR=MC rather than producing where P=MC.

options: All consumer surplus transferred to the firm
Total surplus lost because mutually beneficial units are not produced
P62G-MON-E-024.feedback: DWL is the value of trades between monopoly and efficient output that do not occur.

P62G-MON-E-025.feedback: Consumers value additional units above their marginal production cost.

P62G-MON-E-026.q: Rent seeking occurs when resources are used to:
options: Obtain or protect monopoly privileges rather than produce valuable output
Expand output toward the efficient level
P62G-MON-E-026.feedback: Rent-seeking effort consumes resources to capture economic rents.

P62G-MON-E-027.q: Under marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly, the firm may require a subsidy because:
options: Price can fall below average total cost
P62G-MON-E-027.feedback: With declining ATC, MC lies below ATC, so P=MC may not cover total cost.

P62G-MON-E-028.q: Average-cost pricing regulation sets price where:
P62G-MON-E-028.feedback: P=ATC permits the regulated firm to cover economic cost.

P62G-MON-E-029.q: Price discrimination requires the seller to:
options: Separate customers and prevent profitable resale
Charge every buyer the same price
P62G-MON-E-029.feedback: Segmentation and limits on arbitrage are necessary.

P62G-MON-E-030.q: A third-degree price-discriminating monopolist generally charges the higher price to the group with:
options: The lowest willingness to pay at every quantity
P62G-MON-E-030.feedback: The less responsive group receives the larger markup.

P62G-MON-E-031.q: Refer to the graph. At what quantity does the monopolist maximize profit?
P62G-MON-E-031.feedback: Profit is maximized where MR intersects MC, which occurs at Q = 36.

P62G-MON-E-032.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing quantity, what price does the monopolist charge?
P62G-MON-E-032.feedback: After choosing Q = 36 from MR = MC, move up to demand; the demand curve shows P = $42.

P62G-MON-E-033.q: Refer to the graph. What marginal-revenue value is shown at Q = 36?
P62G-MON-E-033.feedback: At Q = 36, the MR curve meets MC at $24.

P62G-MON-E-034.q: Refer to the graph. What is average total cost at Q = 36?
P62G-MON-E-034.feedback: The ATC guide at the monopoly quantity is $27.

P62G-MON-E-035.q: Refer to the graph. What quantity is selected where MR = MC?
P62G-MON-E-035.feedback: MR and MC intersect at Q = 40.

P62G-MON-E-036.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 40, what price is read from the demand curve?
P62G-MON-E-036.feedback: The demand curve shows P = $40 at Q = 40.

P62G-MON-E-037.q: Refer to the graph. What is ATC at the monopoly quantity?
P62G-MON-E-037.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 40 is $45.

P62G-MON-E-038.q: Refer to the graph. What output does the unregulated natural monopolist choose?
P62G-MON-E-038.feedback: The unregulated monopoly chooses Q where MR = MC, marked at Q = 45.

P62G-MON-E-039.q: Refer to the graph. What price does demand indicate at the monopoly output?
P62G-MON-E-039.feedback: At Q = 45, the demand curve shows a price of $47.

P62G-MON-E-040.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does demand intersect marginal cost?
P62G-MON-E-040.feedback: With MC at $20, demand reaches MC at Q = 90.

P62G-MON-E-041.q: Refer to the graph. Approximately what output does the unregulated monopolist choose where MR = MC?
P62G-MON-E-041.feedback: The MR curve reaches the $10 MC line at about Q = 70.

P62G-MON-E-042.q: Refer to the graph. What price does the demand curve show at the unregulated monopoly output?
P62G-MON-E-042.feedback: At about Q = 70, demand indicates a price of about $27.

PM6-MON-E-014.q: For a single-price monopolist, which curve also shows average revenue at each quantity?
options: A horizontal line at marginal revenue
PM6-MON-E-014.feedback: Because AR = TR/Q = P, average revenue lies on the monopolist’s demand curve.

PM6-MON-E-029.q: A monopolist charges $50, has ATC=$38, and sells 100 units. What is total economic profit?
PM6-MON-E-029.feedback: Profit per unit is $12 and total profit is $12 × 100.

PM6-MON-E-030.q: A monopolist charges $24 while ATC is $30 at its chosen output. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns $6 economic profit per unit
The firm must shut down immediately
The firm has an economic loss of $6 per unit
PM6-MON-E-030.feedback: When P<ATC, the firm incurs a loss equal to ATC−P per unit.

PM6-MON-E-031.q: A monopolist has P=$18, AVC=$12, and ATC=$25 at its best operating output. In the short run it should generally:
options: Exit permanently because any accounting loss requires exit
Produce only if price equals MC at every unit
Produce because price covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost
Shut down because price is below ATC
PM6-MON-E-031.feedback: A short-run loss does not imply shutdown when price remains above AVC.

PM6-MON-E-032.q: When a monopolist’s price equals ATC at its chosen output, economic profit is:
options: Positive because monopoly has market power
Negative because MR is below price
PM6-MON-E-032.feedback: P=ATC means revenue exactly covers explicit and implicit economic costs.

PM6-MON-E-036.q: Compared with an otherwise similar competitive market, a single-price monopoly typically produces:
options: Less output at a lower price
Less output at a higher price
More output at a lower price
The same output at the same price
PM6-MON-E-036.feedback: Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.

PM6-MON-E-037.q: Why is P>MC at the monopoly quantity evidence of allocative inefficiency?
options: Some buyers value additional units more than the marginal cost of producing them
The monopolist must be earning zero profit
Average total cost must be at its minimum
PM6-MON-E-037.feedback: When willingness to pay exceeds MC for foregone units, mutually beneficial trades are left unrealized.

PM6-MON-E-038.q: What does monopoly deadweight loss represent?
options: All profit earned by the monopolist
All consumer surplus transferred to the monopolist
Gains from trade lost because output is restricted below the efficient quantity
PM6-MON-E-038.feedback: Deadweight loss is surplus that disappears rather than being transferred between buyers and sellers.

PM6-MON-E-039.q: If firms spend resources lobbying for an exclusive monopoly privilege, those expenditures are an example of:
PM6-MON-E-039.feedback: Resources used to obtain or protect economic rents can create additional social cost.

PM6-MON-E-040.q: A monopoly price increase transfers some surplus from consumers to the firm. Is that entire transfer deadweight loss?
options: No; because monopoly never changes total surplus
No; transferred surplus changes who receives the surplus, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears
Yes; every dollar of monopoly profit is deadweight loss
Yes; consumer surplus and total surplus are identical
PM6-MON-E-040.feedback: Distributional transfers and efficiency losses are different pieces of monopoly welfare analysis.

PM6-MON-E-048.q: A natural monopoly is most likely when average total cost:
options: Falls over the relevant range of market demand
PM6-MON-E-048.feedback: Large scale economies over market demand can make one producer less costly than several.

PM6-MON-E-049.q: Under marginal-cost regulation, the regulator sets price equal to:

PM6-MON-E-050.q: Average-cost regulation generally targets a price equal to:
PM6-MON-E-050.feedback: P=ATC allows the regulated firm to cover economic cost including normal return.

PM6-MON-E-051.q: Why can P=MC create a financial problem for a natural monopoly?
options: The firm necessarily earns monopoly profit
When ATC exceeds MC, revenue may be insufficient to cover total cost
PM6-MON-E-051.feedback: Declining ATC often implies MC below ATC, so marginal-cost pricing can produce losses.

PM6-MON-E-052.q: A binding price cap below the unregulated monopoly price is intended primarily to:
options: Make the firm a price taker in an unregulated market
Limit the price the regulated monopolist may charge
PM6-MON-E-052.feedback: A price cap constrains the allowable price and can alter incentives and output.

PM6-MON-E-053.q: If a regulator sets P=ATC rather than P=MC, the main efficiency compromise is that:
options: Price may remain above marginal cost even though the firm can cover total cost
The firm must shut down immediately
The firm earns unlimited economic profit
PM6-MON-E-053.feedback: Average-cost pricing addresses financial viability but usually does not attain allocative efficiency.

PM6-MON-E-054.q: If a regulator requires P=MC and the firm would otherwise incur a loss, one possible policy response is:
options: Raise the price back to the unregulated monopoly level
Require output to fall until MR=0
Provide a subsidy financed outside the firm’s price revenue
PM6-MON-E-054.feedback: A subsidy can cover the gap between total cost and revenue under marginal-cost pricing.

PM6-MON-E-055.q: Which example best fits natural monopoly rather than a legal monopoly created only by statute?
options: A license limits taxi entry even though many firms could operate efficiently
A copyright protects a particular book
A single water network has lower ATC than duplicating pipes across several firms
A patent gives one pharmaceutical producer exclusive rights for a fixed term
PM6-MON-E-055.feedback: Natural monopoly is rooted in cost structure and economies of scale rather than legal exclusion alone.

PM6-MON-E-070.q: For price discrimination to be profitable, the seller generally needs:
options: Perfectly competitive pricing and free entry
Identical demand elasticity in every group
A requirement that price equal marginal cost
Market power and some ability to separate buyers by willingness to pay or demand responsiveness
PM6-MON-E-070.feedback: Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.

PM6-MON-E-071.q: Why must a price-discriminating seller often prevent resale between customer groups?
options: Resale guarantees the high-price group becomes less elastic
Resale forces average cost to zero
Low-price buyers could otherwise resell to high-price buyers and undermine the price difference
Resale would make marginal cost negative

PM6-MON-E-072.q: A museum charges local students one price and tourists another based on verifiable group status. This is closest to:
PM6-MON-E-072.feedback: Third-degree discrimination separates identifiable groups and charges them different prices.

PM6-MON-E-073.q: All else equal, which customer group usually receives the higher markup under third-degree price discrimination?
options: The group with less elastic demand
The group with more elastic demand
The group with the lowest fixed cost
The group with the easiest resale opportunities
PM6-MON-E-073.feedback: Less responsive buyers support a larger markup over marginal cost.

PM6-MON-E-074.q: Under perfect first-degree price discrimination, the seller attempts to charge each buyer:
options: Marginal cost for every unit and nothing more
Average total cost regardless of willingness to pay
That buyer’s maximum willingness to pay for each unit
PM6-MON-E-074.feedback: Perfect first-degree discrimination extracts each unit’s willingness to pay.

PM6-MON-E-075.q: A theater can identify student status but students can freely transfer discounted tickets to anyone. Which requirement is missing?
options: Effective prevention of arbitrage or resale
PM6-MON-E-075.feedback: Identification alone is not enough if buyers can defeat segmentation through resale.

PM6-MON-E-076.q: A seller faces two separated groups with the same MC. Group A has more elastic demand than Group B. Which pricing pattern is generally expected?
options: Zero price in the more elastic group
A lower price in Group A and a higher price in Group B
A higher price in Group A and a lower price in Group B
The same price because MC is the same
PM6-MON-E-076.feedback: The more elastic group receives the smaller markup.

PM6-MON-E-077.q: Can price discrimination ever increase output relative to single-price monopoly?
options: Yes; serving additional low-value or elastic-market buyers can expand output in some cases
No; discrimination always leaves output unchanged
No; discrimination always eliminates all consumer purchases
Yes, but only if marginal cost is zero
PM6-MON-E-077.feedback: The welfare effect depends partly on whether discrimination expands or contracts total output.

P62G-MON-M-001.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $60, $56, $52, $48, $44, $40. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
P62G-MON-M-001.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-002.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $72, $67, $62, $57, $52, $47. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
P62G-MON-M-002.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-003.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $84, $78, $72, $66, $60, $54. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 4 to 5 units?
P62G-MON-M-003.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-004.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $55, $52, $49, $46, $43, $40. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
P62G-MON-M-004.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-005.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $90, $83, $76, $69, $62, $55. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
P62G-MON-M-005.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-006.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $64, $60, $56, $52, $48, $44. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 4 to 5 units?
P62G-MON-M-006.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-007.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $75, $70, $65, $60, $55, $50. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
P62G-MON-M-007.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-008.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $96, $88, $80, $72, $64, $56. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
P62G-MON-M-008.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

P62G-MON-M-009.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q and marginal cost MC = 20 + 0Q. What output maximizes profit?
P62G-MON-M-009.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

P62G-MON-M-010.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 120 − 2Q and MC = 24 + 0Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
P62G-MON-M-010.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

P62G-MON-M-011.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 90 − 1.5Q and marginal cost MC = 18 + 0Q. What output maximizes profit?
P62G-MON-M-011.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

P62G-MON-M-012.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 110 − 2.5Q and MC = 20 + 0Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
P62G-MON-M-012.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

P62G-MON-M-013.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 96 − 1.6Q and marginal cost MC = 16 + 0.2Q. What output maximizes profit?
P62G-MON-M-013.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

P62G-MON-M-014.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 105 − 2.1Q and MC = 18 + 0.3Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
P62G-MON-M-014.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

P62G-MON-M-015.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 84 − 1.4Q and marginal cost MC = 14 + 0.2Q. What output maximizes profit?
P62G-MON-M-015.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

P62G-MON-M-016.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 115 − 2.5Q and MC = 25 + 0.25Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
P62G-MON-M-016.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

P62G-MON-M-017.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $60; ATC is $35 and AVC is $20. What is the correct short-run outcome?
P62G-MON-M-017.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

P62G-MON-M-018.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $60; ATC is $65 and AVC is $20. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $100
P62G-MON-M-018.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

P62G-MON-M-019.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 22.5 units at $56.25; ATC is $58.03 and AVC is $20.25. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $40
P62G-MON-M-019.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

P62G-MON-M-020.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $70; ATC is $40 and AVC is $27.50. What is the correct short-run outcome?
P62G-MON-M-020.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

P62G-MON-M-021.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 4.88 units at $60.24; ATC is $111.74 and AVC is $50.24. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $251.22
P62G-MON-M-021.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

P62G-MON-M-022.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 19.33 units at $64.40; ATC is $54.52 and AVC is $20.90. What is the correct short-run outcome?
P62G-MON-M-022.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

P62G-MON-M-023.q: A single-price monopolist produces 20 units, while the competitive benchmark is 40 units. What does the output gap represent?
options: Mutually beneficial units not produced by the monopoly
Units that cost more than buyers value
P62G-MON-M-023.feedback: Between Qm and Qc, demand exceeds MC, so those units would create surplus.

P62G-MON-M-024.q: For a market with monopoly price $66.19 and competitive price $26.36 under the stated linear demand and MC, which statement is correct?
options: All consumer loss becomes monopoly profit
Monopoly transfers some surplus and destroys additional surplus
P62G-MON-M-024.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

P62G-MON-M-025.q: A single-price monopolist produces 22.73 units, while the competitive benchmark is 41.67 units. What does the output gap represent?
options: Units that cost more than buyers value
Mutually beneficial units not produced by the monopoly
P62G-MON-M-025.feedback: Between Qm and Qc, demand exceeds MC, so those units would create surplus.

P62G-MON-M-026.q: For a market with monopoly price $74.33 and competitive price $32.04 under the stated linear demand and MC, which statement is correct?
options: All consumer loss becomes monopoly profit
Monopoly transfers some surplus and destroys additional surplus
P62G-MON-M-026.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

P62G-MON-M-027.q: A natural monopoly regulated at marginal cost has P < ATC. What additional policy issue arises?
options: The firm needs a subsidy or another way to cover its loss
The firm earns monopoly profit automatically
Output must be reduced below monopoly output
P62G-MON-M-027.feedback: P=MC can be efficient but fail to cover fixed cost.

P62G-MON-M-028.q: Compared with marginal-cost pricing, average-cost pricing for a natural monopoly generally produces:
options: A lower price and higher output with larger losses
A higher price and lower output but avoids an operating subsidy
The unregulated monopoly price and output
P62G-MON-M-028.feedback: P=ATC covers cost but leaves P above MC.

P62G-MON-M-029.q: A theater charges students less than adults for the same seat. Which condition is essential for the pricing strategy to work?
options: Students must have less elastic demand
Marginal cost must differ by buyer
Adults cannot cheaply buy and use student tickets
The theater must face horizontal demand

P62G-MON-M-030.q: Two customer groups have the same marginal cost, but Group A has less elastic demand than Group B. A profit-maximizing discriminator will usually:
options: Charge Group B a higher price
Charge both groups the same price regardless of elasticity
Charge Group A a higher price
P62G-MON-M-030.feedback: The less elastic market supports a larger markup.

P62G-MON-M-031.q: Refer to the graph. What is the monopolist’s economic profit per unit at Q = 36?
P62G-MON-M-031.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC: $42 − $27 = $15.

P62G-MON-M-032.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit?

P62G-MON-M-033.q: Refer to the graph. Compared with the D = MC benchmark, how many fewer units does the monopoly produce?
P62G-MON-M-033.feedback: The monopoly produces 36 units, while D = MC occurs at 60, a difference of 24 units.

P62G-MON-M-034.q: Refer to the graph. What price is associated with the D = MC benchmark?
P62G-MON-M-034.feedback: Demand and MC intersect at Q = 60 and P = $30.

P62G-MON-M-035.q: Refer to the graph. What economic loss per unit is shown at Q = 40?
P62G-MON-M-035.feedback: Price is $40 and ATC is $45, so the loss is $5 per unit.

P62G-MON-M-036.q: Refer to the graph. What is the total economic loss at the monopoly output?
P62G-MON-M-036.feedback: The firm loses $5 on each of 40 units, for a total loss of $200.

P62G-MON-M-037.q: Refer to the graph. At the monopoly quantity, what common value do MR and MC have?
P62G-MON-M-037.feedback: The MR and MC curves meet at $20 when Q = 40.

P62G-MON-M-038.q: Refer to the graph. Approximately what quantity and price mark the D = MC benchmark?
P62G-MON-M-038.feedback: The graph marks the demand-MC intersection at about Q = 67 and P = $27.

P62G-MON-M-039.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, what is economic profit per unit?

P62G-MON-M-040.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at Q = 45?

P62G-MON-M-041.q: Refer to the graph. What price corresponds to the D = MC quantity?
P62G-MON-M-041.feedback: Demand intersects the horizontal MC curve at P = $20 and Q = 90.

P62G-MON-M-042.q: Refer to the graph. Which marked outcome corresponds to average-cost, or fair-return, pricing?
P62G-MON-M-042.feedback: Fair-return pricing sets price equal to ATC; the graph marks D = ATC near Q = 116 and P = $16.

P62G-MON-M-043.q: Refer to the graph. Which marked outcome corresponds to marginal-cost pricing?
P62G-MON-M-043.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing sets demand price equal to MC, shown at Q = 140 and P = $10.

P62G-MON-M-044.q: Refer to the graph. At the marginal-cost-pricing output, what is the economic loss per unit?
P62G-MON-M-044.feedback: The per-unit loss is ATC minus price: $15 − $10 = $5.

PM6-MON-M-001.q: A town currently has one ambulance provider, but licenses are readily available and several firms can enter with ordinary equipment. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The current one-seller market does not by itself establish durable monopoly power
The provider is a natural monopoly because only one firm operates today
The provider must have a patent protecting ambulance service
The provider can charge any price because entry has not happened yet
PM6-MON-M-001.feedback: A monopoly requires meaningful barriers to entry, not merely one seller at a moment in time.

PM6-MON-M-002.q: A patented medical device is profitable while the patent remains in force. What is the patent doing economically?
options: Making the firm’s demand curve horizontal
Forcing marginal revenue to equal price
Guaranteeing that average total cost will fall forever
Restricting entry and helping preserve the incumbent’s market power
PM6-MON-M-002.feedback: A patent is a legal barrier that can prevent rivals from copying the protected product.

PM6-MON-M-003.q: A messaging platform becomes more useful as more friends and businesses join it. Why can this discourage entry by a rival platform?
options: The rival automatically faces perfectly inelastic demand
Network effects remove the need for consumer choice
Users may prefer the established network because its large user base raises its value
The incumbent’s marginal cost must be zero
PM6-MON-M-003.feedback: Network effects can create a demand-side barrier because users value access to the existing network.

PM6-MON-M-004.q: A firm owns the only economically viable source of a rare input required to make a specialized product. Which mechanism protects its market position most directly?
options: Its customers cannot respond to price changes
Control of an essential resource blocks rivals from obtaining a necessary input
Its price must equal marginal cost
Its fixed costs disappear as output rises
PM6-MON-M-004.feedback: Exclusive control of a critical resource can prevent otherwise capable rivals from entering.

PM6-MON-M-005.q: A regional water network requires an enormous pipe system, and duplicating the network would raise average cost. Which fact best supports natural-monopoly status?
options: One firm can serve market demand at lower average cost than multiple duplicative networks
The provider has the legal right to discriminate among all buyers
The firm earns accounting profit in the current year
PM6-MON-M-005.feedback: Natural monopoly comes from scale economies over the relevant range of market demand.

PM6-MON-M-015.q: A monopolist cuts price to sell one additional unit. Why can marginal revenue be far below the new price?
options: Average revenue becomes zero when price falls
The demand curve becomes horizontal after the price cut
The extra unit adds revenue, but the lower price also reduces revenue collected on earlier units
Marginal cost is automatically subtracted from marginal revenue
PM6-MON-M-015.feedback: Marginal revenue reflects both the output effect and the price effect on units already sold.

PM6-MON-M-021.q: At 40 units a monopolist has MR=$28 and MC=$22; at 41 units MR=$24 and MC=$25. Which output is the better marginal choice?
options: 40 units, because the 41st unit costs more at the margin than it adds to revenue
41 units, because price must still exceed marginal revenue
41 units, because a monopolist always produces until price equals MC
40 units only if average total cost is minimized there
PM6-MON-M-021.feedback: Produce units for which MR covers MC and stop before the next unit has MC greater than MR.

PM6-MON-M-022.q: A monopolist has already found its profit-maximizing quantity using MR=MC. What is the next step for determining the monopoly price?
options: Use the MR curve value as the price
Set price equal to average total cost
Choose the lowest price on the demand curve
Move up to the demand curve at that quantity
PM6-MON-M-022.feedback: MR determines the quantity condition; demand gives the price buyers will pay for that quantity.

PM6-MON-M-041.q: Suppose competition would produce 100 units at $20, while monopoly produces 70 units at $35. Which change is the clearest source of efficiency loss?
options: The 30 units between 70 and 100 that would have generated gains from trade are not produced
The monopolist receives revenue on the 70 units it sells
The market price is written in dollars rather than units
Consumers buy positive quantities under monopoly
PM6-MON-M-041.feedback: The efficiency loss comes from mutually beneficial transactions forgone because of restricted output.

PM6-MON-M-042.q: If a monopolist reduces output farther below the competitive quantity while demand and cost curves are unchanged, what generally happens to deadweight loss?
options: It necessarily falls because the firm earns more profit
It becomes zero when price rises
It is unchanged because transfers do not matter
It increases because more mutually beneficial units are forgone
PM6-MON-M-042.feedback: Greater output restriction usually widens the range of lost gains from trade.

PM6-MON-M-056.q: A natural monopoly has MC=$12 and ATC=$20 at the allocatively efficient quantity. If regulation sets P=$12, which outcome is most likely without a subsidy?
options: The firm must reduce output to zero by definition
The firm incurs an economic loss because price is below ATC
The firm earns $8 profit per unit
The firm breaks even because P=MC
PM6-MON-M-056.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.

PM6-MON-M-057.q: A regulator sets price where demand intersects ATC for a natural monopoly. Which combination best describes the result?
options: The firm can cover total economic cost, but price generally remains above MC
The firm earns maximum monopoly profit and output falls to zero
Price equals MC and allocative efficiency is guaranteed
The firm necessarily faces a horizontal demand curve
PM6-MON-M-057.feedback: Average-cost pricing aims for financial viability, not full P=MC efficiency.

PM6-MON-M-058.q: A price cap is set above the price the monopolist would charge without regulation. What is the immediate effect?
options: The firm must charge the cap even if it prefers a lower price
The firm’s fixed cost becomes zero
The cap is nonbinding and does not constrain the firm’s chosen price
PM6-MON-M-058.feedback: A ceiling above the unregulated price does not bind.

PM6-MON-M-059.q: A regulator wants lower prices but also wants the utility to maintain infrastructure and innovate. Which concern best captures the tradeoff?
options: Investment incentives are unrelated to expected returns
Any regulation automatically produces the competitive quantity
Aggressive price limits can improve consumer terms while weakening incentives or revenue for cost recovery and investment
Lower prices always increase monopoly profit
PM6-MON-M-059.feedback: Regulation balances static consumer/efficiency goals against financial and dynamic incentives.

PM6-MON-M-060.q: Demand for a utility expands enough that the relevant output range moves beyond the region where ATC is falling. What does that suggest about the natural-monopoly argument?
options: It guarantees marginal cost is zero
It may weaken because one firm may no longer have a cost advantage over multiple firms across the new relevant range
It becomes stronger automatically because demand increased
It proves that price discrimination is efficient
PM6-MON-M-060.feedback: Natural-monopoly status depends on cost conditions over the relevant market-demand range.

PM6-MON-M-078.q: A firm has market power and observes two groups with different demand elasticities, but buyers can costlessly resell the product. What happens to the proposed two-price strategy?
options: The firm can preserve both prices indefinitely
The high-price group automatically becomes less elastic
Marginal cost becomes different across groups
Arbitrage tends to collapse the price difference
PM6-MON-M-078.feedback: Segmentation must be enforceable; costless resale undermines differentiated prices.

PM6-MON-M-079.q: Why does a third-degree discriminator compare MR from each market with the common MC?
options: Average revenue must equal average cost in every market
Profit is increased by allocating another unit to a market whenever that market’s MR exceeds MC
The firm must make prices identical across markets
PM6-MON-M-079.feedback: The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.

PM6-MON-M-080.q: Two groups have identical MC. Seniors have less elastic demand than students. What happens to the optimal markup?
PM6-MON-M-080.feedback: A less elastic market supports a larger markup over common marginal cost.

PM6-MON-M-081.q: Compared with a single-price monopoly, perfect first-degree price discrimination can eliminate the standard output deadweight loss when:
options: The firm sells every unit for which willingness to pay is at least MC
The firm charges one common price above MC
The firm ignores willingness to pay
PM6-MON-M-081.feedback: Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.

PM6-MON-M-082.q: A discriminatory pricing plan raises total output by serving a new low-price market. What is the most defensible welfare conclusion?
options: Total surplus must fall because prices differ
Consumer surplus must rise in every group
Total surplus may rise because additional mutually beneficial trades occur, though distribution also changes
PM6-MON-M-082.feedback: Welfare effects depend on output as well as how surplus is redistributed.

PM6-MON-M-083.q: An airline sells a discounted ticket that cannot be transferred and imposes restrictions that separate leisure from business travelers. What economic purpose do the restrictions serve?
options: They force the same elasticity in both groups
They eliminate the airline’s fixed costs
They help prevent arbitrage and maintain market segmentation
They make the airline a price taker
PM6-MON-M-083.feedback: Restrictions can help keep low-price buyers from reselling or masquerading as high-value segments.

PM6-MON-M-084.q: A firm can separate buyers perfectly but faces a perfectly competitive market with many identical sellers. Why is discrimination difficult to sustain?
options: Buyer groups necessarily have identical elasticities
The firm lacks enough market power to set different markups without losing customers
Resale prevention becomes irrelevant only because MC is zero
PM6-MON-M-084.feedback: Segmentation is not enough; the seller also needs pricing power.

PM6-MON-M-085.q: A monopolist starts charging different prices to two isolated groups. The high-price group is observed to have less elastic demand. Which fact best explains the pricing pattern?
options: Optimal monopoly markup is inversely related to demand responsiveness
The high-price group must have higher marginal cost
The low-price group must have higher fixed cost
Price discrimination requires equal prices when MC is common
PM6-MON-M-085.feedback: Lower elasticity supports a larger markup over marginal cost.

P62G-MON-H-001.q: Refer to the graph. Q1 is selected where MR intersects MC. What does P1 represent?
options: The price on the demand curve at Q1
P62G-MON-H-001.feedback: Quantity comes from MR=MC; price comes from demand.

P62G-MON-H-002.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison determines whether the monopolist earns economic profit at Q1?
options: P1 compared with MC at Q1
P1 compared with ATC at Q1
MR compared with demand at Q1
ATC compared with AVC at zero output

P62G-MON-H-003.q: Refer to the graph. At Q1, why is price greater than marginal revenue?
options: Lowering price to sell Q1 creates a price effect on prior units
P62G-MON-H-003.feedback: For single-price monopoly, MR reflects both the output and price effects.

P62G-MON-H-004.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose fixed cost rises while demand, MR, and MC remain unchanged. What happens in the short run?
options: Q1 and P1 remain unchanged, but profit falls
P62G-MON-H-004.feedback: Fixed cost shifts ATC but does not change the MR=MC output.

P62G-MON-H-005.q: Refer to the graph. If P1 equals ATC at Q1, the monopoly earns:
options: Zero economic profit while covering all opportunity costs
A loss equal to fixed cost
Positive profit because P1 exceeds MC
P62G-MON-H-005.feedback: P=ATC means all explicit and implicit costs are covered.

P62G-MON-H-006.q: Refer to the graph. P1 is below ATC but above AVC at Q1. What should the monopolist do?
options: Shut down because P1 is below ATC
Produce Q1 and minimize its short-run loss
P62G-MON-H-006.feedback: Covering AVC and part of fixed cost reduces the loss.

P62G-MON-H-007.q: Refer to the graph. What is the monopolist’s total economic loss if the vertical gap between ATC and P1 is L?
options: One-half of L multiplied by Q1
The gap between P1 and MC multiplied by Q1
P62G-MON-H-007.feedback: Loss is a rectangle: loss per unit times output.

P62G-MON-H-008.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the MR = MC rule remain relevant even when the monopolist is taking an economic loss?
options: It identifies the shutdown price directly
It makes price equal marginal cost
It identifies the output that minimizes the loss, provided price covers AVC
P62G-MON-H-008.feedback: Marginal analysis chooses the best feasible output, not necessarily a profitable one.

P62G-MON-H-009.q: Refer to the graph. The best available price is below AVC. What should the monopolist do in the short run?
options: Produce zero in the short run
Ignore AVC because it has market power
P62G-MON-H-009.feedback: Price below AVC means revenue cannot cover avoidable cost.

P62G-MON-H-010.q: Refer to the graph. After short-run shutdown, which cost remains?
options: Variable cost of the unproduced units
P62G-MON-H-010.feedback: Shutdown avoids variable cost but not short-run fixed cost.

P62G-MON-H-011.q: Refer to the graph. Q1 is monopoly output and Q2 is the D=MC quantity. The interval from Q1 to Q2 consists of units for which:
options: Average total cost is necessarily falling
Buyer willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost
P62G-MON-H-011.feedback: Those omitted units would add to total surplus.

options: A transfer equal to all monopoly profit
