Set demand=MC for Q, use MR for P, then compare P with AVC
Minimize ATC for Q, set P=MC, then calculate revenue
Choose the highest price, then produce the demanded quantity

Competition uses P=MC, while monopoly uses MR=MC
Monopoly minimizes ATC, while competition maximizes revenue
Monopoly has lower marginal cost at every quantity

options: Set demand=MC for Q, use MR for P, then compare P with AVC

P62G-MON-H-022.q: Why does average-cost regulation usually produce less output than marginal-cost regulation for a natural monopoly?

P62G-MON-H-023.q: A price cap lets a natural monopoly keep cost savings until the cap is reviewed. What incentive does this create?

A requirement to increase fixed cost

P62G-MON-H-024.q: A regulator cannot observe the monopoly’s true cost curve. Which problem does this create?

P62G-MON-H-025.q: Which statement best describes the natural-monopoly policy problem?
options: One firm may minimize production cost, yet unregulated pricing restricts output
Multiple firms always have lower ATC
Marginal-cost pricing always covers total cost
P62G-MON-H-025.feedback: Natural monopoly creates a production-cost advantage and a pricing problem.

P62G-MON-H-026.q: A seller can identify two groups with different elasticities, but customers can freely resell. What blocks third-degree price discrimination?
P62G-MON-H-026.feedback: Resale lets low-price buyers undercut the high-price market.

P62G-MON-H-027.q: Under perfect first-degree price discrimination, why can output reach the efficient quantity?
options: Marginal revenue remains below every buyer’s price
The firm sets one price above demand
The seller serves every buyer whose willingness to pay covers marginal cost
Consumer surplus causes output to contract
P62G-MON-H-027.feedback: Unit-specific pricing makes the marginal buyer’s price equal willingness to pay.

P62G-MON-H-028.q: Perfect first-degree discrimination eliminates the single-price monopoly DWL but:

Transfers the benchmark consumer surplus to the seller
P62G-MON-H-028.feedback: Efficiency can rise while distribution shifts sharply.

P62G-MON-H-029.q: A group-pricing scheme increases total output relative to one-price monopoly. What is the most defensible welfare conclusion?
options: Total welfare may rise, though distribution across groups changes
Consumer surplus must rise for every group
The policy is identical to perfect competition
P62G-MON-H-029.feedback: Output expansion can recover trades, but consumer effects differ.

P62G-MON-H-030.q: A software firm charges a lower price in a market with highly elastic demand. The economic rationale is:

The elastic market requires a smaller markup over marginal cost
The firm’s marginal cost is necessarily lower there
P62G-MON-H-030.feedback: Optimal markups are smaller where demand is more responsive.

P62G-MON-H-031.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, why is the price read from demand above marginal revenue?
options: An extra sale requires lowering price on earlier units
Marginal cost is already embedded in the downward demand curve
Average total cost must exceed marginal revenue at every output
The monopolist takes a fixed market price on all units sold
P62G-MON-H-031.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, expanding sales lowers the price received on previous units, so MR lies below price.

P62G-MON-H-032.q: Refer to the graph. Why would moving output from 36 toward 60 units reduce profit?
options: Demand exceeds ATC over the entire interval
Price becomes greater than marginal revenue
P62G-MON-H-032.feedback: Once output passes MR = MC, the additional units cost more at the margin than they add to revenue.

P62G-MON-H-033.q: Refer to the graph. At the monopoly output, what is the markup of price over marginal cost?
P62G-MON-H-033.feedback: At Q = 36, P = $42 and MC = $24, so the markup is $18.

P62G-MON-H-034.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison correctly describes the monopoly outcome and the D = MC benchmark?

Monopoly: P = $24, Q = 36; benchmark: P = $27, Q = 60
Monopoly and the benchmark both have P = $30 and Q = 60
Monopoly: P = $42, Q = 36; D = MC benchmark: P = $30, Q = 60

P62G-MON-H-035.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison shows that the monopolist is taking an economic loss?

MC $20 is below demand at Q = 40

MC rises faster than demand throughout the relevant range

Demand must become perfectly elastic when a second firm enters

The entrant necessarily has higher marginal revenue than price

The franchise forces the firm to charge average total cost
The franchise guarantees efficient output because rivals are excluded

Q = 40 and P = $40 stay; the firm still loses $200

MC is horizontal between the monopoly and benchmark outputs

P62G-MON-R-001.q: A city has one coffee shop today, but entry is easy and several rivals are preparing to open. Is the current seller necessarily a durable monopoly?
options: Yes; one seller at any moment is always a permanent monopoly
Yes; size alone creates a legal barrier
No; one current seller without a meaningful barrier may only have temporary market leadership
No; because monopoly requires horizontal demand
P62G-MON-R-001.feedback: Durable monopoly power depends on the relevant market and barriers to entry.

P62G-MON-R-002.q: Which fact most strongly supports classifying a firm as a monopoly?
options: It is the largest of twenty similar firms
Its accounting profit rose this year
It is the only supplier and rivals cannot enter because it controls an essential input
P62G-MON-R-002.feedback: One seller plus a durable barrier supports monopoly classification.

P62G-MON-R-003.q: A monopolist lowers price from $20 to $19 to sell one more unit. Why can MR be less than $19?
options: The $1 price cut also applies to units the firm was already selling
The new unit costs more than $19 to produce
Fixed cost rises by $1 per unit
P62G-MON-R-003.feedback: MR subtracts the lost revenue on previous units.

P62G-MON-R-004.q: For a single-price monopolist, which curve gives price at each output?
options: Demand, which is also average revenue
P62G-MON-R-004.feedback: Price is read from demand, while MR lies below it.

P62G-MON-R-005.q: If demand is inelastic at the current output, reducing output will usually:
options: Lower total revenue and raise total cost
Raise total revenue and lower total cost, increasing profit
Force marginal revenue to equal price
P62G-MON-R-005.feedback: On inelastic demand, a price increase raises total revenue; lower output also reduces cost.

P62G-MON-R-006.q: At the unit-elastic point of a demand curve, marginal revenue is:
P62G-MON-R-006.feedback: Total revenue is maximized where MR=0.

P62G-MON-R-007.q: What is the correct order for solving a monopoly graph?
options: Find Q where MR=MC, then read P from demand
Find P where MR=MC, then read Q from ATC
Find Q where demand=MC, then read P from MR
Choose the highest demand intercept as price

P62G-MON-R-008.q: A table has no output where MR exactly equals MC. The monopolist should:
options: Produce zero because equality is absent
Produce through the last unit whose MR is at least MC
Choose the unit with the lowest ATC
P62G-MON-R-008.feedback: Discrete marginal analysis uses the last profitable unit.

P62G-MON-R-009.q: At Q=20, price is $50, ATC is $38, and MC is $30. What is profit?

P62G-MON-R-010.q: Why does P>MC not prove positive economic profit?
P62G-MON-R-010.feedback: Profit depends on price relative to ATC.

P62G-MON-R-011.q: A monopolist has P below ATC but above AVC at its best output. It should:
options: Produce in the short run and minimize its loss
Shut down because any loss requires zero output
Exit and erase fixed cost immediately
P62G-MON-R-011.feedback: Revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

P62G-MON-R-012.q: Short-run shutdown allows a monopolist to avoid:
options: Variable cost but not fixed cost
Fixed cost but not variable cost
P62G-MON-R-012.feedback: Only avoidable variable cost disappears at zero output.

P62G-MON-R-013.q: Which part of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss?
options: The portion not transferred to the monopolist because output is not produced
The price increase on units still sold
P62G-MON-R-013.feedback: DWL comes from unrealized trades; the remaining loss can be a transfer.

P62G-MON-R-014.q: Price above MC is evidence of:
options: Allocative inefficiency, because some buyers value additional output above its marginal cost
P62G-MON-R-014.feedback: P>MC indicates forgone surplus at the margin.

P62G-MON-R-015.q: Why can P=MC cause a regulated natural monopoly to lose money?
options: Declining ATC leaves ATC above MC over the relevant range
P62G-MON-R-015.feedback: Efficient price may not recover large fixed cost.

P62G-MON-R-016.q: What is the main compromise under average-cost pricing?
options: The firm earns unlimited monopoly profit
The firm covers cost, but price remains above MC and output stays below the efficient level
P62G-MON-R-016.feedback: P=ATC addresses solvency but not full allocative efficiency.

P62G-MON-R-017.q: A seller can identify student buyers but cannot prevent ticket resale. What fails?

P62G-MON-R-018.q: Which group normally receives the higher price under third-degree discrimination?
options: The group with more elastic demand
The group with the highest marginal cost even when costs are equal
The group that can resell most easily
The group with less elastic demand
P62G-MON-R-018.feedback: Less elastic demand supports a larger markup.

P62G-MON-R-019.q: Does perfect first-degree discrimination eliminate the single-price monopoly DWL?
options: Yes, in the benchmark model, because output expands to where willingness to pay equals MC
No, because MR remains below every personalized price
P62G-MON-R-019.feedback: Efficient output can be restored even though consumer surplus is extracted.

P62G-MON-R-020.q: Can ordinary group price discrimination increase total welfare?
options: No; any price difference always increases DWL
Yes, when it expands total output enough to recover otherwise lost trades
Yes only when all groups pay the same price
P62G-MON-R-020.feedback: Welfare depends on the output change, not the mere existence of multiple prices.

PM6-MON-R-010.q: What must accompany a single seller for monopoly power to be durable?
options: A requirement that price equal marginal cost
A meaningful barrier that makes entry difficult
PM6-MON-R-010.feedback: One seller becomes a durable monopoly only when entry is meaningfully blocked.

PM6-MON-R-016.q: A monopolist lowers price from $20 to $19 to increase sales. Is the marginal revenue from the added unit necessarily $19?
options: No; marginal revenue must always be negative
No; the lower price may also reduce revenue on units that were already being sold
Yes; marginal revenue always equals price for every seller
Yes; average revenue and marginal revenue are identical for a monopolist
PM6-MON-R-016.feedback: For a single-price monopolist, MR includes the lost revenue caused by lowering price on previous units.

PM6-MON-R-017.q: Where should a monopolist read the price consumers will pay for a chosen quantity?
options: From the minimum of average total cost
PM6-MON-R-017.feedback: Demand gives price at each quantity; MR is used for the marginal output decision.

PM6-MON-R-023.q: Which equality identifies the candidate output for a single-price monopolist?
PM6-MON-R-023.feedback: The monopoly output decision uses marginal revenue and marginal cost.

PM6-MON-R-024.q: After finding Q where MR=MC, where is monopoly price found?
PM6-MON-R-024.feedback: Demand maps the chosen quantity into the price consumers will pay.

PM6-MON-R-025.q: If MR exceeds MC at the current output, what should a profit-maximizing monopolist generally do?
options: Keep output unchanged because price exceeds MR
PM6-MON-R-025.feedback: When MR exceeds MC, another unit adds more revenue than cost.

PM6-MON-R-026.q: If the MR=MC intersection occurs where MC is falling and another later intersection occurs where MC is rising, which is the usual profit-maximizing candidate?
options: The first intersection on the falling portion of MC
Both intersections necessarily give identical profit
Neither intersection because monopoly uses P=MC
The intersection on the rising portion of MC
PM6-MON-R-026.feedback: The stable maximum uses MR=MC with MC rising through MR.

PM6-MON-R-033.q: Which expression gives total economic profit for a monopolist producing Q units?
PM6-MON-R-033.feedback: Economic profit equals profit per unit times quantity.

PM6-MON-R-034.q: A monopolist is losing money because P<ATC, but P>AVC. What does the shutdown rule say?
options: Shut down immediately because any loss requires shutdown
Exit the industry immediately regardless of fixed costs
Continue producing in the short run if the chosen output minimizes the loss
PM6-MON-R-034.feedback: Covering variable cost makes continued short-run production better than shutting down when fixed cost is unavoidable.

PM6-MON-R-043.q: Which area is conceptually deadweight loss from monopoly?
options: Consumer spending on units still purchased
The lost surplus on units between monopoly output and the efficient output
PM6-MON-R-043.feedback: Deadweight loss comes from trades not made, not from surplus merely transferred.

PM6-MON-R-044.q: At the monopoly output, price is $50 and MC is $30. What does the $20 gap imply at the margin?
options: Output is productively efficient because price exceeds MC
Buyers value another unit more than its production cost, so output is too low from an allocative-efficiency standpoint
The firm is necessarily earning $20 profit per unit
PM6-MON-R-044.feedback: P>MC means potential gains from additional output remain.

PM6-MON-R-045.q: If a monopoly captures $100 of consumer surplus without changing total output, what happens to total surplus from that transfer alone?
PM6-MON-R-045.feedback: A pure transfer changes distribution; deadweight loss requires lost gains from trade.

PM6-MON-R-046.q: Why can rent-seeking expenditures make monopoly socially more costly than the standard deadweight-loss triangle alone suggests?
options: They automatically expand output to the competitive level
They convert monopoly demand into perfectly elastic demand
Real resources may be spent obtaining or defending monopoly privileges rather than producing valued goods and services
PM6-MON-R-046.feedback: Rent seeking can consume resources in addition to the surplus loss from restricted output.

PM6-MON-R-061.q: What cost pattern is the key starting point for natural-monopoly analysis?
options: ATC falls over the relevant range of market demand
PM6-MON-R-061.feedback: Economies of scale over market demand can make a single supplier lowest-cost.

PM6-MON-R-062.q: What is the efficiency goal of setting a regulated natural-monopoly price equal to MC?
options: Produce units up to the point where willingness to pay equals the marginal production cost

PM6-MON-R-063.q: Why does P=ATC usually allow a regulated natural monopoly to remain financially viable?
options: Revenue per unit covers average economic cost at the chosen output
It guarantees marginal revenue is zero
PM6-MON-R-063.feedback: Average-cost pricing permits recovery of total economic cost including normal profit.

PM6-MON-R-064.q: When is a price cap actually binding on an unregulated monopolist?
options: Only when demand is perfectly inelastic
When the cap is below the price the firm would otherwise charge
Whenever a regulator announces any maximum price
Only when the cap equals ATC
PM6-MON-R-064.feedback: A ceiling constrains behavior only when it lies below the unconstrained price.

PM6-MON-R-089.q: Which two conditions are especially important for sustaining price discrimination?
options: Market power and the ability to segment buyers while limiting resale
Perfect competition and identical buyer demand
Zero marginal cost and free resale
A horizontal demand curve and free entry
PM6-MON-R-089.feedback: The seller needs pricing power and enforceable segmentation.

PM6-MON-R-090.q: Under third-degree price discrimination, which group normally pays the higher price when marginal cost is the same?
options: The group with more elastic demand
The group with the easiest resale opportunity
The group with lower willingness to pay at every quantity
The group with less elastic demand
PM6-MON-R-090.feedback: Less elastic demand supports a larger optimal markup.

P62G-MON-BR-001.q: Why is the competitive quantity larger than the monopoly quantity in the standard benchmark?
options: Competition uses MR=MC and monopoly uses minimum ATC
Monopoly has a horizontal demand curve
Competition expands output until P=MC, while monopoly stops where MR=MC
Competition faces stronger barriers to entry
P62G-MON-BR-001.feedback: The revenue wedge causes the monopoly to stop earlier.

P62G-MON-BR-002.q: Which equality holds for a competitive firm but not a single-price monopolist?
P62G-MON-BR-002.feedback: A price taker sells each unit at the same price; a monopolist lowers price to expand output.

P62G-MON-BR-003.q: Why can monopoly profit persist when competitive profit is eroded?
options: Barriers prevent the entry response that expands supply
Monopoly fixed cost is always zero
P62G-MON-BR-003.feedback: Entry is the key long-run difference.

P62G-MON-BR-004.q: At the competitive benchmark, allocative efficiency requires P=MC. What is typical under single-price monopoly?
options: P exceeds MC at the chosen output
P62G-MON-BR-004.feedback: Monopoly restricts output below the P=MC quantity.

P62G-MON-BR-005.q: Zero economic profit is common in long-run perfect competition. Can a monopoly also earn zero economic profit?
options: No; every monopoly earns positive profit
No; zero profit requires horizontal demand
Yes; barriers prevent entry but do not guarantee strong enough demand to cover cost
Yes only under perfect price discrimination
P62G-MON-BR-005.feedback: Market structure does not guarantee the profit outcome.

P62G-MON-BR-006.q: Which cost curve determines the monopolist’s output at the margin?
P62G-MON-BR-006.feedback: MR is compared with MC for output choice.

P62G-MON-BR-007.q: Which cost measure determines monopoly profit per unit after output and price are chosen?

P62G-MON-BR-008.q: A pure increase in monopoly fixed cost shifts ATC but leaves which curves unchanged?
P62G-MON-BR-008.feedback: Fixed cost does not change demand or marginal and variable cost.

P62G-MON-BR-009.q: Which cost threshold governs short-run monopoly shutdown?
P62G-MON-BR-009.feedback: The firm must cover avoidable variable cost.

P62G-MON-BR-010.q: Why will a single-price monopolist with nonnegative MC avoid the inelastic part of demand?
options: Reducing output there raises revenue and lowers cost
P62G-MON-BR-010.feedback: Negative MR makes the inelastic range inconsistent with profit maximization.

P62G-MON-BR-011.q: Under third-degree discrimination, which market generally receives the lower markup?
options: The market with more elastic demand
The market with less elastic demand
The market with higher fixed cost
The market where resale is easiest
P62G-MON-BR-011.feedback: A responsive market requires a smaller markup.

P62G-MON-BR-012.q: At the quantity where total revenue is maximized, demand is unit elastic and MR is:
P62G-MON-BR-012.feedback: The derivative or marginal change in TR is zero at the maximum.

P62G-MON-BR-013.q: What distinguishes monopoly profit from monopoly deadweight loss?
options: Profit is consumer surplus and DWL is fixed cost
Profit includes surplus transferred to the seller; DWL is surplus that disappears
P62G-MON-BR-013.feedback: Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not.

P62G-MON-BR-014.q: Why does reducing monopoly output below the competitive quantity create DWL?
options: Some buyers value omitted units above their marginal cost
P62G-MON-BR-014.feedback: The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade.

P62G-MON-BR-015.q: Under perfect first-degree discrimination, what happens to the competitive gains from trade in the benchmark model?
options: They are realized, but the seller captures nearly all of the surplus
They disappear because output is zero
Consumer surplus rises above total surplus
P62G-MON-BR-015.feedback: Personalized prices can restore output while changing distribution.

P62G-MON-BR-016.q: What marginal comparison determines monopoly output?
options: TR compared with fixed cost only
P62G-MON-BR-016.feedback: Produce units whose marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

P62G-MON-BR-017.q: If the next unit has MR greater than MC, what does marginal analysis imply?
options: Reject the unit because it lowers price
Produce the unit because it increases profit
P62G-MON-BR-017.feedback: The incremental benefit exceeds the incremental cost.

P62G-MON-BR-018.q: A patent can create monopoly pricing while encouraging research. What tradeoff should policy evaluate?
options: Fixed cost versus sunk cost only
Static output loss versus dynamic innovation incentives
P62G-MON-BR-018.feedback: Patent policy can sacrifice static efficiency to encourage innovation.

P62G-MON-BR-019.q: A domestic monopolist gains access to a larger export market. Which monopoly tool still determines total output?
options: Compare marginal revenue from available markets with marginal cost
Set price equal to world price in every case
Produce where domestic demand equals MC only
P62G-MON-BR-019.feedback: Market expansion changes demand opportunities, but marginal analysis remains central.

P62G-MON-BR-020.q: Why is monopoly classified as a market-failure source in the standard model?
options: Market power can keep price above MC and block beneficial trades
Fixed cost is always socially wasteful
P62G-MON-BR-020.feedback: The output restriction prevents allocatively efficient exchange.

PM6-MON-BR-011.q: How do barriers to entry connect monopoly structure to persistent economic profit?
options: They make total cost independent of output
They guarantee that the monopolist chooses the efficient quantity
They prevent new rivals from entering quickly when profit appears
They force demand to become perfectly elastic
PM6-MON-BR-011.feedback: Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets.

PM6-MON-BR-012.q: Why does natural-monopoly cost structure often lead directly to a regulation question?
options: Regulation is needed only when a patent expires
Efficient scale may favor one supplier, yet that supplier still has market power over price and output
Natural monopolies always produce where price equals marginal cost without policy
Scale economies make demand perfectly elastic
PM6-MON-BR-012.feedback: Natural monopoly can make one-firm production cost-efficient while still creating a market-power problem.

PM6-MON-BR-013.q: What happens to a patent-based barrier when the patent expires, holding other barriers constant?
options: Legal protection weakens and potential entry becomes easier
The firm’s marginal revenue becomes equal to price automatically
Average total cost must rise above price
PM6-MON-BR-013.feedback: Removing a legal barrier increases contestability even if the incumbent remains large.

PM6-MON-BR-018.q: How does the monopolist’s downward-sloping demand curve create the MR curve used for output choice?
options: Demand forces MR to equal MC at every quantity
The demand curve makes ATC horizontal
MR is simply the vertical distance between demand and MC
Selling more generally requires a lower price, so MR falls below price
PM6-MON-BR-018.feedback: The price effect from expanding sales makes marginal revenue lower than the price on demand.

PM6-MON-BR-019.q: What does positive marginal revenue tell you about the portion of a monopolist’s demand curve?
options: Demand is perfectly inelastic at that output
Demand must have unit elasticity at every output
Demand is elastic at that output
Demand is inelastic at that output
PM6-MON-BR-019.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.

PM6-MON-BR-020.q: Why does P = MR hold for a competitive firm but not for a single-price monopolist?
options: The monopolist’s average revenue is unrelated to price
The competitive firm can sell another unit at the unchanged market price, while the monopolist generally must lower price to expand sales
The monopolist has no demand curve
The competitive firm always has zero marginal cost
PM6-MON-BR-020.feedback: Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price.

PM6-MON-BR-027.q: How do monopoly revenue analysis and marginal cost combine into the output decision?
options: ATC determines quantity before revenue is considered
Price is chosen first and forces MR to equal MC
Demand generates MR, and the firm compares that MR with MC to choose quantity
Demand sets MC directly, so MR is unnecessary
PM6-MON-BR-027.feedback: The monopolist’s demand conditions determine MR; costs determine MC; their marginal comparison selects output.

PM6-MON-BR-028.q: Why is monopoly price determined only after the profit-maximizing quantity is chosen?
options: Average total cost sets price before marginal analysis begins
The firm first uses MR and MC to choose output, then demand reveals the highest single price consistent with that output
Price is unrelated to demand until output is produced
The monopolist has no control over quantity
PM6-MON-BR-028.feedback: Monopoly analysis is a two-step decision: marginal output choice first, demand-based price second.

PM6-MON-BR-035.q: How does the MR = MC output rule connect to the firm’s profit-or-loss calculation?
options: Profit is known before quantity is chosen
The shutdown rule replaces MR=MC whenever the firm has market power
MR=MC identifies the best quantity; price from demand and ATC at that quantity determine profit or loss
ATC determines output first and MR then determines price
PM6-MON-BR-035.feedback: Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis.

PM6-MON-BR-047.q: How does the monopolist’s MR=MC output choice create the welfare result P>MC?
options: Average total cost replaces demand in setting price
Market power makes willingness to pay irrelevant
MR lies below demand, so choosing Q where MR=MC typically leaves price on demand above MC
The firm sets price equal to MC and then raises output
PM6-MON-BR-047.feedback: The gap between demand price and MC at monopoly output is the link between firm optimization and allocative inefficiency.

PM6-MON-BR-065.q: How does declining ATC connect the natural-monopoly cost story to the case for one network rather than duplicated networks?
options: Serving the market through one larger network can avoid duplicative fixed infrastructure and lower average cost
Declining ATC makes price equal MR
It guarantees one firm will choose the efficient quantity without oversight
PM6-MON-BR-065.feedback: Scale economies explain why breaking the firm into many duplicative networks may raise production cost.

PM6-MON-BR-066.q: How does marginal-cost regulation connect monopoly policy to the competitive efficiency benchmark?
options: Both require P=ATC at every output
Both eliminate the need for demand
Both target P=MC so the last unit’s willingness to pay matches its marginal production cost
PM6-MON-BR-066.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing tries to reproduce the allocative condition associated with competitive equilibrium.

PM6-MON-BR-067.q: Why might a subsidy accompany marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly?
options: A subsidy prevents all entry barriers
P=MC can leave revenue below total cost when ATC exceeds MC
A subsidy is required because MR always exceeds price
PM6-MON-BR-067.feedback: The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC.

PM6-MON-BR-068.q: How does average-cost regulation trade some allocative efficiency for financial sustainability?
options: P=ATC makes marginal revenue equal price
P=ATC covers total cost, but price can remain above MC and output below the P=MC level
P=ATC forces the firm to price below MC
PM6-MON-BR-068.feedback: Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark.

PM6-MON-BR-069.q: How can a well-designed price cap change a regulated monopolist’s cost incentives compared with simply reimbursing whatever costs it reports?
options: If the firm can keep some gains from lowering cost below the cap, it may have stronger cost-reduction incentives
A cap guarantees the firm will never invest
A cap automatically sets P=MC regardless of its level
A cap makes fixed costs irrelevant
PM6-MON-BR-069.feedback: Price-cap design can affect incentives to control cost, not just the allowed price.

PM6-MON-BR-091.q: How does elasticity connect directly to third-degree discriminatory pricing?
options: Elasticity determines fixed cost rather than price
Elasticity matters only under perfect competition
Groups with less elastic demand can sustain larger markups over marginal cost
More elastic groups always pay more
PM6-MON-BR-091.feedback: Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.

PM6-MON-BR-092.q: How does resale connect segmented pricing back toward a single price?
options: Arbitrage lets low-price buyers supply high-price buyers, eroding the price gap
Resale raises marginal cost only in the low-price market
PM6-MON-BR-092.feedback: Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist.

PM6-MON-BR-093.q: How should welfare analysis of price discrimination differ from simply asking whether some buyers pay more?
options: Track how total output and total surplus change as well as how surplus is redistributed among buyers and the seller
Any price difference is automatically deadweight loss
Only monopoly profit matters for welfare
Consumer surplus alone always equals total surplus
PM6-MON-BR-093.feedback: Distribution and efficiency are separate questions; output changes can alter total surplus.

PM6-MON-BR-094.q: How does perfect first-degree discrimination connect willingness to pay to the efficient-output condition?
options: The firm must stop where one common price equals MR
The firm ignores willingness to pay and charges ATC
The firm produces only where demand is unit elastic
The firm can sell units until the next buyer’s willingness to pay falls below MC
PM6-MON-BR-094.feedback: Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.

P62H-MCMP-E-001.q: Which combination best describes monopolistic competition?
options: Many firms, differentiated products, and relatively easy entry and exit
One seller, no close substitutes, and barriers that prevent every rival from entering
Many firms selling an identical product
P62H-MCMP-E-001.feedback: The model combines many firms and entry with differentiated products.

P62H-MCMP-E-002.q: What gives a monopolistically competitive firm limited market power?
options: Its product is differentiated from close substitutes
A government franchise that prevents all potential competitors from entering the market
P62H-MCMP-E-002.feedback: Differentiation makes the firm’s own demand slope downward.

P62H-MCMP-E-003.q: A neighborhood café competes through atmosphere, menu, and location. Which feature is being illustrated?
P62H-MCMP-E-003.feedback: Atmosphere, menu, and location can distinguish one seller from close substitutes.

P62H-MCMP-E-004.q: Which example is physical product differentiation?
options: A salon opens closer to commuters
A hotel trains staff to provide faster service
A retailer creates a memorable logo
A shoe brand uses a more durable sole
P62H-MCMP-E-004.feedback: The durable sole changes a physical characteristic of the product.

options: Two similar pharmacies serve different neighborhoods
One pharmacy offers a longer warranty
One pharmacy uses a nationally advertised brand and standardized package design
P62H-MCMP-E-005.feedback: Convenient location can differentiate otherwise similar sellers.

options: A shop changes its wall color
A repair shop guarantees same-day updates
A repair shop owns a patented machine that lowers the cost of each service call
A shop sells an identical commodity
P62H-MCMP-E-006.feedback: The guarantee changes the service experience.

P62H-MCMP-E-007.q: What does branding differentiation primarily create?
options: A legal prohibition on all entry
A perceived identity that may make buyers view close substitutes differently
A legal franchise that prevents rival brands from entering the relevant market
P62H-MCMP-E-007.feedback: Branding can shape perceived differences and loyalty.

P62H-MCMP-E-008.q: Products in monopolistic competition are best described as:
options: Products that buyers regard as identical commodities from interchangeable sellers
P62H-MCMP-E-008.feedback: Consumers can switch, but they may not view every variety as identical.

P62H-MCMP-E-009.q: Why does an individual firm face downward-sloping demand?
options: Some buyers prefer its particular variety
The firm takes price as given
Every buyer views all rival products as identical and refuses to switch among sellers
P62H-MCMP-E-009.feedback: Differentiation allows price to affect quantity demanded for the firm’s variety.

P62H-MCMP-E-010.q: For a monopolistically competitive firm, average revenue equals:
P62H-MCMP-E-010.feedback: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price.

P62H-MCMP-E-011.q: Why is marginal revenue below price for the firm?
options: Average total cost falls as fixed cost is spread across a larger number of units
Selling another unit generally requires a lower price on units sold
P62H-MCMP-E-011.feedback: The price effect makes added revenue smaller than the new unit’s price.

P62H-MCMP-E-012.q: A firm’s close substitutes become more numerous. Its demand will generally become:

P62H-MCMP-E-013.q: What output rule does a monopolistically competitive firm use in the short run?
options: Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost on rising MC
Produce where demand intersects average total cost at the lowest attainable unit cost
Produce at minimum average fixed cost
P62H-MCMP-E-013.feedback: The firm applies the same marginal rule as other profit-maximizing firms.

P62H-MCMP-E-014.q: After choosing output where MR equals MC, where does the firm find its price?
options: On the marginal-revenue curve at the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
On its demand curve at that output
P62H-MCMP-E-014.feedback: Demand gives the price buyers will pay for the chosen quantity.

P62H-MCMP-E-015.q: A firm earns positive economic profit when, at its chosen output:
P62H-MCMP-E-015.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC.

P62H-MCMP-E-016.q: A firm incurs an economic loss when, at its chosen output:
options: Marginal revenue lies below demand even though price still covers average total cost
Price is below average total cost
P62H-MCMP-E-016.feedback: A price below ATC means revenue does not cover total economic cost.

P62H-MCMP-E-017.q: In the short run, a loss-making firm should continue producing when:
options: Price falls below minimum average variable cost but remains above average total cost
P62H-MCMP-E-017.feedback: Production can cover variable cost and part of fixed cost.

P62H-MCMP-E-018.q: What usually happens when firms earn short-run economic profit?
options: Existing firms gain customers because a larger number of sellers expands demand for every variety
P62H-MCMP-E-018.feedback: Profit attracts entry when entry is relatively easy.

P62H-MCMP-E-019.q: How does entry usually affect an existing firm’s demand?
options: It becomes the market supply curve
P62H-MCMP-E-019.feedback: New varieties take some customers from existing firms.

P62H-MCMP-E-020.q: How does entry usually affect an existing firm’s demand elasticity?
P62H-MCMP-E-020.feedback: More substitutes make buyers more responsive.

P62H-MCMP-E-021.q: What usually happens when firms experience persistent economic losses?
options: Existing firms’ demand shifts left indefinitely
P62H-MCMP-E-021.feedback: Exit removes varieties and relieves losses for survivors.

P62H-MCMP-E-022.q: How does exit usually affect a surviving firm’s demand?
P62H-MCMP-E-022.feedback: Fewer substitutes leave more demand for surviving varieties.

P62H-MCMP-E-023.q: In long-run monopolistic-competition equilibrium, firms earn:
options: A loss equal to fixed cost
P62H-MCMP-E-023.feedback: Entry and exit eliminate economic profit while normal profit remains.

P62H-MCMP-E-024.q: What geometric relationship characterizes long-run equilibrium?
options: Demand crosses ATC at minimum ATC
Marginal cost becomes horizontal and coincides with demand at minimum average total cost
The firm’s demand curve is tangent to ATC at its chosen output
P62H-MCMP-E-024.feedback: Tangency makes price equal ATC at the chosen output.

P62H-MCMP-E-025.q: In long-run equilibrium, price is typically:
P62H-MCMP-E-025.feedback: Differentiation leaves a markup even when economic profit is zero.

P62H-MCMP-E-026.q: What is excess capacity in this model?
options: Any unused chair in a store
The gap between equilibrium output and the output minimizing ATC
The vertical distance between the firm’s price and marginal revenue at equilibrium
P62H-MCMP-E-026.feedback: The firm produces below the output that minimizes average total cost.

options: Output is below the quantity at minimum ATC
Economic profit is zero because price equals average total cost at the chosen output
P62H-MCMP-E-027.feedback: Productive efficiency requires production at minimum ATC.

options: Demand is tangent to average total cost at the firm’s long-run equilibrium output
P62H-MCMP-E-028.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires price equal MC.

P62H-MCMP-E-029.q: Which is an example of informational advertising?
options: An ad lists a clinic’s hours, prices, and services
An ad uses only an emotional celebrity image
A group of rival firms secretly coordinates prices and promotional messages
P62H-MCMP-E-029.feedback: The ad provides facts that reduce search costs.

P62H-MCMP-E-030.q: Which statement best captures the welfare tradeoff?
options: Differentiation can add valued variety while markup and excess capacity create inefficiency
Advertising and differentiation always destroy more value than product variety can create
P62H-MCMP-E-030.feedback: The model involves both variety benefits and efficiency costs.

P62H-MCMP-E-031.q: Refer to the graph. What quantity maximizes the firm’s short-run profit?
P62H-MCMP-E-031.feedback: The profit-maximizing output is where MR = MC, which is Q = 50.

P62H-MCMP-E-032.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing quantity, what price does the firm charge?
P62H-MCMP-E-032.feedback: After choosing Q = 50 from MR = MC, move to the demand curve; price is $37.

P62H-MCMP-E-033.q: Refer to the graph. What value of marginal revenue equals marginal cost at Q = 50?
P62H-MCMP-E-033.feedback: The MR and MC curves intersect at $23 when Q = 50.

P62H-MCMP-E-034.q: Refer to the graph. What average total cost is shown at Q = 50?
P62H-MCMP-E-034.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 50 shows average total cost of $33.

P62H-MCMP-E-035.q: Refer to the graph. What quantity satisfies the firm’s MR = MC rule?
P62H-MCMP-E-035.feedback: MR and MC intersect at Q = 36.

P62H-MCMP-E-036.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 36, what price is shown on the demand curve?
P62H-MCMP-E-036.feedback: At the chosen output, the demand curve shows a price of $27.

P62H-MCMP-E-037.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 36, how does price compare with ATC?
P62H-MCMP-E-037.feedback: The graph shows P = ATC = $27 at Q = 36.

P62H-MCMP-E-038.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s long-run equilibrium quantity?
P62H-MCMP-E-038.feedback: The firm chooses Q = 36 where MR = MC.

P62H-MCMP-E-039.q: Refer to the graph. What output represents the efficient scale?
P62H-MCMP-E-039.feedback: The minimum of ATC is marked at Q = 50.

PM7-MCMP-E-015.q: An advertisement lists a store’s prices, hours, and warranty terms. What type of advertising is this primarily?
PM7-MCMP-E-015.feedback: The message mainly reduces consumers’ information costs by providing facts.

PM7-MCMP-E-016.q: A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information. What type of advertising is this primarily?
PM7-MCMP-E-016.feedback: The ad is trying to shape preferences and brand perception rather than mainly transmit facts.

PM7-MCMP-E-017.q: A café upgrades ingredients and service rather than cutting price. Which strategy is it using?
PM7-MCMP-E-017.feedback: Monopolistically competitive firms often compete through quality and service as well as price.

PM7-MCMP-E-018.q: A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged. This is an example of:
PM7-MCMP-E-018.feedback: The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price.

PM7-MCMP-E-019.q: A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand. If the expense is fixed, which cost curve does it directly raise?
PM7-MCMP-E-019.feedback: A fixed selling cost raises fixed and average total cost but does not directly raise MC or AVC.

PM7-MCMP-E-020.q: A platform charges a promotional fee on every unit a seller sells. The fee acts most like an increase in:
PM7-MCMP-E-020.feedback: A per-unit selling expense rises with output, so it behaves like a variable cost.

PM7-MCMP-E-021.q: A successful brand campaign causes more buyers to want the firm’s product at every price. What happens to the firm’s demand curve?
options: There is a movement down the same demand curve
It becomes the market supply curve
It shifts left because advertising raises cost
PM7-MCMP-E-021.feedback: A change in buyers’ willingness to purchase at each price is a demand shift, not a movement along demand.

PM7-MCMP-E-022.q: A loyalty campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rival brands after a price increase. The firm’s demand has become:
PM7-MCMP-E-022.feedback: Greater brand loyalty reduces responsiveness to the firm’s price, making demand less elastic.

PM7-MCMP-E-023.q: A firm develops a distinctive new feature that rivals have not yet copied. What is the most immediate competitive effect?
PM7-MCMP-E-023.feedback: A distinctive feature can temporarily strengthen differentiation until rivals respond or imitate it.

PM7-MCMP-E-038.q: Why can consumers value monopolistic competition even though firms may not produce at minimum ATC?
options: It guarantees the lowest possible price for every product
It makes every firm a price taker
It offers product variety that can match different preferences
PM7-MCMP-E-038.feedback: Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.

PM7-MCMP-E-039.q: In the standard long-run model, which condition signals allocative inefficiency for a monopolistically competitive firm?
PM7-MCMP-E-039.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires P=MC. A positive markup means some mutually beneficial trades may not occur.

PM7-MCMP-E-040.q: A market has only three differentiated firms, and each changes strategy when a rival cuts price. Why may monopolistic competition be a poor model?
options: Price changes are impossible under monopolistic competition
Few firms automatically create a natural monopoly
PM7-MCMP-E-040.feedback: The monopolistic-competition model assumes many firms whose individual strategic reactions are usually not central.

PM7-MCMP-E-041.q: Why is a larger number of brands not automatically socially better?
options: Additional variety can create benefits but also use resources and duplicate fixed costs
Every new brand necessarily lowers marginal cost
More brands guarantee P=MC for all firms
PM7-MCMP-E-041.feedback: The welfare question compares the value of added variety with the resources used to create and sustain it.

P62H-MCMP-M-001.q: A market has 150 independently owned salons, each with a distinct location and reputation, and new salons can open without major legal barriers. Which model fits best?
options: Perfect competition with identical services and a horizontal demand curve for each salon
P62H-MCMP-M-001.feedback: Many firms, differentiation, and entry fit monopolistic competition.

P62H-MCMP-M-002.q: A clothing store raises price and loses some, but not all, customers to nearby brands. What does this imply?
options: It is a price-taking commodity seller facing a horizontal demand curve at the market price
Its firm demand is downward sloping and relatively elastic
P62H-MCMP-M-002.feedback: Differentiation gives market power, while close substitutes keep demand responsive.

P62H-MCMP-M-003.q: A new cluster of coffee shops opens near an established café. Which immediate effect is most likely for the café?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic
Its demand shifts right and becomes less elastic
Its MC curve shifts down automatically

P62H-MCMP-M-004.q: Several boutique gyms close after sustained losses. Which effect is most likely for a surviving gym?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic because fewer alternatives remain available
Its demand shifts right and may become less elastic
Its MR becomes horizontal at zero
P62H-MCMP-M-004.feedback: Exit removes substitutes and can strengthen surviving demand.

P62H-MCMP-M-005.q: A firm’s price is $42, MC is $31, and ATC is $42 at the chosen output. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns an $11 profit per unit because price exceeds marginal cost by $11
The firm earns zero economic profit but has an $11 markup
P62H-MCMP-M-005.feedback: Price equals ATC, so profit is zero; price minus MC is the markup.

P62H-MCMP-M-006.q: A firm produces 24 units in long-run equilibrium, while ATC is minimized at 36 units. What is its excess capacity?
P62H-MCMP-M-006.feedback: Excess capacity is minimum-ATC output minus equilibrium output.

P62H-MCMP-M-007.q: An advertising campaign merely raises fixed selling cost and leaves demand unchanged. What happens to the short-run MR=MC output?
options: It falls because fixed cost raises MC
P62H-MCMP-M-007.feedback: A pure fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MR or MC.

P62H-MCMP-M-008.q: A per-unit promotional fee is imposed on every unit sold. Which curves are directly raised?
P62H-MCMP-M-008.feedback: A per-unit selling cost is a variable cost.

P62H-MCMP-M-009.q: A brand campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rivals. What is the most direct demand effect?
options: Demand shifts only because the campaign lowers marginal cost and average variable cost
The firm’s demand becomes less elastic
MR equals price at every quantity
P62H-MCMP-M-009.feedback: Greater loyalty reduces responsiveness to price.

P62H-MCMP-M-010.q: A comparison website makes prices and features easier to compare across brands. What is the likely effect?
options: Every seller becomes a monopoly because buyers can now compare all products directly
P62H-MCMP-M-010.feedback: Lower search costs make switching easier.

P62H-MCMP-M-015.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

P62H-MCMP-M-016.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

P62H-MCMP-M-017.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

P62H-MCMP-M-018.q: After Kite Apparel chooses Q=18.49, what price follows from P=120−2.5Q?
P62H-MCMP-M-018.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

P62H-MCMP-M-019.q: Lumen Bistro faces P=92−1.5Q and MC=18+0.35Q. What output satisfies MR=MC?
P62H-MCMP-M-019.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

P62H-MCMP-M-020.q: After Lumen Bistro chooses Q=22.09, what price follows from P=92−1.5Q?
P62H-MCMP-M-020.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

P62H-MCMP-M-023.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-M-024.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

P62H-MCMP-M-025.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-M-026.q: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $64 and MC is $47.80. What is the markup?
P62H-MCMP-M-026.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

P62H-MCMP-M-027.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-M-028.q: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $82 and MC is $48.40. What is the markup?
P62H-MCMP-M-028.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

P62H-MCMP-M-029.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

P62H-MCMP-M-037.q: Refer to the graph. How much excess capacity does the firm have?
P62H-MCMP-M-037.feedback: Excess capacity is efficient-scale output minus actual output: 50 − 36 = 14.

P62H-MCMP-M-038.q: Refer to the graph. What minimum average total cost is shown at the efficient scale?
P62H-MCMP-M-038.feedback: ATC reaches its minimum of $25 at Q = 50.

P62H-MCMP-M-039.q: Refer to the graph. At the long-run output, what is the firm’s markup over marginal cost?

PM7-MCMP-M-001.q: A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away. What best explains this result?
options: Product differentiation gives the restaurant limited price-setting power
Free entry makes the restaurant a pure price taker
Many sellers make the restaurant demand curve perfectly elastic
The restaurant controls the entire market supply
PM7-MCMP-M-001.feedback: Differentiation makes the firm’s product an imperfect substitute, so its individual demand curve slopes downward.

PM7-MCMP-M-002.q: Several new coffee shops open offering very similar drinks and service. Holding other factors constant, what is most likely to happen to the demand facing one existing shop?
options: It becomes less elastic because the market has more sellers
It becomes vertical because each shop is now smaller
It becomes perfectly inelastic because products remain differentiated
It becomes more elastic because customers have more close substitutes
PM7-MCMP-M-002.feedback: More close substitutes make customers more responsive to one firm’s price.

PM7-MCMP-M-003.q: A city has dozens of independently owned fitness studios. Each offers a somewhat different mix of classes, and new studios can enter without major legal barriers. Which model is the best starting point?
PM7-MCMP-M-003.feedback: Many sellers, differentiated products, and relatively easy entry are the defining combination.

PM7-MCMP-M-004.q: A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments. Which source of differentiation is most important?
PM7-MCMP-M-004.feedback: The practice is differentiating the service experience rather than relying on a legal barrier or identical product.

PM7-MCMP-M-024.q: A firm spends $20,000 on a fixed ad campaign. Demand shifts right, but MC is unchanged. Which statement is correct?
options: Profit must rise because demand shifted right
The profit-maximizing output may rise because MR changed, while the fixed ad cost also lowers profit
Output must stay unchanged because every advertising expense is fixed
MC shifts upward by exactly $20,000 at every output
PM7-MCMP-M-024.feedback: The demand shift can change MR and output even though the fixed selling cost itself does not shift MC.

PM7-MCMP-M-025.q: A comparison website makes it easier for buyers to compare nearly identical local services. What effect is most likely on each firm’s demand?
PM7-MCMP-M-025.feedback: Better comparison makes substitution easier, increasing buyers’ responsiveness to one firm’s price.

PM7-MCMP-M-026.q: A firm pays a $3 promotional fee for every unit sold, and demand is unchanged. What is the most direct short-run effect?
options: Only fixed cost rises, so output cannot change
Demand shifts right by $3 at every quantity
ATC falls because advertising spreads fixed cost
MC rises, so the MR=MC output tends to fall
PM7-MCMP-M-026.feedback: A per-unit selling cost raises marginal cost and tends to reduce the profit-maximizing output when demand is unchanged.

PM7-MCMP-M-027.q: A restaurant improves food quality. Customers are willing to pay more, but marginal production cost also rises. What determines the new profit-maximizing output?
options: The old output because quality is nonprice competition
The new MR and MC curves together
PM7-MCMP-M-027.feedback: Quality improvement can affect both willingness to pay and cost, so the new optimum still requires comparing MR and MC.

PM7-MCMP-M-028.q: A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive. What becomes more plausible, other things equal?
options: A lower willingness to pay at every quantity
PM7-MCMP-M-028.feedback: Less elastic demand can support greater price-cost markup for a firm with market power.

PM7-MCMP-M-029.q: Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase. Why might heavy advertising sometimes be interpreted as a quality signal?
options: A high-quality seller may expect repeat business that helps justify the advertising expense
Advertising legally guarantees the product will be high quality
Only low-quality sellers are allowed to advertise heavily
Advertising eliminates all uncertainty before purchase
PM7-MCMP-M-029.feedback: In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales.

PM7-MCMP-M-042.q: A policy causes several niche brands to exit. Average production cost falls, but consumers lose valued variety. What is the correct welfare conclusion?
options: Welfare must rise because average cost fell
Welfare must fall because the number of brands fell
The change is irrelevant because firms earn zero economic profit
The net effect is ambiguous without comparing cost savings with lost variety benefits
PM7-MCMP-M-042.feedback: Efficiency analysis must weigh resource savings against the consumer value of differentiation and variety.

PM7-MCMP-M-043.q: A textbook labels a market monopolistically competitive because it has many differentiated sellers. In one rural town, however, only two sellers actually serve customers. What is the best caution?
options: Two local sellers guarantee a natural monopoly
Differentiation becomes irrelevant whenever geography matters
The local market may display strategic interdependence that the broad model misses
The market must still be perfectly competitive locally
PM7-MCMP-M-043.feedback: Market boundaries matter. A broad national description can hide a much more concentrated local competitive environment.

PM7-MCMP-M-044.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit but charges P>$MC$. What does this show?
options: The firm is producing at minimum ATC
Zero economic profit does not imply allocative efficiency
The firm must be earning an accounting loss
Entry has failed to eliminate all market power
PM7-MCMP-M-044.feedback: Entry can eliminate economic profit while differentiation leaves a markup and P above MC.

PM7-MCMP-M-045.q: Two markets have the same total production cost. Market A offers one standardized product; Market B offers several differentiated versions that consumers value. What can be said?
options: Market B may generate greater consumer benefit because variety itself can have value
Market A must be more allocatively efficient because it has fewer products
Market B must have higher deadweight loss because it has more brands
Both markets provide identical welfare because production cost is the same
PM7-MCMP-M-045.feedback: Equal production cost does not imply equal consumer benefit when differentiated varieties match heterogeneous preferences.

P62H-MCMP-H-001.q: Maple Bakery faces P=108−2Q, MC=18+0.3Q, and fixed cost $250. Which sequence is correct?
options: Choose Q=20.93 by MR=MC, charge $66.14, then compare price with ATC
Set demand equal to MC and use MR as price
Choose output where demand equals marginal cost and then use marginal revenue as the selling price
Charge the demand intercept and produce zero

P62H-MCMP-H-013.q: Refer to the graph. Demand is tangent to ATC at Q1 = 20 and price $70. Which combination is correct?
options: Zero economic profit, positive markup, and excess capacity
Positive economic profit with production at minimum average total cost and price equal to marginal cost
P62H-MCMP-H-013.feedback: Tangency gives P=ATC, while P>MC and Q is below minimum ATC.

P62H-MCMP-H-014.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose the firm’s demand shifts outward while costs are unchanged. What is the immediate short-run effect?
options: The firm must earn zero profit immediately
The firm can earn economic profit, encouraging entry
Existing-firm demand shifts left immediately because entry occurs before the outward demand change
P62H-MCMP-H-014.feedback: An outward demand shift can create short-run profit before entry responds.

P62H-MCMP-H-015.q: Refer to the graph. Which equality at Q1 establishes that the firm earns zero economic profit?
options: Marginal revenue equals average total cost
Average total cost equals minimum average variable cost
P62H-MCMP-H-015.feedback: The demand curve is tangent to ATC at Q1, so price equals average total cost and economic profit is zero.

P62H-MCMP-H-016.q: Refer to the graph. After short-run profit induces entry, what happens to the demand curve facing an existing firm?
options: It shifts left until it is tangent to ATC
It shifts right until price equals marginal cost
It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It remains fixed while marginal cost shifts left
P62H-MCMP-H-016.feedback: Entry provides more substitutes and shifts each existing firm’s demand left until tangency restores zero economic profit.

P62H-MCMP-H-017.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison at Q1 demonstrates allocative inefficiency?
options: Price is below average variable cost
P62H-MCMP-H-017.feedback: At Q1 the demand curve gives price above marginal cost, so the allocative-efficiency condition P = MC is not met.

P62H-MCMP-H-018.q: Refer to the graph. Once entry restores long-run equilibrium, which combination can still persist?
options: Zero economic profit with a positive markup
Positive economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
A shutdown loss with minimum average total cost
Zero economic profit with no excess capacity
P62H-MCMP-H-018.feedback: Tangency gives zero economic profit, while the downward-sloping demand curve leaves price above marginal cost.

P62H-MCMP-H-019.q: Refer to the graph. Q2 marks minimum ATC while the firm produces Q1. What does Q2 − Q1 measure?
P62H-MCMP-H-019.feedback: Excess capacity is the difference between efficient-scale output at minimum ATC and the firm’s profit-maximizing output.

P62H-MCMP-H-020.q: Refer to the graph. Why does entry stop at the long-run outcome shown?
options: Price equals average total cost, so economic profit is zero
Price equals marginal cost, so allocative efficiency is achieved
Output equals efficient scale, so excess capacity is zero
Average variable cost equals zero, so shutdown is impossible
P62H-MCMP-H-020.feedback: Entry stops when the demand curve is tangent to ATC and price equals ATC, eliminating economic profit.

P62H-MCMP-H-021.q: A costly brand campaign shifts demand right but also makes demand less elastic. Which conclusion is safest?
options: Output, price, and profit effects depend on both the demand change and campaign cost
Marginal cost must remain above marginal revenue at every possible quantity after the campaign
P62H-MCMP-H-021.feedback: Demand and cost effects must be evaluated together.

P62H-MCMP-H-022.q: An ad supplies verifiable price and quality information. What possible social benefit follows?
options: Lower search costs and better matching between buyers and varieties
A perfectly horizontal firm demand curve that prevents sellers from differentiating their products
P62H-MCMP-H-022.feedback: Information can improve comparison and matching.

P62H-MCMP-H-023.q: A firm repeatedly spends heavily on a brand name that would lose value if quality disappoints. The spending may function as:
options: A guarantee that demand is inelastic
P62H-MCMP-H-023.feedback: A costly, reputation-dependent campaign can signal confidence in repeat business.

P62H-MCMP-H-024.q: Which statement distinguishes genuine quality competition from purely persuasive differentiation?
options: Quality competition always lowers fixed cost
Persuasive differentiation always provides measured performance data
Quality competition changes the attributes or service buyers receive
P62H-MCMP-H-024.feedback: A genuine quality change alters delivered value.

P62H-MCMP-H-025.q: Why can product variety partly offset the model’s efficiency costs?
options: Consumers may value closer matches to preferences
Variety forces every firm to set price equal to marginal cost at minimum average total cost
P62H-MCMP-H-025.feedback: Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain.

P62H-MCMP-H-026.q: A market has four dominant firms that closely monitor one another’s prices. Why is monopolistic competition a weak model?
options: The products are differentiated, which by itself guarantees monopolistic competition regardless of firm count
P62H-MCMP-H-026.feedback: Few-firm strategic interaction is outside the monopolistic-competition model.

P62H-MCMP-H-027.q: A city has hundreds of differentiated restaurants but zoning makes new locations nearly impossible. Which assumption is weakened most?
options: Product differentiation is weakened because zoning changes the physical attributes of restaurant meals
P62H-MCMP-H-027.feedback: Severe entry barriers undermine the standard long-run adjustment.

P62H-MCMP-H-028.q: A fixed advertising campaign raises ATC above demand at the previous output but leaves MR and MC unchanged. What happens first?
options: Price rises because the fixed advertising expense shifts demand outward at every possible price
AVC rises by the same amount
The short-run output remains the same, but profit falls
P62H-MCMP-H-028.feedback: A pure fixed-cost increase does not alter MR=MC output.

P62H-MCMP-H-029.q: A per-unit delivery promise raises MC and also shifts demand right. Which outcome is certain?
options: No direction for output or profit is certain without magnitudes
Output must rise because a rightward demand shift always dominates any increase in marginal cost
P62H-MCMP-H-029.feedback: Demand and marginal-cost changes push decisions in potentially opposing directions.

P62H-MCMP-H-030.q: Why does a markup not prove that a long-run firm earns economic profit?
options: Price can exceed MC while equaling ATC
Entry forces price below average variable cost even though the firm remains in long-run equilibrium
P62H-MCMP-H-030.feedback: Long-run zero profit coexists with P>MC.

P62H-MCMP-H-031.q: Refer to the graph. Using the chosen output, price, and ATC, which statement correctly describes the firm’s economic result?
options: It earns zero economic profit because MR equals MC
It earns $700 because price exceeds MC by $14
It earns positive economic profit of $200
P62H-MCMP-H-031.feedback: The firm earns ($37 − $33) × 50 = $200 in economic profit.

P62H-MCMP-H-032.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the firm’s price read from the demand curve rather than from the MR = MC intersection?
options: Price is read from demand after output is chosen where MR = MC
Price must equal marginal cost at the profit-maximizing output
The firm chooses price where ATC intersects marginal cost
The $23 value is the price consumers pay on the demand curve
P62H-MCMP-H-032.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, the firm chooses Q where MR = MC and then reads price from demand.

P62H-MCMP-H-033.q: Refer to the graph. What are total revenue and total cost at Q = 50?

P62H-MCMP-H-034.q: Refer to the graph. Why is zero economic profit consistent with the firm continuing to operate?
options: Revenue covers all explicit and implicit economic costs
Zero economic profit means the firm receives no revenue
The firm continues only because price equals marginal cost
The firm must be subsidized whenever economic profit is zero
P62H-MCMP-H-034.feedback: P = ATC means the firm covers all economic costs, including normal return.

P62H-MCMP-H-035.q: Refer to the graph. At the chosen output, compare price with marginal cost. What does the gap imply?
options: The firm is allocatively efficient because economic profit is zero
The firm has a positive markup even though economic profit is zero
The firm must be earning $12 of profit per unit
The firm should raise output until price equals ATC again
P62H-MCMP-H-035.feedback: Zero economic profit does not eliminate markup; P still exceeds MC by $12.

P62H-MCMP-H-036.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement best distinguishes the displayed outcome from a perfectly competitive long-run equilibrium?
options: A competitive firm also faces a downward-sloping demand curve
A competitive firm sets MR below price at its chosen output
The firm can have P = ATC while still having P > MC
Perfect competition requires economic profit to remain positive
P62H-MCMP-H-036.feedback: Monopolistic competition can have zero economic profit with a markup because firm demand slopes downward.

P62H-MCMP-H-037.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the firm not expand from Q = 36 to the efficient scale of Q = 50?
options: The firm is physically unable to produce more than 36 units
Price would rise automatically if output increased to 50
Marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost at every output above 36
Profit maximization is governed by MR = MC, not by minimizing ATC alone
P62H-MCMP-H-037.feedback: The firm stops at MR = MC even though ATC would be lower at a larger output.

P62H-MCMP-H-038.q: Refer to the graph. Which pair of facts demonstrates long-run zero economic profit and productive inefficiency?
options: P = ATC at Q = 36, while minimum ATC occurs at Q = 50
P = MC at Q = 36, while ATC is constant after Q = 50
MR = demand at Q = 36, while MC is minimized at Q = 50
P exceeds ATC at Q = 36, while MR equals zero at Q = 50
P62H-MCMP-H-038.feedback: P = ATC gives zero economic profit, while Q below the minimum-ATC output creates excess capacity.

P62H-MCMP-H-039.q: Refer to the graph. Why is the long-run outcome not allocatively efficient?
options: Price of $27 equals ATC at the chosen quantity of 36
Price of $27 exceeds marginal cost of $15.50 at Q = 36
ATC reaches its minimum of $25 at the efficient scale of 50
Demand is tangent to ATC at the long-run quantity of 36
P62H-MCMP-H-039.feedback: Allocative efficiency requires P = MC, but here price exceeds marginal cost by $11.50.

PM7-MCMP-H-005.q: Firm A sells a differentiated snack with many close substitutes. Firm B holds an exclusive patent on a drug with no close substitute. Which comparison is most plausible?
options: Firm A faces more elastic demand than Firm B
Firm A faces less elastic demand than Firm B
Both firms face perfectly elastic demand
Both firms must face the same elasticity because each has a downward-sloping demand curve
PM7-MCMP-H-005.feedback: Close substitutes make buyers more responsive to Firm A’s price, while the patent shields Firm B from close substitution.

PM7-MCMP-H-006.q: A boutique raises its price by 4 percent and loses 7 percent of its customers, but many buyers remain because they prefer its style. What does this pattern most strongly indicate?
options: The firm is a price taker with perfectly elastic demand
The firm has monopoly power protected by an entry barrier
The market must contain only a few strategically interdependent firms
The firm has limited market power, not complete control of demand
PM7-MCMP-H-006.feedback: Differentiation can give a firm some control over price while close substitutes still constrain it.

PM7-MCMP-H-007.q: A market has many sellers and easy entry. Each seller faces a downward-sloping demand curve for its own product. Which additional fact is most consistent with monopolistic competition?
options: A single legal franchise blocks all new rivals
A few firms closely track each rival’s strategic moves
Products are differentiated but remain close substitutes
Products are identical and firms accept one market price
PM7-MCMP-H-007.feedback: Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.

PM7-MCMP-H-008.q: Food-delivery technology makes customers almost indifferent to which neighborhood a restaurant occupies. Other features are unchanged. What happens to location as a source of differentiation?
options: It turns the market into a natural monopoly
It becomes weaker because distance matters less to customers
It becomes stronger because delivery creates a new legal barrier
It guarantees each restaurant a perfectly inelastic demand curve
PM7-MCMP-H-008.feedback: When location matters less to buyers, location creates less product differentiation and less insulation from rivals.

PM7-MCMP-H-009.q: Suppose all meaningful brand, location, service, and quality differences among many sellers disappear while entry remains easy. Which competitive model does the market move toward?
PM7-MCMP-H-009.feedback: With many sellers, easy entry, and effectively identical products, the key remaining conditions resemble perfect competition.

PM7-MCMP-H-030.q: Two campaigns cost the same fixed amount. Campaign A shifts demand right but leaves elasticity unchanged. Campaign B leaves demand quantity unchanged but makes demand less elastic. Why can the profit effects differ?
options: Fixed advertising cost always changes MC by the same amount
Only Campaign A can affect marginal revenue
Only Campaign B can affect the price the firm charges
The campaigns alter the firm’s revenue conditions in different ways even though both add the same fixed cost
PM7-MCMP-H-030.feedback: A demand shift and an elasticity change can alter MR and optimal price/output differently, while the fixed cost enters profit separately.

PM7-MCMP-H-031.q: A firm can spend on product quality that shifts demand right but also raises MC. Which conclusion is economically sound before seeing the magnitudes?
options: Profit must fall because marginal cost increases
Optimal output cannot change because price was not directly altered
Profit may rise or fall because both revenue and marginal cost conditions change
Profit must rise because buyers value the improvement
PM7-MCMP-H-031.feedback: The net effect depends on how much the improvement changes willingness to pay relative to the increase in marginal cost.

PM7-MCMP-H-046.q: Suppose a regulator could force every differentiated firm to price at marginal cost, but doing so would reduce firms’ ability to cover fixed product-development costs and some varieties would disappear. What is the best conclusion?
options: Marginal-cost pricing must raise welfare because P=MC is always sufficient
Variety loss is irrelevant because all firms initially earned zero economic profit
The policy must lower welfare because regulation can never improve allocation
The welfare effect depends on the gain from lower markups relative to the loss of valued variety
PM7-MCMP-H-046.feedback: The standard markup is inefficient, but differentiated products may create variety benefits and require fixed costs. Both sides matter.

P62H-MCMP-R-002.q: A market has differentiated products but only three firms that react strategically to one another. Which model is the better starting point?
P62H-MCMP-R-002.feedback: Strategic few-firm interaction belongs to oligopoly.

P62H-MCMP-R-003.q: Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?
options: Some customers prefer its variety, but they can switch when price rises
The firm is a price taker
The product has no close substitutes, so buyers cannot switch when the firm raises its price

P62H-MCMP-R-004.q: For a downward-sloping firm demand curve, why is MR below price?
options: Selling more requires a lower price, creating a price effect
Entry raises fixed cost and therefore pushes marginal revenue below the firm’s demand curve
P62H-MCMP-R-004.feedback: Added revenue is reduced by the lower price on units sold.

P62H-MCMP-R-005.q: What is the correct sequence for short-run firm choice?
options: Choose P where demand equals MC, then read Q from MR
Choose minimum ATC, then set P=MC
Choose Q where MR=MC, then read P from demand
Choose the highest price on demand
P62H-MCMP-R-005.feedback: Quantity comes from the marginal rule; demand supplies price.

P62H-MCMP-R-006.q: A table has no exact MR=MC equality. Which output should be selected?
options: The first unit whose MC exceeds price
The last unit whose MR is at least MC
P62H-MCMP-R-006.feedback: The discrete marginal rule compares the added revenue and cost of each unit.

P62H-MCMP-R-007.q: A firm has P>MC but P<ATC. Which statement is correct?
options: It has a markup but an economic loss
It earns economic profit because P>MC
P62H-MCMP-R-007.feedback: Profit depends on P versus ATC, not P versus MC.

P62H-MCMP-R-008.q: A firm has P<ATC but P>AVC. What should it do in the short run?
options: Produce at MR=MC and minimize its loss
Exit immediately because any economic loss requires the firm to leave the market
P62H-MCMP-R-008.feedback: Covering AVC allows production to contribute toward fixed cost.

P62H-MCMP-R-009.q: Short-run profit attracts entry. What happens to an existing firm’s demand?
options: It shifts right because the market is larger
It shifts left as new substitutes appear
P62H-MCMP-R-009.feedback: New varieties divide customers among more firms.

P62H-MCMP-R-010.q: How does entry usually affect the elasticity of an existing firm’s demand?
options: Elasticity is determined by fixed cost

P62H-MCMP-R-011.q: Persistent losses cause exit. What happens to a surviving firm’s demand?
P62H-MCMP-R-011.feedback: Fewer substitutes leave more customers for survivors.

P62H-MCMP-R-012.q: Why does exit help eliminate losses?
options: Exit raises every surviving firm’s fixed cost and directly reduces the quantity each firm supplies
Surviving firms face stronger demand and may charge a higher price
P62H-MCMP-R-012.feedback: The demand recovery improves revenue opportunities for survivors.

P62H-MCMP-R-013.q: What does zero economic profit mean?
options: The owner receives no return for time, capital, or entrepreneurship once economic profit reaches zero
All explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered

P62H-MCMP-R-014.q: Where does long-run tangency occur in the standard model?
options: Where demand intersects marginal cost at the output that minimizes average total cost
On the downward-sloping portion of ATC before its minimum
P62H-MCMP-R-014.feedback: The equilibrium output is below the minimum-ATC quantity.

P62H-MCMP-R-015.q: Why can a firm have a markup with zero economic profit?
options: Price can equal ATC while exceeding MC
Markup equals economic profit by definition
P62H-MCMP-R-015.feedback: Markup and profit use different cost comparisons.

options: Price equals marginal cost at minimum average total cost, eliminating markup and excess capacity
Q at minimum ATC minus the firm’s equilibrium Q
P62H-MCMP-R-016.feedback: It is a cost-curve output gap.

P62H-MCMP-R-017.q: An ad shifts firm demand right. Is that a movement along demand?
options: No, it is a demand shift
No, it is a supply shift
P62H-MCMP-R-017.feedback: The campaign changes demand at each possible price.

P62H-MCMP-R-018.q: A fixed advertising bill rises. Which curve does not shift directly?
P62H-MCMP-R-018.feedback: A pure fixed cost does not alter the cost of one more unit.

P62H-MCMP-R-019.q: Why is product variety not automatically wasteful?
options: Consumers may value closer matches to their preferences
P62H-MCMP-R-019.feedback: Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs.

options: Firms compete through quality, service, location, branding, and other dimensions in addition to price
P62H-MCMP-R-020.feedback: Nonprice dimensions supplement rather than eliminate price competition.

PM7-MCMP-R-010.q: A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product. What key condition for monopolistic competition is missing?
PM7-MCMP-R-010.feedback: Many sellers and easy entry are not enough. Monopolistic competition also requires differentiated products.

PM7-MCMP-R-011.q: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses its MR=MC output. At that output, price is below ATC but above AVC. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Raise output until price equals ATC
Exit the industry immediately because price is below ATC
Continue producing and accept an economic loss
Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
PM7-MCMP-R-011.feedback: If price covers AVC, producing helps pay some fixed cost even though the firm earns an economic loss.

PM7-MCMP-R-032.q: A fixed advertising bill increases but demand does not change. Why does the MR=MC output stay the same?
options: The fixed cost does not directly shift MR or MC
The fixed cost lowers price by the same amount
The fixed cost raises MC at every unit
PM7-MCMP-R-032.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change lowers profit but does not alter the marginal decision when demand is unchanged.

PM7-MCMP-R-033.q: An ad tells buyers the product price and where to buy it. Why is this informational rather than persuasive?
options: It supplies facts that reduce search costs
It guarantees buyers will prefer the brand
It changes the product’s physical quality
It prevents consumers from switching brands
PM7-MCMP-R-033.feedback: Informational advertising communicates useful facts instead of mainly trying to reshape preferences.

PM7-MCMP-R-034.q: After a successful campaign, buyers purchase more at every possible price. Is this a movement along the firm’s demand curve?
options: Yes, because advertising changes the posted price
No, it is a leftward shift of supply
No, it is a rightward shift of demand
PM7-MCMP-R-034.feedback: More demanded at every price is a demand shift. A movement along demand requires a change in the firm’s own price.

PM7-MCMP-R-047.q: A monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit in long-run equilibrium. Does that prove the outcome is fully efficient?
options: Yes. Entry forces price to equal MC and minimum ATC
No. Zero economic profit means the firm should shut down
No. Price can still exceed MC and output can remain below the minimum-ATC quantity
Yes. Zero economic profit guarantees both allocative and productive efficiency
PM7-MCMP-R-047.feedback: Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.

P62H-MCMP-BR-006.q: Which long-run result occurs in both models?

P62H-MCMP-BR-007.q: Why does monopolistic competition retain a markup unlike perfect competition?

P62H-MCMP-BR-008.q: Which model achieves productive efficiency in its standard long-run equilibrium?

P62H-MCMP-BR-009.q: What decision rule is shared by monopoly and monopolistic competition?

P62H-MCMP-BR-010.q: Why is entry more important in monopolistic competition than monopoly?

P62H-MCMP-BR-010.feedback: Relatively easy entry is a defining difference.

P62H-MCMP-BR-011.q: Which structure generally has more close substitutes for each firm’s product?
options: The answer depends only on fixed cost
P62H-MCMP-BR-011.feedback: Many differentiated rivals supply close alternatives.

P62H-MCMP-BR-012.q: Which model can sustain long-run economic profit because barriers block entry?
P62H-MCMP-BR-012.feedback: Entry erodes profit in monopolistic competition.
