P62H-MCMP-BR-015.q: Why can differentiation create consumer value?
options: It offers varieties better matched to heterogeneous preferences
It forces every buyer to pay the same willingness to pay
P62H-MCMP-BR-015.feedback: Different buyers may prefer different attributes.

P62H-MCMP-BR-016.q: A brand changes perceived value without changing physical quality. Which concept is central?
P62H-MCMP-BR-016.feedback: Consumer perceptions can shape demand for a variety.

P62H-MCMP-BR-017.q: Why can markup create lost trades?
options: Every unit becomes a fixed cost
Some units valued above MC are not sold because price exceeds MC
P62H-MCMP-BR-017.feedback: P>MC can exclude mutually beneficial units.

P62H-MCMP-BR-018.q: How can informational advertising improve market performance?
P62H-MCMP-BR-018.feedback: Useful information helps buyers compare alternatives.

P62H-MCMP-BR-019.q: What separates monopolistic competition from oligopoly?
options: Many firms act without central strategic interdependence in the basic model
P62H-MCMP-BR-019.feedback: Strategic few-firm interaction belongs to oligopoly.

P62H-MCMP-BR-020.q: Why can successful product development create temporary economic profit?
options: It makes MC equal price forever
It shifts demand before imitation and entry erode the advantage
It sets accounting profit to zero immediately

PM7-MCMP-BR-012.q: Cost analysis tells a differentiated firm its MC curve. Which additional curve is needed to apply the usual profit-maximizing output rule?
PM7-MCMP-BR-012.feedback: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses output where MR equals MC, subject to the usual marginal condition.

PM7-MCMP-BR-013.q: The shutdown rule from cost analysis carries directly into monopolistic competition. Which comparison determines whether the firm should produce in the short run?
options: Price compared with AVC at the chosen output
Price compared with AFC at the chosen output
Total revenue compared only with fixed cost
PM7-MCMP-BR-013.feedback: A firm should produce in the short run when price covers average variable cost at its profit-maximizing output.

PM7-MCMP-BR-014.q: A firm has already selected output where MR=MC. Which comparison now determines whether it earns profit or loss?
PM7-MCMP-BR-014.feedback: At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.

PM7-MCMP-BR-035.q: Elasticity analysis helps explain branding. If brand loyalty reduces the absolute value of price elasticity of demand, buyers become:
options: Perfectly responsive at one market price
Less responsive to the firm’s price
More responsive to the firm’s price
PM7-MCMP-BR-035.feedback: Lower absolute elasticity means quantity demanded changes less for a given percentage price change.

PM7-MCMP-BR-036.q: Cost analysis helps separate two advertising cases. Which selling expense acts most like variable cost?
options: A fee charged on each unit sold
PM7-MCMP-BR-036.feedback: A per-unit fee varies with output and therefore enters variable and marginal cost.

PM7-MCMP-BR-037.q: A successful new product feature creates short-run profit in a market with easy entry. What long-run force can erode that profit?

Automatic shutdown of the innovating firm
A requirement that demand become perfectly inelastic
PM7-MCMP-BR-037.feedback: With relatively easy entry and close substitutes, successful differentiation can attract rivals and imitation over time.

P62I-OLI-E-001.q: Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition?
options: Firms must account for likely rival responses
Firms can enter and exit the market freely.
Each firm is a price taker
P62I-OLI-E-001.feedback: Strategic interdependence is the defining behavioral feature of oligopoly.

P62I-OLI-E-002.feedback: Duopoly is the two-firm special case of oligopoly.

P62I-OLI-E-003.q: Products in an oligopoly may be:
P62I-OLI-E-003.feedback: Oligopoly describes market structure, not a single product type.

P62I-OLI-E-004.q: Why do barriers to entry matter in oligopoly?
options: They make incumbent firms price takers.
They help a few incumbent firms retain large market shares

P62I-OLI-E-005.q: A four-firm concentration ratio is calculated by:
options: Adding the market shares of the four largest firms
The sum of squared shares for every firm and competitive fringe participant
P62I-OLI-E-005.feedback: A concentration ratio sums selected leading shares.

options: Adding the four largest shares only
Dividing market demand by firm count
P62I-OLI-E-006.feedback: HHI weights larger firms more heavily through squaring.

P62I-OLI-E-007.q: Why does market definition matter when measuring concentration?
options: It fixes the number of firms that must be included at four.
It determines the legal price ceiling
Changing product or geographic boundaries changes which firms and sales are included
P62I-OLI-E-007.feedback: Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.

P62I-OLI-E-008.q: In game theory, a strategy is:
options: The payoff received by every player
The payoff a player receives after all firms choose.
A possible action or plan available to a player
P62I-OLI-E-008.feedback: Strategies are the choices available to players.

P62I-OLI-E-009.q: In a payoff pair written (8, 5), the first number usually belongs to:
P62I-OLI-E-009.feedback: The standard stated order is row player first, column player second.

options: The strategy that maximizes the firms’ combined payoff.
The strategy producing the highest payoff given the rival’s action
The strategy with the lowest fixed cost
P62I-OLI-E-010.feedback: A best response is conditional on what the other player does.

P62I-OLI-E-011.q: A dominant strategy is one that:
options: The action associated with the highest payoff in one isolated cell only
Always gives both firms equal payoffs
Produces a higher payoff than the player’s alternatives for every rival action
P62I-OLI-E-011.feedback: Dominance is a comparison across every possible rival action.

options: The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
Each player is choosing a best response to the other
P62I-OLI-E-012.feedback: No player can improve by changing alone.

P62I-OLI-E-013.q: Why can a Nash equilibrium be inefficient?
options: Mutual best responses need not maximize joint payoff
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
P62I-OLI-E-013.feedback: Individual incentives can lead to a jointly inferior outcome.

P62I-OLI-E-014.q: A prisoner’s dilemma describes a situation in which:
options: Individually attractive choices can make all players worse off
The jointly best outcome is always a Nash equilibrium.
P62I-OLI-E-014.feedback: The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.

options: Independently choose the same price after a common cost shock.
A group of firms that happen to charge similar prices without coordinating.
A group of firms coordinating output or price
P62I-OLI-E-016.feedback: A cartel attempts to act collectively like a monopoly.

P62I-OLI-E-017.q: A profit-maximizing cartel chooses total output where:
options: Industry marginal revenue equals industry marginal cost
Market price equals industry marginal cost.
P62I-OLI-E-017.feedback: The cartel uses the monopoly marginal rule for joint output.

P62I-OLI-E-018.q: Why does a cartel member often want to cheat?
options: Selling extra output at the cartel price can raise its own profit
Cheating guarantees that other members keep cooperating forever.
P62I-OLI-E-018.feedback: Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.

P62I-OLI-E-019.q: Which factor makes cartel cheating harder?
options: Reliable monitoring of member prices and output
A shorter expected relationship among cartel members.
P62I-OLI-E-019.feedback: Monitoring increases the chance that cheating is detected.

P62I-OLI-E-020.q: Repeated interaction may support cooperation because:
options: Future punishment guarantees cooperation regardless of observability or credibility
Current cheating can trigger costly future punishment
P62I-OLI-E-020.feedback: Future consequences can change current incentives.

options: Carrying it out remains in the threatening firm’s interest later
It would hurt only the rival
The announced response is credible because it sounds severe and harms the entrant

P62I-OLI-E-022.q: A price war is most likely to:
options: Guarantee higher profit for every firm
Reduce margins for several rival firms
P62I-OLI-E-022.feedback: Aggressive price cutting can damage all firms’ profits.

P62I-OLI-E-023.q: Tacit coordination differs from explicit collusion because tacit coordination:
options: Occurs only when every firm charges exactly the same price.
Can occur without an explicit agreement
P62I-OLI-E-023.feedback: Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.

options: The largest firm has legal authority to set every rival’s price.
Other firms follow a price announced by a leading firm
P62I-OLI-E-024.feedback: Following can occur without formal control.

options: Coordinating output quotas with rival firms.
P62I-OLI-E-025.feedback: Oligopolists often compete on several dimensions.

options: Setting the monopoly price after entry occurs.
Keeping price low partly to discourage entry
P62I-OLI-E-026.feedback: The incumbent may sacrifice current profit to affect entry.

P62I-OLI-E-027.q: What does the kinked-demand model primarily attempt to explain?
options: How firms determine the original market price.
Price rigidity around an existing price
P62I-OLI-E-027.feedback: The model explains rigidity, not the initial price.

P62I-OLI-E-028.q: Compared with competition, an effective cartel typically produces:
options: More output at a lower price
The same output at minimum ATC
Less output at a higher price
P62I-OLI-E-028.feedback: A successful cartel mimics monopoly restriction.

P62I-OLI-E-029.q: Why is high concentration not enough by itself to prove harmful conduct?
options: Entry conditions, efficiencies, imports, and actual behavior also matter
A high HHI guarantees high economic profit.
P62I-OLI-E-029.feedback: Concentration is evidence, not a complete conclusion.

P62I-OLI-E-030.q: Which statement best captures oligopoly outcomes?
options: They always reproduce the monopoly outcome.
They can range from intense rivalry to substantial coordination
They are determined only by firm count
P62I-OLI-E-030.feedback: Rules, payoffs, timing, and repetition shape outcomes.

PM8-OLI-E-001.q: Why does an oligopoly firm pay unusually close attention to a rival’s likely response before changing price?
options: Because a few large rivals can materially change the payoff from the firm’s decision
Because oligopoly firms are required to match every rival price change in order to remain in the market
Because oligopoly firms sell only identical products
Because market demand is perfectly elastic for each firm
PM8-OLI-E-001.feedback: With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.

PM8-OLI-E-002.q: Which condition most helps a few established firms remain dominant in an oligopoly?
options: Perfectly free entry by many small firms
A requirement that every product be identical
A horizontal demand curve for each individual firm
Significant barriers that make entry difficult
PM8-OLI-E-002.feedback: Entry barriers help preserve a market in which a small number of firms account for much of total sales.

PM8-OLI-E-003.q: A four-firm concentration ratio of 82% means that:
options: The four largest firms together account for 82% of market sales
Each of the four largest firms individually controls 82% of total market sales
PM8-OLI-E-003.feedback: A concentration ratio adds the market shares of the specified number of largest firms.

PM8-OLI-E-012.q: In a two-firm game, what does a payoff represent?
options: The slope of the industry demand curve
The outcome value a player receives from a particular combination of strategies
The maximum number of firms that regulators permit to enter the market under the industry’s legal rules
PM8-OLI-E-012.feedback: A payoff records how well a player does under a particular combination of actions.

PM8-OLI-E-013.q: A payoff cell is written (14, 9), with Row’s payoff listed first. What is Column’s payoff?
PM8-OLI-E-013.feedback: With payoff order (Row, Column), the second number belongs to Column.

PM8-OLI-E-014.q: A best response is the action that:
options: Maximizes the two firms’ combined payoff regardless of incentives
Is chosen by every rival in the market
Always remains best no matter what the rival does
Gives a player the highest payoff given the rival’s chosen action
PM8-OLI-E-014.feedback: A best response is conditional on what the other player does; it need not be a dominant strategy.

PM8-OLI-E-015.q: Which statement describes a Nash equilibrium?
options: Both players must have dominant strategies
Each player is choosing a best response to the other player’s action
The two players necessarily choose the outcome that maximizes their combined payoff even if one could gain by deviating alone
PM8-OLI-E-015.feedback: At a Nash equilibrium, neither player can improve by changing action alone while the other action stays fixed.

PM8-OLI-E-029.q: A cartel that successfully coordinates output tries to behave most like:
options: A single profit-maximizing monopolist for the industry
A group of independent price-taking firms
A perfectly contestable market with free entry
A regulator that sets the market price equal to marginal cost and assigns output to each participating firm
PM8-OLI-E-029.feedback: A successful cartel restricts joint output and chooses the industry outcome that maximizes combined profit.

PM8-OLI-E-030.q: Why can a cartel agreement be unstable even when all members gain from the agreement?
options: Every member must legally charge a different price
Cartels require marginal cost to equal zero
Joint profit is always lower under collusion than under competition because restricting output reduces total sales
An individual member may gain by secretly expanding sales while others keep output restricted
PM8-OLI-E-030.feedback: The group can prefer restriction while each member has a private incentive to capture extra sales.

PM8-OLI-E-031.q: What does monitoring do for a cartel?
options: It makes each firm a price taker
It eliminates the need to restrict output
It helps members detect whether other members are cheating on the agreement
It guarantees that barriers to entry disappear once all cartel members can observe one another’s sales
PM8-OLI-E-031.feedback: Monitoring makes hidden deviations easier to discover and therefore easier to punish.

PM8-OLI-E-032.q: In a one-shot prisoner’s-dilemma-style pricing game, why might both firms cut price even though both would prefer that neither cut?
options: Both firms face perfectly inelastic demand
Each firm has an individual incentive to cut given the rival’s possible action
The firms are maximizing total industry profit because the individually attractive price cut also maximizes their joint payoff
PM8-OLI-E-032.feedback: Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.

PM8-OLI-E-042.q: Why can the expectation of future competition sometimes make cooperation easier to sustain?
options: Future interaction makes current payoffs irrelevant
Repeated games eliminate every incentive to cheat
Firms become price takers when they meet repeatedly
A firm that cheats today may lose future cooperative gains
PM8-OLI-E-042.feedback: When future interaction matters, the short-run gain from cheating can be weighed against future losses after retaliation.

PM8-OLI-E-043.q: What makes a strategic threat credible?
options: The threat would be costly to both firms
Carrying it out would be in the threatening firm’s interest if the situation actually occurred
The threat sounds severe to the rival
PM8-OLI-E-043.feedback: Credibility depends on whether the threatened response would actually be rational when the time comes to act.

PM8-OLI-E-053.q: Compared with a competitive outcome, an effective cartel usually chooses:
options: Lower output and a higher price
Higher output and a lower price
The same output with zero profit
Price equal to minimum average total cost
PM8-OLI-E-053.feedback: A cartel acts like a joint monopolist, restricting output to raise price and combined profit.

PM8-OLI-E-054.q: Why is a high HHI not enough by itself to prove consumers are being harmed?
options: A high HHI guarantees prices equal marginal cost
HHI is unrelated to market shares
Concentration measures structure, while welfare also depends on conduct, entry conditions, efficiencies, and rivalry
PM8-OLI-E-054.feedback: Concentration is evidence about market structure, not a complete welfare verdict.

PM8-OLI-E-055.q: If two firms merge and all other market shares remain unchanged, what happens to market concentration?
options: It cannot change unless market demand shifts
It becomes zero if the merged firm cuts price
It generally increases because two separate shares become one larger share
It must fall because there is one fewer firm
PM8-OLI-E-055.feedback: Combining shares raises concentration measures such as HHI, all else equal.

PM8-OLI-E-056.q: A concentrated industry charges high markups but also spends heavily on research. What is the soundest conclusion?
options: There may be a tradeoff between market-power costs and innovation benefits that requires evidence
High research spending proves the market is efficient
High markups prove innovation has no value
PM8-OLI-E-056.feedback: Oligopoly welfare can involve competing effects rather than a one-variable verdict.

PM8-OLI-E-057.q: What is the basic economic concern behind antitrust scrutiny of collusion?
options: Coordinated restriction of competition can raise price and reduce output below competitive levels
Collusion makes every firm a price taker
PM8-OLI-E-057.feedback: The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss.

PM8-OLI-E-058.q: Why should an economist be cautious about predicting one outcome for every oligopoly market?
options: Every oligopoly has the same payoff matrix
Oligopoly theory assumes firms never respond to rivals
Market concentration fully determines every price
Different numbers of firms, products, information, costs, and strategic settings can produce different behavior
PM8-OLI-E-058.feedback: Oligopoly is a strategic family of models, not a guarantee that every few-firm market behaves identically.

PM8-OLI-E-059.q: Which statement best summarizes why oligopoly welfare analysis can be complicated?
options: Only the number of firms matters for welfare
Oligopoly always produces the monopoly outcome
Few firms may create market power, but rivalry, innovation, efficiencies, and entry conditions also matter
Any market with four firms is automatically inefficient
PM8-OLI-E-059.feedback: A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses.

P62I-OLI-M-001.q: Four firms have market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, and 10%, with the remaining firms holding 10%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
P62I-OLI-M-001.feedback: Add the shares of the four largest firms.

P62I-OLI-M-002.q: A market has shares of 50%, 25%, 15%, and 10%. Which measure gives especially heavy weight to the 50% firm?
P62I-OLI-M-002.feedback: Squaring shares makes a very large firm count disproportionately.

P62I-OLI-M-003.q: A merger combines firms with 20% and 15% market shares. By how much does the HHI rise if all other shares stay unchanged?

P62I-OLI-M-004.q: A national market appears unconcentrated, but each rural town has only two local suppliers. What is the main lesson?
options: Geographic market definition can conceal local concentration
National concentration always measures local competition accurately.
P62I-OLI-M-004.feedback: The relevant geographic market can be narrower than the national market.

P62I-OLI-M-005.q: Two airlines choose whether to cut fares. Each earns more from cutting when the rival holds fares, but both earn less when both cut. This structure is closest to:
P62I-OLI-M-005.feedback: Each airline has an individual incentive that can trigger a jointly harmful price war.

P62I-OLI-M-006.q: Row’s payoff is higher with strategy B whether Column chooses X or Y. What does Row have?
P62I-OLI-M-006.feedback: B beats Row’s alternative under both Column actions.

P62I-OLI-M-007.q: A cell is a Nash equilibrium when:
options: Neither firm can improve by changing strategy alone
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
Both firms chose the same letter
P62I-OLI-M-007.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses.

P62I-OLI-M-008.q: A game has two outcomes in which both players are best responding. What does the game have?
options: Two dominant strategies for each player

P62I-OLI-M-009.q: A firm observes that its rival will respond aggressively to any price cut. This expectation most directly illustrates:
options: A dominant strategy that is best regardless of the rival’s action.
P62I-OLI-M-009.feedback: The firm’s best action depends on the expected response.

P62I-OLI-M-010.q: Two firms agree to restrict output, but one secretly offers rebates. The rebate is best described as:
P62I-OLI-M-010.feedback: Secret discounts undermine the coordinated price.

P62I-OLI-M-011.q: A cartel’s market demand is P = 100 − 2Q and MC is $20. What total quantity maximizes joint profit?

P62I-OLI-M-012.q: Using P = 100 − 2Q and cartel output Q = 20, what price does the cartel charge?

P62I-OLI-M-013.q: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive a larger production quota?
options: It has the largest historical market share.
It can produce part of joint output at lower cost
P62I-OLI-M-013.feedback: Efficient allocation places more output with lower-cost producers.

P62I-OLI-M-014.q: A punishment strategy requires a rival to start a costly price war after cheating. When is the threat credible?
options: The announced response is credible because it sounds severe and harms the entrant
Whenever the price war hurts the cheater
When starting the price war is still the rival’s best response after cheating occurs
P62I-OLI-M-014.feedback: A threat must be rational when its decision node is reached.

P62I-OLI-M-015.q: Firms expect to compete for only one final period. Why is cooperation harder to sustain?
options: Future punishment has little or no value
Future punishment guarantees cooperation regardless of observability or credibility
P62I-OLI-M-015.feedback: A short horizon weakens the future cost of cheating.

P62I-OLI-M-016.q: A market’s largest firm announces a price, and rivals independently match it. This is:
P62I-OLI-M-016.feedback: A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.

P62I-OLI-M-017.q: Several firms raise prices after a common input cost increase. Why does this not by itself prove collusion?
options: Parallel price changes are conclusive evidence of an explicit agreement.
Input costs affect only fixed cost
Independent firms may respond similarly to the same cost shock
Parallel prices always maximize total surplus
P62I-OLI-M-017.feedback: Common conditions can produce parallel conduct without agreement.

P62I-OLI-M-018.q: An incumbent builds capacity that would be useful even if entry occurs. Why can this deter entry?
options: It turns the market into perfect competition
The capacity can make an aggressive post-entry response credible
P62I-OLI-M-018.feedback: A sunk commitment can alter the incumbent’s later incentives.

P62I-OLI-M-019.q: An incumbent threatens to cut price below variable cost after entry, but doing so would be very costly and temporary. The threat is likely:
P62I-OLI-M-019.feedback: The incumbent may not rationally carry out the threat later.

P62I-OLI-M-020.q: A firm maintains a lower price today to reduce expected entrant profit. What is the strategic cost?
options: It raises current monopoly profit automatically
P62I-OLI-M-020.feedback: Limit pricing trades current profit for possible entry deterrence.

P62I-OLI-M-021.q: In the kinked-demand model, rivals are assumed to match:
options: Price cuts more readily than price increases

P62I-OLI-M-022.q: If MC changes within the discontinuity in the kinked-demand MR curve, the model predicts:
options: Price and output may remain unchanged
P62I-OLI-M-022.feedback: The same output can remain optimal while MC crosses the MR gap.

P62I-OLI-M-023.q: An effective cartel raises price and reduces output. Which part of lost consumer surplus is not transferred to producers?
P62I-OLI-M-023.feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades create DWL.

P62I-OLI-M-024.q: A merger raises HHI but also creates verified large cost savings. What is the sound conclusion?
options: Both increased market power and efficiencies must be evaluated
P62I-OLI-M-024.feedback: Concentration and efficiency evidence both matter.

P62I-OLI-M-025.q: A merger lowers marginal cost, but the merged firm keeps price high because rivalry weakens. What does this show?
options: Cost savings need not be passed fully to consumers

P62I-OLI-M-026.q: Why can foreign competition affect a domestic concentration assessment?
options: Imports are excluded from every market definition
Imports may provide substitutes that constrain domestic firms
P62I-OLI-M-026.feedback: Relevant competitors may include foreign suppliers.

P62I-OLI-M-027.q: A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price. This is:
P62I-OLI-M-027.feedback: Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions.

P62I-OLI-M-028.q: Heavy advertising builds brand loyalty and reduces switching. What strategic effect is most plausible?
options: Every firm becomes a price taker
Price competition may soften because firm demand becomes less elastic
P62I-OLI-M-028.feedback: Loyalty can reduce substitution among brands.

P62I-OLI-M-029.q: A market has six firms, but two control 78% of sales and rivals closely watch one another. Which structure is most plausible?
P62I-OLI-M-029.feedback: Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly.

P62I-OLI-M-030.q: Why can game theory yield different predictions across oligopoly markets?
options: Every oligopoly has one dominant strategy
Payoffs, information, timing, and repetition differ

PM8-OLI-M-004.q: A grocery chain has only 8% of national grocery sales but 55% of sales in one isolated county. What does this example show about concentration measures?
options: They measure profit rather than market share
They depend on how the relevant market is defined
They are valid only for national markets
They ignore geographic differences and therefore always produce the same concentration result nationwide
PM8-OLI-M-004.feedback: The same firm can appear small or dominant depending on the economically relevant geographic and product market.

PM8-OLI-M-005.q: Two markets each have a four-firm concentration ratio of 80%. In Market A the four firms have nearly equal shares; in Market B one firm is much larger than the other three. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Market B can have a higher HHI because HHI gives more weight to large shares
Both markets must have the same HHI because an equal CR4 guarantees identical concentration among the leading firms
Market A must have the higher HHI because equal shares are squared
HHI cannot distinguish markets with the same CR4
PM8-OLI-M-005.feedback: Squaring market shares makes HHI more sensitive to a very large firm even when CR4 is unchanged.

PM8-OLI-M-006.q: Three national wireless carriers dominate a market. Before one carrier cuts price, its managers estimate how the other two are likely to respond. Which feature of oligopoly is being illustrated?
PM8-OLI-M-006.feedback: The payoff from one firm’s choice depends partly on how a small number of major rivals react.

PM8-OLI-M-007.q: An industry’s HHI rises after two sizable firms merge. What can the HHI increase tell an analyst directly?
options: The merged firm must now be a monopolist because any increase in HHI implies complete control of the market
Market concentration increased under the chosen market definition
PM8-OLI-M-007.feedback: HHI measures concentration; welfare and policy conclusions require additional evidence about competition and efficiencies.

PM8-OLI-M-016.q: Suppose Firm B chooses a high price. Firm A earns $8 million with a high price and $11 million with a low price. What is Firm A’s best response to B’s high price?
options: Choose whichever action maximizes joint industry profit
PM8-OLI-M-016.feedback: Conditional on B choosing high, A compares its own payoffs and chooses the action paying 11 rather than 8.

PM8-OLI-M-017.q: Firm A earns more from advertising whether Firm B advertises or not. What follows?
options: Advertising is a dominant strategy for Firm A
Advertising must maximize the two firms’ combined profit whenever it is more profitable for Firm A than not advertising
The game has no Nash equilibrium
PM8-OLI-M-017.feedback: A dominant strategy gives the player a higher payoff for every action the rival might take.

PM8-OLI-M-018.q: A strategy is Firm A’s best response when B chooses X, but A prefers a different strategy when B chooses Y. What can be concluded?
options: The first strategy is dominant because it is best once
The joint-payoff maximum must be a Nash equilibrium
The first strategy is not dominant for A
PM8-OLI-M-018.feedback: Dominance requires the same strategy to be best against every rival action.

PM8-OLI-M-019.q: At a proposed outcome, Firm A could gain by changing its action while Firm B kept its action fixed. What does that imply?
options: Firm A has a dominant strategy
The game has no strategic interdependence
The proposed outcome is not a Nash equilibrium
The proposed outcome must maximize joint profit
PM8-OLI-M-019.feedback: A unilateral profitable deviation means at least one player is not best responding, so the cell is not Nash.

PM8-OLI-M-020.q: Two firms could earn $20 million each by coordinating, but the Nash equilibrium gives each $14 million. What does this illustrate?
options: Dominant strategies always produce the joint-payoff maximum
A Nash equilibrium need not maximize combined payoff
PM8-OLI-M-020.feedback: Mutual best responses can lead to a stable outcome with lower total payoff than a cooperative alternative.

PM8-OLI-M-021.q: In payoff order (Row, Column), the cell for Row choosing A and Column choosing Y is (6, 15). Which comparison is relevant when finding Row’s best response to Y?
options: Compare Row’s first-number payoffs across Row’s available actions in column Y
Compare Column’s second-number payoffs across every column, regardless of which action Column has already chosen
Add both payoffs in every cell and choose the largest sum
PM8-OLI-M-021.feedback: A best-response calculation holds the rival action fixed and compares the player’s own payoff across its alternatives.

PM8-OLI-M-022.q: Why can firms end up at an outcome they both consider worse than another available outcome?
options: Firms are required to choose the outcome with the lowest combined payoff whenever their interests conflict
A Nash equilibrium always minimizes profit
Individual incentives to deviate can make the better joint outcome unstable
PM8-OLI-M-022.feedback: A jointly attractive cell need not survive if one player can gain by deviating while the rival cooperates.

PM8-OLI-M-033.q: A cartel has already chosen its joint-profit-maximizing total output. Why might it assign more production to a member with lower marginal cost?
options: Shifting output toward the lower-cost producer can reduce the cartel’s total production cost
Equal quotas always maximize joint profit
Higher-cost firms must produce more to preserve competition
Output allocation cannot affect cartel profit once total output is fixed, even when members have different marginal costs
PM8-OLI-M-033.feedback: For a fixed cartel total, allocating more production to lower-marginal-cost members can raise combined profit.

PM8-OLI-M-034.q: Three firms agree to keep prices high. One firm quietly gives large rebates while publicly posting the agreed price. Economically, the rebates are best interpreted as:
options: Proof that the cartel has eliminated all competition because no member can gain market share without openly cutting the posted price
A required form of price leadership
Cheating that captures extra sales while rivals maintain the collusive price
PM8-OLI-M-034.feedback: Secret rebates undermine the agreement by letting one member expand sales at the others’ expense.

PM8-OLI-M-035.q: Which market condition makes a cartel harder to sustain?
options: A small number of firms with similar objectives
A credible punishment system that quickly detects and penalizes members who secretly exceed their agreed output
Many opportunities for members to make secret sales that rivals cannot observe
Frequent transparent reporting of member sales
PM8-OLI-M-035.feedback: When cheating is hard to observe, deviations are easier and enforcement becomes weaker.

PM8-OLI-M-036.q: A cartel restricts total output below the competitive level. What is the intended effect on the market price?
options: Create a perfectly elastic industry demand curve so the cartel can sell any quantity at the higher price
Raise price by moving up the market demand curve
Force price down to marginal cost
PM8-OLI-M-036.feedback: Restricting industry output raises the price buyers are willing to pay along downward-sloping market demand.

PM8-OLI-M-037.q: Suppose cartel members can observe one another’s sales almost immediately. Why can this improve cartel stability?
options: It makes cheating easier to detect and respond to
It removes each member’s incentive to earn profit
It guarantees the cartel price equals marginal cost
It causes market concentration to fall
PM8-OLI-M-037.feedback: Fast observability reduces the chance that a member can profit from hidden deviations for long.

PM8-OLI-M-060.q: Two firms with market shares of 18% and 12% merge. Holding all other shares fixed, why does HHI rise?
options: The merger automatically removes all smaller rivals
The squared share of the combined 30% firm exceeds the sum of the two firms’ separate squared shares
HHI counts the merged firm twice
Every merger doubles total market sales
PM8-OLI-M-060.feedback: Because shares are squared, combining two positive shares increases HHI by the cross term 2ab.

PM8-OLI-H-039.q: An effective cartel raises price from $30 to $42 and reduces quantity sold. Which statement best separates redistribution from efficiency loss?

Every dollar of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss
PM8-OLI-H-039.feedback: A higher price transfers some surplus, but the output restriction also destroys gains from mutually beneficial trades.

PM8-OLI-H-046.q: Several airlines raise fares within hours of the same publicly observed jet-fuel cost increase. Which conclusion is strongest?

Parallel pricing alone does not establish collusion because a common cost shock can produce similar independent responses
PM8-OLI-H-046.feedback: Similar prices can arise from common incentives or observation of rivals; parallel behavior by itself is not proof of an agreement.

PM8-OLI-H-047.q: A dominant firm posts a new price, and several rivals independently match it without an explicit agreement. What best describes the pattern?

A prisoner’s dilemma requiring both firms to cut price
PM8-OLI-H-047.feedback: Following a recognized price leader can coordinate market behavior, but observation alone does not prove an explicit agreement.

PM8-OLI-H-048.q: Two oligopoly firms avoid matching price cuts and instead compete through warranties, loyalty programs, and product quality. Why might this strategy be attractive?

It guarantees marginal cost will fall

The firm becomes a price taker
The demand curve becomes perfectly elastic
PM8-OLI-H-049.feedback: The MR discontinuity is used to explain why a range of marginal-cost changes may leave the chosen price unchanged.

The merger must increase deadweight loss by exactly the HHI change

PM8-OLI-H-068.feedback: The same structural fact can have different welfare implications depending on switching, multi-homing, and rival expansion.

Only the number of firms can affect oligopoly behavior
PM8-OLI-H-069.feedback: Concentration is informative but does not summarize product differentiation, innovation, information, costs, or strategic conduct.

PM8-OLI-H-070.feedback: Oligopoly welfare requires integrating several margins rather than treating one statistic as decisive.

No, market power, entry, and efficiencies still require analysis
P62I-OLI-R-020.feedback: Concentration is one part of merger analysis.

PM8-OLI-R-008.q: A student says a four-firm concentration ratio squares each firm’s market share. What is the correction?
options: The four-firm ratio averages all firms’ squared shares
The four-firm ratio simply adds the shares of the four largest firms
The four-firm ratio multiplies the market shares of the four largest firms and then converts the product to a percentage
The four-firm ratio subtracts fringe shares from 100
PM8-OLI-R-008.feedback: Squaring shares is part of HHI, not the four-firm concentration ratio.

PM8-OLI-R-009.q: A student describes oligopoly as “a market where each firm can safely ignore rivals.” What is the key error?
options: Oligopoly decisions are strategically interdependent because major rivals can respond
Oligopoly always has exactly two firms, so any market with three or more important firms belongs to another structure
Oligopoly firms are all price takers
PM8-OLI-R-009.feedback: The defining strategic feature is that a few important firms must account for likely rival reactions.

PM8-OLI-R-040.q: A student says “if both firms would be better off cooperating, they will automatically cooperate.” What is missing?
options: Prisoner’s-dilemma incentives exist only in monopoly
Each firm’s unilateral incentive must also be checked; the cooperative outcome can be unstable
Joint payoff is irrelevant in oligopoly
Cooperation requires the firms to have identical costs
PM8-OLI-R-040.feedback: A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.

PM8-OLI-R-041.q: A student calls any concentrated industry a cartel. What is the correction?
options: A cartel requires coordination among firms to restrict competition; concentration alone does not establish that
A cartel is simply any market with fewer than ten firms
A cartel exists whenever HHI is high
A cartel means one firm owns the entire market
PM8-OLI-R-041.feedback: Market structure and collusive conduct are different concepts; a concentrated market need not be a cartel.

PM8-OLI-R-051.q: A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical. What is the key distinction?
options: Explicit collusion means firms ignore rivals
Only tacit coordination can affect price
Tacit coordination can emerge without an explicit agreement among firms
Tacit coordination always requires a written contract
PM8-OLI-R-051.feedback: Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.

PM8-OLI-R-071.q: A student says “high concentration proves firms are colluding.” What is the correction?
options: Collusion is impossible in concentrated markets
Concentration measures directly record secret agreements
High concentration can make strategic interaction important, but it does not by itself prove an agreement or harmful conduct
High concentration means every firm charges marginal cost
PM8-OLI-R-071.feedback: Structure can affect incentives, but conduct and welfare conclusions require additional evidence.

PM8-OLI-R-072.q: A student treats every dollar of consumer-surplus loss from a cartel as deadweight loss. What should the student separate?
options: Surplus transferred to producers from surplus destroyed by trades that no longer occur
PM8-OLI-R-072.feedback: A cartel can redistribute surplus and destroy surplus; only the destroyed gains from trade are deadweight loss.

PM8-OLI-R-073.q: A student says a higher post-merger HHI proves the merger harms consumers. What is the better statement?
options: A higher HHI shows greater concentration, but consumer effects also depend on rivalry, entry, efficiencies, and pass-through
HHI directly measures the change in consumer surplus
Any HHI increase means the merged firm becomes a monopolist
HHI is unrelated to merger analysis
PM8-OLI-R-073.feedback: Concentration is an input to analysis, not a complete welfare conclusion.

PM8-OLI-R-074.q: A student argues that high research spending proves a concentrated market is socially optimal. What is missing?
options: Innovation matters only in perfect competition
High research spending eliminates market power
Innovation benefits must be weighed against possible higher prices, weaker rivalry, and other welfare effects
PM8-OLI-R-074.feedback: Innovation can be beneficial without settling the overall welfare comparison.

PM8-OLI-R-075.q: A student sees several firms charge the same price and immediately labels the behavior collusion. What is the key correction?
options: Price equality proves the firms have equal market shares
Collusion can occur only when prices differ
Similar prices can arise independently from common costs or market conditions, so evidence of coordination is still needed
Identical prices are impossible without a cartel
PM8-OLI-R-075.feedback: Parallel conduct is not automatically evidence of an agreement because firms can respond similarly to the same public conditions.

P62I-OLI-BR-001.q: A fully effective cartel most closely imitates which market structure?
P62I-OLI-BR-001.feedback: A cartel restricts joint output like a monopolist.

P62I-OLI-BR-002.q: How does cartel price compare with the competitive benchmark?
options: It is typically higher because joint output is restricted

P62I-OLI-BR-003.q: Which monopoly rule does a cartel use for total output?
P62I-OLI-BR-003.feedback: Joint output follows monopoly marginal analysis.

P62I-OLI-BR-004.q: What prevents an oligopoly from automatically behaving like one monopolist?
options: Member incentives and rival strategic responses
P62I-OLI-BR-004.feedback: Independent firms may not sustain the joint outcome.

P62I-OLI-BR-005.q: What distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition most sharply?
options: Strategic interdependence among a few major firms
P62I-OLI-BR-005.feedback: Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive.

P62I-OLI-BR-006.q: Why can advertising matter in both structures?
options: It makes every firm a price taker
It can differentiate products and alter substitution
P62I-OLI-BR-006.feedback: Advertising can shape demand in both markets.

P62I-OLI-BR-007.q: Which behavior belongs to oligopoly rather than the basic monopolistic-competition model?
options: Choosing an action after anticipating a specific rival’s response
P62I-OLI-BR-007.feedback: The basic monopolistic-competition model abstracts from strategic interdependence.

P62I-OLI-BR-008.q: Compared with perfect competition, oligopolistic firms are more likely to:
options: Recognize that their own actions affect rivals and market outcomes
Have free entry eliminate market power
P62I-OLI-BR-008.feedback: Oligopolists possess market power and strategic influence.

P62I-OLI-BR-009.q: What competitive benchmark is commonly used to evaluate a cartel?
options: Price equals marginal cost at the efficient output
P62I-OLI-BR-009.feedback: The competitive benchmark helps identify output restriction and DWL.

P62I-OLI-BR-010.q: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive more output?
options: It has the highest fixed cost
It faces the least elastic demand
It is always the largest firm
Allocating production toward lower MC reduces joint cost
P62I-OLI-BR-010.feedback: Joint cost minimization matters for cartel allocation.

P62I-OLI-BR-011.q: How can excess capacity serve as a commitment?
options: Installed capacity can make a large post-entry output response more credible
P62I-OLI-BR-011.feedback: A sunk capacity choice can alter later incentives.

P62I-OLI-BR-012.q: Why does product differentiation sometimes soften price competition?
options: More loyal buyers make firm demand less elastic

P62I-OLI-BR-013.q: Why might a cartel be harder to sustain when close substitutes exist outside it?
options: Consumers can switch away from the cartel after price increases
Mutually beneficial units between cartel and competitive output are not produced

P62I-OLI-BR-015.q: A cartel price increase transfers some surplus from:
P62I-OLI-BR-015.feedback: Higher price transfers part of consumer surplus to producers.

P62I-OLI-BR-016.q: Which basic incentive concept explains cartel cheating?
options: A member compares its private marginal gain with expected punishment
P62I-OLI-BR-016.feedback: Private incentives can undermine collective agreements.

P62I-OLI-BR-017.q: How do network effects affect oligopoly?
options: They can strengthen incumbent advantages and concentration
P62I-OLI-BR-017.feedback: Network effects can reinforce entry barriers.

options: A concentrated structure may make coordination or unilateral market power easier
Lower costs can offset some harm if savings are real and passed through
Cost savings prove no market power
P62I-OLI-BR-019.feedback: Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits.

P62I-OLI-BR-020.q: How can foreign suppliers weaken a domestic cartel?
options: Imports provide alternative sources and can expand outside supply
P62I-OLI-BR-020.feedback: Outside supply can destabilize domestic coordination.

PM8-OLI-BR-010.q: A market has four dominant firms. Which feature would most strongly distinguish oligopoly from monopoly or perfect competition?
options: Assume four dominant firms automatically mean monopolistic competition because any market with multiple sellers and differentiated products fits that model
Classify the market only by whether products are identical
Treat every concentrated market as a legal monopoly
Focus on few-firm strategic interdependence rather than requiring one firm or many tiny price takers
PM8-OLI-BR-010.feedback: Oligopoly sits between monopoly and atomistic competition because a few large firms interact strategically.

PM8-OLI-BR-011.q: A student already understands market shares. What extra step turns those shares into an HHI?
options: Multiply each firm's market share by the market price and add the resulting dollar values across firms
Square each firm’s percentage share and add the squared shares
Add only the four largest shares
PM8-OLI-BR-011.feedback: HHI builds on market shares by squaring each percentage share and summing across firms.

PM8-OLI-BR-023.q: Before trying to find a Nash equilibrium in a payoff matrix, what should a student verify first?
options: Whether the market’s concentration measure is high enough to imply that strategic behavior must be present
Whether both players earn equal payoffs
Which payoff belongs to each player and which actions define the rows and columns
Which cell has the highest combined payoff
PM8-OLI-BR-023.feedback: Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium.

PM8-OLI-BR-024.q: A student keeps searching for one action that is always best, but the player’s preferred action changes with the rival’s move. What concept should the student use?
PM8-OLI-BR-024.feedback: Best responses can vary with the rival’s action even when no dominant strategy exists.

PM8-OLI-BR-025.q: A student has correctly found a player’s best response in each column. How should the student check for a dominant strategy?
options: See whether the same action is the best response in every column
Add the two players’ payoffs in each cell
Choose the action with the highest single payoff anywhere in the matrix
Look only at the rival’s payoffs
PM8-OLI-BR-025.feedback: A dominant strategy must remain the player’s best response to every rival action.

PM8-OLI-BR-026.q: After marking each player’s best responses in a matrix, what identifies a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: The cell with the largest total payoff even if someone wants to deviate
Any cell where the payoffs are equal
The first cell in which one player has a dominant strategy
A cell where both players’ best-response markings coincide
PM8-OLI-BR-026.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses in the same outcome cell.

PM8-OLI-BR-027.q: A student found the cell with the largest combined payoff and calls it the Nash equilibrium. What must still be checked?
options: Whether the firms have equal market shares
Whether the cell lies on the main diagonal
Whether each player would choose to stay there given the other player’s action
Whether the two payoffs are both positive and add to more than the payoffs in every neighboring cell
PM8-OLI-BR-027.feedback: Joint-payoff maximization and Nash stability are separate questions.

PM8-OLI-BR-028.q: How does a noncooperative game differ from an assumed cartel solution?
options: The government chooses each firm’s strategy
Each firm follows its own incentives rather than committing to maximize joint profit
The firms necessarily choose identical actions because noncooperative behavior rules out different strategies
PM8-OLI-BR-028.feedback: Noncooperative analysis asks what individually rational strategies imply without assuming binding joint-profit coordination.

PM8-OLI-BR-044.q: A student understands a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma. What new consideration enters when the firms expect to interact again?
options: Market concentration falls with each round
Today’s action can change future responses and future payoffs
The payoff matrix no longer matters at all
PM8-OLI-BR-044.feedback: Repeated interaction links current choices to future rewards or punishments, which can alter incentives.

PM8-OLI-BR-045.q: A student knows that talk alone may not deter entry. What can make an incumbent’s announced response more believable?
options: A costly action taken in advance that changes the incumbent’s future incentives
A vague promise that entry will be punished somehow
A larger concentration ratio by itself
A public statement with no change in capacity or costs
PM8-OLI-BR-045.feedback: A commitment can make future behavior credible by changing what the incumbent will find profitable after entry.

PM8-OLI-BR-052.q: A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes. What is the next step when firms compete through quality or advertising instead?
options: Ignore rivals because only prices create interdependence
Apply the same strategic logic to nonprice actions because rivals may respond there too
Assume nonprice choices have no effect on demand
Treat advertising as proof of collusion
PM8-OLI-BR-052.feedback: Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price.

costs-of-production.title: Costs of Production
costs-of-production.description: Analyze economic and accounting costs, short-run production, fixed and variable costs, marginal and average cost curves, productivity, sunk costs, long-run scale, and minimum efficient scale.

objectiveLabels.COP.1: Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
objectiveLabels.COP.2: Analyze short-run production using total, marginal, and average product.
objectiveLabels.COP.3: Calculate and interpret fixed, variable, total, average, and marginal costs.
objectiveLabels.COP.4: Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
objectiveLabels.COP.5: Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
objectiveLabels.COP.6: Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.

easy.q: Which item is an explicit cost?
options: A payment to a materials supplier
easy.feedback: Explicit costs are direct monetary payments.

easy.q: Which item is an implicit cost?
options: A wage paid to an employee
The salary an owner gives up elsewhere
easy.feedback: Implicit costs are forgone alternatives of owner-supplied resources.

easy.q: Accounting profit equals:
options: Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
easy.feedback: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs.

easy.q: Economic profit equals:
options: Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
easy.feedback: Economic profit subtracts all opportunity costs.

easy.q: Zero economic profit means:
options: All explicit and implicit costs are covered
easy.feedback: Zero economic profit includes normal profit.

easy.q: The short run is a period with:
options: Less than one year by definition
easy.feedback: The short run is defined by a fixed input.

easy.q: In the long run:
easy.feedback: All inputs are adjustable in the long run.

easy.q: Which is usually variable in a short-run factory model?
easy.feedback: Labor can vary while capital is fixed.

easy.q: Total product is:
options: Output added by the last worker
easy.feedback: TP is total output.

easy.q: Marginal product is:
options: Additional output from one more input unit
easy.feedback: MP is the change in output.

easy.q: Average product equals:
options: Change in output divided by labor
easy.feedback: AP is output per worker.

easy.q: Diminishing marginal product begins when:
easy.feedback: Diminishing MP begins with the first decline in MP.

easy.q: At zero short-run output, which cost remains?
easy.feedback: TFC remains at zero output.

easy.q: Variable cost:
easy.feedback: Variable cost changes with production.

easy.q: Total cost equals:
easy.feedback: TC=TFC+TVC.

easy.q: Average fixed cost equals:
options: Change in TFC divided by output
easy.feedback: AFC=TFC/Q.

easy.q: Average variable cost equals:
options: Change in TC divided by output
easy.feedback: AVC=TVC/Q.

easy.q: Average total cost equals:
easy.feedback: ATC=TC/Q.

easy.q: Marginal cost equals:
options: Change in TC divided by change in output
Change in revenue divided by output
easy.feedback: MC=ΔTC/ΔQ.

easy.q: As output rises, AFC generally:
easy.feedback: Fixed cost is spread over more units.

easy.q: The ATC–AVC gap equals:
easy.feedback: ATC=AVC+AFC.

easy.q: If MC is below ATC, ATC:
easy.feedback: A marginal below the average pulls it down.

easy.q: MC crosses ATC at:
easy.feedback: MC crosses ATC at its minimum.

easy.q: A fixed-cost increase raises:
easy.feedback: Fixed cost affects AFC and ATC.

easy.q: A higher wage raises:
easy.feedback: A wage is a variable-input price.

easy.q: When MP rises at a constant wage, MC:
easy.feedback: MC and MP move inversely.

easy.q: A sunk cost:
options: Exists only in the long run
easy.feedback: Sunk costs are unrecoverable.

easy.q: Economies of scale mean LRATC:
easy.feedback: Scale economies lower LRATC.

easy.q: Diseconomies of scale mean LRATC:
easy.feedback: Scale diseconomies raise LRATC.

easy.q: Minimum efficient scale is:
options: The smallest output at minimum LRATC
easy.feedback: MES is the first minimum-LRATC output.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does AVC reach its minimum?
easy.feedback: The AVC curve bottoms out where MC crosses it, at Q=25.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does the average-cost curve reach its lowest point?
easy.feedback: The AC curve reaches its lowest point at Q=50.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, what is the vertical gap between AC and AVC?
easy.feedback: At Q=50, AC=$40 and AVC=$32, so the gap—and AFC—is $8.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does AVC reach its minimum value of $10?
easy.feedback: AVC bottoms out at Q=200 and $10.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what output is AC minimized?
easy.feedback: AC reaches its minimum at Q=400.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 400, what value of AVC is shown?
easy.feedback: The marked AVC value at Q=400 is $12.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 120, which labeled point lies on the total-cost curve?
easy.feedback: At Q=120, total cost is the upper curve at Point A ($1,200).

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which labeled point marks $800 of variable cost at Q = 120?
easy.feedback: Point B marks TVC=$800 at Q=120.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which labeled point lies on the $400 fixed-cost line at Q = 120?
easy.feedback: Point C lies on the horizontal TFC line at $400.

easy.q: At about how many workers does total product reach its highest point on the graph?
easy.feedback: The TP curve peaks at about 10 workers.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Approximately how much total product is produced at the peak of the TP curve?
easy.feedback: The peak occurs at roughly 150 units of total product.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which curve, MP or AP, reaches its peak at a lower labor input?
options: They peak at the same labor input
easy.feedback: The MP curve peaks before the AP curve.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At about how many workers do MP and AP intersect?
easy.feedback: The curves cross at about seven workers.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does LRAC reach its minimum?
easy.feedback: The LRAC curve bottoms out at Q=60.

easy.q: An owner uses a building she could rent to another business for $2,000 per month. In economic-cost analysis, the forgone rent is:
easy.feedback: Using an owner-supplied resource sacrifices its next-best return, so the forgone rent is an implicit cost.

easy.q: Which cost is explicit for a small restaurant?
options: The owner’s forgone salary at another job
The interest the owner could have earned on invested savings
The rent the owner could earn from an owned building
The monthly payment to its food supplier
easy.feedback: An explicit cost is a direct monetary payment made by the firm.

easy.q: Economic cost includes:
options: Only payments that vary with output
Only costs paid in cash this month
Both explicit payments and implicit opportunity costs
Only costs recorded by an accountant
easy.feedback: Economic cost counts both recorded payments and the value of forgone alternatives.

easy.q: A firm has $150,000 in revenue and $110,000 in explicit costs. Its accounting profit is:
easy.feedback: Accounting profit equals revenue minus explicit costs.

easy.q: Economic profit is calculated as:
options: Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
easy.feedback: Economic profit subtracts all opportunity costs, including implicit costs.

easy.q: Normal profit is best understood as:
options: Revenue remaining after variable cost only
A payment excluded from economic cost
The return needed to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use
easy.feedback: Normal profit is part of implicit cost and represents the opportunity cost of entrepreneurial resources.

easy.q: If accounting profit is $60,000 and implicit costs are $25,000, economic profit is:
easy.feedback: Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs.

easy.q: A firm earning zero economic profit is:
options: Covering both explicit and implicit opportunity costs
easy.feedback: Zero economic profit includes normal compensation for owner resources.

easy.q: A firm can have positive accounting profit but negative economic profit when:
options: Implicit opportunity costs exceed accounting profit
Revenue exceeds all explicit and implicit costs
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
easy.feedback: Accounting profit can look positive even though the owner would earn more in the next-best alternative.

easy.q: Positive economic profit means the firm’s revenue is:
options: Greater than explicit costs but below implicit costs
Exactly equal to total opportunity cost
Greater than all explicit and implicit costs
easy.feedback: Positive economic profit is the return above all opportunity costs.

easy.q: In the short run, total fixed cost generally:
options: Falls to zero whenever output is positive
Does not change when output changes
easy.feedback: Fixed cost is tied to inputs that cannot be adjusted in the short run.

easy.q: At zero output, total variable cost is typically:
easy.feedback: Variable cost is generated by producing output, so it is zero when output is zero in the standard cost model.

easy.q: A workshop has $150 of fixed cost and $90 of variable cost at its current output. Its total cost is:
easy.feedback: Total cost combines fixed and variable cost: $150 + $90 = $240.

easy.q: If total cost is $900 and total variable cost is $650, total fixed cost is:
Which expression gives a firm’s fixed cost per unit of output?
options: Change in TC divided by change in Q
easy.feedback: Average fixed cost spreads total fixed cost across the units produced.

easy.q: Marginal cost measures:
options: The change in total cost from producing additional output
Total cost per unit of output
easy.feedback: MC is the change in cost associated with a change in output.

easy.q: If output rises by 1 unit and total cost rises by $18, marginal cost of that unit is:
easy.feedback: With a one-unit output change, MC equals the increase in total cost.

easy.q: A pure increase in total fixed cost has what direct effect on marginal cost?
options: Raises MC by the full fixed-cost increase
easy.feedback: A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.

easy.q: With a constant wage, when marginal product of labor rises, marginal cost generally:
easy.feedback: More output from an additional worker lowers labor cost per extra unit.

easy.q: With a constant wage, diminishing marginal product eventually causes marginal cost to:
easy.feedback: When additional labor adds less output, each extra unit becomes more costly to produce.

easy.q: If TVC rises from $200 to $236 when output rises from 10 to 12 units, MC over that interval is:
Marginal cost can be calculated from changes in TC or TVC because:
options: TVC is always equal to TC
TFC does not change with output
easy.feedback: Since fixed cost is unchanged, ΔTC = ΔTVC when output changes.

easy.q: If one additional worker costs $120 and adds 8 units of output, the labor-cost contribution to MC is:
easy.feedback: With a constant wage, $120/8 = $15 of labor cost per additional unit.

easy.q: ATC falls up to Q = 40 and rises beyond Q = 40. At Q = 40, which relationship should hold?
easy.feedback: Marginal cost intersects average total cost at ATC’s minimum.

easy.q: At the output where AVC reaches its minimum, which statement is correct?
easy.feedback: The marginal-cost curve passes through average variable cost at AVC’s minimum.

easy.q: A higher fixed license fee shifts which short-run average-cost curves upward?
easy.feedback: A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.

easy.q: A higher wage for production workers shifts which curves upward, other things equal?
easy.feedback: A production wage is a variable cost and affects the cost of additional output.

easy.q: A sunk cost is a cost that:
options: Exists only when economic profit is negative
Has already been incurred and cannot be recovered
Can always be avoided by shutting down today
easy.feedback: A sunk cost is unrecoverable and should not be changed by the current decision.

easy.q: An avoidable cost is a cost that:
options: Can be eliminated by choosing a particular alternative
Has already been paid and cannot be recovered
Must be fixed in every time period
easy.feedback: Avoidable costs differ across the alternatives being considered.

easy.q: A nonrefundable $2,000 design fee was paid last month. For today’s continue-or-cancel decision, the fee is:
easy.feedback: The payment cannot be recovered regardless of the current choice.

easy.q: A monthly service contract can be canceled before next month with no penalty. Next month’s payment is:
easy.feedback: A future cost that disappears under one option is relevant to the decision.

easy.q: Long-run average cost shows the lowest attainable average cost when:
options: At least one input is fixed
easy.feedback: The long run allows the firm to choose among plant sizes and adjust all inputs.

easy.q: LRAC falls from $28 per unit to $21 per unit as a firm expands its long-run output. This pattern indicates:
options: Diminishing marginal product from a fixed plant
easy.feedback: Falling long-run average cost as scale expands indicates economies of scale.

easy.q: A very large firm becomes harder to coordinate, and its long-run cost per unit rises as it expands further. This is:
options: A fall in total product caused by one fixed input
easy.feedback: Rising unit cost at greater scale is diseconomies of scale; coordination problems are a common source.

easy.q: The LRAC curve is often described as an envelope because it:
options: Adds all short-run fixed costs together
Shows the highest ATC at every output
Is identical to one short-run ATC curve
Traces the lowest attainable ATC across available plant sizes
easy.feedback: In the long run, the firm can choose the least-cost plant for each output level.

easy.q: Which is a common source of economies of scale?
options: A fall in marginal product caused by one fixed input
Greater specialization as the firm expands
A fixed input becoming more crowded
easy.feedback: Larger scale can support specialization of labor and capital that lowers average cost.

easy.q: Which is a common source of diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination and communication problems in a very large organization
Spreading fixed cost over more units only
easy.feedback: Large scale can raise organizational and coordination costs per unit.

easy.q: Why can a firm choose a different plant size in long-run cost analysis?
options: All inputs are variable in the long run
Plant size is always variable in the short run
Fixed cost is zero at every output
Marginal cost determines plant size automatically
easy.feedback: The long run is defined by enough time to adjust all inputs, including plant capacity.

easy.q: Minimum efficient scale is the:
options: Largest output the firm can physically produce
Output where total cost is lowest
First output where marginal product is positive
Smallest output at which minimum LRAC is attained
easy.feedback: MES marks the first output level that reaches the minimum long-run average cost.

easy.q: A flat LRAC over a range of output is associated with:
options: Diseconomies of scale throughout the range
Economies of scale throughout the range
easy.feedback: A flat long-run average cost means proportional expansion does not change cost per unit.

easy.q: If LRAC first reaches its minimum at 5,000 units and remains flat until 8,000, MES is:
easy.feedback: MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC.

easy.q: With constant returns to scale, doubling all inputs tends to:
options: Increase output by less than double
easy.feedback: Constant returns means output changes in the same proportion as all inputs.

medium.q: Maya runs Northstar Bakery. Revenue is $186,000, explicit cost $118,000, forgone salary $42,000, and forgone capital income $12,000. Economic profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract explicit and implicit costs.

medium.q: Ironwood Furniture earns $242,000 and pays $151,000 in recorded expenses. Accounting profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract recorded expenses only.

medium.q: Ari runs Harbor Roasters. Revenue is $164,000, explicit cost $97,000, forgone salary $38,000, and forgone capital income $9,000. Economic profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract explicit and implicit costs.

medium.q: Cedar Trail Bikes earns $311,000 and pays $203,000 in recorded expenses. Accounting profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract recorded expenses only.

medium.q: Dev runs Blue Peak Printing. Revenue is $138,000, explicit cost $83,000, forgone salary $32,000, and forgone capital income $7,000. Economic profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract explicit and implicit costs.

medium.q: Riverbend Textiles earns $274,000 and pays $176,000 in recorded expenses. Accounting profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract recorded expenses only.

medium.q: Evan runs Juniper Foods. Revenue is $205,000, explicit cost $132,000, forgone salary $44,000, and forgone capital income $11,000. Economic profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract explicit and implicit costs.

medium.q: Summit Glassworks earns $356,000 and pays $229,000 in recorded expenses. Accounting profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract recorded expenses only.

medium.feedback: Subtract explicit and implicit costs.

medium.q: Granite Toolworks earns $298,000 and pays $188,000 in recorded expenses. Accounting profit?
medium.feedback: Subtract recorded expenses only.

medium.q: At Northstar Bakery, output rises from 8 to 20 when worker 2 is added. MP?
medium.feedback: Subtract the previous total product.
