repairQuestions.q: A business owner says, “My time is free because I do not pay myself.” What correction is needed?
options: Owner time is a fixed cost of zero
The owner’s forgone alternative earnings are an implicit cost
repairQuestions.feedback: Owner-supplied resources still have opportunity costs.

repairQuestions.q: Which cost belongs in economic cost but not recorded accounting cost?
options: Forgone rent on an owner-occupied building
repairQuestions.feedback: Forgone rent is an implicit opportunity cost.

repairQuestions.q: Accounting profit is $60,000 and implicit costs are $45,000. Economic profit?
repairQuestions.feedback: Economic profit subtracts implicit cost from accounting profit.

repairQuestions.q: A firm earns zero economic profit. What has it covered?
options: Explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
Variable costs but not fixed costs
repairQuestions.feedback: Zero economic profit means all opportunity costs are covered.

repairQuestions.q: Why can the short run last several years in one industry?
options: The short run is legally set by industry
A major input may remain fixed for several years
repairQuestions.feedback: The fixed-input constraint, not calendar time, defines the horizon.

repairQuestions.q: In the short run, which statement must be true?
options: At least one input is fixed
repairQuestions.feedback: The short run has at least one fixed input.

repairQuestions.q: Output rises from 40 to 52 when a worker is added. The worker’s MP is:
repairQuestions.feedback: MP is the change in total product.

repairQuestions.q: Five workers produce 60 units. AP is:
repairQuestions.feedback: AP=TP/L.

repairQuestions.q: MP falls from 15 to 12 but remains positive. Which statement is correct?
options: TP still rises, but more slowly
repairQuestions.feedback: Positive MP raises TP; declining MP marks diminishing returns.

repairQuestions.q: Diminishing MP begins when:
options: MP first declines, not when it becomes negative
repairQuestions.feedback: The first decline in MP is the threshold.

repairQuestions.q: At zero output, TFC is $500 and TVC is $0. TC is:
repairQuestions.feedback: TC=TFC+TVC.

repairQuestions.q: TFC is $300 and TVC is $700. TC is:
repairQuestions.feedback: Add fixed and variable cost.

repairQuestions.q: AFC is $4 and AVC is $11. ATC is:
repairQuestions.feedback: ATC=AFC+AVC.

repairQuestions.q: Why does the ATC–AVC gap shrink?
options: The gap is AFC, which falls as output rises
repairQuestions.feedback: AFC is spread over more units.

repairQuestions.q: TC rises from $900 to $1,020 as Q rises from 30 to 36. MC is:
MC is below ATC. What happens to ATC?
options: ATC must be at its maximum
repairQuestions.feedback: A marginal below the average lowers it.

repairQuestions.q: A fixed license fee rises. Which curves shift?
repairQuestions.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.

repairQuestions.q: The wage rises. Which curves shift upward?
repairQuestions.feedback: The wage is a variable-input price.

repairQuestions.q: Diminishing MP and diseconomies of scale differ because:
options: The first is short run with fixed inputs; the second is long run with all inputs variable
repairQuestions.feedback: The concepts apply to different horizons and input changes.

repairQuestions.q: MES is best defined as:
options: The smallest output attaining minimum LRATC
The point where MP becomes negative
repairQuestions.feedback: MES is the first output on the minimum-LRATC range.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says, “If the owner did not write a check, the resource has no cost.
options: Only variable resources have economic costs
Every implicit cost must appear on an invoice
Opportunity cost matters only for consumers
Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
repairQuestions.feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

repairQuestions.q: A learner subtracts the owner’s forgone salary when calculating accounting profit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The forgone salary should be added to revenue
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs; the forgone salary is implicit
Accounting profit subtracts all opportunity costs
repairQuestions.feedback: Implicit costs matter for economic profit, not the accounting-profit calculation.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says economic profit equals accounting profit plus implicit costs. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Economic profit and accounting profit are always equal
Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs
Economic profit equals accounting profit plus explicit costs
Economic profit ignores owner opportunity costs
repairQuestions.feedback: Implicit costs reduce economic profit relative to accounting profit.

repairQuestions.q: A learner calls zero economic profit a “loss.
options: Zero economic profit means all explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
Zero economic profit means revenue is zero
Zero economic profit means explicit costs exceed revenue
Zero economic profit excludes owner compensation
repairQuestions.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost, so zero economic profit can be a sustainable outcome.

repairQuestions.q: A learner finds accounting profit of $50,000 and implicit cost of $70,000, then reports economic profit of $20,000. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: $20,000 is correct because profit cannot be negative
repairQuestions.feedback: Economic profit equals $50,000 − $70,000 = −$20,000.

repairQuestions.q: A learner writes TC = TFC − TVC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: Total cost combines the fixed and variable components.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says fixed cost must fall when output falls. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Fixed cost is another name for marginal cost
Within the short run, total fixed cost does not vary with output
Fixed cost moves one-for-one with output
Fixed cost equals zero below capacity
repairQuestions.feedback: A fixed input creates a cost that remains even as current output changes.

repairQuestions.q: A learner reports positive TVC when output is zero in the standard short-run schedule. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: At zero output, TVC is zero; any remaining cost is fixed
TVC equals TFC at zero output
TVC is always greater than TC
TVC is an implicit cost only
repairQuestions.feedback: Variable costs arise from producing output, while fixed costs remain at zero output.

repairQuestions.q: A row has TFC = $90 and TC = $250, but a learner records TVC = $340. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: TVC = TC − TFC = $250 − $90.

repairQuestions.q: A learner divides output by TFC to calculate AFC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: Average fixed cost is fixed cost per unit of output.

repairQuestions.q: A learner calculates AVC using TC/Q. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: TC/Q is ATC; AVC uses total variable cost only.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says ATC = AVC − AFC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: Average total cost contains both average variable and average fixed cost.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says AFC eventually rises because “all U-shaped costs rise.
options: AFC keeps falling as fixed cost is spread over more output
AFC equals MC at its minimum
repairQuestions.feedback: AFC is not U-shaped in the standard model; it declines as quantity increases.

repairQuestions.q: At Q = 10, AFC = $6 and AVC = $14. A learner reports ATC = $8. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: ATC = AFC + AVC = $6 + $14.

repairQuestions.q: A learner calculates MC as TC/Q. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: TC/Q is average total cost; marginal cost uses changes.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says a higher fixed property tax must raise MC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Every fixed-cost increase raises MC one-for-one
MC equals AFC after a tax
Fixed costs are part of TVC
A pure fixed-cost increase does not change MC
repairQuestions.feedback: MC depends on changes in cost as output changes, and a fixed amount is present at every output.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says falling marginal product causes MC to fall. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Marginal product and MC always move together
Marginal product affects fixed cost only
With a constant input price, falling marginal product raises MC
Falling marginal product lowers both MC and AVC automatically
repairQuestions.feedback: Less extra output from the same variable-input expense raises cost per additional unit.

repairQuestions.q: TC rises by $50 when output rises by 5 units, but a learner reports MC = $50. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
repairQuestions.feedback: Divide the cost change by the output change: $50/5 = $10.

repairQuestions.q: A worker costs $100 and adds 10 units. A learner reports MC from labor as $100 per unit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The labor cost per marginal unit is $10
The labor cost per marginal unit is $100
Marginal product should be added to the wage
The worker’s wage is a fixed cost
repairQuestions.feedback: Divide the worker’s cost by the worker’s marginal product: $100/10 = $10 per unit.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says MC must be falling whenever ATC is falling. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: ATC can fall only if MC is zero
MC and ATC always have the same slope
ATC falls only when AFC rises
MC can be rising while ATC is still falling, as long as MC remains below ATC
repairQuestions.feedback: The direction of the average depends on whether the marginal is above or below it, not on whether the marginal is itself rising.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says a higher fixed insurance premium shifts AVC and MC upward. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: All short-run curves shift by the same amount
A pure fixed-cost increase shifts AFC and ATC, not AVC or MC
A fixed-cost increase shifts only MC
repairQuestions.feedback: Fixed cost does not change the variable cost of current output or the incremental cost of another unit.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says, “Fixed cost and sunk cost mean the same thing.
options: A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
Every sunk cost varies with output
Every fixed cost has already been paid forever
repairQuestions.feedback: Fixed describes how cost behaves with current output; sunk describes whether it can be recovered.

repairQuestions.q: A learner includes a nonrefundable past payment when comparing two current options that both leave the payment unchanged. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Double the payment to reflect risk
Ignore the payment because it is sunk and identical across the options
repairQuestions.feedback: Only costs and benefits that differ across current alternatives should affect the choice.

repairQuestions.q: A learner calls a cancelable future lease payment sunk because the lease is a fixed cost. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Only variable costs can be avoided
A lease payment is always implicit
The future payment is avoidable if canceling the lease eliminates it
repairQuestions.feedback: A cost can be fixed with respect to output yet avoidable with respect to a future decision.

repairQuestions.q: A learner treats LRAC as the ATC curve of one fixed plant. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: LRAC is total variable cost per unit only
LRAC reflects the lowest attainable ATC across alternative plant sizes
LRAC is the same as AFC
repairQuestions.feedback: The long run permits plant adjustment, so LRAC summarizes least-cost choices across plants.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says economies of scale mean total cost must fall as output rises. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Economies of scale mean average cost falls; total cost can still rise
Economies mean fixed cost becomes zero
Economies require marginal product to be negative
repairQuestions.feedback: The concept concerns cost per unit, not necessarily the level of total cost.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says diseconomies of scale begin when marginal product first falls in the short run. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Diseconomies and diminishing marginal product are the same event
Diseconomies require one input to remain fixed
Diseconomies concern long-run expansion of all inputs and rising LRAC
repairQuestions.feedback: The two concepts refer to different horizons and different input adjustments.

repairQuestions.q: A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: LRAC slope says nothing about scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment requires negative output
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents economies of scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents constant returns
repairQuestions.feedback: Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says rising LRAC means output itself must be falling. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Rising LRAC means total cost is falling
LRAC can rise while output expands; the issue is rising cost per unit at larger scale
Output and LRAC always move in opposite directions
repairQuestions.feedback: Diseconomies describe a higher average cost at greater output, not a fall in output.

repairQuestions.q: A learner chooses the largest output on a flat minimum-LRAC segment as MES. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: MES is always the largest efficient output
MES is where LRAC first begins to fall
MES is where total cost is smallest
MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC
repairQuestions.feedback: The definition focuses on the minimum scale required to achieve the lowest long-run unit cost.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says a flat LRAC means output is not changing. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Flat LRAC means economies of scale
Flat LRAC means fixed cost is constant in the short run
Output can rise while LRAC stays constant; that range reflects constant returns to scale
Flat LRAC means output must be zero
repairQuestions.feedback: Constant returns refers to proportional changes in all inputs and output, leaving long-run cost per unit unchanged.

bridgeQuestions.q: A proprietor uses a personally owned storefront. How does opportunity cost enter production cost?
options: Forgone market rent is an implicit cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Owner-supplied property has an opportunity cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: An entrepreneur leaves a $70,000 job to run a firm. In economic-cost analysis, the $70,000 is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The forgone salary is the next-best alternative.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can economic profit be lower than accounting profit?
options: Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs of owner resources
Accounting profit includes all implicit costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Implicit opportunity costs create the gap.

bridgeQuestions.q: Zero economic profit signals that owner resources earn:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Normal profit keeps owner resources in their current use.

bridgeQuestions.q: A firm asks how much cost rises when output expands slightly. Which measure is relevant?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal analysis focuses on incremental changes.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does MC below ATC lower ATC?
options: The added unit costs less than the current average
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down.

bridgeQuestions.q: A worker adds 10 units and costs $200. The labor-based MC is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Divide the input cost by marginal product.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which cost is irrelevant to the marginal cost of one more unit?
options: A fixed payment that does not change with output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A cost that does not change has zero marginal contribution.

bridgeQuestions.q: A productivity improvement raises output per worker. With wages unchanged, what happens to labor cost per unit?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: More output from the same wage lowers unit cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: A factory produces the same output with fewer labor hours. Which cost most directly falls?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Labor-hours savings lower current variable cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can better organization create economies of scale?
options: Specialization and coordination may lower LRATC over an output range
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Scale can permit productive specialization.

bridgeQuestions.q: For a competitive firm considering a change in output, which cost curve measures the incremental production cost?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional cost of producing more output and is the relevant cost measure for incremental output decisions.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does distinguishing AVC from ATC matter for a firm’s short-run production decisions?
options: The two averages contain different cost components
bridgeQuestions.feedback: AVC excludes fixed cost; ATC includes it.

bridgeQuestions.q: Cost curves can be reused across market structures because:
options: Every firm faces the same price
Production technology and input costs determine cost independently of the firm’s demand conditions
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Revenue conditions differ, but cost construction follows production and input prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: A higher wage paid for labor directly raises:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.

bridgeQuestions.q: If the rental price of an adjustable machine service rises, what happens to cost?
options: The cost of outputs using that service rises
bridgeQuestions.feedback: An input-price increase raises production cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can a supply curve reflect marginal cost in a competitive setting?
options: A seller’s minimum acceptable price is tied to the cost of the marginal unit
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal cost helps define willingness to accept.

bridgeQuestions.q: Producer surplus differs from accounting profit partly because:
options: Producer surplus is tied to variable or marginal costs, while accounting profit also subtracts fixed costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The measures use different cost concepts.

bridgeQuestions.q: A monopoly and a competitive firm may use the same cost schedule. What differs later?
options: Their revenue and demand conditions, not the cost identities
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Cost machinery is shared even when revenue conditions differ.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is marginal cost relevant to a competitive firm’s supply decision?
options: It measures the additional resource cost of another unit
It is fixed at every output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional production cost of another unit and therefore helps determine whether expanding output is worthwhile at a given market price.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the general idea of opportunity cost carry into a firm’s production-cost analysis?
options: Opportunity cost is replaced by accounting profit
A firm counts only costs that change with output
Resources supplied by the owner are valued by the best alternative return sacrificed
Only purchased inputs have opportunity cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The same next-best-alternative principle applies to labor, capital, land, and other resources used by a firm.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does opportunity cost explain the difference between accounting profit and economic profit?
options: The two measures differ only when fixed cost changes
Economic profit subtracts the forgone returns of owner-supplied resources
Accounting profit subtracts more opportunity costs than economic profit
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Economic profit extends accounting profit by charging the firm for owner resources at their next-best use.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is normal profit connected to the idea of opportunity cost?
options: It is identical to producer surplus
It compensates entrepreneurial resources for what they could earn in their next-best use
It is a tax on accounting profit
It measures consumer willingness to pay
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Normal profit is the implicit opportunity cost required to keep entrepreneurial resources in the firm.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does marginal decision-making differ from comparing total economic profit?
options: Marginal analysis focuses on changes from one more action, while economic profit compares total revenue with all opportunity costs
Marginal analysis compares total revenue with total explicit costs, while economic profit isolates the value of the next unit
Economic profit evaluates the next incremental action, while marginal analysis measures the return on the entire project
Both methods compare total revenue and total cost, but marginal analysis reports the result per unit of output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The two tools answer different questions: one about incremental choices and one about overall return after opportunity costs.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does marginal product connect the production function to marginal cost when the wage is unchanged?
options: A higher marginal product necessarily raises marginal cost
Marginal cost and marginal product move together in the same direction
A higher marginal product generally means a lower marginal cost of additional output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: When each worker adds more output for the same wage, the labor cost per additional unit falls.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does diminishing marginal product help explain the upward-sloping portion of short-run marginal cost?
options: Total product must fall as soon as diminishing returns begin
Additional variable input eventually adds less output, so each extra unit of output becomes more costly
Fixed cost rises with every worker
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With a fixed input, falling marginal product raises the variable-input cost of producing additional output.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does average product connect to average variable cost when labor is the only variable input and the wage is constant?
options: Average product equals total fixed cost per worker
Higher average product tends to imply lower average variable cost
Higher average product raises average fixed cost
Average product and average variable cost are unrelated
bridgeQuestions.feedback: More output per worker spreads the wage cost across more units of output.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does the short-run/long-run distinction matter when interpreting cost curves?
options: Some inputs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs can vary in the long run
All costs are variable in both horizons
The long run is always exactly one year
Fixed costs rise only in the long run
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Short-run cost curves reflect at least one fixed input; long-run cost analysis allows plant size and all other inputs to change.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the marginal-versus-average rule connect product curves to cost curves?
options: Marginal and average values always move in opposite directions
A marginal below an average always raises the average
The rule applies to product but never to cost
A marginal value above an average pulls the average up; a marginal cost below an average cost pulls that average down
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The same arithmetic relationship governs MP versus AP and MC versus AVC or ATC.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does identifying fixed and variable inputs help classify short-run costs?
options: Variable inputs determine accounting profit but not cost
Payments tied to fixed inputs generate fixed cost, while costs of variable inputs change with output
Every input creates only variable cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Input flexibility is the production-side basis for distinguishing fixed and variable cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a fixed input in the production model connect to fixed cost?
options: Fixed inputs determine revenue rather than cost
A fixed input makes marginal cost zero
A payment associated with an input that cannot be changed in the short run contributes to fixed cost
Every fixed input creates variable cost only
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The production distinction between fixed and variable inputs carries directly into short-run cost classification.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does hiring additional labor connect production decisions to variable cost?
options: Variable cost falls automatically whenever workers are added
If labor is variable, more labor raises total variable cost
Hiring labor changes total fixed cost only
Labor cost is sunk by definition
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Payments to adjustable inputs are part of total variable cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is the vertical distance between TC and TVC constant in a standard short-run total-cost graph?
options: The distance equals TFC, which does not vary with output
The distance equals MC, which is constant
TVC and TC have different output units
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Because TC = TFC + TVC, the fixed-cost amount separates the two curves at every output.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a cost schedule support marginal analysis?
options: A cost schedule eliminates the need to compare changes
Only TFC is needed to calculate marginal cost
Marginal cost is found by adding TC and TVC
Changes in TC or TVC between output levels can be used to calculate marginal cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Cost schedules provide the change in cost associated with a change in output.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does TC = TFC + TVC relate to average total cost?
options: It implies ATC equals TFC at every output
It makes AVC independent of variable cost
Dividing each component by output gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by output gives MC = AFC + AVC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The total-cost identity becomes the average-cost identity after dividing by quantity.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does a pure increase in TFC leave the change in total cost between two output levels unchanged?
options: The increase reduces TVC by the same amount
The same fixed amount is added to TC at both output levels
TFC becomes variable after the increase
MC is defined as total fixed cost per unit
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal cost depends on cost differences across output, so a constant fixed-cost addition cancels out.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the fixed-cost concept connect to the downward slope of AFC?
options: TFC falls automatically as output rises
Variable cost is spread across fewer units
AFC is determined by marginal product only
The same TFC is spread across more units as output rises
bridgeQuestions.feedback: AFC falls because the numerator stays fixed while the denominator grows.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can rising average product of labor affect AVC when the wage is constant?
options: It tends to raise AVC because a worker producing more output increases total wage cost faster than output
It leaves AVC unchanged because a constant wage fixes variable cost per unit regardless of worker productivity
It tends to lower AVC because each worker produces more output per dollar of wage cost
It lowers average fixed cost rather than AVC because labor productivity affects the spreading of fixed cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher output per worker reduces variable labor cost per unit.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the identity TC = TFC + TVC connect to ATC?
options: Dividing by Q gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by Q gives ATC = MC + AVC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The average-cost identity follows directly from the total-cost identity.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can ATC fall even when AVC is flat?
options: Falling AFC can pull ATC downward
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Because ATC = AVC + AFC, a declining fixed-cost component can reduce ATC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is AVC often more relevant than AFC for understanding the cost of current production activity?
options: AFC determines how much extra output one worker adds
AFC changes directly with every unit produced
AVC reflects variable resources used to produce the current output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Variable cost is tied to inputs adjusted as production changes.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a below-average marginal cost affect ATC?
options: It leaves ATC unchanged by definition
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The marginal-versus-average rule applies to costs just as it does to other averages.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the sunk-cost rule connect to marginal analysis?
options: Both rules say fixed costs are always irrelevant
Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
Marginal analysis requires adding all past costs
Sunk cost is another term for marginal cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can a cost be fixed with respect to current output but still relevant to a future decision?
options: It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
Every fixed cost is permanently sunk
Fixed costs always change one-for-one with output
Future fixed costs are excluded from economic cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Cost behavior with output and recoverability across decisions are different classifications.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is “recovering what we already spent” a poor reason by itself to continue a project?
options: Continuing can convert past spending into a relevant marginal benefit if enough future revenue is earned
Past spending should be added to expected future benefits because the project needs to recover its historical cost
A project should continue when accounting profit remains positive, even if future incremental costs exceed benefits
Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does specialization connect to economies of scale?
options: A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
Specialization always creates diminishing marginal product
Specialization raises fixed cost per unit forever
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range.

bridgeQuestions.q: How do coordination problems connect organizational size to diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination problems reduce all input prices
They guarantee constant returns to scale
They turn fixed cost into sunk cost
Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Very large scale can create managerial inefficiencies that push LRAC upward.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the short-run/long-run distinction connect SRATC curves to LRAC?
options: SRATC includes implicit cost but LRAC does not
The curves differ only because of revenue
Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
LRAC fixes plant size while SRATC changes every input
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Long-run flexibility over plant size is what lets LRAC trace the least-cost envelope.

bridgeQuestions.q: How is economies of scale different from spreading a fixed short-run cost over more units?
options: Falling AFC is a long-run scale effect only
Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
Economies of scale requires one input to remain fixed
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Both can lower average cost, but they arise from different mechanisms and horizons.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can productivity improvements affect long-run average cost?
options: If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
Productivity affects revenue but never cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: More output from a given bundle of resources can lower the cost required per unit.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does MES build on the idea of economies of scale?
options: MES is the largest feasible plant regardless of cost
MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
MES is where diseconomies first begin at zero output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does constant returns to scale differ from short-run diminishing marginal product?
options: Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
Constant returns requires a fixed plant
Diminishing marginal product requires all inputs to change proportionally
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The concepts apply to different production experiments and time horizons.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can MES matter when comparing efficient firm scale with the size of a market?
options: It fixes the market price by law
It measures accounting profit rather than cost
It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.

perfect-competition.title: Perfect Competition
perfect-competition.description: Analyze price-taking firm behavior, revenue, marginal output choice, profit and loss, shutdown, short-run supply, entry and exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and competitive efficiency.

objectiveLabels.PC.1: Explain the assumptions and price-taking behavior of perfectly competitive firms.
objectiveLabels.PC.2: Calculate and interpret total, average, and marginal revenue for a competitive firm.
objectiveLabels.PC.3: Determine the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output using marginal analysis.
objectiveLabels.PC.4: Calculate and interpret profit, loss, break-even, and shutdown outcomes.
objectiveLabels.PC.5: Derive and interpret the competitive firm’s short-run supply behavior.
objectiveLabels.PC.6: Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.

easy.q: Which condition is most consistent with perfect competition?
options: Many small firms sell an identical product
One firm controls a unique product
Each seller offers a heavily differentiated brand
easy.feedback: Perfect competition has many small sellers and a standardized product.

easy.q: A perfectly competitive firm is called a price taker because:
options: It is legally forbidden to change output
Its individual output is too small to affect the market price
It sets the price for all firms
easy.feedback: The market determines price; one small firm cannot move it.

easy.q: Which decision remains for a price-taking firm?
easy.feedback: The firm accepts price but chooses quantity.

easy.q: The demand curve facing an individual competitive firm is:
options: The same downward-sloping curve as market demand
easy.feedback: The firm can sell its feasible output at the given price.

easy.q: Market demand differs from the individual firm’s demand because market demand is:
options: Downward sloping while firm demand is horizontal
Horizontal while firm demand slopes downward
Vertical while firm demand is horizontal
easy.feedback: The market determines price; the small firm takes it.

easy.q: For a competitive firm, average revenue equals:
easy.feedback: AR=TR/Q=P.

easy.q: For a competitive firm, marginal revenue equals:
easy.feedback: Each additional unit sells at the constant market price.

easy.q: If price is $12 and the firm sells 20 units, total revenue is:
easy.feedback: TR=P×Q.

easy.q: Which relationship holds for a price-taking firm?
options: P = ATC = AFC at every output
MR falls below price as output rises
easy.feedback: Constant price makes average and marginal revenue equal to price.

easy.q: For a competitive firm, economic profit is calculated as:
options: Total revenue minus total economic cost
Total revenue minus variable cost only
easy.feedback: Economic profit subtracts all explicit and implicit costs.

easy.q: If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost for the next unit, the firm should:
easy.feedback: The unit adds more revenue than cost.

easy.q: For the next unit of output, marginal cost is greater than marginal revenue. Producing that unit would:
easy.feedback: The unit adds more cost than revenue.

easy.q: The standard output rule for a competitive firm is to produce where:
options: MR equals MC on the rising portion of MC
Price equals ATC at every output
easy.feedback: The relevant MR=MC crossing lies on rising MC.

easy.q: Why is the rising-MC condition important?
options: A falling-MC crossing need not be a profit maximum
easy.feedback: Profit is maximized at the crossing where MC rises through MR.

easy.q: If price exceeds ATC at the chosen output, the firm earns:
easy.feedback: P>ATC creates positive profit per unit.

easy.q: If price equals ATC at the chosen output, the firm earns:
options: A loss equal to fixed cost
easy.feedback: P=ATC is the break-even condition.

easy.q: If price is below ATC but above AVC at the chosen output, the firm should generally:
options: Produce in the short run while earning a loss
Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
Exit immediately and erase fixed cost
easy.feedback: Covering AVC and some fixed cost reduces the short-run loss.

easy.q: The short-run shutdown rule compares price with:
easy.feedback: Variable cost is avoidable in the short run.

easy.q: The shutdown price is the minimum of:
easy.feedback: The minimum AVC is the threshold for short-run operation.

easy.q: If a firm shuts down in the short run, its fixed cost:
easy.feedback: Short-run fixed cost is unavoidable even at zero output.

easy.q: Short-run shutdown differs from long-run exit because exit:
options: Removes the firm from the industry and avoids all future costs
Occurs whenever P is below ATC for one day
Means the firm produces at minimum AVC
easy.feedback: Exit is the long-run industry decision.

easy.q: The competitive firm’s short-run supply curve is:
options: The portion of MC at or above AVC
The portion of MC below AVC
easy.feedback: Below AVC the firm shuts down rather than supplies along MC.

easy.q: Market supply in a competitive industry is found by:
options: Horizontally summing firms’ quantities supplied at each price
easy.feedback: At each price, add quantities across firms.

easy.q: Short-run economic profit tends to attract:
easy.feedback: Entry expands market supply and erodes profit.

easy.q: Persistent economic losses tend to cause:
options: A permanent fall in supply price with more firms
easy.feedback: Exit contracts market supply and helps remove losses.

easy.q: In long-run competitive equilibrium, firms earn:
options: A loss equal to fixed cost
easy.feedback: Entry and exit eliminate economic profit and loss.

easy.q: Zero economic profit means the firm covers:
options: All explicit and implicit opportunity costs
easy.feedback: Normal profit is included among implicit costs.

easy.q: Productive efficiency occurs when a firm produces at:
easy.feedback: Minimum ATC is the lowest feasible per-unit cost.

easy.q: Allocative efficiency occurs when:
easy.feedback: P reflects marginal benefit and MC reflects marginal cost.

easy.q: Perfect competition is best understood as:
options: A literal description of every farm or stock market
A benchmark model for studying price taking and efficiency
A model in which firms never choose output
easy.feedback: The model is an analytical benchmark with strong assumptions.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What market price does the competitive firm take as given?
easy.feedback: The horizontal P = MR = AR line is at $30.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the $30 MR line meet rising MC, identifying the profit-maximizing quantity?
easy.feedback: The relevant rising MC curve meets P = MR at Q = 50.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, what is average total cost?
easy.feedback: At Q = 50, the ATC guide is $20.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does the firm operate?
easy.feedback: P = MR intersects rising MC at Q = 50.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, what relationship holds between price and ATC?
easy.feedback: The price line passes through ATC at $25.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the $30 MR line meet rising MC, identifying the firm’s output in the loss-but-operate case?
easy.feedback: The horizontal price line meets rising MC at Q = 30.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What market price does the firm face?
easy.feedback: The P = MR = AR line is at $30.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What price is shown by the horizontal P = MR = AR line?
easy.feedback: The horizontal price line is at $10.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which labeled point marks the minimum of AVC?
easy.feedback: MC crosses AVC at its minimum at point A.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Given the price, what is the firm’s short-run output?
easy.feedback: The $10 price lies below minimum AVC, so the firm shuts down and supplies zero.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What market-clearing price is determined by the intersection of market supply and demand?
easy.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at a price of $40.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. The market panel settles at $40. Reading across to the firm panel, which quantity is selected where MR meets rising MC?
easy.feedback: On the firm panel, P = MR = $40 meets rising MC at Q = 90.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. In the paired loss case, what price is transmitted from the market equilibrium to the representative firm?
easy.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at $15.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. With the market equilibrium price at $15, where does the firm panel place the MR–MC output choice?
easy.feedback: The firm’s P = MR line meets rising MC at Q = 50.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. In the market panel where equilibrium quantity is 100, what equilibrium price is shown?
easy.feedback: Market supply and demand intersect at $25.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At the long-run market price of $25, which firm quantity lies at the rising-MC intersection?
easy.feedback: The firm’s horizontal MR line meets MC at Q = 50.

easy.q: A competitive firm has price $18 and ATC $15 at its chosen output. Economic profit per unit is:
easy.feedback: Profit per unit equals price minus average total cost.

easy.q: A firm sells 40 units at $12 and has ATC of $9. Total economic profit is:
easy.feedback: Total profit equals (P − ATC) × Q = $3 × 40.

easy.q: At a competitive firm’s chosen output, price equals ATC. The firm is:
options: Earning a loss equal to fixed cost
Breaking even with zero economic profit
easy.feedback: When P = ATC, total revenue equals total economic cost.

easy.q: A firm has price $14 and ATC $17 at its chosen output. Its economic loss per unit is:
easy.feedback: Loss per unit is ATC minus price when ATC exceeds price.

easy.q: A firm produces 25 units, receives $10 per unit, and has ATC of $12. Total economic loss is:
Which statement is true when a competitive firm earns zero economic profit?
options: Accounting profit must also be zero because economic and accounting costs are identical in competition
The firm must leave the industry immediately
Economic cost already includes normal profit to owner-supplied resources
The owner receives no return of any kind
easy.feedback: Zero economic profit means revenues cover explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit.

easy.q: A competitive firm should shut down in the short run when price is:
options: Below minimum ATC but above AVC
easy.feedback: If price cannot cover variable cost, producing makes the short-run loss larger than shutting down.

easy.q: A firm has P = $14, AVC = $10, and ATC = $18 at its best positive output. In the short run it should:
options: Shut down because P is below ATC
Produce even though it has an economic loss
easy.feedback: Price covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost, so producing minimizes the short-run loss.

easy.q: Which statement best distinguishes shutdown from exit?
options: Shutdown occurs only when economic profit is positive
Exit refers only to reducing one unit of output
Shutdown is a short-run zero-output decision; exit is a long-run decision to leave the industry
Shutdown and exit are identical because both set output to zero and permanently remove the firm from the market
easy.feedback: A firm can temporarily shut down while fixed commitments remain, whereas exit changes long-run industry participation.

easy.q: For a competitive firm, the short-run supply curve is the portion of:
options: ATC at and above minimum AVC
MC at and above minimum AVC
easy.feedback: The firm follows rising MC when operating and supplies zero below the shutdown price.

easy.q: If market price rises and the competitive firm remains open, the firm typically moves:
options: Along a horizontal MC curve by assumption
To zero output because price changed
Up along its rising MC curve to a larger quantity
Down its ATC curve with no output change
easy.feedback: Since P = MR, a higher price intersects rising MC at a larger output.

easy.q: A rise in a firm’s fixed property tax, with variable costs unchanged, does what to its short-run supply curve?
options: Shifts it left because MC rises
Shifts it right because AVC falls
easy.feedback: Fixed cost does not change MC or AVC, so the firm’s short-run supply schedule is unchanged.

easy.q: A wage increase raises the variable cost of producing each unit. Other things equal, the firm’s short-run supply tends to:
options: Shift right because fixed cost is spread out
Stay unchanged because wages are not marginal costs
easy.feedback: Higher variable input costs raise MC and reduce quantity supplied at each price.

easy.q: To construct market supply from individual competitive firms, economists:
options: Vertically adding each firm’s prices at one quantity
Using the output of the largest firm only
Adding market demand to one firm’s MC curve
Add the quantities each firm supplies at the same price
easy.feedback: Industry quantity supplied is the sum of firm quantities at the same market price.

easy.q: Below the firm’s shutdown price, its short-run quantity supplied is:
easy.feedback: Below minimum AVC, the firm minimizes loss by shutting down.

easy.q: At a price of $20, each of 50 identical firms supplies 8 units. Market quantity supplied is:
easy.feedback: Market supply adds the 8 units supplied by each of 50 firms: 50 × 8 = 400.

easy.q: Which change is most likely to leave a competitive firm’s short-run supply unchanged?
options: A higher fixed annual permit fee
A higher price for raw materials
easy.feedback: Fixed-cost changes do not alter the firm’s MC or AVC schedule.

easy.q: Persistent positive economic profit in a competitive industry tends to encourage:
options: A permanent price increase with no supply response
easy.feedback: Positive economic profit attracts resources and firms when entry is available.

easy.q: Persistent economic losses in a competitive industry tend to encourage:
easy.feedback: Long-run losses push resources toward better alternatives.

easy.q: In the standard long-run competitive equilibrium, economic profit is:
easy.feedback: Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.

easy.q: Zero economic profit means the firm is earning:
options: A normal return included in economic cost
No accounting profit and no return to the owner
A loss equal to fixed cost
easy.feedback: Normal profit compensates owner resources for their opportunity cost and is included in economic cost.

easy.q: When firms enter a competitive industry, market supply generally:
options: Equals market demand at every price
easy.feedback: More firms contribute output at each price, shifting market supply right.

easy.q: Several firms permanently leave a competitive industry. Holding the remaining firms’ cost schedules fixed, market supply:
easy.feedback: Fewer firms supply the market, shifting industry supply left.

easy.q: In a constant-cost competitive industry, industry expansion leaves input prices and firms’ cost curves essentially unchanged. The long-run industry supply curve is typically:
easy.feedback: If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.

easy.q: If industry expansion bids up specialized input prices, the industry is best described as:
easy.feedback: Higher input prices raise firms’ costs as the industry expands.

easy.q: If industry expansion leads to cheaper specialized suppliers and lower unit costs, the industry may be:
easy.feedback: Industry growth can lower firm costs when external economies develop.

easy.q: A permanent demand increase in a competitive industry usually creates what first?
options: Immediate zero economic profit with no price change
A short-run price and profit increase before entry completes
easy.feedback: Demand changes first affect the existing set of firms; entry is a long-run response.

easy.q: Which condition best supports a constant-cost industry?
options: Industry growth creates supplier efficiencies that lower costs
Firms are legally prevented from entering
The industry can expand without materially changing the prices of its inputs
Every new firm makes a key input scarcer and more expensive
easy.feedback: Constant-cost means industry size does not materially shift representative firms’ cost curves.

easy.q: Allocative efficiency in the competitive benchmark is associated with:
easy.feedback: Price reflects marginal willingness to pay while MC reflects marginal opportunity cost.

easy.q: Productive efficiency for a competitive firm is associated with producing at:
easy.feedback: Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.

medium.q: A competitive firm faces price $18. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $6, $9, $12, $16, $20, $25. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?

medium.q: At price $18, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $16. What should the firm do?

medium.q: At price $24, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $21. What should the firm do?

medium.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

medium.q: A competitive firm faces price $30. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $10, $16, $22, $28, $35, $43. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
medium.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

medium.q: At price $30, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $28. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
medium.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

medium.q: A competitive firm faces price $15. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $4, $8, $11, $14, $18, $23. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?

medium.q: At price $27, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $25. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
medium.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output of 50 units, a competitive firm has P=$40, ATC=$32, and AVC=$22. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
medium.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

medium.q: A competitive firm produces 50 units at price $40. ATC at that output is $32. What is profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output of 60 units, a competitive firm has P=$28, ATC=$34, and AVC=$20. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down and eliminate all costs
Produce and incur a loss of $360
medium.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

medium.q: A competitive firm produces 60 units at price $28. ATC at that output is $34. What is profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output of 45 units, a competitive firm has P=$24, ATC=$24, and AVC=$17. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
medium.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

medium.q: A competitive firm produces 45 units at price $24. ATC at that output is $24. What is profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output of 55 units, a competitive firm has P=$19, ATC=$28, and AVC=$16. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down and eliminate all costs
Produce and incur a loss of $495
medium.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

medium.q: A competitive firm produces 55 units at price $19. ATC at that output is $28. What is profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output of 40 units, a competitive firm has P=$14, ATC=$26, and AVC=$18. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down in the short run
medium.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

medium.q: A competitive firm produces 40 units at price $14. ATC at that output is $26. What is profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

medium.q: Competitive firms are earning positive economic profit. What happens as entry occurs?
options: Market supply falls and price rises
Market supply increases and market price falls
medium.feedback: Entry shifts market supply right and erodes profit.

medium.q: Competitive firms are earning economic losses. What happens as firms exit?
options: Market supply increases and price falls
Market supply decreases and market price rises
medium.feedback: Exit shifts market supply left and reduces remaining firms’ losses.

medium.q: In a constant-cost industry, demand rises permanently. After long-run adjustment, price typically:
options: Equals minimum AVC but not ATC
medium.feedback: Entry expands output without changing input prices or cost curves.

medium.q: In an increasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price typically ends:
options: Above the original price but below the short-run price
At zero economic profit only if price is zero
medium.feedback: Industry expansion raises input costs, so long-run price rises.

medium.q: In a decreasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price can end:
options: At the original price by definition
medium.feedback: External economies can lower firms’ costs as the industry expands.

medium.q: At long-run competitive equilibrium, which pair holds?
options: P = MC and P = minimum ATC
medium.feedback: Long-run competition combines allocative and productive efficiency.

medium.q: A fixed annual license fee rises for every competitive firm. In the short run, each firm’s output at a given price is:
options: Unchanged because MC and AVC are unchanged
medium.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change shifts ATC, not MC or AVC.

medium.q: A per-unit production tax is imposed. For a competitive firm, the tax directly shifts:
medium.feedback: A per-unit tax is a variable and marginal cost.

medium.q: A technology improvement lowers marginal cost. At the same market price, the firm generally chooses:
options: The same output because price is fixed
medium.feedback: Lower MC moves the P=MC output to a larger quantity.

medium.q: A competitive outcome has P=MC but the firm is not at minimum ATC. The outcome is:
options: Productively efficient but not allocatively efficient
Allocatively efficient but not productively efficient
medium.feedback: P=MC is allocative efficiency; minimum ATC is productive efficiency.

options: P < AVC and MC < ATC for the displayed firm
P = MC and P = minimum ATC

medium.q: A competitive wheat farm doubles its own output while every other seller and market demand are unchanged. Why is the market price essentially unaffected?
options: The farm is too small relative to the market to influence price
The farm can force buyers to accept any price
Its average total cost determines the market price for all sellers
Doubling output makes its demand curve downward sloping
medium.feedback: A price-taking firm is individually too small to move the market price.

medium.q: The market price of soybeans is $12 per bushel. Which statement best describes the demand curve facing one competitive soybean farm?
options: It slopes downward because the farm must cut price to sell more
It is vertical at the farm’s current quantity
It coincides with the entire market demand curve
It is horizontal at $12 over the farm’s feasible output range
medium.feedback: A competitive firm can sell feasible output at the prevailing market price, so its firm-level demand is horizontal.

medium.q: A competitive firm sells its first 25 units at $18 each. If it can also sell the 26th unit at $18, marginal revenue from the 26th unit is:
medium.feedback: For a price-taking firm, each additional unit adds the unchanged market price to total revenue.

medium.q: A price-taking firm has total revenue of $1,260 from selling 70 units. Its average revenue is:
medium.feedback: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price for a competitive firm.

medium.q: If the competitive market price falls from $24 to $20, what happens to the individual firm’s P, AR, and MR?
options: Price becomes $20 while AR and MR stay $24
MR falls to $20 but AR stays $24
Only total revenue changes; P, AR, and MR do not
medium.feedback: For a price-taking firm, price, average revenue, and marginal revenue all equal the market price.

medium.q: A competitive firm faces a constant market price of $15. Which total-revenue pattern is consistent with price taking?
options: Total revenue rises by a smaller amount with each additional unit
Total revenue is fixed because the firm cannot change price
Total revenue falls whenever output rises
Each additional unit raises total revenue by $15
medium.feedback: With constant price, total revenue increases linearly and each unit adds the same amount.

medium.q: Which pair correctly contrasts market demand with the demand facing one perfectly competitive firm?
options: Market demand is horizontal; firm demand slopes downward
Both curves slope downward because every seller faces the same market demand
Market demand slopes downward; the individual firm faces a horizontal line at market price
Both curves are horizontal because all firms are price takers
medium.feedback: Industry demand determines market price with supply, while an individual competitive firm takes that price as given.

medium.q: A market has many sellers, standardized output, and easy entry. Which additional implication is most consistent with the competitive model?
options: Brand loyalty gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve
No single seller has meaningful control over market price
Each firm chooses a unique profit-maximizing price
Firms must coordinate output to avoid price wars
medium.feedback: The competitive assumptions make individual firms price takers.

medium.q: A competitive firm sells 40 units at $9 and then 45 units at the same price. By how much does total revenue increase?
medium.feedback: Five additional units at $9 each add $45 to total revenue.

medium.q: A competitive firm faces P = $11. At the output where MR = MC, AVC = $8 and ATC = $15. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Exit immediately because fixed cost is positive
Produce in the short run and incur a loss
Shut down because price is below ATC
medium.feedback: Price covers AVC but not ATC, so the firm produces and uses revenue to cover variable cost plus part of fixed cost.

medium.q: At the best positive output, a firm faces P = $7, AVC = $9, and ATC = $13. What should it do in the short run?
options: Shut down because revenue cannot cover variable cost
Produce because price is below ATC
Raise output until ATC falls to $7
medium.feedback: When P < AVC, producing fails to cover avoidable variable cost.

medium.q: A competitive firm has already paid a nonrefundable annual license fee. The fee increases while market price, MC, and AVC are unchanged. What happens to the short-run output decision?
options: Output falls because every fixed-cost increase shifts MC upward
The firm must shut down immediately
Output rises to spread the fee across more units
The profit-maximizing positive output is unchanged, though profit is lower
medium.feedback: A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.

medium.q: A firm’s MC for units 1–5 is $6, $9, $13, $18, and $24. Assume AVC is covered. If price rises from $14 to $20, output changes from:
medium.feedback: The firm produces through the last unit whose MC does not exceed price on rising MC.

medium.q: At price $16, 30 identical firms each supply 5 units. At price $22, each supplies 8 units. What is the industry response?
options: Market quantity supplied falls from 240 to 150 units
Market quantity supplied stays at 30 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 150 to 240 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 35 to 38 units
medium.feedback: Horizontal aggregation multiplies each firm’s quantity by the number of identical firms.

medium.q: A fixed insurance premium increases by $4,000 for every firm in a competitive industry. Market demand and variable costs are unchanged. In the immediate short run, what happens to each operating firm’s supply curve?
options: It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It does not shift because MC and AVC are unchanged
It shifts left because ATC rises
It shifts right because firms need more output
medium.feedback: Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.

medium.q: A per-unit fee raises MC and AVC by $2 at every positive output. Which supply effect is most consistent?
options: The firm requires a higher market price to supply a given quantity
The supply curve is unchanged because the fee is fixed
The firm supplies more at every price
Only ATC changes, so shutdown price cannot change
medium.feedback: A per-unit cost raises marginal and variable cost, shifting the operating supply schedule upward.

medium.q: A firm has minimum AVC of $9. At P = $8, its quantity supplied is zero; at P = $12, it supplies where P = MC. What does this illustrate?
options: The entire MC curve is supply even below AVC
ATC alone determines the firm’s supply
Market demand is the firm’s supply curve
The supply curve includes rising MC only above the shutdown threshold
medium.feedback: The shutdown threshold determines where the rising MC curve becomes the firm’s short-run supply.

medium.q: Ten firms each increase quantity supplied by 3 units when price rises. If no firms enter or exit, industry quantity supplied increases by:
medium.feedback: Industry supply sums the individual output responses: 10 × 3 = 30.

medium.q: Market demand increases in a competitive industry. Before entry occurs, the market price rises. How does one firm respond if its costs are unchanged?
options: It cuts price below the new market price to expand sales
Its P = MR line rises and it moves to a larger quantity on MC
Its ATC becomes the market supply curve
medium.feedback: The market price change is transmitted to the firm as a change in MR, producing movement along its supply curve.

medium.q: A competitive industry earns positive economic profit. What long-run sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Entry decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
Firms keep the profit permanently because they are price takers
Entry increases market supply, price falls, and economic profit is pushed toward zero
Exit decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
medium.feedback: Free entry expands industry supply and erodes positive economic profit.

medium.q: Firms in a competitive industry are sustaining economic losses. What long-run sequence is most likely?
options: Firms shut down for one day and long-run equilibrium is restored automatically
Exit reduces market supply, price rises, and losses are pushed toward zero
Entry raises supply, price falls, and losses deepen indefinitely
Exit raises supply and lowers price
medium.feedback: Long-run exit contracts industry supply and raises the market price relative to the loss-making situation.

medium.q: A firm has positive accounting profit but zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium. How can both be true?
options: Accounting profit can cover the owner’s implicit opportunity costs that economists count as costs
Accounting profit must always equal zero when economic profit is zero
The firm receives a subsidy equal to normal profit
medium.feedback: Economic cost includes owner-supplied resources, so accounting and economic profit need not be equal.

medium.q: A firm temporarily produces zero because price is below AVC, but managers expect conditions to improve next season. This is best described as:
options: Short-run shutdown rather than long-run exit
medium.feedback: A temporary zero-output choice can occur while the firm remains in the industry.

medium.q: For a representative firm in the standard constant-cost competitive benchmark, which condition is associated with long-run equilibrium?
options: P is below AVC while the firm continues forever
MR is zero at the profit-maximizing output
P = MR = MC and P equals minimum ATC
medium.feedback: At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.

medium.q: A competitive industry expands after demand rises. The larger industry raises land rents and skilled-worker wages, shifting firms’ ATC upward. Compared with the original long-run equilibrium, the new long-run price is most likely:
medium.feedback: In an increasing-cost industry, expansion raises input costs, so a higher price is required for zero-profit long-run equilibrium.

medium.q: Demand for an industry rises permanently. As firms enter, specialized suppliers expand and input costs fall. What long-run outcome is consistent with a decreasing-cost industry?
options: Industry output rises and the long-run equilibrium price can fall below its original level
Industry output falls and price must rise
The long-run supply curve must be vertical
medium.feedback: External cost reductions can shift firms’ costs down as the industry grows.

medium.q: Why is P = MC important for competitive allocative efficiency?
options: It means every firm earns positive economic profit
It makes all fixed costs disappear
The value buyers place on the last unit matches the opportunity cost of producing it
It guarantees equal incomes across consumers
medium.feedback: At P = MC, the marginal benefit reflected by price equals marginal resource cost.

medium.q: A representative competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium at the minimum point of ATC. What efficiency idea does that condition illustrate most directly?
medium.feedback: Producing at minimum ATC uses the least-cost scale available to the firm in the benchmark.

medium.q: Which observation is a limitation of using perfect competition as a literal description of many real markets?
options: Products may be differentiated and firms may have some control over price
All real markets contain many tiny firms selling identical products
Entry is always costless and instantaneous
Consumers never care about product differences
medium.feedback: The competitive model is a benchmark; many real markets relax one or more of its assumptions.

medium.q: A competitive allocation maximizes total surplus under the benchmark assumptions, but one household receives very little income. What does this illustrate?
options: The allocation cannot be efficient because incomes differ
Efficiency does not by itself guarantee an equitable distribution
medium.feedback: Total-surplus efficiency and distributional equity are separate evaluative questions.
