monopoly.title: Monopoly
monopoly.description: Analyze monopoly power, barriers to entry, demand and marginal revenue, output and price choice, profit and loss, welfare effects, natural-monopoly regulation, and price discrimination.

objectiveLabels.MON.1: Explain monopoly, market power, and the major barriers to entry.
objectiveLabels.MON.2: Calculate and interpret demand, total revenue, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a monopolist.
objectiveLabels.MON.3: Determine the monopolist’s profit-maximizing output and price using marginal analysis.
objectiveLabels.MON.4: Calculate and interpret monopoly profit, loss, shutdown, and cost changes.
objectiveLabels.MON.5: Compare monopoly and competitive outcomes using surplus, efficiency, and deadweight loss.
objectiveLabels.MON.6: Evaluate natural-monopoly regulation, price discrimination, and monopoly-policy tradeoffs.

easy.q: Which feature most directly distinguishes a monopoly from perfect competition?
options: A single seller is protected by substantial barriers to entry
Many sellers offer an identical product
Each firm faces a horizontal demand curve
easy.feedback: A monopoly is sustained by one seller and barriers that prevent competitive entry.

easy.q: A firm has market power when it can:
options: Choose any price and quantity without losing customers
Influence the price of its product within the limits imposed by demand
Force every consumer to buy the product
easy.feedback: Market power permits price influence, but demand still constrains the firm.

easy.q: Which is a legal barrier to entry?
options: A patent that grants temporary exclusive production rights
A competitive firm earning normal profit
easy.feedback: Patents are government-created, time-limited barriers.

easy.q: Control of the only commercially useful deposit of a critical mineral is an example of:
easy.feedback: Exclusive control of a necessary input can block entry.

easy.q: A network effect can strengthen monopoly power when:
options: The product becomes more valuable as more people use the same network
Average fixed cost rises with output
Consumers can resell the product freely
New firms face no coordination problem
easy.feedback: Network value can make switching and entry difficult.

easy.q: A natural monopoly usually exists because:
options: Marginal revenue equals price at every output
Average total cost falls over the relevant range of market demand
The firm owns a patent forever
easy.feedback: Large scale economies can make one supplier less costly than several.

easy.q: The demand curve facing a single-price monopolist is:
easy.feedback: With one seller, firm demand and market demand are the same.

easy.q: For a monopolist, average revenue equals:
options: Price and therefore the demand curve
easy.feedback: AR=TR/Q=P, so average revenue lies on demand.

easy.q: Why is marginal revenue below price for a single-price monopolist?
options: Selling another unit requires a lower price that also applies to earlier units
Marginal cost always exceeds average cost
The firm pays a tax on every unit
Fixed cost rises when output expands
easy.feedback: The price effect on previous units makes MR less than the new price.

easy.q: The output effect of selling one more unit is:
options: Revenue lost because all earlier units sell for less
Revenue gained from selling the additional unit
The decline in average total cost
easy.feedback: The added unit contributes its sale price to revenue.

easy.q: The price effect of selling one more unit is:
options: Revenue gained from the new unit
Revenue lost because the lower price applies to units already being sold
easy.feedback: A single-price monopolist must lower price on all units.

easy.q: When marginal revenue is positive, total revenue is:
easy.feedback: Positive MR means another unit adds to total revenue.

easy.q: For a downward-sloping linear demand curve, the marginal-revenue curve has:
options: The same price intercept and twice the slope
The same slope and half the price intercept
A horizontal shape at market price
A higher quantity intercept than demand
easy.feedback: Linear MR shares demand’s vertical intercept and is twice as steep.

easy.q: A single-price monopolist with nonnegative marginal cost will choose output on:
options: Only the unit-elastic point regardless of cost
easy.feedback: MR is positive on elastic demand; on inelastic demand, reducing output raises revenue and lowers cost.

easy.q: The standard monopoly output rule is to produce where:
options: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost on rising MC
Total revenue is highest regardless of cost
easy.feedback: MR=MC identifies the profit-maximizing quantity.

easy.q: After finding the monopoly quantity, the monopolist determines price by:
options: Reading the marginal-revenue curve at that quantity
Setting price equal to marginal cost
Reading the demand curve at that quantity
easy.feedback: Demand gives the highest price consumers will pay for the chosen quantity.

easy.q: If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost for the next unit, the monopolist should:
easy.feedback: That unit adds more revenue than cost.

easy.q: If marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue for the next unit, producing it would:
easy.feedback: The unit adds more cost than revenue.

easy.q: Monopoly profit per unit equals:
options: Marginal revenue minus average variable cost
easy.feedback: ATC includes all economic cost per unit.

easy.q: A monopoly can earn an economic loss because:
options: A monopoly is required to charge marginal cost
Barriers to entry force price below AVC
Its demand may be too weak relative to its costs
easy.feedback: Market power does not guarantee profitable demand and cost conditions.

easy.q: A loss-making monopolist should shut down in the short run when:
options: Price at its best output is below average variable cost
Price is below average total cost but above AVC
easy.feedback: The short-run shutdown rule still compares price with AVC.

easy.q: Why can monopoly economic profit persist in the long run?
options: Barriers prevent entry from expanding supply and eroding profit
easy.feedback: Barriers block the entry mechanism that removes competitive profit.

easy.q: Compared with perfect competition, a single-price monopoly generally charges:
options: A lower price and produces a higher quantity
A higher price and produces a lower quantity
A price equal to minimum ATC
easy.feedback: The monopoly restricts output where MR=MC rather than producing where P=MC.

easy.q: Monopoly deadweight loss represents:
options: All consumer surplus transferred to the firm
Total surplus lost because mutually beneficial units are not produced
easy.feedback: DWL is the value of trades between monopoly and efficient output that do not occur.

easy.q: Price above marginal cost signals:
easy.feedback: Consumers value additional units above their marginal production cost.

easy.q: Rent seeking occurs when resources are used to:
options: Obtain or protect monopoly privileges rather than produce valuable output
Expand output toward the efficient level
easy.feedback: Rent-seeking effort consumes resources to capture economic rents.

easy.q: Under marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly, the firm may require a subsidy because:
options: Price can fall below average total cost
easy.feedback: With declining ATC, MC lies below ATC, so P=MC may not cover total cost.

easy.q: Average-cost pricing regulation sets price where:
easy.feedback: P=ATC permits the regulated firm to cover economic cost.

easy.q: Price discrimination requires the seller to:
options: Separate customers and prevent profitable resale
Charge every buyer the same price
easy.feedback: Segmentation and limits on arbitrage are necessary.

easy.q: A third-degree price-discriminating monopolist generally charges the higher price to the group with:
options: The lowest willingness to pay at every quantity
easy.feedback: The less responsive group receives the larger markup.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what quantity does the monopolist maximize profit?
easy.feedback: Profit is maximized where MR intersects MC, which occurs at Q = 36.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing quantity, what price does the monopolist charge?
easy.feedback: After choosing Q = 36 from MR = MC, move up to demand; the demand curve shows P = $42.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What marginal-revenue value is shown at Q = 36?
easy.feedback: At Q = 36, the MR curve meets MC at $24.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What is average total cost at Q = 36?
easy.feedback: The ATC guide at the monopoly quantity is $27.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What quantity is selected where MR = MC?
easy.feedback: MR and MC intersect at Q = 40.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 40, what price is read from the demand curve?
easy.feedback: The demand curve shows P = $40 at Q = 40.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What is ATC at the monopoly quantity?
easy.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 40 is $45.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What output does the unregulated natural monopolist choose?
easy.feedback: The unregulated monopoly chooses Q where MR = MC, marked at Q = 45.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What price does demand indicate at the monopoly output?
easy.feedback: At Q = 45, the demand curve shows a price of $47.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what output does demand intersect marginal cost?
easy.feedback: With MC at $20, demand reaches MC at Q = 90.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Approximately what output does the unregulated monopolist choose where MR = MC?
easy.feedback: The MR curve reaches the $10 MC line at about Q = 70.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. What price does the demand curve show at the unregulated monopoly output?
easy.feedback: At about Q = 70, demand indicates a price of about $27.

easy.q: For a single-price monopolist, which curve also shows average revenue at each quantity?
options: A horizontal line at marginal revenue
easy.feedback: Because AR = TR/Q = P, average revenue lies on the monopolist’s demand curve.

easy.q: A monopolist charges $50, has ATC=$38, and sells 100 units. What is total economic profit?
easy.feedback: Profit per unit is $12 and total profit is $12 × 100.

easy.q: A monopolist charges $24 while ATC is $30 at its chosen output. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns $6 economic profit per unit
The firm must shut down immediately
The firm has an economic loss of $6 per unit
easy.feedback: When P<ATC, the firm incurs a loss equal to ATC−P per unit.

easy.q: A monopolist has P=$18, AVC=$12, and ATC=$25 at its best operating output. In the short run it should generally:
options: Exit permanently because any accounting loss requires exit
Produce only if price equals MC at every unit
Produce because price covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost
Shut down because price is below ATC
easy.feedback: A short-run loss does not imply shutdown when price remains above AVC.

easy.q: When a monopolist’s price equals ATC at its chosen output, economic profit is:
options: Positive because monopoly has market power
Negative because MR is below price
easy.feedback: P=ATC means revenue exactly covers explicit and implicit economic costs.

easy.q: Compared with an otherwise similar competitive market, a single-price monopoly typically produces:
options: Less output at a lower price
Less output at a higher price
More output at a lower price
The same output at the same price
easy.feedback: Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.

easy.q: Why is P>MC at the monopoly quantity evidence of allocative inefficiency?
options: Some buyers value additional units more than the marginal cost of producing them
The monopolist must be earning zero profit
Average total cost must be at its minimum
easy.feedback: When willingness to pay exceeds MC for foregone units, mutually beneficial trades are left unrealized.

easy.q: What does monopoly deadweight loss represent?
options: All profit earned by the monopolist
All consumer surplus transferred to the monopolist
Gains from trade lost because output is restricted below the efficient quantity
easy.feedback: Deadweight loss is surplus that disappears rather than being transferred between buyers and sellers.

easy.q: If firms spend resources lobbying for an exclusive monopoly privilege, those expenditures are an example of:
easy.feedback: Resources used to obtain or protect economic rents can create additional social cost.

easy.q: A monopoly price increase transfers some surplus from consumers to the firm. Is that entire transfer deadweight loss?
options: No; because monopoly never changes total surplus
No; transferred surplus changes who receives the surplus, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears
Yes; every dollar of monopoly profit is deadweight loss
Yes; consumer surplus and total surplus are identical
easy.feedback: Distributional transfers and efficiency losses are different pieces of monopoly welfare analysis.

easy.q: A natural monopoly is most likely when average total cost:
options: Falls over the relevant range of market demand
easy.feedback: Large scale economies over market demand can make one producer less costly than several.

easy.q: Under marginal-cost regulation, the regulator sets price equal to:
easy.feedback: P=MC targets allocative efficiency.

easy.q: Average-cost regulation generally targets a price equal to:
easy.feedback: P=ATC allows the regulated firm to cover economic cost including normal return.

easy.q: Why can P=MC create a financial problem for a natural monopoly?
options: The firm necessarily earns monopoly profit
When ATC exceeds MC, revenue may be insufficient to cover total cost
easy.feedback: Declining ATC often implies MC below ATC, so marginal-cost pricing can produce losses.

easy.q: A binding price cap below the unregulated monopoly price is intended primarily to:
options: Make the firm a price taker in an unregulated market
Limit the price the regulated monopolist may charge
easy.feedback: A price cap constrains the allowable price and can alter incentives and output.

easy.q: If a regulator sets P=ATC rather than P=MC, the main efficiency compromise is that:
options: Price may remain above marginal cost even though the firm can cover total cost
The firm must shut down immediately
The firm earns unlimited economic profit
easy.feedback: Average-cost pricing addresses financial viability but usually does not attain allocative efficiency.

easy.q: If a regulator requires P=MC and the firm would otherwise incur a loss, one possible policy response is:
options: Raise the price back to the unregulated monopoly level
Require output to fall until MR=0
Provide a subsidy financed outside the firm’s price revenue
easy.feedback: A subsidy can cover the gap between total cost and revenue under marginal-cost pricing.

easy.q: Which example best fits natural monopoly rather than a legal monopoly created only by statute?
options: A license limits taxi entry even though many firms could operate efficiently
A copyright protects a particular book
A single water network has lower ATC than duplicating pipes across several firms
A patent gives one pharmaceutical producer exclusive rights for a fixed term
easy.feedback: Natural monopoly is rooted in cost structure and economies of scale rather than legal exclusion alone.

easy.q: For price discrimination to be profitable, the seller generally needs:
options: Perfectly competitive pricing and free entry
Identical demand elasticity in every group
A requirement that price equal marginal cost
Market power and some ability to separate buyers by willingness to pay or demand responsiveness
easy.feedback: Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.

easy.q: Why must a price-discriminating seller often prevent resale between customer groups?
options: Resale guarantees the high-price group becomes less elastic
Resale forces average cost to zero
Low-price buyers could otherwise resell to high-price buyers and undermine the price difference
Resale would make marginal cost negative
easy.feedback: Arbitrage erodes segmented prices.

easy.q: A museum charges local students one price and tourists another based on verifiable group status. This is closest to:
easy.feedback: Third-degree discrimination separates identifiable groups and charges them different prices.

easy.q: All else equal, which customer group usually receives the higher markup under third-degree price discrimination?
options: The group with less elastic demand
The group with more elastic demand
The group with the lowest fixed cost
The group with the easiest resale opportunities
easy.feedback: Less responsive buyers support a larger markup over marginal cost.

easy.q: Under perfect first-degree price discrimination, the seller attempts to charge each buyer:
options: Marginal cost for every unit and nothing more
Average total cost regardless of willingness to pay
That buyer’s maximum willingness to pay for each unit
easy.feedback: Perfect first-degree discrimination extracts each unit’s willingness to pay.

easy.q: A theater can identify student status but students can freely transfer discounted tickets to anyone. Which requirement is missing?
options: Effective prevention of arbitrage or resale
easy.feedback: Identification alone is not enough if buyers can defeat segmentation through resale.

easy.q: A seller faces two separated groups with the same MC. Group A has more elastic demand than Group B. Which pricing pattern is generally expected?
options: Zero price in the more elastic group
A lower price in Group A and a higher price in Group B
A higher price in Group A and a lower price in Group B
The same price because MC is the same
easy.feedback: The more elastic group receives the smaller markup.

easy.q: Can price discrimination ever increase output relative to single-price monopoly?
options: Yes; serving additional low-value or elastic-market buyers can expand output in some cases
No; discrimination always leaves output unchanged
No; discrimination always eliminates all consumer purchases
Yes, but only if marginal cost is zero
easy.feedback: The welfare effect depends partly on whether discrimination expands or contracts total output.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $60, $56, $52, $48, $44, $40. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $72, $67, $62, $57, $52, $47. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $84, $78, $72, $66, $60, $54. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 4 to 5 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $55, $52, $49, $46, $43, $40. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $90, $83, $76, $69, $62, $55. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $64, $60, $56, $52, $48, $44. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 4 to 5 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $75, $70, $65, $60, $55, $50. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $96, $88, $80, $72, $64, $56. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q and marginal cost MC = 20 + 0Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 120 − 2Q and MC = 24 + 0Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 90 − 1.5Q and marginal cost MC = 18 + 0Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 110 − 2.5Q and MC = 20 + 0Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 96 − 1.6Q and marginal cost MC = 16 + 0.2Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 105 − 2.1Q and MC = 18 + 0.3Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 84 − 1.4Q and marginal cost MC = 14 + 0.2Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 115 − 2.5Q and MC = 25 + 0.25Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $60; ATC is $35 and AVC is $20. What is the correct short-run outcome?
medium.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $60; ATC is $65 and AVC is $20. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $100
medium.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 22.5 units at $56.25; ATC is $58.03 and AVC is $20.25. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $40
medium.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $70; ATC is $40 and AVC is $27.50. What is the correct short-run outcome?
medium.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 4.88 units at $60.24; ATC is $111.74 and AVC is $50.24. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $251.22
medium.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 19.33 units at $64.40; ATC is $54.52 and AVC is $20.90. What is the correct short-run outcome?
medium.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

medium.q: A single-price monopolist produces 20 units, while the competitive benchmark is 40 units. What does the output gap represent?
options: Mutually beneficial units not produced by the monopoly
Units that cost more than buyers value
medium.feedback: Between Qm and Qc, demand exceeds MC, so those units would create surplus.

medium.q: For a market with monopoly price $66.19 and competitive price $26.36 under the stated linear demand and MC, which statement is correct?
options: All consumer loss becomes monopoly profit
Monopoly transfers some surplus and destroys additional surplus
medium.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

medium.q: A single-price monopolist produces 22.73 units, while the competitive benchmark is 41.67 units. What does the output gap represent?
options: Units that cost more than buyers value
Mutually beneficial units not produced by the monopoly
medium.feedback: Between Qm and Qc, demand exceeds MC, so those units would create surplus.

medium.q: For a market with monopoly price $74.33 and competitive price $32.04 under the stated linear demand and MC, which statement is correct?
options: All consumer loss becomes monopoly profit
Monopoly transfers some surplus and destroys additional surplus
medium.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

medium.q: A natural monopoly regulated at marginal cost has P < ATC. What additional policy issue arises?
options: The firm needs a subsidy or another way to cover its loss
The firm earns monopoly profit automatically
Output must be reduced below monopoly output
medium.feedback: P=MC can be efficient but fail to cover fixed cost.

medium.q: Compared with marginal-cost pricing, average-cost pricing for a natural monopoly generally produces:
options: A lower price and higher output with larger losses
A higher price and lower output but avoids an operating subsidy
The unregulated monopoly price and output
medium.feedback: P=ATC covers cost but leaves P above MC.

medium.q: A theater charges students less than adults for the same seat. Which condition is essential for the pricing strategy to work?
options: Students must have less elastic demand
Marginal cost must differ by buyer
Adults cannot cheaply buy and use student tickets
The theater must face horizontal demand
medium.feedback: Arbitrage would undermine segmented prices.

medium.q: Two customer groups have the same marginal cost, but Group A has less elastic demand than Group B. A profit-maximizing discriminator will usually:
options: Charge Group B a higher price
Charge both groups the same price regardless of elasticity
Charge Group A a higher price
medium.feedback: The less elastic market supports a larger markup.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the monopolist’s economic profit per unit at Q = 36?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC: $42 − $27 = $15.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit?
medium.feedback: Total profit is ($42 − $27) × 36 = $540.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Compared with the D = MC benchmark, how many fewer units does the monopoly produce?
medium.feedback: The monopoly produces 36 units, while D = MC occurs at 60, a difference of 24 units.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What price is associated with the D = MC benchmark?
medium.feedback: Demand and MC intersect at Q = 60 and P = $30.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What economic loss per unit is shown at Q = 40?
medium.feedback: Price is $40 and ATC is $45, so the loss is $5 per unit.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the total economic loss at the monopoly output?
medium.feedback: The firm loses $5 on each of 40 units, for a total loss of $200.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the monopoly quantity, what common value do MR and MC have?
medium.feedback: The MR and MC curves meet at $20 when Q = 40.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Approximately what quantity and price mark the D = MC benchmark?
medium.feedback: The graph marks the demand-MC intersection at about Q = 67 and P = $27.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, what is economic profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit is $47 − $24 = $23.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at Q = 45?
medium.feedback: Economic profit is ($47 − $24) × 45 = $1,035.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What price corresponds to the D = MC quantity?
medium.feedback: Demand intersects the horizontal MC curve at P = $20 and Q = 90.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Which marked outcome corresponds to average-cost, or fair-return, pricing?
medium.feedback: Fair-return pricing sets price equal to ATC; the graph marks D = ATC near Q = 116 and P = $16.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Which marked outcome corresponds to marginal-cost pricing?
medium.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing sets demand price equal to MC, shown at Q = 140 and P = $10.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the marginal-cost-pricing output, what is the economic loss per unit?
medium.feedback: The per-unit loss is ATC minus price: $15 − $10 = $5.

medium.q: A town currently has one ambulance provider, but licenses are readily available and several firms can enter with ordinary equipment. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The current one-seller market does not by itself establish durable monopoly power
The provider is a natural monopoly because only one firm operates today
The provider must have a patent protecting ambulance service
The provider can charge any price because entry has not happened yet
medium.feedback: A monopoly requires meaningful barriers to entry, not merely one seller at a moment in time.

medium.q: A patented medical device is profitable while the patent remains in force. What is the patent doing economically?
options: Making the firm’s demand curve horizontal
Forcing marginal revenue to equal price
Guaranteeing that average total cost will fall forever
Restricting entry and helping preserve the incumbent’s market power
medium.feedback: A patent is a legal barrier that can prevent rivals from copying the protected product.

medium.q: A messaging platform becomes more useful as more friends and businesses join it. Why can this discourage entry by a rival platform?
options: The rival automatically faces perfectly inelastic demand
Network effects remove the need for consumer choice
Users may prefer the established network because its large user base raises its value
The incumbent’s marginal cost must be zero
medium.feedback: Network effects can create a demand-side barrier because users value access to the existing network.

medium.q: A firm owns the only economically viable source of a rare input required to make a specialized product. Which mechanism protects its market position most directly?
options: Its customers cannot respond to price changes
Control of an essential resource blocks rivals from obtaining a necessary input
Its price must equal marginal cost
Its fixed costs disappear as output rises
medium.feedback: Exclusive control of a critical resource can prevent otherwise capable rivals from entering.

medium.q: A regional water network requires an enormous pipe system, and duplicating the network would raise average cost. Which fact best supports natural-monopoly status?
options: One firm can serve market demand at lower average cost than multiple duplicative networks
The provider has the legal right to discriminate among all buyers
The firm earns accounting profit in the current year
medium.feedback: Natural monopoly comes from scale economies over the relevant range of market demand.

medium.q: A monopolist cuts price to sell one additional unit. Why can marginal revenue be far below the new price?
options: Average revenue becomes zero when price falls
The demand curve becomes horizontal after the price cut
The extra unit adds revenue, but the lower price also reduces revenue collected on earlier units
Marginal cost is automatically subtracted from marginal revenue
medium.feedback: Marginal revenue reflects both the output effect and the price effect on units already sold.

medium.q: At 40 units a monopolist has MR=$28 and MC=$22; at 41 units MR=$24 and MC=$25. Which output is the better marginal choice?
options: 40 units, because the 41st unit costs more at the margin than it adds to revenue
41 units, because price must still exceed marginal revenue
41 units, because a monopolist always produces until price equals MC
40 units only if average total cost is minimized there
medium.feedback: Produce units for which MR covers MC and stop before the next unit has MC greater than MR.

medium.q: A monopolist has already found its profit-maximizing quantity using MR=MC. What is the next step for determining the monopoly price?
options: Use the MR curve value as the price
Set price equal to average total cost
Choose the lowest price on the demand curve
Move up to the demand curve at that quantity
medium.feedback: MR determines the quantity condition; demand gives the price buyers will pay for that quantity.

medium.q: Suppose competition would produce 100 units at $20, while monopoly produces 70 units at $35. Which change is the clearest source of efficiency loss?
options: The 30 units between 70 and 100 that would have generated gains from trade are not produced
The monopolist receives revenue on the 70 units it sells
The market price is written in dollars rather than units
Consumers buy positive quantities under monopoly
medium.feedback: The efficiency loss comes from mutually beneficial transactions forgone because of restricted output.

medium.q: If a monopolist reduces output farther below the competitive quantity while demand and cost curves are unchanged, what generally happens to deadweight loss?
options: It necessarily falls because the firm earns more profit
It becomes zero when price rises
It is unchanged because transfers do not matter
It increases because more mutually beneficial units are forgone
medium.feedback: Greater output restriction usually widens the range of lost gains from trade.

medium.q: A natural monopoly has MC=$12 and ATC=$20 at the allocatively efficient quantity. If regulation sets P=$12, which outcome is most likely without a subsidy?
options: The firm must reduce output to zero by definition
The firm incurs an economic loss because price is below ATC
The firm earns $8 profit per unit
The firm breaks even because P=MC
medium.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.

medium.q: A regulator sets price where demand intersects ATC for a natural monopoly. Which combination best describes the result?
options: The firm can cover total economic cost, but price generally remains above MC
The firm earns maximum monopoly profit and output falls to zero
Price equals MC and allocative efficiency is guaranteed
The firm necessarily faces a horizontal demand curve
medium.feedback: Average-cost pricing aims for financial viability, not full P=MC efficiency.

medium.q: A price cap is set above the price the monopolist would charge without regulation. What is the immediate effect?
options: The firm must charge the cap even if it prefers a lower price
The firm’s fixed cost becomes zero
The cap is nonbinding and does not constrain the firm’s chosen price
medium.feedback: A ceiling above the unregulated price does not bind.

medium.q: A regulator wants lower prices but also wants the utility to maintain infrastructure and innovate. Which concern best captures the tradeoff?
options: Investment incentives are unrelated to expected returns
Any regulation automatically produces the competitive quantity
Aggressive price limits can improve consumer terms while weakening incentives or revenue for cost recovery and investment
Lower prices always increase monopoly profit
medium.feedback: Regulation balances static consumer/efficiency goals against financial and dynamic incentives.

medium.q: Demand for a utility expands enough that the relevant output range moves beyond the region where ATC is falling. What does that suggest about the natural-monopoly argument?
options: It guarantees marginal cost is zero
It may weaken because one firm may no longer have a cost advantage over multiple firms across the new relevant range
It becomes stronger automatically because demand increased
It proves that price discrimination is efficient
medium.feedback: Natural-monopoly status depends on cost conditions over the relevant market-demand range.

medium.q: A firm has market power and observes two groups with different demand elasticities, but buyers can costlessly resell the product. What happens to the proposed two-price strategy?
options: The firm can preserve both prices indefinitely
The high-price group automatically becomes less elastic
Marginal cost becomes different across groups
Arbitrage tends to collapse the price difference
medium.feedback: Segmentation must be enforceable; costless resale undermines differentiated prices.

medium.q: Why does a third-degree discriminator compare MR from each market with the common MC?
options: Average revenue must equal average cost in every market
Profit is increased by allocating another unit to a market whenever that market’s MR exceeds MC
The firm must make prices identical across markets
medium.feedback: The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.

medium.q: Two groups have identical MC. Seniors have less elastic demand than students. What happens to the optimal markup?
medium.feedback: A less elastic market supports a larger markup over common marginal cost.

medium.q: Compared with a single-price monopoly, perfect first-degree price discrimination can eliminate the standard output deadweight loss when:
options: The firm sells every unit for which willingness to pay is at least MC
The firm charges one common price above MC
The firm ignores willingness to pay
medium.feedback: Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.

medium.q: A discriminatory pricing plan raises total output by serving a new low-price market. What is the most defensible welfare conclusion?
options: Total surplus must fall because prices differ
Consumer surplus must rise in every group
Total surplus may rise because additional mutually beneficial trades occur, though distribution also changes
medium.feedback: Welfare effects depend on output as well as how surplus is redistributed.

medium.q: An airline sells a discounted ticket that cannot be transferred and imposes restrictions that separate leisure from business travelers. What economic purpose do the restrictions serve?
options: They force the same elasticity in both groups
They eliminate the airline’s fixed costs
They help prevent arbitrage and maintain market segmentation
They make the airline a price taker
medium.feedback: Restrictions can help keep low-price buyers from reselling or masquerading as high-value segments.

medium.q: A firm can separate buyers perfectly but faces a perfectly competitive market with many identical sellers. Why is discrimination difficult to sustain?
options: Buyer groups necessarily have identical elasticities
The firm lacks enough market power to set different markups without losing customers
Resale prevention becomes irrelevant only because MC is zero
medium.feedback: Segmentation is not enough; the seller also needs pricing power.

medium.q: A monopolist starts charging different prices to two isolated groups. The high-price group is observed to have less elastic demand. Which fact best explains the pricing pattern?
options: Optimal monopoly markup is inversely related to demand responsiveness
The high-price group must have higher marginal cost
The low-price group must have higher fixed cost
Price discrimination requires equal prices when MC is common
medium.feedback: Lower elasticity supports a larger markup over marginal cost.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Q1 is selected where MR intersects MC. What does P1 represent?
options: The price on the demand curve at Q1
hard.feedback: Quantity comes from MR=MC; price comes from demand.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison determines whether the monopolist earns economic profit at Q1?
options: P1 compared with MC at Q1
P1 compared with ATC at Q1
MR compared with demand at Q1
ATC compared with AVC at zero output
hard.feedback: Profit per unit is P−ATC.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. At Q1, why is price greater than marginal revenue?
options: Lowering price to sell Q1 creates a price effect on prior units
hard.feedback: For single-price monopoly, MR reflects both the output and price effects.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose fixed cost rises while demand, MR, and MC remain unchanged. What happens in the short run?
options: Q1 and P1 remain unchanged, but profit falls
hard.feedback: Fixed cost shifts ATC but does not change the MR=MC output.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. If P1 equals ATC at Q1, the monopoly earns:
options: Zero economic profit while covering all opportunity costs
A loss equal to fixed cost
Positive profit because P1 exceeds MC
hard.feedback: P=ATC means all explicit and implicit costs are covered.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. P1 is below ATC but above AVC at Q1. What should the monopolist do?
options: Shut down because P1 is below ATC
Produce Q1 and minimize its short-run loss
hard.feedback: Covering AVC and part of fixed cost reduces the loss.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. What is the monopolist’s total economic loss if the vertical gap between ATC and P1 is L?
options: One-half of L multiplied by Q1
The gap between P1 and MC multiplied by Q1
hard.feedback: Loss is a rectangle: loss per unit times output.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the MR = MC rule remain relevant even when the monopolist is taking an economic loss?
options: It identifies the shutdown price directly
It makes price equal marginal cost
It identifies the output that minimizes the loss, provided price covers AVC
hard.feedback: Marginal analysis chooses the best feasible output, not necessarily a profitable one.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. The best available price is below AVC. What should the monopolist do in the short run?
options: Produce zero in the short run
Ignore AVC because it has market power
hard.feedback: Price below AVC means revenue cannot cover avoidable cost.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. After short-run shutdown, which cost remains?
options: Variable cost of the unproduced units
hard.feedback: Shutdown avoids variable cost but not short-run fixed cost.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Q1 is monopoly output and Q2 is the D=MC quantity. The interval from Q1 to Q2 consists of units for which:
options: Average total cost is necessarily falling
Buyer willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost
hard.feedback: Those omitted units would add to total surplus.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Which area concept is created by restricting output from Q2 to Q1?
options: A transfer equal to all monopoly profit
hard.feedback: The restriction eliminates trades with positive net benefit.

hard.q: A monopolist faces P=100−2Q, MC=20+0Q, and fixed cost $300. Which sequence correctly solves the problem?
options: Set MR=MC for Q, use demand for P, then compare P with ATC
Set demand=MC for Q, use MR for P, then compare P with AVC
Minimize ATC for Q, set P=MC, then calculate revenue
Choose the highest price, then produce the demanded quantity
hard.feedback: Monopoly analysis proceeds quantity, price, then profit or loss.

hard.q: For demand P=100−2Q and MC=20+0Q, the competitive benchmark quantity is 40 and monopoly quantity is 20. Why are they different?
options: Competition uses MR=MC, while monopoly uses P=ATC
Competition uses P=MC, while monopoly uses MR=MC
Monopoly minimizes ATC, while competition maximizes revenue
Monopoly has lower marginal cost at every quantity
hard.feedback: MR lies below demand, so MR=MC occurs at a lower quantity than P=MC.

hard.q: A monopolist faces P=120−3Q, MC=18+0Q, and fixed cost $420. Which sequence correctly solves the problem?
options: Set demand=MC for Q, use MR for P, then compare P with AVC
Minimize ATC for Q, set P=MC, then calculate revenue
Set MR=MC for Q, use demand for P, then compare P with ATC
Choose the highest price, then produce the demanded quantity
hard.feedback: Monopoly analysis proceeds quantity, price, then profit or loss.

hard.q: For demand P=120−3Q and MC=18+0Q, the competitive benchmark quantity is 34 and monopoly quantity is 17. Why are they different?
options: Competition uses MR=MC, while monopoly uses P=ATC
Monopoly minimizes ATC, while competition maximizes revenue
Monopoly has lower marginal cost at every quantity
Competition uses P=MC, while monopoly uses MR=MC
hard.feedback: MR lies below demand, so MR=MC occurs at a lower quantity than P=MC.

hard.q: A monopolist faces P=108−2Q, MC=24+0.4Q, and fixed cost $360. Which sequence correctly solves the problem?
options: Set MR=MC for Q, use demand for P, then compare P with ATC
Set demand=MC for Q, use MR for P, then compare P with AVC
Minimize ATC for Q, set P=MC, then calculate revenue
Choose the highest price, then produce the demanded quantity
hard.feedback: Monopoly analysis proceeds quantity, price, then profit or loss.

hard.q: For demand P=108−2Q and MC=24+0.4Q, the competitive benchmark quantity is 35 and monopoly quantity is 19.09. Why are they different?
options: Competition uses MR=MC, while monopoly uses P=ATC
Competition uses P=MC, while monopoly uses MR=MC
Monopoly minimizes ATC, while competition maximizes revenue
Monopoly has lower marginal cost at every quantity
hard.feedback: MR lies below demand, so MR=MC occurs at a lower quantity than P=MC.

hard.q: A monopolist faces P=96−1.5Q, MC=18+0.3Q, and fixed cost $300. Which sequence correctly solves the problem?
options: Set demand=MC for Q, use MR for P, then compare P with AVC
Minimize ATC for Q, set P=MC, then calculate revenue
Set MR=MC for Q, use demand for P, then compare P with ATC
Choose the highest price, then produce the demanded quantity
hard.feedback: Monopoly analysis proceeds quantity, price, then profit or loss.

hard.q: For demand P=96−1.5Q and MC=18+0.3Q, the competitive benchmark quantity is 43.33 and monopoly quantity is 23.64. Why are they different?
options: Competition uses MR=MC, while monopoly uses P=ATC
Monopoly minimizes ATC, while competition maximizes revenue
Monopoly has lower marginal cost at every quantity
Competition uses P=MC, while monopoly uses MR=MC
hard.feedback: MR lies below demand, so MR=MC occurs at a lower quantity than P=MC.

hard.q: A natural monopoly has MC=$12, fixed cost $900, and demand P=100−1.2Q. Under marginal-cost pricing, what is its operating result?
hard.feedback: At P=MC, revenue covers variable cost but not the fixed cost.

hard.q: Why does average-cost regulation usually produce less output than marginal-cost regulation for a natural monopoly?
options: Average cost pricing sets P below MC
The regulated price remains above MC
It raises marginal revenue above demand
hard.feedback: P=ATC covers cost but exceeds marginal cost.

hard.q: A price cap lets a natural monopoly keep cost savings until the cap is reviewed. What incentive does this create?
options: An automatic guarantee of allocative efficiency
A stronger incentive to reduce cost, with possible quality risks
A requirement to increase fixed cost
hard.feedback: A fixed cap rewards cost reduction but can encourage quality cuts.

hard.q: A regulator cannot observe the monopoly’s true cost curve. Which problem does this create?
options: The firm loses all market power automatically
The regulator may set a price that is too high, too low, or weakens cost incentives
hard.feedback: Regulation depends on imperfect cost and demand information.

hard.q: Which statement best describes the natural-monopoly policy problem?
options: One firm may minimize production cost, yet unregulated pricing restricts output
Multiple firms always have lower ATC
Marginal-cost pricing always covers total cost
hard.feedback: Natural monopoly creates a production-cost advantage and a pricing problem.

hard.q: A seller can identify two groups with different elasticities, but customers can freely resell. What blocks third-degree price discrimination?
hard.feedback: Resale lets low-price buyers undercut the high-price market.

hard.q: Under perfect first-degree price discrimination, why can output reach the efficient quantity?
options: Marginal revenue remains below every buyer’s price
The firm sets one price above demand
The seller serves every buyer whose willingness to pay covers marginal cost
Consumer surplus causes output to contract
hard.feedback: Unit-specific pricing makes the marginal buyer’s price equal willingness to pay.

hard.q: Perfect first-degree discrimination eliminates the single-price monopoly DWL but:
options: Forces the seller to earn zero profit
Transfers the benchmark consumer surplus to the seller
hard.feedback: Efficiency can rise while distribution shifts sharply.

hard.q: A group-pricing scheme increases total output relative to one-price monopoly. What is the most defensible welfare conclusion?
options: Total welfare may rise, though distribution across groups changes
Consumer surplus must rise for every group
The policy is identical to perfect competition
hard.feedback: Output expansion can recover trades, but consumer effects differ.

hard.q: A software firm charges a lower price in a market with highly elastic demand. The economic rationale is:
options: The elastic market has higher willingness to pay at every quantity
The elastic market requires a smaller markup over marginal cost
The firm’s marginal cost is necessarily lower there
hard.feedback: Optimal markups are smaller where demand is more responsive.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, why is the price read from demand above marginal revenue?
options: An extra sale requires lowering price on earlier units
Marginal cost is already embedded in the downward demand curve
Average total cost must exceed marginal revenue at every output
The monopolist takes a fixed market price on all units sold
hard.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, expanding sales lowers the price received on previous units, so MR lies below price.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Why would moving output from 36 toward 60 units reduce profit?
options: Demand exceeds ATC over the entire interval
Price becomes greater than marginal revenue
hard.feedback: Once output passes MR = MC, the additional units cost more at the margin than they add to revenue.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. At the monopoly output, what is the markup of price over marginal cost?
hard.feedback: At Q = 36, P = $42 and MC = $24, so the markup is $18.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison correctly describes the monopoly outcome and the D = MC benchmark?
options: Monopoly: P = $30, Q = 60; benchmark: P = $42, Q = 36
Monopoly: P = $24, Q = 36; benchmark: P = $27, Q = 60
Monopoly and the benchmark both have P = $30 and Q = 60
Monopoly: P = $42, Q = 36; D = MC benchmark: P = $30, Q = 60
hard.feedback: The monopoly restricts output to 36 and charges $42; the D = MC benchmark is 60 units at $30.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison shows that the monopolist is taking an economic loss?
options: Price $40 is above MR $20 at Q = 40
MC $20 is below demand at Q = 40
Price $40 is below ATC $45 at Q = 40
hard.feedback: Economic profit depends on price relative to ATC. Here P < ATC at the chosen quantity.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Why is Q = 67 not the profit-maximizing monopoly output?
options: At Q = 67, marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue
At Q = 67, price is greater than marginal cost
At Q = 67, ATC is necessarily zero
The monopolist must always choose the demand intercept
hard.feedback: A monopolist maximizes profit where MR = MC, not where demand equals MC.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. What is the monopoly markup over marginal cost at Q = 40?
hard.feedback: At Q = 40, price is $40 and MC is $20, a $20 markup.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Relative to the D = MC benchmark, the monopoly approximately:
options: Produces 27 more units and charges $13 less
Produces 20 fewer units and charges $5 more
Produces 27 fewer units and charges $13 more
Produces the same quantity but charges $20 more
hard.feedback: The monopoly is at Q = 40, P = $40; the benchmark is about Q = 67, P = $27.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. How much output is withheld by the unregulated monopoly relative to D = MC?
hard.feedback: The monopoly produces 45 rather than 90 units, a 45-unit restriction.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. At the regulated output shown, how large is price minus marginal cost?
hard.feedback: At the monopoly output, P = $47 and MC = $20, so the markup is $27.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Which feature is consistent with a natural monopoly over the relevant range?
options: ATC declines as output expands toward the efficient quantity
MR is horizontal across the relevant output range
Demand becomes perfectly elastic near the efficient output
MC rises faster than demand throughout the relevant range
hard.feedback: Declining ATC over the relevant output range signals economies of scale that can support natural monopoly.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. What total loss would the regulated firm incur at Q = 140 under marginal-cost pricing?
hard.feedback: A $5 loss per unit on 140 units equals $700.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Why does the fair-return outcome near Q = 116 and P = $16 imply approximately zero economic profit?
options: P = ATC at the fair-return output
P = MR at the fair-return output
MC = ATC at the $10 regulated price
Total revenue equals zero near Q = 116
hard.feedback: Average-cost pricing sets P = ATC, covering economic costs without positive economic profit.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Which ordering of quantities is shown?
options: Marginal-cost output < fair-return output < unregulated monopoly
Unregulated monopoly < fair-return output < marginal-cost output
Fair-return output < unregulated monopoly < marginal-cost output
All three policies produce the same quantity

boss.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change does not alter MR, MC, or demand.

boss.q: Refer to the graph. At the monopoly output shown, what total cost is implied by ATC before comparing it with revenue?
boss.feedback: ATC is $45 at Q = 40, so total cost is $45 × 40 = $1,800.

boss.q: Monopoly output is 19.05 and the efficient output is 36.36. Which condition identifies the efficient benchmark?
boss.feedback: The competitive benchmark produces until marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

boss.q: The demand–MC gap at monopoly output is $38.10 and the quantity gap between monopoly and efficient output is 17.32. What is monopoly deadweight loss?
boss.feedback: Use the area of the lost-trade triangle.

boss.q: When a single-price monopolist raises price and restricts output relative to the competitive benchmark, what happens to the resulting loss of consumer surplus?
options: Part becomes producer surplus and part becomes deadweight loss
Total surplus rises by the full loss
boss.feedback: The price increase transfers surplus on units sold; output restriction destroys surplus.

boss.q: Monopoly output is 19.79 and the efficient output is 37.25. Which condition identifies the efficient benchmark?

boss.q: The demand–MC gap at monopoly output is $44.53 and the quantity gap between monopoly and efficient output is 17.46. What is monopoly deadweight loss?
boss.feedback: Use the area of the lost-trade triangle.

boss.q: How is the loss of consumer surplus from monopoly pricing divided between transfers and deadweight loss?
options: Total surplus rises by the full loss
Part becomes producer surplus and part becomes deadweight loss
boss.feedback: The price increase transfers surplus on units sold; output restriction destroys surplus.

boss.q: A natural monopoly has demand P = 100 − 1.2Q and constant MC = $12. Which output is allocatively efficient?
boss.feedback: Set demand equal to MC.

boss.q: A natural monopoly has large fixed costs, so ATC remains above MC at the efficient output. Why would marginal-cost pricing create an economic loss?
options: ATC remains above MC because large fixed cost is spread over output
The regulation raises fixed cost per unit indefinitely
boss.feedback: P=MC does not cover the natural monopoly’s fixed cost.

boss.q: For a regulated natural monopoly, what does average-cost pricing typically accomplish?
options: It restores the unregulated monopoly output
It permits cost recovery but leaves price above MC
It eliminates all regulatory information problems
boss.feedback: P=ATC balances solvency against allocative efficiency.

It restores the unregulated monopoly output
It eliminates all regulatory information problems

boss.q: A monopolist can separate two markets and prevent resale between them. With a common marginal cost, what marginal condition maximizes profit?

Set the two prices equal regardless of demand
Set MR in each market equal to the common marginal cost
Set demand equal to MR in both markets
boss.feedback: The last unit in each market must contribute the same marginal revenue equal to MC.

boss.q: A price-discriminating monopolist charges $60 in Market A and $50 in Market B. What best explains the difference?
options: Marginal cost must differ by the full price gap
The seller has no market power in the lower-price group
The groups have different demand responsiveness, so optimal markups differ
boss.feedback: Different elasticities support different markups over the same MC.

boss.q: What condition is necessary for different monopoly prices across two customer groups to persist?

Both groups must have identical demand
The seller must charge below MC in one group
Consumer surplus must be zero in both groups
boss.feedback: Arbitrage would collapse the segmented prices.

boss.q: A monopolist can price discriminate across two isolated markets with the same marginal cost. How should it allocate sales at the margin?
options: Set each price equal to average total cost
Set MR in each market equal to the common marginal cost
Set the two prices equal regardless of demand
Set demand equal to MR in both markets
boss.feedback: The last unit in each market must contribute the same marginal revenue equal to MC.

boss.q: A price-discriminating monopolist charges $72 in Market A and $57 in Market B. What best explains the difference?
options: Marginal cost must differ by the full price gap
The groups have different demand responsiveness, so optimal markups differ

boss.feedback: Different elasticities support different markups over the same MC.

boss.q: Why must a price-discriminating monopolist generally prevent resale between low-price and high-price customers?
options: Both groups must have identical demand
The seller must charge below MC in one group
Consumer surplus must be zero in both groups
Low-price customers cannot profitably resell to high-price customers
boss.feedback: Arbitrage would collapse the segmented prices.

boss.q: Refer to the graph. Which comparison best captures the unregulated monopoly outcome and the allocatively efficient outcome?

Unregulated: Q = 45, P = $47; efficient D = MC: Q = 90, P = $20
Unregulated: Q = 45, P = $20; efficient: Q = 90, P = $47

boss.feedback: MR = MC determines the unregulated monopoly output, while D = MC identifies the allocatively efficient benchmark.

boss.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly contrasts fair-return pricing with marginal-cost pricing?

Both rules preserve the unregulated price near $27 and leave output close to Q = 70
MC pricing produces less output than fair-return pricing because the MC curve is horizontal
Fair-return covers ATC near Q = 116; MC pricing reaches Q = 140 but P < ATC
boss.feedback: The graph shows the classic tradeoff: average-cost pricing supports break-even, while marginal-cost pricing reaches the efficient quantity but may require a subsidy.
