oligopoly.title: Oligopoly
oligopoly.description: Analyze few-firm strategic interdependence, concentration, payoff matrices, Nash equilibrium, collusion, cartels, repeated interaction, entry deterrence, welfare, mergers, and policy tradeoffs.

objectiveLabels.OLI.1: Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
objectiveLabels.OLI.2: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
objectiveLabels.OLI.3: Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
objectiveLabels.OLI.4: Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
objectiveLabels.OLI.5: Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
objectiveLabels.OLI.6: Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

easy.q: Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition?
options: Firms must account for likely rival responses
Firms can enter and exit the market freely.
Each firm is a price taker
easy.feedback: Strategic interdependence is the defining behavioral feature of oligopoly.

easy.q: A duopoly is:
easy.feedback: Duopoly is the two-firm special case of oligopoly.

easy.q: Products in an oligopoly may be:
easy.feedback: Oligopoly describes market structure, not a single product type.

easy.q: Why do barriers to entry matter in oligopoly?
options: They make incumbent firms price takers.
They help a few incumbent firms retain large market shares
easy.feedback: Entry barriers help sustain concentration.

easy.q: A four-firm concentration ratio is calculated by:
options: Adding the market shares of the four largest firms
The sum of squared shares for every firm and competitive fringe participant
easy.feedback: A concentration ratio sums selected leading shares.

easy.q: The HHI is calculated by:
options: Adding the four largest shares only
Dividing market demand by firm count
easy.feedback: HHI weights larger firms more heavily through squaring.

easy.q: Why does market definition matter when measuring concentration?
options: It fixes the number of firms that must be included at four.
It determines the legal price ceiling
Changing product or geographic boundaries changes which firms and sales are included
easy.feedback: Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.

easy.q: In game theory, a strategy is:
options: The payoff received by every player
The payoff a player receives after all firms choose.
A possible action or plan available to a player
easy.feedback: Strategies are the choices available to players.

easy.q: In a payoff pair written (8, 5), the first number usually belongs to:
easy.feedback: The standard stated order is row player first, column player second.

easy.q: A best response is:
options: The strategy that maximizes the firms’ combined payoff.
The strategy producing the highest payoff given the rival’s action
The strategy with the lowest fixed cost
easy.feedback: A best response is conditional on what the other player does.

easy.q: A dominant strategy is one that:
options: The action associated with the highest payoff in one isolated cell only
Always gives both firms equal payoffs
Produces a higher payoff than the player’s alternatives for every rival action
easy.feedback: Dominance is a comparison across every possible rival action.

easy.q: A Nash equilibrium occurs when:
options: The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
Each player is choosing a best response to the other
easy.feedback: No player can improve by changing alone.

easy.q: Why can a Nash equilibrium be inefficient?
options: Mutual best responses need not maximize joint payoff
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
easy.feedback: Individual incentives can lead to a jointly inferior outcome.

easy.q: A prisoner’s dilemma describes a situation in which:
options: Individually attractive choices can make all players worse off
The jointly best outcome is always a Nash equilibrium.
easy.feedback: The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.

easy.q: Collusion occurs when firms:
options: Independently choose the same price after a common cost shock.
easy.feedback: Collusion involves coordinated conduct.

easy.q: A cartel is:
options: A group of firms that happen to charge similar prices without coordinating.
A group of firms coordinating output or price
easy.feedback: A cartel attempts to act collectively like a monopoly.

easy.q: A profit-maximizing cartel chooses total output where:
options: Industry marginal revenue equals industry marginal cost
Market price equals industry marginal cost.
easy.feedback: The cartel uses the monopoly marginal rule for joint output.

easy.q: Why does a cartel member often want to cheat?
options: Selling extra output at the cartel price can raise its own profit
Cheating guarantees that other members keep cooperating forever.
easy.feedback: Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.

easy.q: Which factor makes cartel cheating harder?
options: Reliable monitoring of member prices and output
A shorter expected relationship among cartel members.
easy.feedback: Monitoring increases the chance that cheating is detected.

easy.q: Repeated interaction may support cooperation because:
options: Future punishment guarantees cooperation regardless of observability or credibility
Current cheating can trigger costly future punishment
easy.feedback: Future consequences can change current incentives.

easy.q: A threat is credible when:
options: Carrying it out remains in the threatening firm’s interest later
It would hurt only the rival
The announced response is credible because it sounds severe and harms the entrant
easy.feedback: Credibility requires sequential rationality.

easy.q: A price war is most likely to:
options: Guarantee higher profit for every firm
Reduce margins for several rival firms
easy.feedback: Aggressive price cutting can damage all firms’ profits.

easy.q: Tacit coordination differs from explicit collusion because tacit coordination:
options: Occurs only when every firm charges exactly the same price.
Can occur without an explicit agreement
easy.feedback: Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.

easy.q: Price leadership occurs when:
options: The largest firm has legal authority to set every rival’s price.
Other firms follow a price announced by a leading firm
easy.feedback: Following can occur without formal control.

easy.q: Nonprice competition includes competition through:
options: Coordinating output quotas with rival firms.
easy.feedback: Oligopolists often compete on several dimensions.

easy.q: Limit pricing refers to:
options: Setting the monopoly price after entry occurs.
Keeping price low partly to discourage entry
easy.feedback: The incumbent may sacrifice current profit to affect entry.

easy.q: What does the kinked-demand model primarily attempt to explain?
options: How firms determine the original market price.
Price rigidity around an existing price
easy.feedback: The model explains rigidity, not the initial price.

easy.q: Compared with competition, an effective cartel typically produces:
options: More output at a lower price
The same output at minimum ATC
Less output at a higher price
easy.feedback: A successful cartel mimics monopoly restriction.

easy.q: Why is high concentration not enough by itself to prove harmful conduct?
options: Entry conditions, efficiencies, imports, and actual behavior also matter
A high HHI guarantees high economic profit.
easy.feedback: Concentration is evidence, not a complete conclusion.

easy.q: Which statement best captures oligopoly outcomes?
options: They always reproduce the monopoly outcome.
They can range from intense rivalry to substantial coordination
They are determined only by firm count
easy.feedback: Rules, payoffs, timing, and repetition shape outcomes.

easy.q: Why does an oligopoly firm pay unusually close attention to a rival’s likely response before changing price?
options: Because a few large rivals can materially change the payoff from the firm’s decision
Because oligopoly firms are required to match every rival price change in order to remain in the market
Because oligopoly firms sell only identical products
Because market demand is perfectly elastic for each firm
easy.feedback: With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.

easy.q: Which condition most helps a few established firms remain dominant in an oligopoly?
options: Perfectly free entry by many small firms
A requirement that every product be identical
A horizontal demand curve for each individual firm
Significant barriers that make entry difficult
easy.feedback: Entry barriers help preserve a market in which a small number of firms account for much of total sales.

easy.q: A four-firm concentration ratio of 82% means that:
options: The four largest firms together account for 82% of market sales
Each of the four largest firms individually controls 82% of total market sales
easy.feedback: A concentration ratio adds the market shares of the specified number of largest firms.

easy.q: In a two-firm game, what does a payoff represent?
options: The slope of the industry demand curve
The outcome value a player receives from a particular combination of strategies
The maximum number of firms that regulators permit to enter the market under the industry’s legal rules
easy.feedback: A payoff records how well a player does under a particular combination of actions.

easy.q: A payoff cell is written (14, 9), with Row’s payoff listed first. What is Column’s payoff?
easy.feedback: With payoff order (Row, Column), the second number belongs to Column.

easy.q: A best response is the action that:
options: Maximizes the two firms’ combined payoff regardless of incentives
Is chosen by every rival in the market
Always remains best no matter what the rival does
Gives a player the highest payoff given the rival’s chosen action
easy.feedback: A best response is conditional on what the other player does; it need not be a dominant strategy.

easy.q: Which statement describes a Nash equilibrium?
options: Both players must have dominant strategies
Each player is choosing a best response to the other player’s action
The two players necessarily choose the outcome that maximizes their combined payoff even if one could gain by deviating alone
easy.feedback: At a Nash equilibrium, neither player can improve by changing action alone while the other action stays fixed.

easy.q: A cartel that successfully coordinates output tries to behave most like:
options: A single profit-maximizing monopolist for the industry
A group of independent price-taking firms
A perfectly contestable market with free entry
A regulator that sets the market price equal to marginal cost and assigns output to each participating firm
easy.feedback: A successful cartel restricts joint output and chooses the industry outcome that maximizes combined profit.

easy.q: Why can a cartel agreement be unstable even when all members gain from the agreement?
options: Every member must legally charge a different price
Cartels require marginal cost to equal zero
Joint profit is always lower under collusion than under competition because restricting output reduces total sales
An individual member may gain by secretly expanding sales while others keep output restricted
easy.feedback: The group can prefer restriction while each member has a private incentive to capture extra sales.

easy.q: What does monitoring do for a cartel?
options: It makes each firm a price taker
It eliminates the need to restrict output
It helps members detect whether other members are cheating on the agreement
It guarantees that barriers to entry disappear once all cartel members can observe one another’s sales
easy.feedback: Monitoring makes hidden deviations easier to discover and therefore easier to punish.

easy.q: In a one-shot prisoner’s-dilemma-style pricing game, why might both firms cut price even though both would prefer that neither cut?
options: Both firms face perfectly inelastic demand
Each firm has an individual incentive to cut given the rival’s possible action
The firms are maximizing total industry profit because the individually attractive price cut also maximizes their joint payoff
easy.feedback: Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.

easy.q: Why can the expectation of future competition sometimes make cooperation easier to sustain?
options: Future interaction makes current payoffs irrelevant
Repeated games eliminate every incentive to cheat
Firms become price takers when they meet repeatedly
A firm that cheats today may lose future cooperative gains
easy.feedback: When future interaction matters, the short-run gain from cheating can be weighed against future losses after retaliation.

easy.q: What makes a strategic threat credible?
options: The threat would be costly to both firms
Carrying it out would be in the threatening firm’s interest if the situation actually occurred
The threat sounds severe to the rival
easy.feedback: Credibility depends on whether the threatened response would actually be rational when the time comes to act.

easy.q: Compared with a competitive outcome, an effective cartel usually chooses:
options: Lower output and a higher price
Higher output and a lower price
The same output with zero profit
Price equal to minimum average total cost
easy.feedback: A cartel acts like a joint monopolist, restricting output to raise price and combined profit.

easy.q: Why is a high HHI not enough by itself to prove consumers are being harmed?
options: A high HHI guarantees prices equal marginal cost
HHI is unrelated to market shares
Concentration measures structure, while welfare also depends on conduct, entry conditions, efficiencies, and rivalry
easy.feedback: Concentration is evidence about market structure, not a complete welfare verdict.

easy.q: If two firms merge and all other market shares remain unchanged, what happens to market concentration?
options: It cannot change unless market demand shifts
It becomes zero if the merged firm cuts price
It generally increases because two separate shares become one larger share
It must fall because there is one fewer firm
easy.feedback: Combining shares raises concentration measures such as HHI, all else equal.

easy.q: A concentrated industry charges high markups but also spends heavily on research. What is the soundest conclusion?
options: There may be a tradeoff between market-power costs and innovation benefits that requires evidence
High research spending proves the market is efficient
High markups prove innovation has no value
easy.feedback: Oligopoly welfare can involve competing effects rather than a one-variable verdict.

easy.q: What is the basic economic concern behind antitrust scrutiny of collusion?
options: Coordinated restriction of competition can raise price and reduce output below competitive levels
Collusion makes every firm a price taker
easy.feedback: The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss.

easy.q: Why should an economist be cautious about predicting one outcome for every oligopoly market?
options: Every oligopoly has the same payoff matrix
Oligopoly theory assumes firms never respond to rivals
Market concentration fully determines every price
Different numbers of firms, products, information, costs, and strategic settings can produce different behavior
easy.feedback: Oligopoly is a strategic family of models, not a guarantee that every few-firm market behaves identically.

easy.q: Which statement best summarizes why oligopoly welfare analysis can be complicated?
options: Only the number of firms matters for welfare
Oligopoly always produces the monopoly outcome
Few firms may create market power, but rivalry, innovation, efficiencies, and entry conditions also matter
Any market with four firms is automatically inefficient
easy.feedback: A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses.

medium.q: Four firms have market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, and 10%, with the remaining firms holding 10%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
medium.feedback: Add the shares of the four largest firms.

medium.q: A market has shares of 50%, 25%, 15%, and 10%. Which measure gives especially heavy weight to the 50% firm?
medium.feedback: Squaring shares makes a very large firm count disproportionately.

medium.q: A merger combines firms with 20% and 15% market shares. By how much does the HHI rise if all other shares stay unchanged?
medium.feedback: The change is 2ab = 2(20)(15) = 600.

medium.q: A national market appears unconcentrated, but each rural town has only two local suppliers. What is the main lesson?
options: Geographic market definition can conceal local concentration
National concentration always measures local competition accurately.
medium.feedback: The relevant geographic market can be narrower than the national market.

medium.q: Two airlines choose whether to cut fares. Each earns more from cutting when the rival holds fares, but both earn less when both cut. This structure is closest to:
medium.feedback: Each airline has an individual incentive that can trigger a jointly harmful price war.

medium.q: Row’s payoff is higher with strategy B whether Column chooses X or Y. What does Row have?
medium.feedback: B beats Row’s alternative under both Column actions.

medium.q: A cell is a Nash equilibrium when:
options: Neither firm can improve by changing strategy alone
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
Both firms chose the same letter
medium.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses.

medium.q: A game has two outcomes in which both players are best responding. What does the game have?
options: Two dominant strategies for each player
medium.feedback: Games can have multiple equilibria.

medium.q: A firm observes that its rival will respond aggressively to any price cut. This expectation most directly illustrates:
options: A dominant strategy that is best regardless of the rival’s action.
medium.feedback: The firm’s best action depends on the expected response.

medium.q: Two firms agree to restrict output, but one secretly offers rebates. The rebate is best described as:
medium.feedback: Secret discounts undermine the coordinated price.

medium.q: A cartel’s market demand is P = 100 − 2Q and MC is $20. What total quantity maximizes joint profit?
medium.feedback: MR = 100 − 4Q; setting MR = 20 gives Q = 20.

medium.q: Using P = 100 − 2Q and cartel output Q = 20, what price does the cartel charge?
medium.feedback: Read price from demand: 100 − 2(20) = 60.

medium.q: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive a larger production quota?
options: It has the largest historical market share.
It can produce part of joint output at lower cost
medium.feedback: Efficient allocation places more output with lower-cost producers.

medium.q: A punishment strategy requires a rival to start a costly price war after cheating. When is the threat credible?
options: The announced response is credible because it sounds severe and harms the entrant
Whenever the price war hurts the cheater
When starting the price war is still the rival’s best response after cheating occurs
medium.feedback: A threat must be rational when its decision node is reached.

medium.q: Firms expect to compete for only one final period. Why is cooperation harder to sustain?
options: Future punishment has little or no value
Future punishment guarantees cooperation regardless of observability or credibility
medium.feedback: A short horizon weakens the future cost of cheating.

medium.q: A market’s largest firm announces a price, and rivals independently match it. This is:
medium.feedback: A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.

medium.q: Several firms raise prices after a common input cost increase. Why does this not by itself prove collusion?
options: Parallel price changes are conclusive evidence of an explicit agreement.
Input costs affect only fixed cost
Independent firms may respond similarly to the same cost shock
Parallel prices always maximize total surplus
medium.feedback: Common conditions can produce parallel conduct without agreement.

medium.q: An incumbent builds capacity that would be useful even if entry occurs. Why can this deter entry?
options: It turns the market into perfect competition
The capacity can make an aggressive post-entry response credible
medium.feedback: A sunk commitment can alter the incumbent’s later incentives.

medium.q: An incumbent threatens to cut price below variable cost after entry, but doing so would be very costly and temporary. The threat is likely:
medium.feedback: The incumbent may not rationally carry out the threat later.

medium.q: A firm maintains a lower price today to reduce expected entrant profit. What is the strategic cost?
options: It raises current monopoly profit automatically
medium.feedback: Limit pricing trades current profit for possible entry deterrence.

medium.q: In the kinked-demand model, rivals are assumed to match:
options: Price cuts more readily than price increases
medium.feedback: This asymmetry creates the kink.

medium.q: If MC changes within the discontinuity in the kinked-demand MR curve, the model predicts:
options: Price and output may remain unchanged
medium.feedback: The same output can remain optimal while MC crosses the MR gap.

medium.q: An effective cartel raises price and reduces output. Which part of lost consumer surplus is not transferred to producers?
medium.feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades create DWL.

medium.q: A merger raises HHI but also creates verified large cost savings. What is the sound conclusion?
options: Both increased market power and efficiencies must be evaluated
medium.feedback: Concentration and efficiency evidence both matter.

medium.q: A merger lowers marginal cost, but the merged firm keeps price high because rivalry weakens. What does this show?
options: Cost savings need not be passed fully to consumers
medium.feedback: Pass-through depends on competitive pressure.

medium.q: Why can foreign competition affect a domestic concentration assessment?
options: Imports are excluded from every market definition
Imports may provide substitutes that constrain domestic firms
medium.feedback: Relevant competitors may include foreign suppliers.

medium.q: A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price. This is:
medium.feedback: Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions.

medium.q: Heavy advertising builds brand loyalty and reduces switching. What strategic effect is most plausible?
options: Every firm becomes a price taker
Price competition may soften because firm demand becomes less elastic
medium.feedback: Loyalty can reduce substitution among brands.

medium.q: A market has six firms, but two control 78% of sales and rivals closely watch one another. Which structure is most plausible?
medium.feedback: Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly.

medium.q: Why can game theory yield different predictions across oligopoly markets?
options: Every oligopoly has one dominant strategy
Payoffs, information, timing, and repetition differ
medium.feedback: Strategic settings differ across industries.

medium.q: A grocery chain has only 8% of national grocery sales but 55% of sales in one isolated county. What does this example show about concentration measures?
options: They measure profit rather than market share
They depend on how the relevant market is defined
They are valid only for national markets
They ignore geographic differences and therefore always produce the same concentration result nationwide
medium.feedback: The same firm can appear small or dominant depending on the economically relevant geographic and product market.

medium.q: Two markets each have a four-firm concentration ratio of 80%. In Market A the four firms have nearly equal shares; in Market B one firm is much larger than the other three. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Market B can have a higher HHI because HHI gives more weight to large shares
Both markets must have the same HHI because an equal CR4 guarantees identical concentration among the leading firms
Market A must have the higher HHI because equal shares are squared
HHI cannot distinguish markets with the same CR4
medium.feedback: Squaring market shares makes HHI more sensitive to a very large firm even when CR4 is unchanged.

medium.q: Three national wireless carriers dominate a market. Before one carrier cuts price, its managers estimate how the other two are likely to respond. Which feature of oligopoly is being illustrated?
medium.feedback: The payoff from one firm’s choice depends partly on how a small number of major rivals react.

medium.q: An industry’s HHI rises after two sizable firms merge. What can the HHI increase tell an analyst directly?
options: The merged firm must now be a monopolist because any increase in HHI implies complete control of the market
Market concentration increased under the chosen market definition
medium.feedback: HHI measures concentration; welfare and policy conclusions require additional evidence about competition and efficiencies.

medium.q: Suppose Firm B chooses a high price. Firm A earns $8 million with a high price and $11 million with a low price. What is Firm A’s best response to B’s high price?
options: Choose whichever action maximizes joint industry profit
medium.feedback: Conditional on B choosing high, A compares its own payoffs and chooses the action paying 11 rather than 8.

medium.q: Firm A earns more from advertising whether Firm B advertises or not. What follows?
options: Advertising is a dominant strategy for Firm A
Advertising must maximize the two firms’ combined profit whenever it is more profitable for Firm A than not advertising
The game has no Nash equilibrium
medium.feedback: A dominant strategy gives the player a higher payoff for every action the rival might take.

medium.q: A strategy is Firm A’s best response when B chooses X, but A prefers a different strategy when B chooses Y. What can be concluded?
options: The first strategy is dominant because it is best once
The joint-payoff maximum must be a Nash equilibrium
The first strategy is not dominant for A
medium.feedback: Dominance requires the same strategy to be best against every rival action.

medium.q: At a proposed outcome, Firm A could gain by changing its action while Firm B kept its action fixed. What does that imply?
options: Firm A has a dominant strategy
The game has no strategic interdependence
The proposed outcome is not a Nash equilibrium
The proposed outcome must maximize joint profit
medium.feedback: A unilateral profitable deviation means at least one player is not best responding, so the cell is not Nash.

medium.q: Two firms could earn $20 million each by coordinating, but the Nash equilibrium gives each $14 million. What does this illustrate?
options: Dominant strategies always produce the joint-payoff maximum
A Nash equilibrium need not maximize combined payoff
medium.feedback: Mutual best responses can lead to a stable outcome with lower total payoff than a cooperative alternative.

medium.q: In payoff order (Row, Column), the cell for Row choosing A and Column choosing Y is (6, 15). Which comparison is relevant when finding Row’s best response to Y?
options: Compare Row’s first-number payoffs across Row’s available actions in column Y
Compare Column’s second-number payoffs across every column, regardless of which action Column has already chosen
Add both payoffs in every cell and choose the largest sum
medium.feedback: A best-response calculation holds the rival action fixed and compares the player’s own payoff across its alternatives.

medium.q: Why can firms end up at an outcome they both consider worse than another available outcome?
options: Firms are required to choose the outcome with the lowest combined payoff whenever their interests conflict
A Nash equilibrium always minimizes profit
Individual incentives to deviate can make the better joint outcome unstable
medium.feedback: A jointly attractive cell need not survive if one player can gain by deviating while the rival cooperates.

medium.q: A cartel has already chosen its joint-profit-maximizing total output. Why might it assign more production to a member with lower marginal cost?
options: Shifting output toward the lower-cost producer can reduce the cartel’s total production cost
Equal quotas always maximize joint profit
Higher-cost firms must produce more to preserve competition
Output allocation cannot affect cartel profit once total output is fixed, even when members have different marginal costs
medium.feedback: For a fixed cartel total, allocating more production to lower-marginal-cost members can raise combined profit.

medium.q: Three firms agree to keep prices high. One firm quietly gives large rebates while publicly posting the agreed price. Economically, the rebates are best interpreted as:
options: Proof that the cartel has eliminated all competition because no member can gain market share without openly cutting the posted price
A required form of price leadership
Cheating that captures extra sales while rivals maintain the collusive price
medium.feedback: Secret rebates undermine the agreement by letting one member expand sales at the others’ expense.

medium.q: Which market condition makes a cartel harder to sustain?
options: A small number of firms with similar objectives
A credible punishment system that quickly detects and penalizes members who secretly exceed their agreed output
Many opportunities for members to make secret sales that rivals cannot observe
Frequent transparent reporting of member sales
medium.feedback: When cheating is hard to observe, deviations are easier and enforcement becomes weaker.

medium.q: A cartel restricts total output below the competitive level. What is the intended effect on the market price?
options: Create a perfectly elastic industry demand curve so the cartel can sell any quantity at the higher price
Raise price by moving up the market demand curve
Force price down to marginal cost
medium.feedback: Restricting industry output raises the price buyers are willing to pay along downward-sloping market demand.

medium.q: Suppose cartel members can observe one another’s sales almost immediately. Why can this improve cartel stability?
options: It makes cheating easier to detect and respond to
It removes each member’s incentive to earn profit
It guarantees the cartel price equals marginal cost
It causes market concentration to fall
medium.feedback: Fast observability reduces the chance that a member can profit from hidden deviations for long.

medium.q: Two firms with market shares of 18% and 12% merge. Holding all other shares fixed, why does HHI rise?
options: The merger automatically removes all smaller rivals
The squared share of the combined 30% firm exceeds the sum of the two firms’ separate squared shares
HHI counts the merged firm twice
Every merger doubles total market sales
medium.feedback: Because shares are squared, combining two positive shares increases HHI by the cross term 2ab.

medium.q: A proposed merger would eliminate the closest competitor but also reduce marginal cost substantially. What is the best economic approach?
options: Compare the likely loss of rivalry with the magnitude and pass-through of verifiable efficiencies
Approve the merger automatically because costs fall
Block the merger automatically because concentration rises
Ignore cost effects because only the number of firms matters
medium.feedback: Merger analysis requires weighing competitive harm against genuine efficiencies rather than using one fact mechanically.

medium.q: When a cartel raises price, some lost consumer surplus becomes additional producer surplus. What happens to the remaining loss associated with trades that no longer occur?
options: It is automatically recovered through innovation
medium.feedback: Foregone mutually beneficial trades destroy total surplus rather than transfer it to another market participant.

medium.q: A domestic industry has a high concentration ratio, but buyers can readily switch to imported substitutes when domestic prices rise. What does this imply?
options: The market must be a monopoly
Domestic concentration alone may overstate the firms’ effective market power
Imports are irrelevant to market definition
medium.feedback: Competitive constraints from close substitutes, including imports when relevant, matter to the economic market definition.

medium.q: A merger creates a larger research budget but also reduces head-to-head price competition. Which statement is most defensible?
options: The merger must lower HHI because research increases
Both innovation benefits and reduced-rivalry costs should be evaluated rather than assuming one dominates
A larger research budget proves consumer welfare will rise
Reduced rivalry is irrelevant whenever innovation is possible
medium.feedback: The welfare question is empirical: innovation gains can matter, but so can weaker price and quality competition.

hard.feedback: Sum the four largest market shares.

hard.feedback: Sum the four largest market shares.

hard.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. With payoffs ordered (Row, Column), which cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
hard.feedback: A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.

hard.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. Which statement about the Row firm’s dominant strategy is correct?
hard.feedback: Compare Row’s two payoffs separately under each Column strategy.

hard.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. Which cell maximizes the two firms’ combined payoff?
options: Row A, Column X; Row B, Column Y
hard.feedback: Add the two payoffs in each cell.

options: Row A, Column X; Row B, Column X
Row A, Column Y; Row B, Column X
Row A, Column Y; Row B, Column Y
Row A, Column X; Row B, Column Y
hard.feedback: A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.

hard.feedback: Compare Row’s two payoffs separately under each Column strategy.

hard.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. With payoffs ordered (Row, Column), which cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?

options: Row has no strictly dominant strategy
hard.feedback: Compare Row’s two payoffs separately under each Column strategy.

hard.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. Which cell maximizes the two firms’ combined payoff?
options: Row A, Column X; Row B, Column Y

hard.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. With payoffs ordered (Row, Column), which cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: Row A, Column X; Row A, Column Y; Row B, Column X; Row B, Column Y
hard.feedback: A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.

hard.feedback: Compare Row’s two payoffs separately under each Column strategy.

hard.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. Which cell maximizes the two firms’ combined payoff?
hard.feedback: Add the two payoffs in each cell.

hard.feedback: Set industry MR equal to industry MC.

hard.q: In the airlines market, an incumbent announces a severe post-entry price cut. Internal documents show the cut would reduce the incumbent’s own post-entry payoff below accommodation. What is the best interpretation?
options: The threat is credible because it hurts the entrant
The announcement creates a dominant strategy for the entrant
hard.feedback: A threat is noncredible when carrying it out is not optimal after entry.

hard.q: In the wireless carriers market, an incumbent announces a severe post-entry price cut. Internal documents show the cut would reduce the incumbent’s own post-entry payoff below accommodation. What is the best interpretation?
options: The threat is credible because it hurts the entrant
The announcement creates a dominant strategy for the entrant
hard.feedback: A threat is noncredible when carrying it out is not optimal after entry.

hard.q: In the soft-drink producers market, an incumbent announces a severe post-entry price cut. Internal documents show the cut would reduce the incumbent’s own post-entry payoff below accommodation. What is the best interpretation?
options: The threat is credible because it hurts the entrant
The announcement creates a dominant strategy for the entrant
hard.feedback: A threat is noncredible when carrying it out is not optimal after entry.

hard.q: In the cement companies market, an incumbent announces a severe post-entry price cut. Internal documents show the cut would reduce the incumbent’s own post-entry payoff below accommodation. What is the best interpretation?
options: The threat is credible because it hurts the entrant
The announcement creates a dominant strategy for the entrant
hard.feedback: A threat is noncredible when carrying it out is not optimal after entry.

hard.q: In the chip manufacturers market, an incumbent announces a severe post-entry price cut. Internal documents show the cut would reduce the incumbent’s own post-entry payoff below accommodation. What is the best interpretation?
options: The threat is credible because it hurts the entrant
The announcement creates a dominant strategy for the entrant
hard.feedback: A threat is noncredible when carrying it out is not optimal after entry.

hard.q: A cartel’s members all prefer the collusive outcome to the competitive outcome, yet the agreement repeatedly breaks down. Which explanation is most consistent with oligopoly incentives?
options: The cartel outcome cannot produce positive profit
Members have no information about market demand
A jointly preferred outcome is automatically a Nash equilibrium
Each firm can gain privately from expanding output if it expects rivals to keep restricting theirs
hard.feedback: Joint gains do not erase the unilateral incentive to cheat when other members are expected to cooperate.

hard.q: An effective cartel raises price from $30 to $42 and reduces quantity sold. Which statement best separates redistribution from efficiency loss?
options: Higher cartel profit proves total surplus rose
Deadweight loss is the cartel’s entire increase in revenue
Some consumer surplus becomes producer gain, while trades no longer made create deadweight loss
Every dollar of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss
hard.feedback: A higher price transfers some surplus, but the output restriction also destroys gains from mutually beneficial trades.

hard.q: Several airlines raise fares within hours of the same publicly observed jet-fuel cost increase. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The matching fare increases prove an illegal agreement
The airlines must be following a dominant strategy in a payoff matrix
The market cannot be oligopolistic because prices moved together
Parallel pricing alone does not establish collusion because a common cost shock can produce similar independent responses
hard.feedback: Similar prices can arise from common incentives or observation of rivals; parallel behavior by itself is not proof of an agreement.

hard.q: A dominant firm posts a new price, and several rivals independently match it without an explicit agreement. What best describes the pattern?
options: Perfect competition because all firms charge the same price
Price leadership that may coordinate expectations without proving explicit collusion
A prisoner’s dilemma requiring both firms to cut price
hard.feedback: Following a recognized price leader can coordinate market behavior, but observation alone does not prove an explicit agreement.

hard.q: Two oligopoly firms avoid matching price cuts and instead compete through warranties, loyalty programs, and product quality. Why might this strategy be attractive?
options: It converts the market into perfect competition
It can attract customers without immediately triggering a market-wide price war
It guarantees marginal cost will fall
hard.feedback: Nonprice competition can shift demand or strengthen loyalty while avoiding direct price retaliation.

hard.q: In the kinked-demand model, a modest marginal-cost change occurs entirely within the discontinuity in marginal revenue. What does the model predict?
options: The profit-maximizing price can remain unchanged
Price must immediately fall by the same amount as marginal cost
The firm becomes a price taker
The demand curve becomes perfectly elastic
hard.feedback: The MR discontinuity is used to explain why a range of marginal-cost changes may leave the chosen price unchanged.

hard.q: One firm mistakes a temporary rival discount for a permanent price cut and responds aggressively. Rivals retaliate, producing several rounds of lower prices. What does this illustrate?
options: Price wars require a formal cartel agreement
The firms have stopped being strategically interdependent
A price war necessarily raises joint industry profit
Strategic reactions can amplify an initial move into a price war
hard.feedback: In oligopoly, reactions and counterreactions can turn even a misread signal into sustained price rivalry.

hard.q: A merger sharply raises HHI, but entry is easy and several well-funded firms can expand quickly if price rises. What is the strongest economic inference?
options: The concentration increase is relevant, but ease of entry and expansion can limit post-merger market power
The HHI increase proves prices will rise
Easy entry is irrelevant once concentration increases
The merger must increase deadweight loss by exactly the HHI change
hard.feedback: Concentration is one piece of evidence; credible entry and expansion can constrain the merged firm.

hard.q: Four firms independently raise price after the same large increase in a key input cost. What additional evidence would be needed before inferring collusion?
options: A high market price by itself
Proof that the firms earn positive accounting profit
A calculation showing consumer demand slopes downward
Evidence that the firms coordinated rather than merely responding to the common cost shock
hard.feedback: Parallel pricing can have competitive explanations; an inference of collusion needs evidence that distinguishes coordination from common incentives.

hard.q: A cartel restriction transfers $9 million of surplus from consumers to producers and destroys another $3 million of mutually beneficial trade. What is the deadweight loss?
hard.feedback: Transfers change who receives surplus; only the destroyed gains from trade are deadweight loss.

hard.q: A platform market is highly concentrated because network effects make a large user base valuable, but users can easily use multiple platforms at once. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: The market must be perfectly competitive because users can switch
Network effects can support concentration, while easy multi-homing may still preserve meaningful competitive pressure
High concentration proves the platform has unconstrained monopoly power
hard.feedback: The same structural fact can have different welfare implications depending on switching, multi-homing, and rival expansion.

hard.q: Two industries have identical CR4 and HHI values. One has standardized products and transparent prices; the other has differentiated products and rapid innovation. Why might their competitive outcomes differ?
options: Concentration measures do not capture every strategic and product-market feature that shapes rivalry
Equal concentration measures guarantee equal prices and profits
Only the number of firms can affect oligopoly behavior
hard.feedback: Concentration is informative but does not summarize product differentiation, innovation, information, costs, or strategic conduct.

hard.q: A concentrated industry has high prices, strong product innovation, and frequent entry by niche rivals. Which analysis is strongest?
options: Conclude the industry is harmful solely because prices are high
Conclude the industry is efficient solely because innovation is high
Ignore entry because the incumbent firms are large
Evaluate market power, innovation benefits, entry conditions, and consumer substitution together
hard.feedback: Oligopoly welfare requires integrating several margins rather than treating one statistic as decisive.

elite.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. After identifying both firms’ best responses, which pure-strategy Nash equilibrium follows?
elite.feedback: Trace both players’ best responses; only mutual best responses are Nash equilibria.

elite.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. How does the Nash equilibrium compare with the joint-payoff-maximizing outcome?
options: Every Nash equilibrium must maximize joint payoff
The jointly best cell is automatically a dominant strategy
Equal payoffs are required for equilibrium
The equilibrium can differ from the cell maximizing joint payoff
elite.feedback: Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum.

elite.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. After identifying both firms’ best responses, which pure-strategy Nash equilibrium follows?
options: Row A, Column X; Row A, Column Y
elite.feedback: Trace both players’ best responses; only mutual best responses are Nash equilibria.

elite.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. How does the Nash equilibrium compare with the joint-payoff-maximizing outcome?
options: Every Nash equilibrium must maximize joint payoff
The equilibrium can differ from the cell maximizing joint payoff
The jointly best cell is automatically a dominant strategy

legendaryBoss.q: Cable providers assess local concentration. A cartel is disrupted by imports, new technology, and member cheating. Which integrated conclusion is strongest?
options: Outside competition and internal instability both weaken coordination
legendaryBoss.feedback: Integrated policy analysis combines structure, entry, conduct, efficiencies, and consumer effects.

repairQuestions.q: A market has three firms that closely track one another’s pricing. What feature matters most?
repairQuestions.feedback: Rival response is central.

repairQuestions.q: Why can an industry with six firms still be oligopolistic?
options: Any market with more than two firms is competitive
Six firms means monopolistic competition automatically
A few firms may dominate sales and react strategically
repairQuestions.feedback: Firm count alone is insufficient.

repairQuestions.q: Which measure squares market shares?
repairQuestions.feedback: HHI squares shares.

repairQuestions.q: What does a four-firm concentration ratio do?
options: Adds the four largest market shares
repairQuestions.feedback: The ratio is a sum, not a proof of conduct.

repairQuestions.q: In payoff order (Row, Column), whose payoff is second?
repairQuestions.feedback: Payoff order must be read consistently.

repairQuestions.q: Why must payoff order be stated?
options: It changes the number of strategies
Reversing the order changes each firm’s incentives
repairQuestions.feedback: Each number belongs to a different player.

repairQuestions.q: What is a best response?
options: The highest-payoff action given the rival’s action
The action with the highest single payoff anywhere
repairQuestions.feedback: Best responses are conditional.

repairQuestions.q: What makes a strategy dominant?
options: It beats the player’s alternative under every rival action
repairQuestions.feedback: Dominance requires comparison across rival actions.

repairQuestions.q: What defines Nash equilibrium?
repairQuestions.feedback: Nash is stability against unilateral deviation.

repairQuestions.q: Can a Nash equilibrium be jointly inferior?
options: No, Nash always maximizes total payoff
Only if firms are price takers
Yes, individual incentives can lead to a lower combined payoff
repairQuestions.feedback: Equilibrium and efficiency are distinct.

repairQuestions.q: Why is cooperation unstable in a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma?
options: Each firm can gain by deviating when the other cooperates
Cooperation gives the lowest joint payoff
repairQuestions.feedback: The private incentive to defect destabilizes cooperation.

repairQuestions.q: What does mutual defection show?
options: Individually rational actions can produce a jointly worse result
repairQuestions.feedback: The dilemma is the conflict between private and collective incentives.

repairQuestions.q: How does a cartel select joint output?
options: At minimum ATC for every member
Where industry MR equals industry MC
repairQuestions.feedback: A successful cartel applies monopoly logic.

repairQuestions.q: Why is cartel profit not equal to deadweight loss?
options: Some consumer loss is transferred to producers while DWL is lost surplus
repairQuestions.feedback: Separate transfers from lost trades.

repairQuestions.q: When can future punishment discourage cheating?
options: When future losses are large enough and punishment is credible
repairQuestions.feedback: Repetition helps only when incentives support punishment.

repairQuestions.q: What makes a threat credible?
options: The threatening firm would rationally carry it out later
repairQuestions.feedback: Credibility is tested at the future decision point.

repairQuestions.q: Does parallel pricing prove collusion?
options: No, firms may respond independently to common conditions
repairQuestions.feedback: Parallel conduct needs context and evidence.

repairQuestions.q: What is price leadership?
options: A dominant strategy in every game
Rivals follow a leading firm’s announced price without legal control
repairQuestions.feedback: Leadership can create a focal price.

repairQuestions.q: Does low pricing prove predation?
options: No, it may reflect low cost or vigorous competition
Yes, every price cut is exclusionary
No, low prices never affect entry
repairQuestions.feedback: Intent and recoupment cannot be inferred from low price alone.

repairQuestions.q: Does a higher post-merger HHI settle the welfare question?
options: Yes, concentration is the only issue
No, market power, entry, and efficiencies still require analysis
repairQuestions.feedback: Concentration is one part of merger analysis.

repairQuestions.q: A student says a four-firm concentration ratio squares each firm’s market share. What is the correction?
options: The four-firm ratio averages all firms’ squared shares
The four-firm ratio simply adds the shares of the four largest firms
The four-firm ratio multiplies the market shares of the four largest firms and then converts the product to a percentage
The four-firm ratio subtracts fringe shares from 100
repairQuestions.feedback: Squaring shares is part of HHI, not the four-firm concentration ratio.

repairQuestions.q: A student describes oligopoly as “a market where each firm can safely ignore rivals.” What is the key error?
options: Oligopoly decisions are strategically interdependent because major rivals can respond
Oligopoly always has exactly two firms, so any market with three or more important firms belongs to another structure
Oligopoly firms are all price takers
repairQuestions.feedback: The defining strategic feature is that a few important firms must account for likely rival reactions.

repairQuestions.q: A student says “if both firms would be better off cooperating, they will automatically cooperate.” What is missing?
options: Prisoner’s-dilemma incentives exist only in monopoly
Each firm’s unilateral incentive must also be checked; the cooperative outcome can be unstable
Joint payoff is irrelevant in oligopoly
Cooperation requires the firms to have identical costs
repairQuestions.feedback: A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.

repairQuestions.q: A student calls any concentrated industry a cartel. What is the correction?
options: A cartel requires coordination among firms to restrict competition; concentration alone does not establish that
A cartel is simply any market with fewer than ten firms
A cartel exists whenever HHI is high
A cartel means one firm owns the entire market
repairQuestions.feedback: Market structure and collusive conduct are different concepts; a concentrated market need not be a cartel.

repairQuestions.q: A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical. What is the key distinction?
options: Explicit collusion means firms ignore rivals
Only tacit coordination can affect price
Tacit coordination can emerge without an explicit agreement among firms
Tacit coordination always requires a written contract
repairQuestions.feedback: Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.

repairQuestions.q: A student says “high concentration proves firms are colluding.” What is the correction?
options: Collusion is impossible in concentrated markets
Concentration measures directly record secret agreements
High concentration can make strategic interaction important, but it does not by itself prove an agreement or harmful conduct
High concentration means every firm charges marginal cost
repairQuestions.feedback: Structure can affect incentives, but conduct and welfare conclusions require additional evidence.

repairQuestions.q: A student treats every dollar of consumer-surplus loss from a cartel as deadweight loss. What should the student separate?
options: Surplus transferred to producers from surplus destroyed by trades that no longer occur
repairQuestions.feedback: A cartel can redistribute surplus and destroy surplus; only the destroyed gains from trade are deadweight loss.

repairQuestions.q: A student says a higher post-merger HHI proves the merger harms consumers. What is the better statement?
options: A higher HHI shows greater concentration, but consumer effects also depend on rivalry, entry, efficiencies, and pass-through
HHI directly measures the change in consumer surplus
Any HHI increase means the merged firm becomes a monopolist
HHI is unrelated to merger analysis
repairQuestions.feedback: Concentration is an input to analysis, not a complete welfare conclusion.

repairQuestions.q: A student argues that high research spending proves a concentrated market is socially optimal. What is missing?
options: Innovation matters only in perfect competition
High research spending eliminates market power
Innovation benefits must be weighed against possible higher prices, weaker rivalry, and other welfare effects
repairQuestions.feedback: Innovation can be beneficial without settling the overall welfare comparison.

repairQuestions.q: A student sees several firms charge the same price and immediately labels the behavior collusion. What is the key correction?
options: Price equality proves the firms have equal market shares
Collusion can occur only when prices differ
Similar prices can arise independently from common costs or market conditions, so evidence of coordination is still needed
Identical prices are impossible without a cartel
repairQuestions.feedback: Parallel conduct is not automatically evidence of an agreement because firms can respond similarly to the same public conditions.

bridgeQuestions.q: A fully effective cartel most closely imitates which market structure?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A cartel restricts joint output like a monopolist.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does cartel price compare with the competitive benchmark?
options: It is typically higher because joint output is restricted
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Coordination can reproduce monopoly-like outcomes.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which monopoly rule does a cartel use for total output?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Joint output follows monopoly marginal analysis.

bridgeQuestions.q: What prevents an oligopoly from automatically behaving like one monopolist?
options: Member incentives and rival strategic responses
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Independent firms may not sustain the joint outcome.

bridgeQuestions.q: What distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition most sharply?
options: Strategic interdependence among a few major firms
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can advertising matter in both structures?
options: It makes every firm a price taker
It can differentiate products and alter substitution
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Advertising can shape demand in both markets.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which behavior belongs to oligopoly rather than the basic monopolistic-competition model?
options: Choosing an action after anticipating a specific rival’s response
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The basic monopolistic-competition model abstracts from strategic interdependence.

bridgeQuestions.q: Compared with perfect competition, oligopolistic firms are more likely to:
options: Recognize that their own actions affect rivals and market outcomes
Have free entry eliminate market power
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Oligopolists possess market power and strategic influence.

bridgeQuestions.q: What competitive benchmark is commonly used to evaluate a cartel?
options: Price equals marginal cost at the efficient output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The competitive benchmark helps identify output restriction and DWL.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive more output?
options: It has the highest fixed cost
It faces the least elastic demand
It is always the largest firm
Allocating production toward lower MC reduces joint cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Joint cost minimization matters for cartel allocation.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can excess capacity serve as a commitment?
options: Installed capacity can make a large post-entry output response more credible
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A sunk capacity choice can alter later incentives.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does product differentiation sometimes soften price competition?
options: More loyal buyers make firm demand less elastic
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lower elasticity reduces customer switching.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why might a cartel be harder to sustain when close substitutes exist outside it?
options: Consumers can switch away from the cartel after price increases
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Outside substitutes constrain cartel pricing.

bridgeQuestions.q: What creates cartel deadweight loss?
options: Mutually beneficial units between cartel and competitive output are not produced
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lost trades reduce total surplus.

bridgeQuestions.q: A cartel price increase transfers some surplus from:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher price transfers part of consumer surplus to producers.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which basic incentive concept explains cartel cheating?
options: A member compares its private marginal gain with expected punishment
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Private incentives can undermine collective agreements.

bridgeQuestions.q: How do network effects affect oligopoly?
options: They can strengthen incumbent advantages and concentration
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Network effects can reinforce entry barriers.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does antitrust examine concentration?
options: A concentrated structure may make coordination or unilateral market power easier
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Structure can affect competitive risk.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why are merger efficiencies relevant?
options: Lower costs can offset some harm if savings are real and passed through
Cost savings prove no market power
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can foreign suppliers weaken a domestic cartel?
options: Imports provide alternative sources and can expand outside supply
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Outside supply can destabilize domestic coordination.

bridgeQuestions.q: A market has four dominant firms. Which feature would most strongly distinguish oligopoly from monopoly or perfect competition?
options: Assume four dominant firms automatically mean monopolistic competition because any market with multiple sellers and differentiated products fits that model
Classify the market only by whether products are identical
Treat every concentrated market as a legal monopoly
Focus on few-firm strategic interdependence rather than requiring one firm or many tiny price takers
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Oligopoly sits between monopoly and atomistic competition because a few large firms interact strategically.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student already understands market shares. What extra step turns those shares into an HHI?
options: Multiply each firm's market share by the market price and add the resulting dollar values across firms
Square each firm’s percentage share and add the squared shares
Add only the four largest shares
bridgeQuestions.feedback: HHI builds on market shares by squaring each percentage share and summing across firms.

bridgeQuestions.q: Before trying to find a Nash equilibrium in a payoff matrix, what should a student verify first?
options: Whether the market’s concentration measure is high enough to imply that strategic behavior must be present
Whether both players earn equal payoffs
Which payoff belongs to each player and which actions define the rows and columns
Which cell has the highest combined payoff
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student keeps searching for one action that is always best, but the player’s preferred action changes with the rival’s move. What concept should the student use?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Best responses can vary with the rival’s action even when no dominant strategy exists.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student has correctly found a player’s best response in each column. How should the student check for a dominant strategy?
options: See whether the same action is the best response in every column
Add the two players’ payoffs in each cell
Choose the action with the highest single payoff anywhere in the matrix
Look only at the rival’s payoffs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A dominant strategy must remain the player’s best response to every rival action.

bridgeQuestions.q: After marking each player’s best responses in a matrix, what identifies a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: The cell with the largest total payoff even if someone wants to deviate
Any cell where the payoffs are equal
The first cell in which one player has a dominant strategy
A cell where both players’ best-response markings coincide
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses in the same outcome cell.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student found the cell with the largest combined payoff and calls it the Nash equilibrium. What must still be checked?
options: Whether the firms have equal market shares
Whether the cell lies on the main diagonal
Whether each player would choose to stay there given the other player’s action
Whether the two payoffs are both positive and add to more than the payoffs in every neighboring cell
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Joint-payoff maximization and Nash stability are separate questions.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a noncooperative game differ from an assumed cartel solution?
options: The government chooses each firm’s strategy
Each firm follows its own incentives rather than committing to maximize joint profit
The firms necessarily choose identical actions because noncooperative behavior rules out different strategies
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Noncooperative analysis asks what individually rational strategies imply without assuming binding joint-profit coordination.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student understands a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma. What new consideration enters when the firms expect to interact again?
options: Market concentration falls with each round
Today’s action can change future responses and future payoffs
The payoff matrix no longer matters at all
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Repeated interaction links current choices to future rewards or punishments, which can alter incentives.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student knows that talk alone may not deter entry. What can make an incumbent’s announced response more believable?
options: A costly action taken in advance that changes the incumbent’s future incentives
A vague promise that entry will be punished somehow
A larger concentration ratio by itself
A public statement with no change in capacity or costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A commitment can make future behavior credible by changing what the incumbent will find profitable after entry.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes. What is the next step when firms compete through quality or advertising instead?
options: Ignore rivals because only prices create interdependence
Apply the same strategic logic to nonprice actions because rivals may respond there too
Assume nonprice choices have no effect on demand
Treat advertising as proof of collusion
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price.
