medium.q: Competitive firms are earning positive economic profit. What happens as entry occurs?
options: Market supply falls and price rises
Market supply increases and market price falls
medium.feedback: Entry shifts market supply right and erodes profit.

medium.q: Competitive firms are earning economic losses. What happens as firms exit?
options: Market supply increases and price falls
Market supply decreases and market price rises
medium.feedback: Exit shifts market supply left and reduces remaining firms’ losses.

medium.q: In a constant-cost industry, demand rises permanently. After long-run adjustment, price typically:
options: Equals minimum AVC but not ATC
medium.feedback: Entry expands output without changing input prices or cost curves.

medium.q: In an increasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price typically ends:
options: Above the original price but below the short-run price
At zero economic profit only if price is zero
medium.feedback: Industry expansion raises input costs, so long-run price rises.

medium.q: In a decreasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price can end:
options: At the original price by definition
medium.feedback: External economies can lower firms’ costs as the industry expands.

medium.q: At long-run competitive equilibrium, which pair holds?
options: P = MC and P = minimum ATC
medium.feedback: Long-run competition combines allocative and productive efficiency.

medium.q: A fixed annual license fee rises for every competitive firm. In the short run, each firm’s output at a given price is:
options: Unchanged because MC and AVC are unchanged
medium.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change shifts ATC, not MC or AVC.

medium.q: A per-unit production tax is imposed. For a competitive firm, the tax directly shifts:
medium.feedback: A per-unit tax is a variable and marginal cost.

medium.q: A technology improvement lowers marginal cost. At the same market price, the firm generally chooses:
options: The same output because price is fixed
medium.feedback: Lower MC moves the P=MC output to a larger quantity.

medium.q: A competitive outcome has P=MC but the firm is not at minimum ATC. The outcome is:
options: Productively efficient but not allocatively efficient
Allocatively efficient but not productively efficient
medium.feedback: P=MC is allocative efficiency; minimum ATC is productive efficiency.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, what is average variable cost?
medium.feedback: The AVC guide at Q = 50 is $10.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the 50-unit output, what vertical price–ATC gap represents profit on each unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit is P − ATC = $30 − $20 = $10.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at the profit-maximizing output?
medium.feedback: Total profit is ($30 − $20) × 50 = $500.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What economic profit does the firm earn at the output?
medium.feedback: Because P equals ATC at Q = 50, economic profit is zero.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s total revenue at the break-even price and output shown?
Refer to the graph. The blue ATC guide at the chosen 30-unit output lands on which dollar value?
medium.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 30 is $40.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. The green AVC marker at Q = 30 gives what variable cost per unit?
medium.feedback: The AVC guide at Q = 30 is $20.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the firm’s chosen output in the loss graph, what is the loss per unit?
medium.feedback: Loss per unit is ATC − P = $40 − $30 = $10.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s shutdown price?
medium.feedback: Minimum AVC is $20 at point A.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Where does the firm’s short-run supply curve begin?
options: At the left end of the entire MC curve
At point C and then along ATC
At point A and then along rising MC
Along the AVC curve below A
medium.feedback: Short-run supply is rising MC at and above minimum AVC.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the 90-unit output in the paired profit graph, what vertical price–ATC gap represents profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Price is $40 and ATC is $20, so profit per unit is $20.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit for the representative firm?
Refer to the graph. How does the market-panel equilibrium price enter the representative firm’s decision?
options: It becomes the firm’s ATC curve, determining average cost at every possible output level
It becomes the firm’s quantity of 75, so market quantity and individual output are identical
It becomes the firm’s horizontal P = MR = AR line used to choose output along MC
It shifts the firm’s MC curve upward, changing production cost without changing marginal revenue
medium.feedback: A price-taking firm accepts the market price as its marginal and average revenue.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Use the price and ATC at the representative firm’s chosen output. What is the loss per unit?
medium.feedback: ATC is $18 and price is $15, so loss per unit is $3.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the representative firm’s total economic loss?
Refer to the graph. Use price and AVC at the chosen output. Why does the representative firm continue producing in the short run?
options: P = $15 exceeds AVC = $10 at Q = 50, so revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost
P = $15 exceeds ATC = $18 at Q = 50, so the firm is earning positive economic profit
The competitive firm can raise its own price above $15, so it avoids the loss shown by ATC
Producing at Q = 50 eliminates fixed cost, so any price above AVC guarantees zero economic loss
medium.feedback: The firm covers variable cost and part of fixed cost because P > AVC.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What economic profit does the representative firm earn at the long-run equilibrium?
medium.feedback: Price equals ATC at the selected output, so economic profit is zero.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Which pair of conditions holds at the representative firm’s selected output?
options: P < AVC and MC < ATC for the displayed firm
P = MC and P = minimum ATC
medium.feedback: Long-run competitive equilibrium has P = MC and P at minimum ATC.

medium.q: A competitive wheat farm doubles its own output while every other seller and market demand are unchanged. Why is the market price essentially unaffected?
options: The farm is too small relative to the market to influence price
The farm can force buyers to accept any price
Its average total cost determines the market price for all sellers
Doubling output makes its demand curve downward sloping
medium.feedback: A price-taking firm is individually too small to move the market price.

medium.q: The market price of soybeans is $12 per bushel. Which statement best describes the demand curve facing one competitive soybean farm?
options: It slopes downward because the farm must cut price to sell more
It is vertical at the farm’s current quantity
It coincides with the entire market demand curve
It is horizontal at $12 over the farm’s feasible output range
medium.feedback: A competitive firm can sell feasible output at the prevailing market price, so its firm-level demand is horizontal.

medium.q: A competitive firm sells its first 25 units at $18 each. If it can also sell the 26th unit at $18, marginal revenue from the 26th unit is:
medium.feedback: For a price-taking firm, each additional unit adds the unchanged market price to total revenue.

medium.q: A price-taking firm has total revenue of $1,260 from selling 70 units. Its average revenue is:
medium.feedback: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price for a competitive firm.

medium.q: If the competitive market price falls from $24 to $20, what happens to the individual firm’s P, AR, and MR?
options: Price becomes $20 while AR and MR stay $24
MR falls to $20 but AR stays $24
Only total revenue changes; P, AR, and MR do not
medium.feedback: For a price-taking firm, price, average revenue, and marginal revenue all equal the market price.

medium.q: A competitive firm faces a constant market price of $15. Which total-revenue pattern is consistent with price taking?
options: Total revenue rises by a smaller amount with each additional unit
Total revenue is fixed because the firm cannot change price
Total revenue falls whenever output rises
Each additional unit raises total revenue by $15
medium.feedback: With constant price, total revenue increases linearly and each unit adds the same amount.

medium.q: Which pair correctly contrasts market demand with the demand facing one perfectly competitive firm?
options: Market demand is horizontal; firm demand slopes downward
Both curves slope downward because every seller faces the same market demand
Market demand slopes downward; the individual firm faces a horizontal line at market price
Both curves are horizontal because all firms are price takers
medium.feedback: Industry demand determines market price with supply, while an individual competitive firm takes that price as given.

medium.q: A market has many sellers, standardized output, and easy entry. Which additional implication is most consistent with the competitive model?
options: Brand loyalty gives each firm a downward-sloping demand curve
No single seller has meaningful control over market price
Each firm chooses a unique profit-maximizing price
Firms must coordinate output to avoid price wars
medium.feedback: The competitive assumptions make individual firms price takers.

medium.q: A competitive firm sells 40 units at $9 and then 45 units at the same price. By how much does total revenue increase?
medium.feedback: Five additional units at $9 each add $45 to total revenue.

medium.q: A competitive firm faces P = $11. At the output where MR = MC, AVC = $8 and ATC = $15. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Exit immediately because fixed cost is positive
Produce in the short run and incur a loss
Shut down because price is below ATC
medium.feedback: Price covers AVC but not ATC, so the firm produces and uses revenue to cover variable cost plus part of fixed cost.

medium.q: At the best positive output, a firm faces P = $7, AVC = $9, and ATC = $13. What should it do in the short run?
options: Shut down because revenue cannot cover variable cost
Produce because price is below ATC
Raise output until ATC falls to $7
medium.feedback: When P < AVC, producing fails to cover avoidable variable cost.

medium.q: A competitive firm has already paid a nonrefundable annual license fee. The fee increases while market price, MC, and AVC are unchanged. What happens to the short-run output decision?
options: Output falls because every fixed-cost increase shifts MC upward
The firm must shut down immediately
Output rises to spread the fee across more units
The profit-maximizing positive output is unchanged, though profit is lower
medium.feedback: A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.

medium.q: A firm’s MC for units 1–5 is $6, $9, $13, $18, and $24. Assume AVC is covered. If price rises from $14 to $20, output changes from:
medium.feedback: The firm produces through the last unit whose MC does not exceed price on rising MC.

medium.q: At price $16, 30 identical firms each supply 5 units. At price $22, each supplies 8 units. What is the industry response?
options: Market quantity supplied falls from 240 to 150 units
Market quantity supplied stays at 30 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 150 to 240 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 35 to 38 units
medium.feedback: Horizontal aggregation multiplies each firm’s quantity by the number of identical firms.

medium.q: A fixed insurance premium increases by $4,000 for every firm in a competitive industry. Market demand and variable costs are unchanged. In the immediate short run, what happens to each operating firm’s supply curve?
options: It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It does not shift because MC and AVC are unchanged
It shifts left because ATC rises
It shifts right because firms need more output
medium.feedback: Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.

medium.q: A per-unit fee raises MC and AVC by $2 at every positive output. Which supply effect is most consistent?
options: The firm requires a higher market price to supply a given quantity
The supply curve is unchanged because the fee is fixed
The firm supplies more at every price
Only ATC changes, so shutdown price cannot change
medium.feedback: A per-unit cost raises marginal and variable cost, shifting the operating supply schedule upward.

medium.q: A firm has minimum AVC of $9. At P = $8, its quantity supplied is zero; at P = $12, it supplies where P = MC. What does this illustrate?
options: The entire MC curve is supply even below AVC
ATC alone determines the firm’s supply
Market demand is the firm’s supply curve
The supply curve includes rising MC only above the shutdown threshold
medium.feedback: The shutdown threshold determines where the rising MC curve becomes the firm’s short-run supply.

medium.q: Ten firms each increase quantity supplied by 3 units when price rises. If no firms enter or exit, industry quantity supplied increases by:
medium.feedback: Industry supply sums the individual output responses: 10 × 3 = 30.

medium.q: Market demand increases in a competitive industry. Before entry occurs, the market price rises. How does one firm respond if its costs are unchanged?
options: It cuts price below the new market price to expand sales
Its P = MR line rises and it moves to a larger quantity on MC
Its ATC becomes the market supply curve
medium.feedback: The market price change is transmitted to the firm as a change in MR, producing movement along its supply curve.

medium.q: A competitive industry earns positive economic profit. What long-run sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Entry decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
Firms keep the profit permanently because they are price takers
Entry increases market supply, price falls, and economic profit is pushed toward zero
Exit decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
medium.feedback: Free entry expands industry supply and erodes positive economic profit.

medium.q: Firms in a competitive industry are sustaining economic losses. What long-run sequence is most likely?
options: Firms shut down for one day and long-run equilibrium is restored automatically
Exit reduces market supply, price rises, and losses are pushed toward zero
Entry raises supply, price falls, and losses deepen indefinitely
Exit raises supply and lowers price
medium.feedback: Long-run exit contracts industry supply and raises the market price relative to the loss-making situation.

medium.q: A firm has positive accounting profit but zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium. How can both be true?
options: Accounting profit can cover the owner’s implicit opportunity costs that economists count as costs
Accounting profit must always equal zero when economic profit is zero
The firm receives a subsidy equal to normal profit
medium.feedback: Economic cost includes owner-supplied resources, so accounting and economic profit need not be equal.

medium.q: A firm temporarily produces zero because price is below AVC, but managers expect conditions to improve next season. This is best described as:
options: Short-run shutdown rather than long-run exit
medium.feedback: A temporary zero-output choice can occur while the firm remains in the industry.

medium.q: For a representative firm in the standard constant-cost competitive benchmark, which condition is associated with long-run equilibrium?
options: P is below AVC while the firm continues forever
MR is zero at the profit-maximizing output
P = MR = MC and P equals minimum ATC
medium.feedback: At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.

medium.q: A competitive industry expands after demand rises. The larger industry raises land rents and skilled-worker wages, shifting firms’ ATC upward. Compared with the original long-run equilibrium, the new long-run price is most likely:
medium.feedback: In an increasing-cost industry, expansion raises input costs, so a higher price is required for zero-profit long-run equilibrium.

medium.q: Demand for an industry rises permanently. As firms enter, specialized suppliers expand and input costs fall. What long-run outcome is consistent with a decreasing-cost industry?
options: Industry output rises and the long-run equilibrium price can fall below its original level
Industry output falls and price must rise
The long-run supply curve must be vertical
medium.feedback: External cost reductions can shift firms’ costs down as the industry grows.

medium.q: Why is P = MC important for competitive allocative efficiency?
options: It means every firm earns positive economic profit
It makes all fixed costs disappear
The value buyers place on the last unit matches the opportunity cost of producing it
It guarantees equal incomes across consumers
medium.feedback: At P = MC, the marginal benefit reflected by price equals marginal resource cost.

medium.q: A representative competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium at the minimum point of ATC. What efficiency idea does that condition illustrate most directly?
medium.feedback: Producing at minimum ATC uses the least-cost scale available to the firm in the benchmark.

medium.q: Which observation is a limitation of using perfect competition as a literal description of many real markets?
options: Products may be differentiated and firms may have some control over price
All real markets contain many tiny firms selling identical products
Entry is always costless and instantaneous
Consumers never care about product differences
medium.feedback: The competitive model is a benchmark; many real markets relax one or more of its assumptions.

medium.q: A competitive allocation maximizes total surplus under the benchmark assumptions, but one household receives very little income. What does this illustrate?
options: The allocation cannot be efficient because incomes differ
Efficiency does not by itself guarantee an equitable distribution
medium.feedback: Total-surplus efficiency and distributional equity are separate evaluative questions.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $60, $56, $52, $48, $44, $40. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $72, $67, $62, $57, $52, $47. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $84, $78, $72, $66, $60, $54. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 4 to 5 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $55, $52, $49, $46, $43, $40. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $90, $83, $76, $69, $62, $55. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $64, $60, $56, $52, $48, $44. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 4 to 5 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $75, $70, $65, $60, $55, $50. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 2 to 3 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist’s prices for quantities 0–5 are $96, $88, $80, $72, $64, $56. What is marginal revenue from increasing output from 3 to 4 units?
medium.feedback: MR is the change in total revenue from the additional unit.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q and marginal cost MC = 20 + 0Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 120 − 2Q and MC = 24 + 0Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 90 − 1.5Q and marginal cost MC = 18 + 0Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 110 − 2.5Q and MC = 20 + 0Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 96 − 1.6Q and marginal cost MC = 16 + 0.2Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 105 − 2.1Q and MC = 18 + 0.3Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 84 − 1.4Q and marginal cost MC = 14 + 0.2Q. What output maximizes profit?
medium.feedback: Set MR equal to MC to find quantity.

medium.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 115 − 2.5Q and MC = 25 + 0.25Q. After choosing the profit-maximizing output, what price should it charge?
medium.feedback: Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $60; ATC is $35 and AVC is $20. What is the correct short-run outcome?
medium.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $60; ATC is $65 and AVC is $20. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $100
medium.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 22.5 units at $56.25; ATC is $58.03 and AVC is $20.25. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $40
medium.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 20 units at $70; ATC is $40 and AVC is $27.50. What is the correct short-run outcome?
medium.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 4.88 units at $60.24; ATC is $111.74 and AVC is $50.24. What is the correct short-run outcome?
options: Produce and incur an economic loss of $251.22
medium.feedback: If P covers AVC, producing minimizes the short-run loss.

medium.q: At its MR=MC output, a monopolist sells 19.33 units at $64.40; ATC is $54.52 and AVC is $20.90. What is the correct short-run outcome?
medium.feedback: Profit equals (P−ATC)Q at the MR=MC output.

medium.q: A single-price monopolist produces 20 units, while the competitive benchmark is 40 units. What does the output gap represent?
options: Mutually beneficial units not produced by the monopoly
Units that cost more than buyers value
medium.feedback: Between Qm and Qc, demand exceeds MC, so those units would create surplus.

medium.q: For a market with monopoly price $66.19 and competitive price $26.36 under the stated linear demand and MC, which statement is correct?
options: All consumer loss becomes monopoly profit
Monopoly transfers some surplus and destroys additional surplus
medium.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

medium.q: A single-price monopolist produces 22.73 units, while the competitive benchmark is 41.67 units. What does the output gap represent?
options: Units that cost more than buyers value
Mutually beneficial units not produced by the monopoly
medium.feedback: Between Qm and Qc, demand exceeds MC, so those units would create surplus.

medium.q: For a market with monopoly price $74.33 and competitive price $32.04 under the stated linear demand and MC, which statement is correct?
options: All consumer loss becomes monopoly profit
Monopoly transfers some surplus and destroys additional surplus
medium.feedback: Some consumer surplus is transferred; the output restriction creates DWL.

medium.q: A natural monopoly regulated at marginal cost has P < ATC. What additional policy issue arises?
options: The firm needs a subsidy or another way to cover its loss
The firm earns monopoly profit automatically
Output must be reduced below monopoly output
medium.feedback: P=MC can be efficient but fail to cover fixed cost.

medium.q: Compared with marginal-cost pricing, average-cost pricing for a natural monopoly generally produces:
options: A lower price and higher output with larger losses
A higher price and lower output but avoids an operating subsidy
The unregulated monopoly price and output
medium.feedback: P=ATC covers cost but leaves P above MC.

medium.q: A theater charges students less than adults for the same seat. Which condition is essential for the pricing strategy to work?
options: Students must have less elastic demand
Marginal cost must differ by buyer
Adults cannot cheaply buy and use student tickets
The theater must face horizontal demand
medium.feedback: Arbitrage would undermine segmented prices.

medium.q: Two customer groups have the same marginal cost, but Group A has less elastic demand than Group B. A profit-maximizing discriminator will usually:
options: Charge Group B a higher price
Charge both groups the same price regardless of elasticity
Charge Group A a higher price
medium.feedback: The less elastic market supports a larger markup.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the monopolist’s economic profit per unit at Q = 36?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC: $42 − $27 = $15.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit?
medium.feedback: Total profit is ($42 − $27) × 36 = $540.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Compared with the D = MC benchmark, how many fewer units does the monopoly produce?
medium.feedback: The monopoly produces 36 units, while D = MC occurs at 60, a difference of 24 units.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What price is associated with the D = MC benchmark?
medium.feedback: Demand and MC intersect at Q = 60 and P = $30.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What economic loss per unit is shown at Q = 40?
medium.feedback: Price is $40 and ATC is $45, so the loss is $5 per unit.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the total economic loss at the monopoly output?
medium.feedback: The firm loses $5 on each of 40 units, for a total loss of $200.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the monopoly quantity, what common value do MR and MC have?
medium.feedback: The MR and MC curves meet at $20 when Q = 40.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Approximately what quantity and price mark the D = MC benchmark?
medium.feedback: The graph marks the demand-MC intersection at about Q = 67 and P = $27.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the profit-maximizing output, what is economic profit per unit?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit is $47 − $24 = $23.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at Q = 45?
medium.feedback: Economic profit is ($47 − $24) × 45 = $1,035.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What price corresponds to the D = MC quantity?
medium.feedback: Demand intersects the horizontal MC curve at P = $20 and Q = 90.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Which marked outcome corresponds to average-cost, or fair-return, pricing?
medium.feedback: Fair-return pricing sets price equal to ATC; the graph marks D = ATC near Q = 116 and P = $16.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Which marked outcome corresponds to marginal-cost pricing?
medium.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing sets demand price equal to MC, shown at Q = 140 and P = $10.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the marginal-cost-pricing output, what is the economic loss per unit?
medium.feedback: The per-unit loss is ATC minus price: $15 − $10 = $5.

medium.q: A town currently has one ambulance provider, but licenses are readily available and several firms can enter with ordinary equipment. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The current one-seller market does not by itself establish durable monopoly power
The provider is a natural monopoly because only one firm operates today
The provider must have a patent protecting ambulance service
The provider can charge any price because entry has not happened yet
medium.feedback: A monopoly requires meaningful barriers to entry, not merely one seller at a moment in time.

medium.q: A patented medical device is profitable while the patent remains in force. What is the patent doing economically?
options: Making the firm’s demand curve horizontal
Forcing marginal revenue to equal price
Guaranteeing that average total cost will fall forever
Restricting entry and helping preserve the incumbent’s market power
medium.feedback: A patent is a legal barrier that can prevent rivals from copying the protected product.

medium.q: A messaging platform becomes more useful as more friends and businesses join it. Why can this discourage entry by a rival platform?
options: The rival automatically faces perfectly inelastic demand
Network effects remove the need for consumer choice
Users may prefer the established network because its large user base raises its value
The incumbent’s marginal cost must be zero
medium.feedback: Network effects can create a demand-side barrier because users value access to the existing network.

medium.q: A firm owns the only economically viable source of a rare input required to make a specialized product. Which mechanism protects its market position most directly?
options: Its customers cannot respond to price changes
Control of an essential resource blocks rivals from obtaining a necessary input
Its price must equal marginal cost
Its fixed costs disappear as output rises
medium.feedback: Exclusive control of a critical resource can prevent otherwise capable rivals from entering.

medium.q: A regional water network requires an enormous pipe system, and duplicating the network would raise average cost. Which fact best supports natural-monopoly status?
options: One firm can serve market demand at lower average cost than multiple duplicative networks
The provider has the legal right to discriminate among all buyers
The firm earns accounting profit in the current year
medium.feedback: Natural monopoly comes from scale economies over the relevant range of market demand.

medium.q: A monopolist cuts price to sell one additional unit. Why can marginal revenue be far below the new price?
options: Average revenue becomes zero when price falls
The demand curve becomes horizontal after the price cut
The extra unit adds revenue, but the lower price also reduces revenue collected on earlier units
Marginal cost is automatically subtracted from marginal revenue
medium.feedback: Marginal revenue reflects both the output effect and the price effect on units already sold.

medium.q: At 40 units a monopolist has MR=$28 and MC=$22; at 41 units MR=$24 and MC=$25. Which output is the better marginal choice?
options: 40 units, because the 41st unit costs more at the margin than it adds to revenue
41 units, because price must still exceed marginal revenue
41 units, because a monopolist always produces until price equals MC
40 units only if average total cost is minimized there
medium.feedback: Produce units for which MR covers MC and stop before the next unit has MC greater than MR.

medium.q: A monopolist has already found its profit-maximizing quantity using MR=MC. What is the next step for determining the monopoly price?
options: Use the MR curve value as the price
Set price equal to average total cost
Choose the lowest price on the demand curve
Move up to the demand curve at that quantity
medium.feedback: MR determines the quantity condition; demand gives the price buyers will pay for that quantity.

medium.q: Suppose competition would produce 100 units at $20, while monopoly produces 70 units at $35. Which change is the clearest source of efficiency loss?
options: The 30 units between 70 and 100 that would have generated gains from trade are not produced
The monopolist receives revenue on the 70 units it sells
The market price is written in dollars rather than units
Consumers buy positive quantities under monopoly
medium.feedback: The efficiency loss comes from mutually beneficial transactions forgone because of restricted output.

medium.q: If a monopolist reduces output farther below the competitive quantity while demand and cost curves are unchanged, what generally happens to deadweight loss?
options: It necessarily falls because the firm earns more profit
It becomes zero when price rises
It is unchanged because transfers do not matter
It increases because more mutually beneficial units are forgone
medium.feedback: Greater output restriction usually widens the range of lost gains from trade.

medium.q: A natural monopoly has MC=$12 and ATC=$20 at the allocatively efficient quantity. If regulation sets P=$12, which outcome is most likely without a subsidy?
options: The firm must reduce output to zero by definition
The firm incurs an economic loss because price is below ATC
The firm earns $8 profit per unit
The firm breaks even because P=MC
medium.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.

medium.q: A regulator sets price where demand intersects ATC for a natural monopoly. Which combination best describes the result?
options: The firm can cover total economic cost, but price generally remains above MC
The firm earns maximum monopoly profit and output falls to zero
Price equals MC and allocative efficiency is guaranteed
The firm necessarily faces a horizontal demand curve
medium.feedback: Average-cost pricing aims for financial viability, not full P=MC efficiency.

medium.q: A price cap is set above the price the monopolist would charge without regulation. What is the immediate effect?
options: The firm must charge the cap even if it prefers a lower price
The firm’s fixed cost becomes zero
The cap is nonbinding and does not constrain the firm’s chosen price
medium.feedback: A ceiling above the unregulated price does not bind.

medium.q: A regulator wants lower prices but also wants the utility to maintain infrastructure and innovate. Which concern best captures the tradeoff?
options: Investment incentives are unrelated to expected returns
Any regulation automatically produces the competitive quantity
Aggressive price limits can improve consumer terms while weakening incentives or revenue for cost recovery and investment
Lower prices always increase monopoly profit
medium.feedback: Regulation balances static consumer/efficiency goals against financial and dynamic incentives.

medium.q: Demand for a utility expands enough that the relevant output range moves beyond the region where ATC is falling. What does that suggest about the natural-monopoly argument?
options: It guarantees marginal cost is zero
It may weaken because one firm may no longer have a cost advantage over multiple firms across the new relevant range
It becomes stronger automatically because demand increased
It proves that price discrimination is efficient
medium.feedback: Natural-monopoly status depends on cost conditions over the relevant market-demand range.

medium.q: A firm has market power and observes two groups with different demand elasticities, but buyers can costlessly resell the product. What happens to the proposed two-price strategy?
options: The firm can preserve both prices indefinitely
The high-price group automatically becomes less elastic
Marginal cost becomes different across groups
Arbitrage tends to collapse the price difference
medium.feedback: Segmentation must be enforceable; costless resale undermines differentiated prices.

medium.q: Why does a third-degree discriminator compare MR from each market with the common MC?
options: Average revenue must equal average cost in every market
Profit is increased by allocating another unit to a market whenever that market’s MR exceeds MC
The firm must make prices identical across markets
medium.feedback: The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.

medium.q: Two groups have identical MC. Seniors have less elastic demand than students. What happens to the optimal markup?
medium.feedback: A less elastic market supports a larger markup over common marginal cost.

medium.q: Compared with a single-price monopoly, perfect first-degree price discrimination can eliminate the standard output deadweight loss when:
options: The firm sells every unit for which willingness to pay is at least MC
The firm charges one common price above MC
The firm ignores willingness to pay
medium.feedback: Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.

medium.q: A discriminatory pricing plan raises total output by serving a new low-price market. What is the most defensible welfare conclusion?
options: Total surplus must fall because prices differ
Consumer surplus must rise in every group
Total surplus may rise because additional mutually beneficial trades occur, though distribution also changes
medium.feedback: Welfare effects depend on output as well as how surplus is redistributed.

medium.q: An airline sells a discounted ticket that cannot be transferred and imposes restrictions that separate leisure from business travelers. What economic purpose do the restrictions serve?
options: They force the same elasticity in both groups
They eliminate the airline’s fixed costs
They help prevent arbitrage and maintain market segmentation
They make the airline a price taker
medium.feedback: Restrictions can help keep low-price buyers from reselling or masquerading as high-value segments.

medium.q: A firm can separate buyers perfectly but faces a perfectly competitive market with many identical sellers. Why is discrimination difficult to sustain?
options: Buyer groups necessarily have identical elasticities
The firm lacks enough market power to set different markups without losing customers
Resale prevention becomes irrelevant only because MC is zero
medium.feedback: Segmentation is not enough; the seller also needs pricing power.

medium.q: A monopolist starts charging different prices to two isolated groups. The high-price group is observed to have less elastic demand. Which fact best explains the pricing pattern?
options: Optimal monopoly markup is inversely related to demand responsiveness
The high-price group must have higher marginal cost
The low-price group must have higher fixed cost
Price discrimination requires equal prices when MC is common
medium.feedback: Lower elasticity supports a larger markup over marginal cost.

medium.q: A market has 150 independently owned salons, each with a distinct location and reputation, and new salons can open without major legal barriers. Which model fits best?
options: Perfect competition with identical services and a horizontal demand curve for each salon
medium.feedback: Many firms, differentiation, and entry fit monopolistic competition.

medium.q: A clothing store raises price and loses some, but not all, customers to nearby brands. What does this imply?
options: It is a price-taking commodity seller facing a horizontal demand curve at the market price
Its firm demand is downward sloping and relatively elastic
medium.feedback: Differentiation gives market power, while close substitutes keep demand responsive.

medium.q: A new cluster of coffee shops opens near an established café. Which immediate effect is most likely for the café?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic
Its demand shifts right and becomes less elastic
Its MC curve shifts down automatically
medium.feedback: Entry creates more close substitutes.

medium.q: Several boutique gyms close after sustained losses. Which effect is most likely for a surviving gym?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic because fewer alternatives remain available
Its demand shifts right and may become less elastic
Its MR becomes horizontal at zero
medium.feedback: Exit removes substitutes and can strengthen surviving demand.

medium.q: A firm’s price is $42, MC is $31, and ATC is $42 at the chosen output. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns an $11 profit per unit because price exceeds marginal cost by $11
The firm earns zero economic profit but has an $11 markup
medium.feedback: Price equals ATC, so profit is zero; price minus MC is the markup.

medium.q: A firm produces 24 units in long-run equilibrium, while ATC is minimized at 36 units. What is its excess capacity?
medium.feedback: Excess capacity is minimum-ATC output minus equilibrium output.

medium.q: An advertising campaign merely raises fixed selling cost and leaves demand unchanged. What happens to the short-run MR=MC output?
options: It falls because fixed cost raises MC
medium.feedback: A pure fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MR or MC.

medium.q: A per-unit promotional fee is imposed on every unit sold. Which curves are directly raised?
medium.feedback: A per-unit selling cost is a variable cost.

medium.q: A brand campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rivals. What is the most direct demand effect?
options: Demand shifts only because the campaign lowers marginal cost and average variable cost
The firm’s demand becomes less elastic
MR equals price at every quantity
medium.feedback: Greater loyalty reduces responsiveness to price.

medium.q: A comparison website makes prices and features easier to compare across brands. What is the likely effect?
options: Every seller becomes a monopoly because buyers can now compare all products directly
medium.feedback: Lower search costs make switching easier.

medium.q: Harbor Café faces P=100−2Q and MC=18+0.3Q. What output satisfies MR=MC?
medium.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

medium.q: After Harbor Café chooses Q=19.07, what price follows from P=100−2Q?
medium.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

medium.q: Iris Salon faces P=112−2.4Q and MC=20+0.35Q. What output satisfies MR=MC?
medium.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

medium.q: After Iris Salon chooses Q=17.86, what price follows from P=112−2.4Q?
medium.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

medium.q: Juniper Fitness faces P=96−1.6Q and MC=16+0.4Q. What output satisfies MR=MC?
medium.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

medium.q: After Juniper Fitness chooses Q=22.22, what price follows from P=96−1.6Q?
medium.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

medium.q: Kite Apparel faces P=120−2.5Q and MC=22+0.3Q. What output satisfies MR=MC?
medium.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

medium.q: After Kite Apparel chooses Q=18.49, what price follows from P=120−2.5Q?
medium.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

medium.q: Lumen Bistro faces P=92−1.5Q and MC=18+0.35Q. What output satisfies MR=MC?
medium.feedback: Use MR=a−2bQ and set it equal to MC.

medium.q: After Lumen Bistro chooses Q=22.09, what price follows from P=92−1.5Q?
medium.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

medium.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm produces Q1=20 while ATC is minimized at Q2=36.67. What is excess capacity?
medium.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

medium.q: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $70 and MC is $50. What is the markup?
medium.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

medium.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm produces Q1=24 while ATC is minimized at Q2=39.71. What is excess capacity?
medium.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

medium.q: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $76 and MC is $49.60. What is the markup?
medium.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

medium.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm produces Q1=18 while ATC is minimized at Q2=34.07. What is excess capacity?
medium.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

medium.q: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $64 and MC is $47.80. What is the markup?
medium.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

medium.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm produces Q1=28 while ATC is minimized at Q2=43. What is excess capacity?
medium.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

medium.q: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $82 and MC is $48.40. What is the markup?
medium.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

medium.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm produces Q1=22 while ATC is minimized at Q2=38. What is excess capacity?
medium.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

medium.q: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $68 and MC is $50.40. What is the markup?
medium.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s economic profit per unit at Q = 50?
medium.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC: $37 − $33 = $4.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at the profit-maximizing output?
medium.feedback: Total profit is ($37 − $33) × 50 = $200.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, by how much does price exceed marginal cost?
medium.feedback: The markup over marginal cost is $37 − $23 = $14.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What economic profit does the firm earn?
medium.feedback: Because price equals ATC, economic profit is zero.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total revenue at Q = 36?
medium.feedback: Total revenue is $27 × 36 = $972.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total cost at Q = 36?
medium.feedback: ATC is $27, so total cost is $27 × 36 = $972.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. How much excess capacity does the firm have?
medium.feedback: Excess capacity is efficient-scale output minus actual output: 50 − 36 = 14.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What minimum average total cost is shown at the efficient scale?
medium.feedback: ATC reaches its minimum of $25 at Q = 50.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. At the long-run output, what is the firm’s markup over marginal cost?
medium.feedback: The markup is P − MC = $27 − $15.50 = $11.50.

medium.q: A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away. What best explains this result?
options: Product differentiation gives the restaurant limited price-setting power
Free entry makes the restaurant a pure price taker
Many sellers make the restaurant demand curve perfectly elastic
The restaurant controls the entire market supply
medium.feedback: Differentiation makes the firm’s product an imperfect substitute, so its individual demand curve slopes downward.

medium.q: Several new coffee shops open offering very similar drinks and service. Holding other factors constant, what is most likely to happen to the demand facing one existing shop?
options: It becomes less elastic because the market has more sellers
It becomes vertical because each shop is now smaller
It becomes perfectly inelastic because products remain differentiated
It becomes more elastic because customers have more close substitutes
medium.feedback: More close substitutes make customers more responsive to one firm’s price.

medium.q: A city has dozens of independently owned fitness studios. Each offers a somewhat different mix of classes, and new studios can enter without major legal barriers. Which model is the best starting point?
medium.feedback: Many sellers, differentiated products, and relatively easy entry are the defining combination.

medium.q: A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments. Which source of differentiation is most important?
medium.feedback: The practice is differentiating the service experience rather than relying on a legal barrier or identical product.

medium.q: A firm spends $20,000 on a fixed ad campaign. Demand shifts right, but MC is unchanged. Which statement is correct?
options: Profit must rise because demand shifted right
The profit-maximizing output may rise because MR changed, while the fixed ad cost also lowers profit
Output must stay unchanged because every advertising expense is fixed
MC shifts upward by exactly $20,000 at every output
medium.feedback: The demand shift can change MR and output even though the fixed selling cost itself does not shift MC.

medium.q: A comparison website makes it easier for buyers to compare nearly identical local services. What effect is most likely on each firm’s demand?
medium.feedback: Better comparison makes substitution easier, increasing buyers’ responsiveness to one firm’s price.

medium.q: A firm pays a $3 promotional fee for every unit sold, and demand is unchanged. What is the most direct short-run effect?
options: Only fixed cost rises, so output cannot change
Demand shifts right by $3 at every quantity
ATC falls because advertising spreads fixed cost
MC rises, so the MR=MC output tends to fall
medium.feedback: A per-unit selling cost raises marginal cost and tends to reduce the profit-maximizing output when demand is unchanged.

medium.q: A restaurant improves food quality. Customers are willing to pay more, but marginal production cost also rises. What determines the new profit-maximizing output?
options: The old output because quality is nonprice competition
The new MR and MC curves together
medium.feedback: Quality improvement can affect both willingness to pay and cost, so the new optimum still requires comparing MR and MC.

medium.q: A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive. What becomes more plausible, other things equal?
options: A lower willingness to pay at every quantity
medium.feedback: Less elastic demand can support greater price-cost markup for a firm with market power.

medium.q: Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase. Why might heavy advertising sometimes be interpreted as a quality signal?
options: A high-quality seller may expect repeat business that helps justify the advertising expense
Advertising legally guarantees the product will be high quality
Only low-quality sellers are allowed to advertise heavily
Advertising eliminates all uncertainty before purchase
medium.feedback: In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales.

medium.q: A policy causes several niche brands to exit. Average production cost falls, but consumers lose valued variety. What is the correct welfare conclusion?
options: Welfare must rise because average cost fell
Welfare must fall because the number of brands fell
The change is irrelevant because firms earn zero economic profit
The net effect is ambiguous without comparing cost savings with lost variety benefits
medium.feedback: Efficiency analysis must weigh resource savings against the consumer value of differentiation and variety.

medium.q: A textbook labels a market monopolistically competitive because it has many differentiated sellers. In one rural town, however, only two sellers actually serve customers. What is the best caution?
options: Two local sellers guarantee a natural monopoly
Differentiation becomes irrelevant whenever geography matters
The local market may display strategic interdependence that the broad model misses
The market must still be perfectly competitive locally
medium.feedback: Market boundaries matter. A broad national description can hide a much more concentrated local competitive environment.

medium.q: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit but charges P>$MC$. What does this show?
options: The firm is producing at minimum ATC
Zero economic profit does not imply allocative efficiency
The firm must be earning an accounting loss
Entry has failed to eliminate all market power
medium.feedback: Entry can eliminate economic profit while differentiation leaves a markup and P above MC.

medium.q: Two markets have the same total production cost. Market A offers one standardized product; Market B offers several differentiated versions that consumers value. What can be said?
options: Market B may generate greater consumer benefit because variety itself can have value
Market A must be more allocatively efficient because it has fewer products
Market B must have higher deadweight loss because it has more brands
Both markets provide identical welfare because production cost is the same
medium.feedback: Equal production cost does not imply equal consumer benefit when differentiated varieties match heterogeneous preferences.

medium.q: Four firms have market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, and 10%, with the remaining firms holding 10%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
medium.feedback: Add the shares of the four largest firms.

medium.q: A market has shares of 50%, 25%, 15%, and 10%. Which measure gives especially heavy weight to the 50% firm?
medium.feedback: Squaring shares makes a very large firm count disproportionately.

medium.q: A merger combines firms with 20% and 15% market shares. By how much does the HHI rise if all other shares stay unchanged?
medium.feedback: The change is 2ab = 2(20)(15) = 600.

medium.q: A national market appears unconcentrated, but each rural town has only two local suppliers. What is the main lesson?
options: Geographic market definition can conceal local concentration
National concentration always measures local competition accurately.
medium.feedback: The relevant geographic market can be narrower than the national market.

medium.q: Two airlines choose whether to cut fares. Each earns more from cutting when the rival holds fares, but both earn less when both cut. This structure is closest to:
medium.feedback: Each airline has an individual incentive that can trigger a jointly harmful price war.

medium.q: Row’s payoff is higher with strategy B whether Column chooses X or Y. What does Row have?
medium.feedback: B beats Row’s alternative under both Column actions.

medium.q: A cell is a Nash equilibrium when:
options: Neither firm can improve by changing strategy alone
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
Both firms chose the same letter
medium.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses.

medium.q: A game has two outcomes in which both players are best responding. What does the game have?
options: Two dominant strategies for each player
medium.feedback: Games can have multiple equilibria.

medium.q: A firm observes that its rival will respond aggressively to any price cut. This expectation most directly illustrates:
options: A dominant strategy that is best regardless of the rival’s action.
medium.feedback: The firm’s best action depends on the expected response.

medium.q: Two firms agree to restrict output, but one secretly offers rebates. The rebate is best described as:
medium.feedback: Secret discounts undermine the coordinated price.

medium.q: A cartel’s market demand is P = 100 − 2Q and MC is $20. What total quantity maximizes joint profit?
medium.feedback: MR = 100 − 4Q; setting MR = 20 gives Q = 20.

medium.q: Using P = 100 − 2Q and cartel output Q = 20, what price does the cartel charge?
medium.feedback: Read price from demand: 100 − 2(20) = 60.

medium.q: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive a larger production quota?
options: It has the largest historical market share.
It can produce part of joint output at lower cost
medium.feedback: Efficient allocation places more output with lower-cost producers.

medium.q: A punishment strategy requires a rival to start a costly price war after cheating. When is the threat credible?
options: The announced response is credible because it sounds severe and harms the entrant
Whenever the price war hurts the cheater
When starting the price war is still the rival’s best response after cheating occurs
medium.feedback: A threat must be rational when its decision node is reached.

medium.q: Firms expect to compete for only one final period. Why is cooperation harder to sustain?
options: Future punishment has little or no value
Future punishment guarantees cooperation regardless of observability or credibility
medium.feedback: A short horizon weakens the future cost of cheating.

medium.q: A market’s largest firm announces a price, and rivals independently match it. This is:
medium.feedback: A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.

medium.q: Several firms raise prices after a common input cost increase. Why does this not by itself prove collusion?
options: Parallel price changes are conclusive evidence of an explicit agreement.
Input costs affect only fixed cost
Independent firms may respond similarly to the same cost shock
Parallel prices always maximize total surplus
medium.feedback: Common conditions can produce parallel conduct without agreement.

medium.q: An incumbent builds capacity that would be useful even if entry occurs. Why can this deter entry?
options: It turns the market into perfect competition
The capacity can make an aggressive post-entry response credible
medium.feedback: A sunk commitment can alter the incumbent’s later incentives.

medium.q: An incumbent threatens to cut price below variable cost after entry, but doing so would be very costly and temporary. The threat is likely:
medium.feedback: The incumbent may not rationally carry out the threat later.

medium.q: A firm maintains a lower price today to reduce expected entrant profit. What is the strategic cost?
options: It raises current monopoly profit automatically
medium.feedback: Limit pricing trades current profit for possible entry deterrence.

medium.q: In the kinked-demand model, rivals are assumed to match:
options: Price cuts more readily than price increases
medium.feedback: This asymmetry creates the kink.

medium.q: If MC changes within the discontinuity in the kinked-demand MR curve, the model predicts:
options: Price and output may remain unchanged
medium.feedback: The same output can remain optimal while MC crosses the MR gap.

medium.q: An effective cartel raises price and reduces output. Which part of lost consumer surplus is not transferred to producers?
medium.feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades create DWL.

medium.q: A merger raises HHI but also creates verified large cost savings. What is the sound conclusion?
options: Both increased market power and efficiencies must be evaluated
medium.feedback: Concentration and efficiency evidence both matter.

medium.q: A merger lowers marginal cost, but the merged firm keeps price high because rivalry weakens. What does this show?
options: Cost savings need not be passed fully to consumers
medium.feedback: Pass-through depends on competitive pressure.

medium.q: Why can foreign competition affect a domestic concentration assessment?
options: Imports are excluded from every market definition
Imports may provide substitutes that constrain domestic firms
medium.feedback: Relevant competitors may include foreign suppliers.

medium.q: A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price. This is:
medium.feedback: Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions.

medium.q: Heavy advertising builds brand loyalty and reduces switching. What strategic effect is most plausible?
options: Every firm becomes a price taker
Price competition may soften because firm demand becomes less elastic
medium.feedback: Loyalty can reduce substitution among brands.

medium.q: A market has six firms, but two control 78% of sales and rivals closely watch one another. Which structure is most plausible?
medium.feedback: Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly.

medium.q: Why can game theory yield different predictions across oligopoly markets?
options: Every oligopoly has one dominant strategy
Payoffs, information, timing, and repetition differ
medium.feedback: Strategic settings differ across industries.

medium.q: A grocery chain has only 8% of national grocery sales but 55% of sales in one isolated county. What does this example show about concentration measures?
options: They measure profit rather than market share
They depend on how the relevant market is defined
They are valid only for national markets
They ignore geographic differences and therefore always produce the same concentration result nationwide
medium.feedback: The same firm can appear small or dominant depending on the economically relevant geographic and product market.

medium.q: Two markets each have a four-firm concentration ratio of 80%. In Market A the four firms have nearly equal shares; in Market B one firm is much larger than the other three. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Market B can have a higher HHI because HHI gives more weight to large shares
Both markets must have the same HHI because an equal CR4 guarantees identical concentration among the leading firms
Market A must have the higher HHI because equal shares are squared
HHI cannot distinguish markets with the same CR4
medium.feedback: Squaring market shares makes HHI more sensitive to a very large firm even when CR4 is unchanged.

medium.q: Three national wireless carriers dominate a market. Before one carrier cuts price, its managers estimate how the other two are likely to respond. Which feature of oligopoly is being illustrated?
medium.feedback: The payoff from one firm’s choice depends partly on how a small number of major rivals react.

medium.q: An industry’s HHI rises after two sizable firms merge. What can the HHI increase tell an analyst directly?
options: The merged firm must now be a monopolist because any increase in HHI implies complete control of the market
Market concentration increased under the chosen market definition
medium.feedback: HHI measures concentration; welfare and policy conclusions require additional evidence about competition and efficiencies.

medium.q: Suppose Firm B chooses a high price. Firm A earns $8 million with a high price and $11 million with a low price. What is Firm A’s best response to B’s high price?
options: Choose whichever action maximizes joint industry profit
medium.feedback: Conditional on B choosing high, A compares its own payoffs and chooses the action paying 11 rather than 8.

medium.q: Firm A earns more from advertising whether Firm B advertises or not. What follows?
options: Advertising is a dominant strategy for Firm A
Advertising must maximize the two firms’ combined profit whenever it is more profitable for Firm A than not advertising
The game has no Nash equilibrium
medium.feedback: A dominant strategy gives the player a higher payoff for every action the rival might take.

medium.q: A strategy is Firm A’s best response when B chooses X, but A prefers a different strategy when B chooses Y. What can be concluded?
options: The first strategy is dominant because it is best once
The joint-payoff maximum must be a Nash equilibrium
The first strategy is not dominant for A
medium.feedback: Dominance requires the same strategy to be best against every rival action.

medium.q: At a proposed outcome, Firm A could gain by changing its action while Firm B kept its action fixed. What does that imply?
options: Firm A has a dominant strategy
The game has no strategic interdependence
The proposed outcome is not a Nash equilibrium
The proposed outcome must maximize joint profit
medium.feedback: A unilateral profitable deviation means at least one player is not best responding, so the cell is not Nash.

medium.q: Two firms could earn $20 million each by coordinating, but the Nash equilibrium gives each $14 million. What does this illustrate?
options: Dominant strategies always produce the joint-payoff maximum
A Nash equilibrium need not maximize combined payoff
medium.feedback: Mutual best responses can lead to a stable outcome with lower total payoff than a cooperative alternative.

medium.q: In payoff order (Row, Column), the cell for Row choosing A and Column choosing Y is (6, 15). Which comparison is relevant when finding Row’s best response to Y?
options: Compare Row’s first-number payoffs across Row’s available actions in column Y
Compare Column’s second-number payoffs across every column, regardless of which action Column has already chosen
Add both payoffs in every cell and choose the largest sum
medium.feedback: A best-response calculation holds the rival action fixed and compares the player’s own payoff across its alternatives.

medium.q: Why can firms end up at an outcome they both consider worse than another available outcome?
options: Firms are required to choose the outcome with the lowest combined payoff whenever their interests conflict
A Nash equilibrium always minimizes profit
Individual incentives to deviate can make the better joint outcome unstable
medium.feedback: A jointly attractive cell need not survive if one player can gain by deviating while the rival cooperates.

medium.q: A cartel has already chosen its joint-profit-maximizing total output. Why might it assign more production to a member with lower marginal cost?
options: Shifting output toward the lower-cost producer can reduce the cartel’s total production cost
Equal quotas always maximize joint profit
Higher-cost firms must produce more to preserve competition
Output allocation cannot affect cartel profit once total output is fixed, even when members have different marginal costs
medium.feedback: For a fixed cartel total, allocating more production to lower-marginal-cost members can raise combined profit.

medium.q: Three firms agree to keep prices high. One firm quietly gives large rebates while publicly posting the agreed price. Economically, the rebates are best interpreted as:
options: Proof that the cartel has eliminated all competition because no member can gain market share without openly cutting the posted price
A required form of price leadership
Cheating that captures extra sales while rivals maintain the collusive price
medium.feedback: Secret rebates undermine the agreement by letting one member expand sales at the others’ expense.

medium.q: Which market condition makes a cartel harder to sustain?
options: A small number of firms with similar objectives
A credible punishment system that quickly detects and penalizes members who secretly exceed their agreed output
Many opportunities for members to make secret sales that rivals cannot observe
Frequent transparent reporting of member sales
medium.feedback: When cheating is hard to observe, deviations are easier and enforcement becomes weaker.

medium.q: A cartel restricts total output below the competitive level. What is the intended effect on the market price?
options: Create a perfectly elastic industry demand curve so the cartel can sell any quantity at the higher price
Raise price by moving up the market demand curve
Force price down to marginal cost
medium.feedback: Restricting industry output raises the price buyers are willing to pay along downward-sloping market demand.

medium.q: Suppose cartel members can observe one another’s sales almost immediately. Why can this improve cartel stability?
options: It makes cheating easier to detect and respond to
It removes each member’s incentive to earn profit
It guarantees the cartel price equals marginal cost
It causes market concentration to fall
medium.feedback: Fast observability reduces the chance that a member can profit from hidden deviations for long.

medium.q: Two firms with market shares of 18% and 12% merge. Holding all other shares fixed, why does HHI rise?
options: The merger automatically removes all smaller rivals
The squared share of the combined 30% firm exceeds the sum of the two firms’ separate squared shares
HHI counts the merged firm twice
Every merger doubles total market sales
medium.feedback: Because shares are squared, combining two positive shares increases HHI by the cross term 2ab.

medium.q: A proposed merger would eliminate the closest competitor but also reduce marginal cost substantially. What is the best economic approach?
options: Compare the likely loss of rivalry with the magnitude and pass-through of verifiable efficiencies
Approve the merger automatically because costs fall
Block the merger automatically because concentration rises
Ignore cost effects because only the number of firms matters
medium.feedback: Merger analysis requires weighing competitive harm against genuine efficiencies rather than using one fact mechanically.

medium.q: When a cartel raises price, some lost consumer surplus becomes additional producer surplus. What happens to the remaining loss associated with trades that no longer occur?
options: It is automatically recovered through innovation
medium.feedback: Foregone mutually beneficial trades destroy total surplus rather than transfer it to another market participant.

medium.q: A domestic industry has a high concentration ratio, but buyers can readily switch to imported substitutes when domestic prices rise. What does this imply?
options: The market must be a monopoly
Domestic concentration alone may overstate the firms’ effective market power
Imports are irrelevant to market definition
medium.feedback: Competitive constraints from close substitutes, including imports when relevant, matter to the economic market definition.

medium.q: A merger creates a larger research budget but also reduces head-to-head price competition. Which statement is most defensible?
options: The merger must lower HHI because research increases
Both innovation benefits and reduced-rivalry costs should be evaluated rather than assuming one dominates
A larger research budget proves consumer welfare will rise
Reduced rivalry is irrelevant whenever innovation is possible
medium.feedback: The welfare question is empirical: innovation gains can matter, but so can weaker price and quality competition.

hard.q: Northstar Bakery pays each worker $120. Worker 3 raises output from 20 to 34. Which pair is correct?
options: MP=14 units and MC=$8.57 per unit
hard.feedback: MP is the output change; with a constant wage, MC is wage divided by MP.

hard.q: At Ironwood Furniture, Q=41, TFC=$300, and 4 workers each cost $135. Which cost identity is correct?
hard.feedback: Divide each total by output and verify ATC=AFC+AVC.
