It lowers average fixed cost rather than AVC because labor productivity affects the spreading of fixed cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher output per worker reduces variable labor cost per unit.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the identity TC = TFC + TVC connect to ATC?
options: Dividing by Q gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by Q gives ATC = MC + AVC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The average-cost identity follows directly from the total-cost identity.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can ATC fall even when AVC is flat?
options: Falling AFC can pull ATC downward
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Because ATC = AVC + AFC, a declining fixed-cost component can reduce ATC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is AVC often more relevant than AFC for understanding the cost of current production activity?
options: AFC determines how much extra output one worker adds
AFC changes directly with every unit produced
AVC reflects variable resources used to produce the current output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Variable cost is tied to inputs adjusted as production changes.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a below-average marginal cost affect ATC?
options: It leaves ATC unchanged by definition
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The marginal-versus-average rule applies to costs just as it does to other averages.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the sunk-cost rule connect to marginal analysis?
options: Both rules say fixed costs are always irrelevant
Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
Marginal analysis requires adding all past costs
Sunk cost is another term for marginal cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can a cost be fixed with respect to current output but still relevant to a future decision?
options: It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
Every fixed cost is permanently sunk
Fixed costs always change one-for-one with output
Future fixed costs are excluded from economic cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Cost behavior with output and recoverability across decisions are different classifications.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is “recovering what we already spent” a poor reason by itself to continue a project?
options: Continuing can convert past spending into a relevant marginal benefit if enough future revenue is earned
Past spending should be added to expected future benefits because the project needs to recover its historical cost
A project should continue when accounting profit remains positive, even if future incremental costs exceed benefits
Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does specialization connect to economies of scale?
options: A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
Specialization always creates diminishing marginal product
Specialization raises fixed cost per unit forever
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range.

bridgeQuestions.q: How do coordination problems connect organizational size to diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination problems reduce all input prices
They guarantee constant returns to scale
They turn fixed cost into sunk cost
Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Very large scale can create managerial inefficiencies that push LRAC upward.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the short-run/long-run distinction connect SRATC curves to LRAC?
options: SRATC includes implicit cost but LRAC does not
The curves differ only because of revenue
Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
LRAC fixes plant size while SRATC changes every input
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Long-run flexibility over plant size is what lets LRAC trace the least-cost envelope.

bridgeQuestions.q: How is economies of scale different from spreading a fixed short-run cost over more units?
options: Falling AFC is a long-run scale effect only
Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
Economies of scale requires one input to remain fixed
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Both can lower average cost, but they arise from different mechanisms and horizons.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can productivity improvements affect long-run average cost?
options: If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
Productivity affects revenue but never cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: More output from a given bundle of resources can lower the cost required per unit.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does MES build on the idea of economies of scale?
options: MES is the largest feasible plant regardless of cost
MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
MES is where diseconomies first begin at zero output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does constant returns to scale differ from short-run diminishing marginal product?
options: Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
Constant returns requires a fixed plant
Diminishing marginal product requires all inputs to change proportionally
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The concepts apply to different production experiments and time horizons.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can MES matter when comparing efficient firm scale with the size of a market?
options: It fixes the market price by law
It measures accounting profit rather than cost
It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.

bridgeQuestions.q: A competitive firm uses which cost curve to decide whether another unit should be produced?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The incremental output decision compares MR with MC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which average cost determines profit per unit after output is chosen?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Profit per unit=P−ATC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which average cost determines the short-run shutdown threshold?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does a fixed-cost increase not change short-run competitive output?
options: It does not change MC or AVC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Output and shutdown depend on marginal and variable costs.

bridgeQuestions.q: Zero economic profit includes which owner return?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Normal profit covers entrepreneurial opportunity cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: How is a competitive firm’s supply response connected to cost?
options: It follows rising MC above AVC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: MC gives the additional cost of supply.

bridgeQuestions.q: What converts individual competitive firm supplies into market supply?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Add firm quantities supplied at each price.

bridgeQuestions.q: Entry affects market supply by:
options: Moving upward along the same supply curve
bridgeQuestions.feedback: More firms supply more total output at each price.

bridgeQuestions.q: Exit affects market supply by:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Fewer firms reduce total quantity supplied.

bridgeQuestions.q: A competitive firm should expand output while:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal benefit to the firm exceeds marginal cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: The last profitable unit in a discrete table is the last unit with:
options: MR at least as large as MC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The next unit would reduce profit once MC exceeds MR.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is the rising-MC crossing used?
options: It is the crossing where moving beyond the output makes MC exceed MR
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The local profit maximum occurs where MC rises through MR.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is P=MC associated with allocative efficiency?
options: The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal unit’s cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The last unit’s marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: What does entry after profit tend to do to consumer surplus?
options: Raise price and lower consumer surplus
Lower price tends to increase consumer surplus
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Entry expands supply and lowers price.

bridgeQuestions.q: A per-unit tax on competitive output directly raises:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The tax is tied to each unit produced.

bridgeQuestions.q: A lump-sum annual tax on a competitive firm directly raises:
options: Average total cost but not marginal cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: A higher wage shifts a competitive firm’s cost curves because labor is:
options: A variable input in the standard short-run model
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher variable input cost raises AVC and MC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Compared with a price-taking firm, a firm with market power generally faces:
options: A horizontal demand curve at all outputs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Market power changes the firm’s revenue conditions; the competitive firm takes price.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can a perfectly competitive outcome fail to maximize social surplus?
options: Private marginal cost may omit external costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The benchmark requires private and social marginal costs to align.

bridgeQuestions.q: A small competitive firm selling a traded good takes which price as given in the open-market model?
options: The relevant market or world price
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Competitive firms respond to the price established in the wider market.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the competitive firm’s price-taking assumption connect market equilibrium to the firm’s decision problem?
options: Market demand determines the firm’s fixed cost
Market supply and demand determine price; the firm then chooses quantity at that price
The firm chooses price first from its cost curves and then the market determines how much buyers take
The firm’s ATC determines the market equilibrium price directly
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The market establishes the price signal, and the individual firm responds by selecting output.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does P = AR = MR connect the competitive revenue model to marginal analysis?
options: The market price is both revenue per unit and the added revenue from one more unit
Average revenue equals fixed cost while marginal revenue equals price
Marginal revenue falls below price because selling more requires the firm to cut price on all earlier units
Price equals marginal cost at every possible output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With price fixed, each additional unit adds the same amount to total revenue, so marginal revenue equals price. The firm then compares that marginal revenue with marginal cost when choosing output.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a horizontal firm demand curve connect to the shape of the competitive firm’s total-revenue function?
options: A horizontal demand curve makes total revenue constant even when the firm sells additional units
A constant price makes total revenue fall as quantity rises
The total-revenue function must be U-shaped
A constant price makes total revenue rise proportionally with quantity
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With price fixed, TR = P × Q rises by the same dollar amount for each additional unit.

bridgeQuestions.q: What prior market concept helps explain why the individual competitive firm can face a horizontal demand line even though market demand slopes downward?
options: The firm owns the market supply curve
The firm faces no scarcity in its inputs
The firm is a tiny participant taking the equilibrium price generated by the whole market
The law of demand stops applying at the firm level because competitive sellers can choose any price they want
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Firm-level price taking is consistent with a downward-sloping market demand curve because the individual seller is negligible relative to the market.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the competitive firm’s MR = MC rule connect to the broader marginal-analysis principle?
options: Maximize output whenever average benefit is positive
Expand an activity while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost and stop near equality
Choose the activity with the largest total cost because total cost identifies the strongest marginal gain
Ignore incremental effects once fixed cost exists
bridgeQuestions.feedback: For the firm, marginal revenue is the marginal benefit of another unit and MC is its marginal cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a market-price increase reach a competitive firm’s profit-maximizing output decision?
options: The higher price raises the firm’s MR line, so the firm moves along rising MC to a larger output
The higher price shifts the firm’s MC curve left automatically while leaving its marginal revenue line unchanged
The higher price lowers MR and therefore output
The firm ignores market price once its plant is built
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?
options: ATC is irrelevant once output is chosen
The vertical gap P − ATC measures profit per unit when positive and loss per unit when negative
The gap P − AVC always equals total profit because fixed cost is irrelevant once the firm chooses output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Average total cost converts the firm’s chosen price and quantity into a per-unit economic-profit measure.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does total economic profit connect the revenue and cost frameworks?
options: Profit equals total revenue minus total economic cost
Profit equals total revenue minus variable cost only
Profit equals price minus marginal cost on the last unit only
Profit equals accounting revenue plus implicit cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can a firm remain in long-run competitive equilibrium when economic profit is zero?
options: The firm has no opportunity costs
Zero economic profit means total revenue is zero
Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Normal profit is part of economic cost, so zero economic profit can still keep resources in their current use.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does break-even connect the firm’s revenue line to its average-cost curve?
options: MR equals zero at minimum ATC
At the chosen output, price equals ATC so total revenue equals total cost
Price equals AVC so fixed cost disappears
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Break-even is the point where the per-unit revenue and total-cost averages match.

bridgeQuestions.q: How should a measured short-run economic loss connect to the next decision?
options: The firm should compare price with AFC instead
After measuring the loss, separately compare price with AVC to decide produce versus shut down
Any loss automatically implies exit today because a competitive firm should never operate while ATC exceeds price
A loss means the firm should maximize quantity
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Loss measurement uses ATC; the short-run operating decision uses AVC.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the shutdown rule connect to the distinction between fixed and variable costs?
options: Variable cost is sunk in the short run
Price must cover variable cost because fixed cost is unavoidable in the short run
Price must cover fixed cost before variable cost matters
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The shutdown test asks whether operating revenue covers the costs that can be avoided by not producing.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does producing at a loss connect to incremental decision making?
options: Use average fixed cost as the marginal benefit of output
Produce if operating adds more revenue than avoidable variable cost, even if total profit is negative
Produce only if accounting profit is positive
Ignore revenue because fixed cost is already paid
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the shutdown-versus-exit distinction connect to the short-run/long-run distinction in cost theory?
options: Some inputs and costs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs are adjustable in the long run
All costs are variable in the short run and fixed in the long run
Exit changes only marginal cost, not industry participation
Shutdown requires the firm to sell all fixed inputs immediately
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Temporary shutdown occurs with short-run fixed commitments; exit becomes possible when those commitments can be changed.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the firm’s short-run supply curve connect the MR = MC rule to market supply?
options: The firm supplies where ATC equals AFC
The firm’s supply is its horizontal demand curve
At each price above shutdown, P = MR identifies the quantity on rising MC that the firm supplies
Market supply is unrelated to the firm’s marginal choice
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The output rule becomes a price-to-quantity supply schedule when repeated across possible market prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does individual-firm supply become the competitive industry supply curve?
options: Use the market demand curve instead
Add firms’ quantities supplied at each common price
Add firms’ prices at each quantity
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Horizontal aggregation connects firm-level marginal-cost decisions to the market supply schedule.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does entry connect firm-level profit to a market-level supply response?
options: Positive economic profit attracts firms, and additional firms increase industry supply
Positive profit shifts market demand left
Entry makes each incumbent’s MC automatically fall
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The profit signal changes the number of firms, linking firm outcomes to market supply.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does exit connect economic loss to long-run resource allocation?
options: Resources leave uses that fail to cover opportunity cost and move toward better alternatives
Exit increases the number of firms in the industry
Economic loss means variable cost is always zero
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Long-run exit is an opportunity-cost response: resources seek higher-valued uses.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does normal profit connect long-run competitive equilibrium to economic cost?
options: Normal profit is a monopoly markup above economic cost
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
Normal profit exists only when P exceeds ATC
Normal profit is the implicit return required to keep owner resources in the industry
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Zero economic profit can be sustainable because normal profit is already included among opportunity costs.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a constant-cost industry connect entry/exit to the long-run supply curve?
options: Entry permanently raises every firm’s ATC
The number of firms cannot change
Entry changes industry quantity without permanently shifting representative firms’ cost curves, producing horizontal long-run supply
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Stable input costs let entry absorb demand changes while long-run price returns to the original cost level.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does an increasing-cost industry connect output-market expansion to input markets?
options: Input prices cannot matter in perfect competition
Higher input prices shift market demand rather than supply
Industry growth raises demand for scarce inputs, which can raise input prices and firm costs
Industry growth reduces input demand automatically
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a demand increase connect short-run profit to the eventual long-run industry response?
options: Long-run price is always the short-run peak price
Higher short-run price can create profit, attracting entry; final price depends on the industry’s cost condition
Demand changes cause immediate exit before price changes
Profit has no connection to entry
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is the competitive quantity larger than the monopoly quantity in the standard benchmark?
options: Competition uses MR=MC and monopoly uses minimum ATC
Monopoly has a horizontal demand curve
Competition expands output until P=MC, while monopoly stops where MR=MC
Competition faces stronger barriers to entry
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The revenue wedge causes the monopoly to stop earlier.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which equality holds for a competitive firm but not a single-price monopolist?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A price taker sells each unit at the same price; a monopolist lowers price to expand output.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can monopoly profit persist when competitive profit is eroded?
options: Barriers prevent the entry response that expands supply
Monopoly fixed cost is always zero
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Entry is the key long-run difference.

bridgeQuestions.q: At the competitive benchmark, allocative efficiency requires P=MC. What is typical under single-price monopoly?
options: P exceeds MC at the chosen output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Monopoly restricts output below the P=MC quantity.

bridgeQuestions.q: Zero economic profit is common in long-run perfect competition. Can a monopoly also earn zero economic profit?
options: No; every monopoly earns positive profit
No; zero profit requires horizontal demand
Yes; barriers prevent entry but do not guarantee strong enough demand to cover cost
Yes only under perfect price discrimination
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Market structure does not guarantee the profit outcome.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which cost curve determines the monopolist’s output at the margin?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: MR is compared with MC for output choice.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which cost measure determines monopoly profit per unit after output and price are chosen?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Profit per unit is P−ATC.

bridgeQuestions.q: A pure increase in monopoly fixed cost shifts ATC but leaves which curves unchanged?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Fixed cost does not change demand or marginal and variable cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which cost threshold governs short-run monopoly shutdown?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The firm must cover avoidable variable cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why will a single-price monopolist with nonnegative MC avoid the inelastic part of demand?
options: Reducing output there raises revenue and lowers cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Negative MR makes the inelastic range inconsistent with profit maximization.

bridgeQuestions.q: Under third-degree discrimination, which market generally receives the lower markup?
options: The market with more elastic demand
The market with less elastic demand
The market with higher fixed cost
The market where resale is easiest
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A responsive market requires a smaller markup.

bridgeQuestions.q: At the quantity where total revenue is maximized, demand is unit elastic and MR is:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The derivative or marginal change in TR is zero at the maximum.

bridgeQuestions.q: What distinguishes monopoly profit from monopoly deadweight loss?
options: Profit is consumer surplus and DWL is fixed cost
Profit includes surplus transferred to the seller; DWL is surplus that disappears
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does reducing monopoly output below the competitive quantity create DWL?
options: Some buyers value omitted units above their marginal cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade.

bridgeQuestions.q: Under perfect first-degree discrimination, what happens to the competitive gains from trade in the benchmark model?
options: They are realized, but the seller captures nearly all of the surplus
They disappear because output is zero
Consumer surplus rises above total surplus
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Personalized prices can restore output while changing distribution.

bridgeQuestions.q: What marginal comparison determines monopoly output?
options: TR compared with fixed cost only
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Produce units whose marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: If the next unit has MR greater than MC, what does marginal analysis imply?
options: Reject the unit because it lowers price
Produce the unit because it increases profit
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The incremental benefit exceeds the incremental cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: A patent can create monopoly pricing while encouraging research. What tradeoff should policy evaluate?
options: Fixed cost versus sunk cost only
Static output loss versus dynamic innovation incentives
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Patent policy can sacrifice static efficiency to encourage innovation.

bridgeQuestions.q: A domestic monopolist gains access to a larger export market. Which monopoly tool still determines total output?
options: Compare marginal revenue from available markets with marginal cost
Set price equal to world price in every case
Produce where domestic demand equals MC only
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Market expansion changes demand opportunities, but marginal analysis remains central.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is monopoly classified as a market-failure source in the standard model?
options: Market power can keep price above MC and block beneficial trades
Fixed cost is always socially wasteful
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The output restriction prevents allocatively efficient exchange.

bridgeQuestions.q: How do barriers to entry connect monopoly structure to persistent economic profit?
options: They make total cost independent of output
They guarantee that the monopolist chooses the efficient quantity
They prevent new rivals from entering quickly when profit appears
They force demand to become perfectly elastic
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does natural-monopoly cost structure often lead directly to a regulation question?
options: Regulation is needed only when a patent expires
Efficient scale may favor one supplier, yet that supplier still has market power over price and output
Natural monopolies always produce where price equals marginal cost without policy
Scale economies make demand perfectly elastic
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Natural monopoly can make one-firm production cost-efficient while still creating a market-power problem.

bridgeQuestions.q: What happens to a patent-based barrier when the patent expires, holding other barriers constant?
options: Legal protection weakens and potential entry becomes easier
The firm’s marginal revenue becomes equal to price automatically
Average total cost must rise above price
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Removing a legal barrier increases contestability even if the incumbent remains large.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the monopolist’s downward-sloping demand curve create the MR curve used for output choice?
options: Demand forces MR to equal MC at every quantity
The demand curve makes ATC horizontal
MR is simply the vertical distance between demand and MC
Selling more generally requires a lower price, so MR falls below price
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The price effect from expanding sales makes marginal revenue lower than the price on demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: What does positive marginal revenue tell you about the portion of a monopolist’s demand curve?
options: Demand is perfectly inelastic at that output
Demand must have unit elasticity at every output
Demand is elastic at that output
Demand is inelastic at that output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does P = MR hold for a competitive firm but not for a single-price monopolist?
options: The monopolist’s average revenue is unrelated to price
The competitive firm can sell another unit at the unchanged market price, while the monopolist generally must lower price to expand sales
The monopolist has no demand curve
The competitive firm always has zero marginal cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price.

bridgeQuestions.q: How do monopoly revenue analysis and marginal cost combine into the output decision?
options: ATC determines quantity before revenue is considered
Price is chosen first and forces MR to equal MC
Demand generates MR, and the firm compares that MR with MC to choose quantity
Demand sets MC directly, so MR is unnecessary
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The monopolist’s demand conditions determine MR; costs determine MC; their marginal comparison selects output.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is monopoly price determined only after the profit-maximizing quantity is chosen?
options: Average total cost sets price before marginal analysis begins
The firm first uses MR and MC to choose output, then demand reveals the highest single price consistent with that output
Price is unrelated to demand until output is produced
The monopolist has no control over quantity
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Monopoly analysis is a two-step decision: marginal output choice first, demand-based price second.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the MR = MC output rule connect to the firm’s profit-or-loss calculation?
options: Profit is known before quantity is chosen
The shutdown rule replaces MR=MC whenever the firm has market power
MR=MC identifies the best quantity; price from demand and ATC at that quantity determine profit or loss
ATC determines output first and MR then determines price
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the monopolist’s MR=MC output choice create the welfare result P>MC?
options: Average total cost replaces demand in setting price
Market power makes willingness to pay irrelevant
MR lies below demand, so choosing Q where MR=MC typically leaves price on demand above MC
The firm sets price equal to MC and then raises output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The gap between demand price and MC at monopoly output is the link between firm optimization and allocative inefficiency.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does declining ATC connect the natural-monopoly cost story to the case for one network rather than duplicated networks?
options: Serving the market through one larger network can avoid duplicative fixed infrastructure and lower average cost
Declining ATC makes price equal MR
It guarantees one firm will choose the efficient quantity without oversight
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Scale economies explain why breaking the firm into many duplicative networks may raise production cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does marginal-cost regulation connect monopoly policy to the competitive efficiency benchmark?
options: Both require P=ATC at every output
Both eliminate the need for demand
Both target P=MC so the last unit’s willingness to pay matches its marginal production cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing tries to reproduce the allocative condition associated with competitive equilibrium.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why might a subsidy accompany marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly?
options: A subsidy prevents all entry barriers
P=MC can leave revenue below total cost when ATC exceeds MC
A subsidy is required because MR always exceeds price
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does average-cost regulation trade some allocative efficiency for financial sustainability?
options: P=ATC makes marginal revenue equal price
P=ATC covers total cost, but price can remain above MC and output below the P=MC level
P=ATC forces the firm to price below MC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can a well-designed price cap change a regulated monopolist’s cost incentives compared with simply reimbursing whatever costs it reports?
options: If the firm can keep some gains from lowering cost below the cap, it may have stronger cost-reduction incentives
A cap guarantees the firm will never invest
A cap automatically sets P=MC regardless of its level
A cap makes fixed costs irrelevant
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Price-cap design can affect incentives to control cost, not just the allowed price.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does elasticity connect directly to third-degree discriminatory pricing?
options: Elasticity determines fixed cost rather than price
Elasticity matters only under perfect competition
Groups with less elastic demand can sustain larger markups over marginal cost
More elastic groups always pay more
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does resale connect segmented pricing back toward a single price?
options: Arbitrage lets low-price buyers supply high-price buyers, eroding the price gap
Resale raises marginal cost only in the low-price market
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist.

bridgeQuestions.q: How should welfare analysis of price discrimination differ from simply asking whether some buyers pay more?
options: Track how total output and total surplus change as well as how surplus is redistributed among buyers and the seller
Any price difference is automatically deadweight loss
Only monopoly profit matters for welfare
Consumer surplus alone always equals total surplus
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Distribution and efficiency are separate questions; output changes can alter total surplus.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does perfect first-degree discrimination connect willingness to pay to the efficient-output condition?
options: The firm must stop where one common price equals MR
The firm ignores willingness to pay and charges ATC
The firm produces only where demand is unit elastic
The firm can sell units until the next buyer’s willingness to pay falls below MC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.

bridgeQuestions.q: A differentiated firm uses MC, AVC, and ATC from cost analysis. Which curve chooses output?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Output follows the marginal comparison.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which cost measure determines short-run shutdown?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which cost measure determines whether long-run economic profit is zero?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: P=ATC means all economic cost is covered.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does minimum ATC matter for excess capacity?
options: It identifies the price on demand
It identifies the output that minimizes unit cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which feature does monopolistic competition share with perfect competition?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Entry and exit operate in both models.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which long-run result occurs in both models?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does monopolistic competition retain a markup unlike perfect competition?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Limited market power keeps P above MC.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which model achieves productive efficiency in its standard long-run equilibrium?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The competitive firm produces at minimum ATC.

bridgeQuestions.q: What decision rule is shared by monopoly and monopolistic competition?
options: Choose output where MR=MC and read price from demand
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Both firms face downward-sloping demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is entry more important in monopolistic competition than monopoly?
options: Entry shifts each existing firm’s demand and erodes profit
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Relatively easy entry is a defining difference.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which structure generally has more close substitutes for each firm’s product?
options: The answer depends only on fixed cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Many differentiated rivals supply close alternatives.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which model can sustain long-run economic profit because barriers block entry?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Entry erodes profit in monopolistic competition.

bridgeQuestions.q: More close substitutes make a firm’s demand:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Substitution opportunities increase responsiveness.

bridgeQuestions.q: A successful loyalty program makes demand less elastic. What market-power effect follows?
options: The firm may sustain a larger markup
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lower elasticity generally strengthens pricing power.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can differentiation create consumer value?
options: It offers varieties better matched to heterogeneous preferences
It forces every buyer to pay the same willingness to pay
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Different buyers may prefer different attributes.

bridgeQuestions.q: A brand changes perceived value without changing physical quality. Which concept is central?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Consumer perceptions can shape demand for a variety.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can markup create lost trades?
options: Every unit becomes a fixed cost
Some units valued above MC are not sold because price exceeds MC
bridgeQuestions.feedback: P>MC can exclude mutually beneficial units.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can informational advertising improve market performance?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Useful information helps buyers compare alternatives.

bridgeQuestions.q: What separates monopolistic competition from oligopoly?
options: Many firms act without central strategic interdependence in the basic model
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Strategic few-firm interaction belongs to oligopoly.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can successful product development create temporary economic profit?
options: It makes MC equal price forever
It shifts demand before imitation and entry erode the advantage
It sets accounting profit to zero immediately
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Innovation can temporarily strengthen demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: Cost analysis tells a differentiated firm its MC curve. Which additional curve is needed to apply the usual profit-maximizing output rule?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses output where MR equals MC, subject to the usual marginal condition.

bridgeQuestions.q: The shutdown rule from cost analysis carries directly into monopolistic competition. Which comparison determines whether the firm should produce in the short run?
options: Price compared with AVC at the chosen output
Price compared with AFC at the chosen output
Total revenue compared only with fixed cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A firm should produce in the short run when price covers average variable cost at its profit-maximizing output.

bridgeQuestions.q: A firm has already selected output where MR=MC. Which comparison now determines whether it earns profit or loss?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.

bridgeQuestions.q: Elasticity analysis helps explain branding. If brand loyalty reduces the absolute value of price elasticity of demand, buyers become:
options: Perfectly responsive at one market price
Less responsive to the firm’s price
More responsive to the firm’s price
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lower absolute elasticity means quantity demanded changes less for a given percentage price change.

bridgeQuestions.q: Cost analysis helps separate two advertising cases. Which selling expense acts most like variable cost?
options: A fee charged on each unit sold
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A per-unit fee varies with output and therefore enters variable and marginal cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: A successful new product feature creates short-run profit in a market with easy entry. What long-run force can erode that profit?
options: A permanent legal ban on substitutes
Automatic shutdown of the innovating firm
A requirement that demand become perfectly inelastic
bridgeQuestions.feedback: With relatively easy entry and close substitutes, successful differentiation can attract rivals and imitation over time.

bridgeQuestions.q: A fully effective cartel most closely imitates which market structure?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A cartel restricts joint output like a monopolist.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does cartel price compare with the competitive benchmark?
options: It is typically higher because joint output is restricted
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Coordination can reproduce monopoly-like outcomes.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which monopoly rule does a cartel use for total output?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Joint output follows monopoly marginal analysis.

bridgeQuestions.q: What prevents an oligopoly from automatically behaving like one monopolist?
options: Member incentives and rival strategic responses
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Independent firms may not sustain the joint outcome.

bridgeQuestions.q: What distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition most sharply?
options: Strategic interdependence among a few major firms
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can advertising matter in both structures?
options: It makes every firm a price taker
It can differentiate products and alter substitution
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Advertising can shape demand in both markets.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which behavior belongs to oligopoly rather than the basic monopolistic-competition model?
options: Choosing an action after anticipating a specific rival’s response
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The basic monopolistic-competition model abstracts from strategic interdependence.

bridgeQuestions.q: Compared with perfect competition, oligopolistic firms are more likely to:
options: Recognize that their own actions affect rivals and market outcomes
Have free entry eliminate market power
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Oligopolists possess market power and strategic influence.

bridgeQuestions.q: What competitive benchmark is commonly used to evaluate a cartel?
options: Price equals marginal cost at the efficient output
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The competitive benchmark helps identify output restriction and DWL.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive more output?
options: It has the highest fixed cost
It faces the least elastic demand
It is always the largest firm
Allocating production toward lower MC reduces joint cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Joint cost minimization matters for cartel allocation.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can excess capacity serve as a commitment?
options: Installed capacity can make a large post-entry output response more credible
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A sunk capacity choice can alter later incentives.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does product differentiation sometimes soften price competition?
options: More loyal buyers make firm demand less elastic
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lower elasticity reduces customer switching.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why might a cartel be harder to sustain when close substitutes exist outside it?
options: Consumers can switch away from the cartel after price increases
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Outside substitutes constrain cartel pricing.

bridgeQuestions.q: What creates cartel deadweight loss?
options: Mutually beneficial units between cartel and competitive output are not produced
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Lost trades reduce total surplus.

bridgeQuestions.q: A cartel price increase transfers some surplus from:
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Higher price transfers part of consumer surplus to producers.

bridgeQuestions.q: Which basic incentive concept explains cartel cheating?
options: A member compares its private marginal gain with expected punishment
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Private incentives can undermine collective agreements.

bridgeQuestions.q: How do network effects affect oligopoly?
options: They can strengthen incumbent advantages and concentration
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Network effects can reinforce entry barriers.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does antitrust examine concentration?
options: A concentrated structure may make coordination or unilateral market power easier
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Structure can affect competitive risk.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why are merger efficiencies relevant?
options: Lower costs can offset some harm if savings are real and passed through
Cost savings prove no market power
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can foreign suppliers weaken a domestic cartel?
options: Imports provide alternative sources and can expand outside supply
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Outside supply can destabilize domestic coordination.

bridgeQuestions.q: A market has four dominant firms. Which feature would most strongly distinguish oligopoly from monopoly or perfect competition?
options: Assume four dominant firms automatically mean monopolistic competition because any market with multiple sellers and differentiated products fits that model
Classify the market only by whether products are identical
Treat every concentrated market as a legal monopoly
Focus on few-firm strategic interdependence rather than requiring one firm or many tiny price takers
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Oligopoly sits between monopoly and atomistic competition because a few large firms interact strategically.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student already understands market shares. What extra step turns those shares into an HHI?
options: Multiply each firm's market share by the market price and add the resulting dollar values across firms
Square each firm’s percentage share and add the squared shares
Add only the four largest shares
bridgeQuestions.feedback: HHI builds on market shares by squaring each percentage share and summing across firms.

bridgeQuestions.q: Before trying to find a Nash equilibrium in a payoff matrix, what should a student verify first?
options: Whether the market’s concentration measure is high enough to imply that strategic behavior must be present
Whether both players earn equal payoffs
Which payoff belongs to each player and which actions define the rows and columns
Which cell has the highest combined payoff
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student keeps searching for one action that is always best, but the player’s preferred action changes with the rival’s move. What concept should the student use?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Best responses can vary with the rival’s action even when no dominant strategy exists.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student has correctly found a player’s best response in each column. How should the student check for a dominant strategy?
options: See whether the same action is the best response in every column
Add the two players’ payoffs in each cell
Choose the action with the highest single payoff anywhere in the matrix
Look only at the rival’s payoffs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A dominant strategy must remain the player’s best response to every rival action.

bridgeQuestions.q: After marking each player’s best responses in a matrix, what identifies a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: The cell with the largest total payoff even if someone wants to deviate
Any cell where the payoffs are equal
The first cell in which one player has a dominant strategy
A cell where both players’ best-response markings coincide
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses in the same outcome cell.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student found the cell with the largest combined payoff and calls it the Nash equilibrium. What must still be checked?
options: Whether the firms have equal market shares
Whether the cell lies on the main diagonal
Whether each player would choose to stay there given the other player’s action
Whether the two payoffs are both positive and add to more than the payoffs in every neighboring cell
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Joint-payoff maximization and Nash stability are separate questions.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a noncooperative game differ from an assumed cartel solution?
options: The government chooses each firm’s strategy
Each firm follows its own incentives rather than committing to maximize joint profit
The firms necessarily choose identical actions because noncooperative behavior rules out different strategies
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Noncooperative analysis asks what individually rational strategies imply without assuming binding joint-profit coordination.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student understands a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma. What new consideration enters when the firms expect to interact again?
options: Market concentration falls with each round
Today’s action can change future responses and future payoffs
The payoff matrix no longer matters at all
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Repeated interaction links current choices to future rewards or punishments, which can alter incentives.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student knows that talk alone may not deter entry. What can make an incumbent’s announced response more believable?
options: A costly action taken in advance that changes the incumbent’s future incentives
A vague promise that entry will be punished somehow
A larger concentration ratio by itself
A public statement with no change in capacity or costs
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A commitment can make future behavior credible by changing what the incumbent will find profitable after entry.

bridgeQuestions.q: A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes. What is the next step when firms compete through quality or advertising instead?
options: Ignore rivals because only prices create interdependence
Apply the same strategic logic to nonprice actions because rivals may respond there too
Assume nonprice choices have no effect on demand
Treat advertising as proof of collusion
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price.

repair_explicit_implicit_cost.q: A business owner says, “My time is free because I do not pay myself.” What correction is needed?
options: Owner time is a fixed cost of zero
The owner’s forgone alternative earnings are an implicit cost
repair_explicit_implicit_cost.feedback: Owner-supplied resources still have opportunity costs.

repair_explicit_implicit_cost.q: Which cost belongs in economic cost but not recorded accounting cost?
options: Forgone rent on an owner-occupied building
repair_explicit_implicit_cost.feedback: Forgone rent is an implicit opportunity cost.

repair_accounting_economic_profit.q: Accounting profit is $60,000 and implicit costs are $45,000. Economic profit?
repair_accounting_economic_profit.feedback: Economic profit subtracts implicit cost from accounting profit.

repair_accounting_economic_profit.q: A firm earns zero economic profit. What has it covered?
options: Explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
Variable costs but not fixed costs
repair_accounting_economic_profit.feedback: Zero economic profit means all opportunity costs are covered.

repair_short_run_long_run.q: Why can the short run last several years in one industry?
options: The short run is legally set by industry
A major input may remain fixed for several years
repair_short_run_long_run.feedback: The fixed-input constraint, not calendar time, defines the horizon.

repair_short_run_long_run.q: In the short run, which statement must be true?
options: At least one input is fixed
repair_short_run_long_run.feedback: The short run has at least one fixed input.

repair_product_measures.q: Output rises from 40 to 52 when a worker is added. The worker’s MP is:
repair_product_measures.feedback: MP is the change in total product.

repair_product_measures.q: Five workers produce 60 units. AP is:

repair_diminishing_marginal_product.q: MP falls from 15 to 12 but remains positive. Which statement is correct?
options: TP still rises, but more slowly
repair_diminishing_marginal_product.feedback: Positive MP raises TP; declining MP marks diminishing returns.

options: MP first declines, not when it becomes negative
repair_diminishing_marginal_product.feedback: The first decline in MP is the threshold.

repair_total_cost_identity.q: At zero output, TFC is $500 and TVC is $0. TC is:
TFC is $300 and TVC is $700. TC is:

repair_average_cost_identity.q: AFC is $4 and AVC is $11. ATC is:
Why does the ATC–AVC gap shrink?
options: The gap is AFC, which falls as output rises
repair_average_cost_identity.feedback: AFC is spread over more units.

repair_marginal_cost.q: TC rises from $900 to $1,020 as Q rises from 30 to 36. MC is:
MC is below ATC. What happens to ATC?
options: ATC must be at its maximum
repair_marginal_cost.feedback: A marginal below the average lowers it.

repair_cost_curve_shifts.q: A fixed license fee rises. Which curves shift?
repair_cost_curve_shifts.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.

repair_cost_curve_shifts.q: The wage rises. Which curves shift upward?
repair_cost_curve_shifts.feedback: The wage is a variable-input price.

repair_scale_sunk_mes.q: Diminishing MP and diseconomies of scale differ because:
options: The first is short run with fixed inputs; the second is long run with all inputs variable
repair_scale_sunk_mes.feedback: The concepts apply to different horizons and input changes.

options: The smallest output attaining minimum LRATC
The point where MP becomes negative
repair_scale_sunk_mes.feedback: MES is the first output on the minimum-LRATC range.

opportunity_cost_firm.q: A learner says, “If the owner did not write a check, the resource has no cost.
options: Only variable resources have economic costs
Every implicit cost must appear on an invoice
Opportunity cost matters only for consumers
Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
opportunity_cost_firm.feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

accounting_profit.q: A learner subtracts the owner’s forgone salary when calculating accounting profit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The forgone salary should be added to revenue
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs; the forgone salary is implicit
Accounting profit subtracts all opportunity costs
accounting_profit.feedback: Implicit costs matter for economic profit, not the accounting-profit calculation.

economic_profit.q: A learner says economic profit equals accounting profit plus implicit costs. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Economic profit and accounting profit are always equal
Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs
Economic profit equals accounting profit plus explicit costs
Economic profit ignores owner opportunity costs
economic_profit.feedback: Implicit costs reduce economic profit relative to accounting profit.

economic_profit.q: A learner finds accounting profit of $50,000 and implicit cost of $70,000, then reports economic profit of $20,000. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: $20,000 is correct because profit cannot be negative

normal_profit.q: A learner calls zero economic profit a “loss.
options: Zero economic profit means all explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
Zero economic profit means revenue is zero
Zero economic profit means explicit costs exceed revenue
Zero economic profit excludes owner compensation
normal_profit.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost, so zero economic profit can be a sustainable outcome.

total_cost.q: A learner writes TC = TFC − TVC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
total_cost.feedback: Total cost combines the fixed and variable components.

fixed_cost.q: A learner says fixed cost must fall when output falls. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Fixed cost is another name for marginal cost
Within the short run, total fixed cost does not vary with output
Fixed cost moves one-for-one with output
Fixed cost equals zero below capacity
fixed_cost.feedback: A fixed input creates a cost that remains even as current output changes.

variable_cost.q: A learner reports positive TVC when output is zero in the standard short-run schedule. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: At zero output, TVC is zero; any remaining cost is fixed
TVC equals TFC at zero output
TVC is always greater than TC
TVC is an implicit cost only
variable_cost.feedback: Variable costs arise from producing output, while fixed costs remain at zero output.

cost_schedule_completion.q: A row has TFC = $90 and TC = $250, but a learner records TVC = $340. Which statement best corrects this mistake?

average_fixed_cost.q: A learner divides output by TFC to calculate AFC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
average_fixed_cost.feedback: Average fixed cost is fixed cost per unit of output.

average_fixed_cost.q: A learner says AFC eventually rises because “all U-shaped costs rise.
options: AFC keeps falling as fixed cost is spread over more output
AFC equals MC at its minimum
average_fixed_cost.feedback: AFC is not U-shaped in the standard model; it declines as quantity increases.

average_variable_cost.q: A learner calculates AVC using TC/Q. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
average_variable_cost.feedback: TC/Q is ATC; AVC uses total variable cost only.

average_total_cost.q: A learner says ATC = AVC − AFC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
average_total_cost.feedback: Average total cost contains both average variable and average fixed cost.

average_total_cost.q: At Q = 10, AFC = $6 and AVC = $14. A learner reports ATC = $8. Which statement best corrects this mistake?

marginal_cost.q: A learner calculates MC as TC/Q. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
marginal_cost.feedback: TC/Q is average total cost; marginal cost uses changes.

marginal_cost.q: A learner says a higher fixed property tax must raise MC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Every fixed-cost increase raises MC one-for-one
MC equals AFC after a tax
Fixed costs are part of TVC
A pure fixed-cost increase does not change MC
marginal_cost.feedback: MC depends on changes in cost as output changes, and a fixed amount is present at every output.

marginal_cost.q: TC rises by $50 when output rises by 5 units, but a learner reports MC = $50. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
marginal_cost.feedback: Divide the cost change by the output change: $50/5 = $10.

marginal_product_marginal_cost.q: A learner says falling marginal product causes MC to fall. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Marginal product and MC always move together
Marginal product affects fixed cost only
With a constant input price, falling marginal product raises MC
Falling marginal product lowers both MC and AVC automatically
marginal_product_marginal_cost.feedback: Less extra output from the same variable-input expense raises cost per additional unit.

marginal_product_marginal_cost.q: A worker costs $100 and adds 10 units. A learner reports MC from labor as $100 per unit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The labor cost per marginal unit is $10
The labor cost per marginal unit is $100
Marginal product should be added to the wage
The worker’s wage is a fixed cost
marginal_product_marginal_cost.feedback: Divide the worker’s cost by the worker’s marginal product: $100/10 = $10 per unit.

marginal_average_relationship.q: A learner says MC must be falling whenever ATC is falling. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: ATC can fall only if MC is zero
MC and ATC always have the same slope
ATC falls only when AFC rises
MC can be rising while ATC is still falling, as long as MC remains below ATC
marginal_average_relationship.feedback: The direction of the average depends on whether the marginal is above or below it, not on whether the marginal is itself rising.

short_run_cost_analysis.q: A learner says a higher fixed insurance premium shifts AVC and MC upward. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: All short-run curves shift by the same amount
A pure fixed-cost increase shifts AFC and ATC, not AVC or MC
A fixed-cost increase shifts only MC
short_run_cost_analysis.feedback: Fixed cost does not change the variable cost of current output or the incremental cost of another unit.

sunk_cost.q: A learner says, “Fixed cost and sunk cost mean the same thing.
options: A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
Every sunk cost varies with output
Every fixed cost has already been paid forever
sunk_cost.feedback: Fixed describes how cost behaves with current output; sunk describes whether it can be recovered.

sunk_cost.q: A learner includes a nonrefundable past payment when comparing two current options that both leave the payment unchanged. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Double the payment to reflect risk
Ignore the payment because it is sunk and identical across the options
sunk_cost.feedback: Only costs and benefits that differ across current alternatives should affect the choice.

avoidable_cost.q: A learner calls a cancelable future lease payment sunk because the lease is a fixed cost. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Only variable costs can be avoided
A lease payment is always implicit
The future payment is avoidable if canceling the lease eliminates it
avoidable_cost.feedback: A cost can be fixed with respect to output yet avoidable with respect to a future decision.

long_run_average_cost.q: A learner treats LRAC as the ATC curve of one fixed plant. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: LRAC is total variable cost per unit only
LRAC reflects the lowest attainable ATC across alternative plant sizes
LRAC is the same as AFC
long_run_average_cost.feedback: The long run permits plant adjustment, so LRAC summarizes least-cost choices across plants.

economies_of_scale.q: A learner says economies of scale mean total cost must fall as output rises. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Economies of scale mean average cost falls; total cost can still rise
Economies mean fixed cost becomes zero
Economies require marginal product to be negative
economies_of_scale.feedback: The concept concerns cost per unit, not necessarily the level of total cost.

economies_of_scale.q: A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: LRAC slope says nothing about scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment requires negative output
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents economies of scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents constant returns
economies_of_scale.feedback: Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.

diseconomies_of_scale.q: A learner says diseconomies of scale begin when marginal product first falls in the short run. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Diseconomies and diminishing marginal product are the same event
Diseconomies require one input to remain fixed
Diseconomies concern long-run expansion of all inputs and rising LRAC
diseconomies_of_scale.feedback: The two concepts refer to different horizons and different input adjustments.

diseconomies_of_scale.q: A learner says rising LRAC means output itself must be falling. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Rising LRAC means total cost is falling
LRAC can rise while output expands; the issue is rising cost per unit at larger scale
Output and LRAC always move in opposite directions
diseconomies_of_scale.feedback: Diseconomies describe a higher average cost at greater output, not a fall in output.

minimum_efficient_scale.q: A learner chooses the largest output on a flat minimum-LRAC segment as MES. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: MES is always the largest efficient output
MES is where LRAC first begins to fall
MES is where total cost is smallest
MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC
minimum_efficient_scale.feedback: The definition focuses on the minimum scale required to achieve the lowest long-run unit cost.

constant_returns_to_scale.q: A learner says a flat LRAC means output is not changing. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Flat LRAC means economies of scale
Flat LRAC means fixed cost is constant in the short run
Output can rise while LRAC stays constant; that range reflects constant returns to scale
Flat LRAC means output must be zero
constant_returns_to_scale.feedback: Constant returns refers to proportional changes in all inputs and output, leaving long-run cost per unit unchanged.

repair_price_taker.q: A student says a competitive firm chooses both price and quantity. What is the correction?
options: The firm sets price but not quantity
The market sets price; the firm chooses quantity
repair_price_taker.feedback: A small competitive firm takes market price as given.

repair_price_taker.q: Why does a competitive firm not cut price below the market price?
options: It can sell its feasible output at the market price
repair_price_taker.feedback: A price taker gains nothing by charging less.

repair_market_vs_firm.q: Which curve slopes downward in the standard model?
repair_market_vs_firm.feedback: The individual firm faces horizontal demand at market price.

repair_market_vs_firm.q: A graph labels the horizontal firm line “D=AR=MR.” What does it represent?
options: Market demand for the entire industry
The market price faced by the individual firm
repair_market_vs_firm.feedback: The horizontal line is the firm’s demand and revenue line.

repair_revenue_relationships.q: A firm sells 10 units at $8 each. What are AR and MR?
Why does total revenue rise linearly with output?
options: The firm raises price each time
Each additional unit adds the same market price
repair_revenue_relationships.feedback: Constant MR makes TR a straight line.

repair_marginal_output_rule.q: MR is $25 and the next unit’s MC is $19. What should the firm do?
MR is $25 and the next unit’s MC is $31. What should the firm do?
options: Produce it because revenue is positive
Do not produce the next unit
Raise output until ATC is minimum
repair_marginal_output_rule.feedback: The unit would reduce profit by $6.

repair_profit_measurement.q: At the chosen output, P=$30 and ATC=$24. Profit per unit is:
A firm earns $4 per unit on 50 units. Total profit is:
repair_profit_measurement.feedback: Multiply the per-unit gap by quantity.

repair_profit_measurement.q: At Q=20, price is $50, ATC is $38, and MC is $30. What is profit?
Why does P>MC not prove positive economic profit?
repair_profit_measurement.feedback: Profit depends on price relative to ATC.

repair_zero_profit.q: For a competitive firm, earning zero economic profit means:
options: All explicit and implicit costs are covered
repair_zero_profit.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost.

repair_zero_profit.q: Why can accounting profit be positive at zero economic profit?
options: Accounting profit does not subtract implicit costs
repair_zero_profit.feedback: Implicit costs account for the difference.

repair_shutdown_rule.q: P is below ATC but above AVC. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
repair_shutdown_rule.feedback: Operating covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

repair_shutdown_rule.q: P is below minimum AVC. What should the firm do?
options: Exit and erase fixed cost immediately
repair_shutdown_rule.feedback: Revenue does not cover avoidable variable cost.

repair_firm_supply.q: Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?
options: MC at and above minimum AVC
repair_firm_supply.feedback: The firm supplies along MC only when operating.

repair_firm_supply.q: At a price below minimum AVC, a firm’s quantity supplied is:
repair_firm_supply.feedback: The firm shuts down below the threshold.

repair_entry_exit.q: Positive economic profit causes entry. What does entry do to market supply and price?
Economic loss causes exit. What does exit do to market supply and price?

repair_efficiency_industry_cost.feedback: Price reflects marginal benefit and MC reflects marginal resource cost.

marginal_rule.q: A learner says a competitive firm should keep expanding whenever MR is above ATC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Stop whenever total revenue exceeds total cost
Compare MR with MC for the next unit, not MR with ATC
Compare price only with fixed cost because fixed cost determines whether the next unit should be produced
Expand until ATC is as large as possible
marginal_rule.feedback: The output rule is marginal: add units while MR is at least as large as rising MC.

rising_mc_condition.q: A learner finds an output where MR = MC but MC is falling at that point and declares it profit maximizing. What condition is missing?
options: MC should be rising through MR for the usual maximum
ATC must equal zero so the firm has no cost burden at the point where MR and MC meet
Market demand must be horizontal at zero
rising_mc_condition.feedback: The standard profit maximum occurs where rising MC crosses MR from below.

discrete_output_choice.q: A learner sees MR = $20, the next unit’s MC = $18, and stops production at the current output. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Stop because any positive marginal cost reduces profit even when marginal revenue is larger
Raise price to $22 before adding output
Shut down because MR exceeds MC
Add the next unit because it adds $20 of revenue and only $18 of cost
discrete_output_choice.feedback: A unit with MR greater than MC increases profit or reduces loss.

profit_maximizing_output.q: A learner chooses the output with the lowest ATC as the profit-maximizing quantity. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Choose output where AFC is minimized
Choose output where total revenue is smallest
Choose output using MR and MC; minimum ATC answers a different question
Choose the largest feasible output instead because spreading fixed cost always maximizes profit
profit_maximizing_output.feedback: Productive efficiency and profit maximization are distinct decisions.

profit_maximizing_output.q: Which equality identifies the candidate output for a single-price monopolist?
profit_maximizing_output.feedback: The monopoly output decision uses marginal revenue and marginal cost.

profit_maximizing_output.q: If MR exceeds MC at the current output, what should a profit-maximizing monopolist generally do?
options: Keep output unchanged because price exceeds MR
profit_maximizing_output.feedback: When MR exceeds MC, another unit adds more revenue than cost.

profit_maximizing_output.q: If the MR=MC intersection occurs where MC is falling and another later intersection occurs where MC is rising, which is the usual profit-maximizing candidate?
options: The first intersection on the falling portion of MC
Both intersections necessarily give identical profit
Neither intersection because monopoly uses P=MC
The intersection on the rising portion of MC
profit_maximizing_output.feedback: The stable maximum uses MR=MC with MC rising through MR.

profit_per_unit.q: A learner computes profit per unit as ATC − P when P exceeds ATC. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Use P − ATC for profit per unit
Use P − AVC for economic profit per unit
Use TR − TC without dividing by quantity and call it per-unit profit
profit_per_unit.feedback: When price exceeds ATC, the vertical gap P − ATC is profit per unit.

total_profit.q: A learner reports $5 of total profit because P − ATC = $5 and the firm sells 60 units. What is missing?
options: Multiply the $5 per-unit profit by 60 units
Subtract fixed cost a second time
Use only the last unit’s marginal cost
total_profit.feedback: The price-ATC gap is per unit; total profit requires multiplying by quantity.

break_even.q: A learner says P = ATC means the firm has no accounting profit and no return to the owner. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: P = ATC means the firm is shutting down because covering total cost leaves no reason to produce
P = ATC means marginal revenue is zero
P = ATC guarantees an accounting loss
P = ATC means zero economic profit; normal profit is included in economic cost
break_even.feedback: Economic cost includes implicit opportunity costs, including the normal return needed to keep owner resources in the firm.

total_loss.q: A learner sees P < ATC and concludes the firm must shut down. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Shutdown depends on P versus AFC
Losses matter only in the long run
P < ATC establishes an economic loss, but shutdown depends on P versus AVC
Any economic loss requires immediate shutdown even when the market price still covers variable cost
total_loss.feedback: Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons.

shutdown_rule.q: A learner uses P < ATC as the shutdown rule. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Compare MR with total fixed cost
Compare price with AVC for shutdown; ATC determines profit or loss
Compare price with AFC for shutdown
shutdown_rule.feedback: The firm may rationally produce at a loss if price covers variable cost.

produce_at_loss.q: A learner says producing at a loss is irrational under any circumstances. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Fixed cost is avoidable whenever profit is negative
In the short run, producing can reduce the loss when price covers AVC and contributes to fixed cost
A firm should produce whenever price is positive
Losses disappear if output rises enough
produce_at_loss.feedback: The relevant comparison is the loss from producing versus the fixed-cost loss from shutting down.

short_run_fixed_cost.q: A learner says shutting down eliminates all costs immediately. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Short-run fixed costs remain even when output is zero
Shutdown makes fixed cost become variable
The firm earns zero economic profit when shut down
Shutdown raises average fixed cost to zero
short_run_fixed_cost.feedback: Shutdown avoids variable production cost but does not erase fixed commitments in the short run.

short_run_fixed_cost.q: A learner shifts short-run supply left after a fixed-cost increase. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Supply shifts right because firms spread the cost
Fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MC or AVC, so short-run supply does not shift
Any cost increase must shift MC
short_run_fixed_cost.feedback: The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.

shutdown_vs_exit.q: A learner treats a one-month shutdown as permanent industry exit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Exit is the short-run version of shutdown
A shut-down firm has no fixed cost
Shutdown can be temporary; exit means leaving the industry in the long run
shutdown_vs_exit.feedback: Time horizon separates the temporary operating decision from long-run participation.

firm_short_run_supply.q: A learner labels the entire MC curve as the firm’s short-run supply curve. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Use MC only below minimum AVC
Use average fixed cost above its minimum
Use only the rising MC portion at and above minimum AVC
Use the entire ATC curve instead
firm_short_run_supply.feedback: Below minimum AVC the firm shuts down rather than supplying the MC-indicated positive quantity.

firm_short_run_supply.q: A learner says a higher wage cannot shift supply because the firm is a price taker. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Price-taking means the market price is given, so input-cost changes affect profit but not the firm's marginal cost curve
A higher wage changes average fixed cost because labor payments become fixed after the firm hires its workers
A wage increase changes the firm's demand curve by raising the price required to cover its labor costs
Price taking fixes the output price, not the firm’s costs; a wage increase can raise MC and shift supply
firm_short_run_supply.feedback: Competitive firms take price as given but still respond to changes in production costs.

market_supply_aggregation.q: A learner adds firms’ supply prices vertically to build market supply. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: At each price, add the quantities supplied across firms horizontally
At each quantity, add firms’ fixed costs
Use only the median firm’s output
Add market demand to firm supply
market_supply_aggregation.feedback: Market supply sums how much all firms supply at a common market price.

entry.q: A learner says positive economic profit causes existing firms to raise the market price. What is the long-run repair?
options: Profit causes exit, which raises price
Each firm can raise price independently because profit is positive
Economic profit has no effect on industry size
Profit attracts entry, which increases market supply and tends to lower price
entry.feedback: In competition, the adjustment occurs through entry and market supply, not unilateral price setting.

exit.q: A learner says loss-making competitive firms can remain forever with no industry adjustment. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Long-run fixed costs prevent any firm from leaving
Persistent losses encourage exit when firms can leave in the long run
exit.feedback: Long-run mobility lets resources leave industries that do not cover opportunity cost.

constant_cost_industry.q: A learner says every competitive industry has a horizontal long-run supply curve. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Long-run supply depends only on market demand
A horizontal curve requires monopoly power
Horizontal long-run supply is the constant-cost case; other cost conditions can slope up or down
Competition always makes long-run supply vertical
constant_cost_industry.feedback: The slope depends on how industry expansion affects input costs and firms’ cost curves.

increasing_cost_industry.q: A learner says entry can never raise production costs because each firm is a price taker. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Competitive firms do not buy inputs
Industry expansion can bid up shared input prices even though firms take output price as given
Price-taking firms also take every input price as permanently fixed
Entry always creates economies that lower cost
increasing_cost_industry.feedback: Output-market price taking does not prevent industry growth from affecting input markets.
