decreasing_cost_industry.q: A learner interprets a downward-sloping long-run industry supply curve as a violation of competition. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: It can arise when industry expansion lowers firms’ costs through external economies
It means demand is perfectly elastic
It means firms are operating below AVC
decreasing_cost_industry.feedback: A decreasing-cost industry can remain competitive while industry growth reduces input or supplier costs.

allocative_efficiency.q: A learner says productive efficiency and allocative efficiency are the same condition. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Allocative efficiency means every firm earns positive profit
Productive efficiency concerns minimum ATC; allocative efficiency concerns P = MC
allocative_efficiency.feedback: The two efficiency concepts answer different questions: least-cost production versus whether marginal value equals marginal cost.

repair_monopoly_definition_barriers.q: A city has one coffee shop today, but entry is easy and several rivals are preparing to open. Is the current seller necessarily a durable monopoly?
options: Yes; one seller at any moment is always a permanent monopoly
Yes; size alone creates a legal barrier
No; one current seller without a meaningful barrier may only have temporary market leadership
No; because monopoly requires horizontal demand
repair_monopoly_definition_barriers.feedback: Durable monopoly power depends on the relevant market and barriers to entry.

repair_monopoly_definition_barriers.q: Which fact most strongly supports classifying a firm as a monopoly?
options: It is the largest of twenty similar firms
Its accounting profit rose this year
It is the only supplier and rivals cannot enter because it controls an essential input
repair_monopoly_definition_barriers.feedback: One seller plus a durable barrier supports monopoly classification.

repair_demand_mr_relationship.q: A monopolist lowers price from $20 to $19 to sell one more unit. Why can MR be less than $19?
options: The $1 price cut also applies to units the firm was already selling
The new unit costs more than $19 to produce
Fixed cost rises by $1 per unit
repair_demand_mr_relationship.feedback: MR subtracts the lost revenue on previous units.

repair_demand_mr_relationship.q: For a single-price monopolist, which curve gives price at each output?
options: Demand, which is also average revenue
repair_demand_mr_relationship.feedback: Price is read from demand, while MR lies below it.

repair_elasticity_mr.q: If demand is inelastic at the current output, reducing output will usually:
options: Lower total revenue and raise total cost
Raise total revenue and lower total cost, increasing profit
Force marginal revenue to equal price
repair_elasticity_mr.feedback: On inelastic demand, a price increase raises total revenue; lower output also reduces cost.

repair_elasticity_mr.q: At the unit-elastic point of a demand curve, marginal revenue is:
repair_elasticity_mr.feedback: Total revenue is maximized where MR=0.

repair_monopoly_output_price.q: What is the correct order for solving a monopoly graph?
options: Find Q where MR=MC, then read P from demand
Find P where MR=MC, then read Q from ATC
Find Q where demand=MC, then read P from MR
Choose the highest demand intercept as price

repair_monopoly_output_price.q: A table has no output where MR exactly equals MC. The monopolist should:
options: Produce zero because equality is absent
Produce through the last unit whose MR is at least MC
Choose the unit with the lowest ATC
repair_monopoly_output_price.feedback: Discrete marginal analysis uses the last profitable unit.

repair_monopoly_shutdown.q: A monopolist has P below ATC but above AVC at its best output. It should:
options: Produce in the short run and minimize its loss
Shut down because any loss requires zero output
Exit and erase fixed cost immediately
repair_monopoly_shutdown.feedback: Revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.

repair_monopoly_shutdown.q: Short-run shutdown allows a monopolist to avoid:
options: Variable cost but not fixed cost
Fixed cost but not variable cost
repair_monopoly_shutdown.feedback: Only avoidable variable cost disappears at zero output.

repair_monopoly_welfare.q: Which part of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss?
options: The portion not transferred to the monopolist because output is not produced
The price increase on units still sold
repair_monopoly_welfare.feedback: DWL comes from unrealized trades; the remaining loss can be a transfer.

repair_monopoly_welfare.q: Price above MC is evidence of:
options: Allocative inefficiency, because some buyers value additional output above its marginal cost
repair_monopoly_welfare.feedback: P>MC indicates forgone surplus at the margin.

repair_natural_monopoly_regulation.q: Why can P=MC cause a regulated natural monopoly to lose money?
options: Declining ATC leaves ATC above MC over the relevant range
repair_natural_monopoly_regulation.feedback: Efficient price may not recover large fixed cost.

repair_natural_monopoly_regulation.q: What is the main compromise under average-cost pricing?
options: The firm earns unlimited monopoly profit
The firm covers cost, but price remains above MC and output stays below the efficient level
repair_natural_monopoly_regulation.feedback: P=ATC addresses solvency but not full allocative efficiency.

repair_price_discrimination_conditions.q: A seller can identify student buyers but cannot prevent ticket resale. What fails?
Which group normally receives the higher price under third-degree discrimination?
options: The group with more elastic demand
The group with the highest marginal cost even when costs are equal
The group that can resell most easily
The group with less elastic demand
repair_price_discrimination_conditions.feedback: Less elastic demand supports a larger markup.

repair_price_discrimination_welfare.q: Does perfect first-degree discrimination eliminate the single-price monopoly DWL?
options: Yes, in the benchmark model, because output expands to where willingness to pay equals MC
No, because MR remains below every personalized price
repair_price_discrimination_welfare.feedback: Efficient output can be restored even though consumer surplus is extracted.

repair_price_discrimination_welfare.q: Can ordinary group price discrimination increase total welfare?
options: No; any price difference always increases DWL
Yes, when it expands total output enough to recover otherwise lost trades
Yes only when all groups pay the same price
repair_price_discrimination_welfare.feedback: Welfare depends on the output change, not the mere existence of multiple prices.

barriers_to_entry.q: What must accompany a single seller for monopoly power to be durable?
options: A requirement that price equal marginal cost
A meaningful barrier that makes entry difficult
barriers_to_entry.feedback: One seller becomes a durable monopoly only when entry is meaningfully blocked.

marginal_revenue_monopoly.q: A monopolist lowers price from $20 to $19 to increase sales. Is the marginal revenue from the added unit necessarily $19?
options: No; marginal revenue must always be negative
No; the lower price may also reduce revenue on units that were already being sold
Yes; marginal revenue always equals price for every seller
Yes; average revenue and marginal revenue are identical for a monopolist
marginal_revenue_monopoly.feedback: For a single-price monopolist, MR includes the lost revenue caused by lowering price on previous units.

average_revenue_monopoly.q: Where should a monopolist read the price consumers will pay for a chosen quantity?
options: From the minimum of average total cost
average_revenue_monopoly.feedback: Demand gives price at each quantity; MR is used for the marginal output decision.

monopoly_price.q: After finding Q where MR=MC, where is monopoly price found?
monopoly_price.feedback: Demand maps the chosen quantity into the price consumers will pay.

monopoly_profit.q: Which expression gives total economic profit for a monopolist producing Q units?
monopoly_profit.feedback: Economic profit equals profit per unit times quantity.

monopoly_shutdown.q: A monopolist is losing money because P<ATC, but P>AVC. What does the shutdown rule say?
options: Shut down immediately because any loss requires shutdown
Exit the industry immediately regardless of fixed costs
Continue producing in the short run if the chosen output minimizes the loss
monopoly_shutdown.feedback: Covering variable cost makes continued short-run production better than shutting down when fixed cost is unavoidable.

monopoly_deadweight_loss.q: Which area is conceptually deadweight loss from monopoly?
options: Consumer spending on units still purchased
The lost surplus on units between monopoly output and the efficient output
monopoly_deadweight_loss.feedback: Deadweight loss comes from trades not made, not from surplus merely transferred.

allocative_inefficiency.q: At the monopoly output, price is $50 and MC is $30. What does the $20 gap imply at the margin?
options: Output is productively efficient because price exceeds MC
Buyers value another unit more than its production cost, so output is too low from an allocative-efficiency standpoint
The firm is necessarily earning $20 profit per unit
allocative_inefficiency.feedback: P>MC means potential gains from additional output remain.

allocative_inefficiency.q: A monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit in long-run equilibrium. Does that prove the outcome is fully efficient?
options: Yes. Entry forces price to equal MC and minimum ATC
No. Zero economic profit means the firm should shut down
No. Price can still exceed MC and output can remain below the minimum-ATC quantity
Yes. Zero economic profit guarantees both allocative and productive efficiency
allocative_inefficiency.feedback: Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.

consumer_surplus_monopoly.q: If a monopoly captures $100 of consumer surplus without changing total output, what happens to total surplus from that transfer alone?
consumer_surplus_monopoly.feedback: A pure transfer changes distribution; deadweight loss requires lost gains from trade.

rent_seeking.q: Why can rent-seeking expenditures make monopoly socially more costly than the standard deadweight-loss triangle alone suggests?
options: They automatically expand output to the competitive level
They convert monopoly demand into perfectly elastic demand
Real resources may be spent obtaining or defending monopoly privileges rather than producing valued goods and services
rent_seeking.feedback: Rent seeking can consume resources in addition to the surplus loss from restricted output.

natural_monopoly_cost.q: What cost pattern is the key starting point for natural-monopoly analysis?
options: ATC falls over the relevant range of market demand
natural_monopoly_cost.feedback: Economies of scale over market demand can make a single supplier lowest-cost.

marginal_cost_regulation.q: What is the efficiency goal of setting a regulated natural-monopoly price equal to MC?
options: Produce units up to the point where willingness to pay equals the marginal production cost

average_cost_regulation.q: Why does P=ATC usually allow a regulated natural monopoly to remain financially viable?
options: Revenue per unit covers average economic cost at the chosen output
It guarantees marginal revenue is zero
average_cost_regulation.feedback: Average-cost pricing permits recovery of total economic cost including normal profit.

price_cap_regulation.q: When is a price cap actually binding on an unregulated monopolist?
options: Only when demand is perfectly inelastic
When the cap is below the price the firm would otherwise charge
Whenever a regulator announces any maximum price
Only when the cap equals ATC
price_cap_regulation.feedback: A ceiling constrains behavior only when it lies below the unconstrained price.

price_discrimination_conditions.q: Which two conditions are especially important for sustaining price discrimination?
options: Market power and the ability to segment buyers while limiting resale
Perfect competition and identical buyer demand
Zero marginal cost and free resale
A horizontal demand curve and free entry
price_discrimination_conditions.feedback: The seller needs pricing power and enforceable segmentation.

third_degree_price_discrimination.q: Under third-degree price discrimination, which group normally pays the higher price when marginal cost is the same?
options: The group with more elastic demand
The group with the easiest resale opportunity
The group with lower willingness to pay at every quantity
The group with less elastic demand
third_degree_price_discrimination.feedback: Less elastic demand supports a larger optimal markup.

repair_market_structure_characteristics.q: A market has many sellers but all products are identical. Why is that not enough for monopolistic competition?
options: Many sellers automatically imply monopolistic competition
repair_market_structure_characteristics.feedback: The model requires both many firms and differentiated varieties.

repair_market_structure_characteristics.q: A market has differentiated products but only three firms that react strategically to one another. Which model is the better starting point?
repair_market_structure_characteristics.feedback: Strategic few-firm interaction belongs to oligopoly.

repair_firm_demand_mr.q: Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?
options: Some customers prefer its variety, but they can switch when price rises
The firm is a price taker
The product has no close substitutes, so buyers cannot switch when the firm raises its price

repair_firm_demand_mr.q: For a downward-sloping firm demand curve, why is MR below price?
options: Selling more requires a lower price, creating a price effect
Entry raises fixed cost and therefore pushes marginal revenue below the firm’s demand curve
repair_firm_demand_mr.feedback: Added revenue is reduced by the lower price on units sold.

repair_output_price_choice.q: What is the correct sequence for short-run firm choice?
options: Choose P where demand equals MC, then read Q from MR
Choose minimum ATC, then set P=MC
Choose Q where MR=MC, then read P from demand
Choose the highest price on demand
repair_output_price_choice.feedback: Quantity comes from the marginal rule; demand supplies price.

repair_output_price_choice.q: A table has no exact MR=MC equality. Which output should be selected?
options: The first unit whose MC exceeds price
The last unit whose MR is at least MC
repair_output_price_choice.feedback: The discrete marginal rule compares the added revenue and cost of each unit.

repair_short_run_profit_loss.q: A firm has P>MC but P<ATC. Which statement is correct?
options: It has a markup but an economic loss
It earns economic profit because P>MC
repair_short_run_profit_loss.feedback: Profit depends on P versus ATC, not P versus MC.

repair_short_run_profit_loss.q: A firm has P<ATC but P>AVC. What should it do in the short run?
options: Produce at MR=MC and minimize its loss
Exit immediately because any economic loss requires the firm to leave the market
repair_short_run_profit_loss.feedback: Covering AVC allows production to contribute toward fixed cost.

repair_entry_adjustment.q: Short-run profit attracts entry. What happens to an existing firm’s demand?
options: It shifts right because the market is larger
It shifts left as new substitutes appear
repair_entry_adjustment.feedback: New varieties divide customers among more firms.

repair_entry_adjustment.q: How does entry usually affect the elasticity of an existing firm’s demand?
options: Elasticity is determined by fixed cost

repair_exit_adjustment.q: Persistent losses cause exit. What happens to a surviving firm’s demand?
repair_exit_adjustment.feedback: Fewer substitutes leave more customers for survivors.

repair_exit_adjustment.q: Why does exit help eliminate losses?
options: Exit raises every surviving firm’s fixed cost and directly reduces the quantity each firm supplies
Surviving firms face stronger demand and may charge a higher price
repair_exit_adjustment.feedback: The demand recovery improves revenue opportunities for survivors.

repair_long_run_zero_profit.q: What does zero economic profit mean?
options: The owner receives no return for time, capital, or entrepreneurship once economic profit reaches zero
All explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered

repair_long_run_zero_profit.q: Where does long-run tangency occur in the standard model?
options: Where demand intersects marginal cost at the output that minimizes average total cost
On the downward-sloping portion of ATC before its minimum
repair_long_run_zero_profit.feedback: The equilibrium output is below the minimum-ATC quantity.

repair_excess_capacity_markup.q: Why can a firm have a markup with zero economic profit?
options: Price can equal ATC while exceeding MC
Markup equals economic profit by definition
repair_excess_capacity_markup.feedback: Markup and profit use different cost comparisons.

options: Price equals marginal cost at minimum average total cost, eliminating markup and excess capacity
Q at minimum ATC minus the firm’s equilibrium Q
repair_excess_capacity_markup.feedback: It is a cost-curve output gap.

repair_advertising_effects.q: An ad shifts firm demand right. Is that a movement along demand?
options: No, it is a demand shift
No, it is a supply shift
repair_advertising_effects.feedback: The campaign changes demand at each possible price.

repair_advertising_effects.q: A fixed advertising bill rises. Which curve does not shift directly?
repair_advertising_effects.feedback: A pure fixed cost does not alter the cost of one more unit.

repair_variety_nonprice_competition.q: Why is product variety not automatically wasteful?
options: Consumers may value closer matches to their preferences
repair_variety_nonprice_competition.feedback: Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs.

options: Firms compete through quality, service, location, branding, and other dimensions in addition to price
repair_variety_nonprice_competition.feedback: Nonprice dimensions supplement rather than eliminate price competition.

market_structure_characteristics.q: A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product. What key condition for monopolistic competition is missing?
market_structure_characteristics.feedback: Many sellers and easy entry are not enough. Monopolistic competition also requires differentiated products.

short_run_shutdown.q: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses its MR=MC output. At that output, price is below ATC but above AVC. What should the firm do in the short run?
options: Raise output until price equals ATC
Exit the industry immediately because price is below ATC
Continue producing and accept an economic loss
Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
short_run_shutdown.feedback: If price covers AVC, producing helps pay some fixed cost even though the firm earns an economic loss.

selling_cost.q: A fixed advertising bill increases but demand does not change. Why does the MR=MC output stay the same?
options: The fixed cost does not directly shift MR or MC
The fixed cost lowers price by the same amount
The fixed cost raises MC at every unit
selling_cost.feedback: A pure fixed-cost change lowers profit but does not alter the marginal decision when demand is unchanged.

advertising_informational.q: An ad tells buyers the product price and where to buy it. Why is this informational rather than persuasive?
options: It supplies facts that reduce search costs
It guarantees buyers will prefer the brand
It changes the product’s physical quality
It prevents consumers from switching brands
advertising_informational.feedback: Informational advertising communicates useful facts instead of mainly trying to reshape preferences.

advertising_demand_shift.q: After a successful campaign, buyers purchase more at every possible price. Is this a movement along the firm’s demand curve?
options: Yes, because advertising changes the posted price
No, it is a leftward shift of supply
No, it is a rightward shift of demand
advertising_demand_shift.feedback: More demanded at every price is a demand shift. A movement along demand requires a change in the firm’s own price.

repair_oligopoly_characteristics.q: A market has three firms that closely track one another’s pricing. What feature matters most?
Why can an industry with six firms still be oligopolistic?
options: Any market with more than two firms is competitive
Six firms means monopolistic competition automatically
A few firms may dominate sales and react strategically

repair_concentration_measures.q: What does a four-firm concentration ratio do?
options: Adds the four largest market shares
repair_concentration_measures.feedback: The ratio is a sum, not a proof of conduct.

repair_payoff_matrix_reading.q: In payoff order (Row, Column), whose payoff is second?
repair_payoff_matrix_reading.feedback: Payoff order must be read consistently.

repair_payoff_matrix_reading.q: Why must payoff order be stated?
options: It changes the number of strategies
Reversing the order changes each firm’s incentives
repair_payoff_matrix_reading.feedback: Each number belongs to a different player.

options: The highest-payoff action given the rival’s action
The action with the highest single payoff anywhere
It beats the player’s alternative under every rival action
repair_dominant_best_response.feedback: Dominance requires comparison across rival actions.

repair_nash_vs_joint_payoff.feedback: Nash is stability against unilateral deviation.

repair_nash_vs_joint_payoff.q: Can a Nash equilibrium be jointly inferior?
options: No, Nash always maximizes total payoff
Only if firms are price takers
Yes, individual incentives can lead to a lower combined payoff

repair_prisoners_dilemma.q: Why is cooperation unstable in a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma?
options: Each firm can gain by deviating when the other cooperates
Cooperation gives the lowest joint payoff
repair_prisoners_dilemma.feedback: The private incentive to defect destabilizes cooperation.

options: Individually rational actions can produce a jointly worse result
repair_prisoners_dilemma.feedback: The dilemma is the conflict between private and collective incentives.

repair_cartel_output_welfare.q: How does a cartel select joint output?
options: At minimum ATC for every member
Where industry MR equals industry MC
repair_cartel_output_welfare.feedback: A successful cartel applies monopoly logic.

repair_cartel_output_welfare.q: Why is cartel profit not equal to deadweight loss?
options: Some consumer loss is transferred to producers while DWL is lost surplus

repair_repeated_game_credibility.q: When can future punishment discourage cheating?
options: When future losses are large enough and punishment is credible
repair_repeated_game_credibility.feedback: Repetition helps only when incentives support punishment.

options: The threatening firm would rationally carry it out later
repair_repeated_game_credibility.feedback: Credibility is tested at the future decision point.

options: No, firms may respond independently to common conditions
repair_tacit_price_behavior.feedback: Parallel conduct needs context and evidence.

options: A dominant strategy in every game
Rivals follow a leading firm’s announced price without legal control
repair_tacit_price_behavior.feedback: Leadership can create a focal price.

options: No, it may reflect low cost or vigorous competition
Yes, every price cut is exclusionary
No, low prices never affect entry
repair_entry_merger_policy.feedback: Intent and recoupment cannot be inferred from low price alone.

repair_entry_merger_policy.q: Does a higher post-merger HHI settle the welfare question?
options: Yes, concentration is the only issue
No, market power, entry, and efficiencies still require analysis
repair_entry_merger_policy.feedback: Concentration is one part of merger analysis.

concentration_ratio.q: A student says a four-firm concentration ratio squares each firm’s market share. What is the correction?
options: The four-firm ratio averages all firms’ squared shares
The four-firm ratio simply adds the shares of the four largest firms
The four-firm ratio multiplies the market shares of the four largest firms and then converts the product to a percentage
The four-firm ratio subtracts fringe shares from 100
concentration_ratio.feedback: Squaring shares is part of HHI, not the four-firm concentration ratio.

strategic_interdependence.q: A student describes oligopoly as “a market where each firm can safely ignore rivals.” What is the key error?
options: Oligopoly decisions are strategically interdependent because major rivals can respond
Oligopoly always has exactly two firms, so any market with three or more important firms belongs to another structure
Oligopoly firms are all price takers
strategic_interdependence.feedback: The defining strategic feature is that a few important firms must account for likely rival reactions.

prisoners_dilemma.q: A student says “if both firms would be better off cooperating, they will automatically cooperate.” What is missing?
options: Prisoner’s-dilemma incentives exist only in monopoly
Each firm’s unilateral incentive must also be checked; the cooperative outcome can be unstable
Joint payoff is irrelevant in oligopoly
Cooperation requires the firms to have identical costs
prisoners_dilemma.feedback: A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.

cartel.q: A student calls any concentrated industry a cartel. What is the correction?
options: A cartel requires coordination among firms to restrict competition; concentration alone does not establish that
A cartel is simply any market with fewer than ten firms
A cartel exists whenever HHI is high
A cartel means one firm owns the entire market
cartel.feedback: Market structure and collusive conduct are different concepts; a concentrated market need not be a cartel.

tacit_coordination.q: A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical. What is the key distinction?
options: Explicit collusion means firms ignore rivals
Only tacit coordination can affect price
Tacit coordination can emerge without an explicit agreement among firms
Tacit coordination always requires a written contract
tacit_coordination.feedback: Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.

concentration_limitations.q: A student says “high concentration proves firms are colluding.” What is the correction?
options: Collusion is impossible in concentrated markets
Concentration measures directly record secret agreements
High concentration can make strategic interaction important, but it does not by itself prove an agreement or harmful conduct
High concentration means every firm charges marginal cost
concentration_limitations.feedback: Structure can affect incentives, but conduct and welfare conclusions require additional evidence.

cartel_welfare.q: A student treats every dollar of consumer-surplus loss from a cartel as deadweight loss. What should the student separate?
options: Surplus transferred to producers from surplus destroyed by trades that no longer occur
cartel_welfare.feedback: A cartel can redistribute surplus and destroy surplus; only the destroyed gains from trade are deadweight loss.

merger_concentration.q: A student says a higher post-merger HHI proves the merger harms consumers. What is the better statement?
options: A higher HHI shows greater concentration, but consumer effects also depend on rivalry, entry, efficiencies, and pass-through
HHI directly measures the change in consumer surplus
Any HHI increase means the merged firm becomes a monopolist
HHI is unrelated to merger analysis
merger_concentration.feedback: Concentration is an input to analysis, not a complete welfare conclusion.

innovation_tradeoff.q: A student argues that high research spending proves a concentrated market is socially optimal. What is missing?
options: Innovation matters only in perfect competition
High research spending eliminates market power
Innovation benefits must be weighed against possible higher prices, weaker rivalry, and other welfare effects
innovation_tradeoff.feedback: Innovation can be beneficial without settling the overall welfare comparison.

antitrust_rationale.q: A student sees several firms charge the same price and immediately labels the behavior collusion. What is the key correction?
options: Price equality proves the firms have equal market shares
Collusion can occur only when prices differ
Similar prices can arise independently from common costs or market conditions, so evidence of coordination is still needed
Identical prices are impossible without a cartel
antitrust_rationale.feedback: Parallel conduct is not automatically evidence of an agreement because firms can respond similarly to the same public conditions.

opportunity-cost.q: A proprietor uses a personally owned storefront. How does opportunity cost enter production cost?
options: Forgone market rent is an implicit cost
opportunity-cost.feedback: Owner-supplied property has an opportunity cost.

opportunity-cost.q: An entrepreneur leaves a $70,000 job to run a firm. In economic-cost analysis, the $70,000 is:
opportunity-cost.feedback: The forgone salary is the next-best alternative.

opportunity-cost.q: Why can economic profit be lower than accounting profit?
options: Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs of owner resources
Accounting profit includes all implicit costs
opportunity-cost.feedback: Implicit opportunity costs create the gap.

opportunity-cost.q: Zero economic profit signals that owner resources earn:
opportunity-cost.feedback: Normal profit keeps owner resources in their current use.

marginal-analysis.q: A firm asks how much cost rises when output expands slightly. Which measure is relevant?
marginal-analysis.feedback: Marginal analysis focuses on incremental changes.

marginal-analysis.q: Why does MC below ATC lower ATC?
options: The added unit costs less than the current average
marginal-analysis.feedback: A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down.

marginal-analysis.q: A worker adds 10 units and costs $200. The labor-based MC is:
marginal-analysis.feedback: Divide the input cost by marginal product.

marginal-analysis.q: Which cost is irrelevant to the marginal cost of one more unit?
options: A fixed payment that does not change with output
marginal-analysis.feedback: A cost that does not change has zero marginal contribution.

marginal-analysis.q: A competitive firm should expand output while:
marginal-analysis.feedback: Marginal benefit to the firm exceeds marginal cost.

marginal-analysis.q: The last profitable unit in a discrete table is the last unit with:
options: MR at least as large as MC
marginal-analysis.feedback: The next unit would reduce profit once MC exceeds MR.

marginal-analysis.q: Why is the rising-MC crossing used?
options: It is the crossing where moving beyond the output makes MC exceed MR
marginal-analysis.feedback: The local profit maximum occurs where MC rises through MR.

productivity.q: A productivity improvement raises output per worker. With wages unchanged, what happens to labor cost per unit?
productivity.feedback: More output from the same wage lowers unit cost.

productivity.q: A factory produces the same output with fewer labor hours. Which cost most directly falls?
productivity.feedback: Labor-hours savings lower current variable cost.

productivity.q: How can better organization create economies of scale?
options: Specialization and coordination may lower LRATC over an output range

perfect-competition.q: For a competitive firm considering a change in output, which cost curve measures the incremental production cost?
perfect-competition.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional cost of producing more output and is the relevant cost measure for incremental output decisions.

perfect-competition.q: Why does distinguishing AVC from ATC matter for a firm’s short-run production decisions?
options: The two averages contain different cost components
perfect-competition.feedback: AVC excludes fixed cost; ATC includes it.

perfect-competition.q: Cost curves can be reused across market structures because:
options: Every firm faces the same price
Production technology and input costs determine cost independently of the firm’s demand conditions
perfect-competition.feedback: Revenue conditions differ, but cost construction follows production and input prices.

factor-markets.q: A higher wage paid for labor directly raises:
factor-markets.feedback: Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.

factor-markets.q: If the rental price of an adjustable machine service rises, what happens to cost?
options: The cost of outputs using that service rises
factor-markets.feedback: An input-price increase raises production cost.

factor-markets.q: A higher wage shifts a competitive firm’s cost curves because labor is:
options: A variable input in the standard short-run model
factor-markets.feedback: Higher variable input cost raises AVC and MC.

consumer-and-producer-surplus.q: Why can a supply curve reflect marginal cost in a competitive setting?
options: A seller’s minimum acceptable price is tied to the cost of the marginal unit
consumer-and-producer-surplus.feedback: Marginal cost helps define willingness to accept.

consumer-and-producer-surplus.q: Producer surplus differs from accounting profit partly because:
options: Producer surplus is tied to variable or marginal costs, while accounting profit also subtracts fixed costs
consumer-and-producer-surplus.feedback: The measures use different cost concepts.

consumer-and-producer-surplus.q: Why is P=MC associated with allocative efficiency?
options: The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal unit’s cost
consumer-and-producer-surplus.feedback: The last unit’s marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

consumer-and-producer-surplus.q: What does entry after profit tend to do to consumer surplus?
options: Raise price and lower consumer surplus
Lower price tends to increase consumer surplus
consumer-and-producer-surplus.feedback: Entry expands supply and lowers price.

market-structures.q: A monopoly and a competitive firm may use the same cost schedule. What differs later?
options: Their revenue and demand conditions, not the cost identities
market-structures.feedback: Cost machinery is shared even when revenue conditions differ.

supply.q: Why is marginal cost relevant to a competitive firm’s supply decision?
options: It measures the additional resource cost of another unit
It is fixed at every output
supply.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional production cost of another unit and therefore helps determine whether expanding output is worthwhile at a given market price.

supply.q: How is a competitive firm’s supply response connected to cost?
options: It follows rising MC above AVC
supply.feedback: MC gives the additional cost of supply.

supply.q: What converts individual competitive firm supplies into market supply?
supply.feedback: Add firm quantities supplied at each price.

options: Moving upward along the same supply curve
supply.feedback: More firms supply more total output at each price.
Fewer firms reduce total quantity supplied.

opportunity_cost_firm.q: How does the general idea of opportunity cost carry into a firm’s production-cost analysis?
options: Opportunity cost is replaced by accounting profit
A firm counts only costs that change with output
Resources supplied by the owner are valued by the best alternative return sacrificed
Only purchased inputs have opportunity cost
opportunity_cost_firm.feedback: The same next-best-alternative principle applies to labor, capital, land, and other resources used by a firm.

economic_profit.q: How does opportunity cost explain the difference between accounting profit and economic profit?
options: The two measures differ only when fixed cost changes
Economic profit subtracts the forgone returns of owner-supplied resources
Accounting profit subtracts more opportunity costs than economic profit
economic_profit.feedback: Economic profit extends accounting profit by charging the firm for owner resources at their next-best use.

normal_profit.q: Why is normal profit connected to the idea of opportunity cost?
options: It is identical to producer surplus
It compensates entrepreneurial resources for what they could earn in their next-best use
It is a tax on accounting profit
It measures consumer willingness to pay
normal_profit.feedback: Normal profit is the implicit opportunity cost required to keep entrepreneurial resources in the firm.

normal_profit.q: How does normal profit connect long-run competitive equilibrium to economic cost?
options: Normal profit is a monopoly markup above economic cost
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
Normal profit exists only when P exceeds ATC
Normal profit is the implicit return required to keep owner resources in the industry
normal_profit.feedback: Zero economic profit can be sustainable because normal profit is already included among opportunity costs.

integrated_cost_analysis.q: How does marginal decision-making differ from comparing total economic profit?
options: Marginal analysis focuses on changes from one more action, while economic profit compares total revenue with all opportunity costs
Marginal analysis compares total revenue with total explicit costs, while economic profit isolates the value of the next unit
Economic profit evaluates the next incremental action, while marginal analysis measures the return on the entire project
Both methods compare total revenue and total cost, but marginal analysis reports the result per unit of output
integrated_cost_analysis.feedback: The two tools answer different questions: one about incremental choices and one about overall return after opportunity costs.

marginal_product.q: How does marginal product connect the production function to marginal cost when the wage is unchanged?
options: A higher marginal product necessarily raises marginal cost
Marginal cost and marginal product move together in the same direction
A higher marginal product generally means a lower marginal cost of additional output
marginal_product.feedback: When each worker adds more output for the same wage, the labor cost per additional unit falls.

diminishing_marginal_product.q: Why does diminishing marginal product help explain the upward-sloping portion of short-run marginal cost?
options: Total product must fall as soon as diminishing returns begin
Additional variable input eventually adds less output, so each extra unit of output becomes more costly
Fixed cost rises with every worker
diminishing_marginal_product.feedback: With a fixed input, falling marginal product raises the variable-input cost of producing additional output.

average_product.q: How does average product connect to average variable cost when labor is the only variable input and the wage is constant?
options: Average product equals total fixed cost per worker
Higher average product tends to imply lower average variable cost
Higher average product raises average fixed cost
Average product and average variable cost are unrelated
average_product.feedback: More output per worker spreads the wage cost across more units of output.

short_run_long_run.q: Why does the short-run/long-run distinction matter when interpreting cost curves?
options: Some inputs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs can vary in the long run
All costs are variable in both horizons
The long run is always exactly one year
Fixed costs rise only in the long run
short_run_long_run.feedback: Short-run cost curves reflect at least one fixed input; long-run cost analysis allows plant size and all other inputs to change.

marginal_average_relationship.q: How does the marginal-versus-average rule connect product curves to cost curves?
options: Marginal and average values always move in opposite directions
A marginal below an average always raises the average
The rule applies to product but never to cost
A marginal value above an average pulls the average up; a marginal cost below an average cost pulls that average down
marginal_average_relationship.feedback: The same arithmetic relationship governs MP versus AP and MC versus AVC or ATC.

fixed_variable_inputs.q: How does identifying fixed and variable inputs help classify short-run costs?
options: Variable inputs determine accounting profit but not cost
Payments tied to fixed inputs generate fixed cost, while costs of variable inputs change with output
Every input creates only variable cost
fixed_variable_inputs.feedback: Input flexibility is the production-side basis for distinguishing fixed and variable cost.

fixed_cost.q: How does a fixed input in the production model connect to fixed cost?
options: Fixed inputs determine revenue rather than cost
A fixed input makes marginal cost zero
A payment associated with an input that cannot be changed in the short run contributes to fixed cost
Every fixed input creates variable cost only
fixed_cost.feedback: The production distinction between fixed and variable inputs carries directly into short-run cost classification.

fixed_cost.q: Why does a pure increase in TFC leave the change in total cost between two output levels unchanged?
options: The increase reduces TVC by the same amount
The same fixed amount is added to TC at both output levels
TFC becomes variable after the increase
MC is defined as total fixed cost per unit
fixed_cost.feedback: Marginal cost depends on cost differences across output, so a constant fixed-cost addition cancels out.

variable_cost.q: How does hiring additional labor connect production decisions to variable cost?
options: Variable cost falls automatically whenever workers are added
If labor is variable, more labor raises total variable cost
Hiring labor changes total fixed cost only
Labor cost is sunk by definition
variable_cost.feedback: Payments to adjustable inputs are part of total variable cost.

total_cost.q: Why is the vertical distance between TC and TVC constant in a standard short-run total-cost graph?
options: The distance equals TFC, which does not vary with output
The distance equals MC, which is constant
TVC and TC have different output units
total_cost.feedback: Because TC = TFC + TVC, the fixed-cost amount separates the two curves at every output.

total_cost.q: How does TC = TFC + TVC relate to average total cost?
options: It implies ATC equals TFC at every output
It makes AVC independent of variable cost
Dividing each component by output gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by output gives MC = AFC + AVC
total_cost.feedback: The total-cost identity becomes the average-cost identity after dividing by quantity.

cost_schedule_completion.q: How does a cost schedule support marginal analysis?
options: A cost schedule eliminates the need to compare changes
Only TFC is needed to calculate marginal cost
Marginal cost is found by adding TC and TVC
Changes in TC or TVC between output levels can be used to calculate marginal cost
cost_schedule_completion.feedback: Cost schedules provide the change in cost associated with a change in output.

average_fixed_cost.q: How does the fixed-cost concept connect to the downward slope of AFC?
options: TFC falls automatically as output rises
Variable cost is spread across fewer units
AFC is determined by marginal product only
The same TFC is spread across more units as output rises
average_fixed_cost.feedback: AFC falls because the numerator stays fixed while the denominator grows.

average_variable_cost.q: How can rising average product of labor affect AVC when the wage is constant?
options: It tends to raise AVC because a worker producing more output increases total wage cost faster than output
It leaves AVC unchanged because a constant wage fixes variable cost per unit regardless of worker productivity
It tends to lower AVC because each worker produces more output per dollar of wage cost
It lowers average fixed cost rather than AVC because labor productivity affects the spreading of fixed cost
average_variable_cost.feedback: Higher output per worker reduces variable labor cost per unit.

average_variable_cost.q: Why is AVC often more relevant than AFC for understanding the cost of current production activity?
options: AFC determines how much extra output one worker adds
AFC changes directly with every unit produced
AVC reflects variable resources used to produce the current output
average_variable_cost.feedback: Variable cost is tied to inputs adjusted as production changes.

average_total_cost.q: How does the identity TC = TFC + TVC connect to ATC?
options: Dividing by Q gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by Q gives ATC = MC + AVC
average_total_cost.feedback: The average-cost identity follows directly from the total-cost identity.

average_total_cost.q: Why can ATC fall even when AVC is flat?
options: Falling AFC can pull ATC downward
average_total_cost.feedback: Because ATC = AVC + AFC, a declining fixed-cost component can reduce ATC.

average_total_cost.q: How does a below-average marginal cost affect ATC?
options: It leaves ATC unchanged by definition
average_total_cost.feedback: The marginal-versus-average rule applies to costs just as it does to other averages.

sunk_cost.q: How does the sunk-cost rule connect to marginal analysis?
options: Both rules say fixed costs are always irrelevant
Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
Marginal analysis requires adding all past costs
Sunk cost is another term for marginal cost
sunk_cost.feedback: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision.

sunk_cost.q: Why is “recovering what we already spent” a poor reason by itself to continue a project?
options: Continuing can convert past spending into a relevant marginal benefit if enough future revenue is earned
Past spending should be added to expected future benefits because the project needs to recover its historical cost
A project should continue when accounting profit remains positive, even if future incremental costs exceed benefits
Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
sunk_cost.feedback: The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment.

avoidable_cost.q: How can a cost be fixed with respect to current output but still relevant to a future decision?
options: It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
Every fixed cost is permanently sunk
Fixed costs always change one-for-one with output
Future fixed costs are excluded from economic cost
avoidable_cost.feedback: Cost behavior with output and recoverability across decisions are different classifications.

economies_of_scale.q: How does specialization connect to economies of scale?
options: A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
Specialization always creates diminishing marginal product
Specialization raises fixed cost per unit forever
economies_of_scale.feedback: Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range.

economies_of_scale.q: How is economies of scale different from spreading a fixed short-run cost over more units?
options: Falling AFC is a long-run scale effect only
Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
Economies of scale requires one input to remain fixed
economies_of_scale.feedback: Both can lower average cost, but they arise from different mechanisms and horizons.

diseconomies_of_scale.q: How do coordination problems connect organizational size to diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination problems reduce all input prices
They guarantee constant returns to scale
They turn fixed cost into sunk cost
Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
diseconomies_of_scale.feedback: Very large scale can create managerial inefficiencies that push LRAC upward.

long_run_average_cost.q: How does the short-run/long-run distinction connect SRATC curves to LRAC?
options: SRATC includes implicit cost but LRAC does not
The curves differ only because of revenue
Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
LRAC fixes plant size while SRATC changes every input
long_run_average_cost.feedback: Long-run flexibility over plant size is what lets LRAC trace the least-cost envelope.

long_run_average_cost.q: How can productivity improvements affect long-run average cost?
options: If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
Productivity affects revenue but never cost
long_run_average_cost.feedback: More output from a given bundle of resources can lower the cost required per unit.

minimum_efficient_scale.q: How does MES build on the idea of economies of scale?
options: MES is the largest feasible plant regardless of cost
MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
MES is where diseconomies first begin at zero output
minimum_efficient_scale.feedback: Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached.

minimum_efficient_scale.q: Why can MES matter when comparing efficient firm scale with the size of a market?
options: It fixes the market price by law
It measures accounting profit rather than cost
It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
minimum_efficient_scale.feedback: MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.

constant_returns_to_scale.q: How does constant returns to scale differ from short-run diminishing marginal product?
options: Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
Constant returns requires a fixed plant
Diminishing marginal product requires all inputs to change proportionally
constant_returns_to_scale.feedback: The concepts apply to different production experiments and time horizons.

costs-of-production.q: A competitive firm uses which cost curve to decide whether another unit should be produced?
costs-of-production.feedback: The incremental output decision compares MR with MC.

costs-of-production.q: Which average cost determines profit per unit after output is chosen?
Which average cost determines the short-run shutdown threshold?
costs-of-production.feedback: AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run.

costs-of-production.q: Why does a fixed-cost increase not change short-run competitive output?
options: It does not change MC or AVC
costs-of-production.feedback: Output and shutdown depend on marginal and variable costs.

costs-of-production.q: Zero economic profit includes which owner return?
costs-of-production.feedback: Normal profit covers entrepreneurial opportunity cost.

taxes-and-deadweight-loss.q: A per-unit tax on competitive output directly raises:
taxes-and-deadweight-loss.feedback: The tax is tied to each unit produced.

taxes-and-deadweight-loss.q: A lump-sum annual tax on a competitive firm directly raises:
options: Average total cost but not marginal cost
taxes-and-deadweight-loss.feedback: A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost.

monopoly.q: Compared with a price-taking firm, a firm with market power generally faces:
options: A horizontal demand curve at all outputs
monopoly.feedback: Market power changes the firm’s revenue conditions; the competitive firm takes price.

monopoly.q: What decision rule is shared by monopoly and monopolistic competition?
options: Choose output where MR=MC and read price from demand

monopoly.q: Why is entry more important in monopolistic competition than monopoly?
options: Entry shifts each existing firm’s demand and erodes profit
monopoly.feedback: Relatively easy entry is a defining difference.

monopoly.q: Which structure generally has more close substitutes for each firm’s product?
options: The answer depends only on fixed cost
monopoly.feedback: Many differentiated rivals supply close alternatives.

monopoly.q: Which model can sustain long-run economic profit because barriers block entry?
monopoly.feedback: Entry erodes profit in monopolistic competition.

externalities.q: Why can a perfectly competitive outcome fail to maximize social surplus?
options: Private marginal cost may omit external costs
externalities.feedback: The benchmark requires private and social marginal costs to align.

international-trade-and-trade-policy.q: A small competitive firm selling a traded good takes which price as given in the open-market model?
options: The relevant market or world price
international-trade-and-trade-policy.feedback: Competitive firms respond to the price established in the wider market.

price_taker.q: How does the competitive firm’s price-taking assumption connect market equilibrium to the firm’s decision problem?
options: Market demand determines the firm’s fixed cost
Market supply and demand determine price; the firm then chooses quantity at that price
The firm chooses price first from its cost curves and then the market determines how much buyers take
The firm’s ATC determines the market equilibrium price directly
price_taker.feedback: The market establishes the price signal, and the individual firm responds by selecting output.

price_ar_mr_relationship.q: How does P = AR = MR connect the competitive revenue model to marginal analysis?
options: The market price is both revenue per unit and the added revenue from one more unit
Average revenue equals fixed cost while marginal revenue equals price
Marginal revenue falls below price because selling more requires the firm to cut price on all earlier units
Price equals marginal cost at every possible output
price_ar_mr_relationship.feedback: With price fixed, each additional unit adds the same amount to total revenue, so marginal revenue equals price. The firm then compares that marginal revenue with marginal cost when choosing output.

total_revenue.q: How does a horizontal firm demand curve connect to the shape of the competitive firm’s total-revenue function?
options: A horizontal demand curve makes total revenue constant even when the firm sells additional units
A constant price makes total revenue fall as quantity rises
The total-revenue function must be U-shaped
A constant price makes total revenue rise proportionally with quantity
total_revenue.feedback: With price fixed, TR = P × Q rises by the same dollar amount for each additional unit.

market_vs_firm.q: What prior market concept helps explain why the individual competitive firm can face a horizontal demand line even though market demand slopes downward?
options: The firm owns the market supply curve
The firm faces no scarcity in its inputs
The firm is a tiny participant taking the equilibrium price generated by the whole market
The law of demand stops applying at the firm level because competitive sellers can choose any price they want
market_vs_firm.feedback: Firm-level price taking is consistent with a downward-sloping market demand curve because the individual seller is negligible relative to the market.

market_vs_firm.q: How does a market-price increase reach a competitive firm’s profit-maximizing output decision?
options: The higher price raises the firm’s MR line, so the firm moves along rising MC to a larger output
The higher price shifts the firm’s MC curve left automatically while leaving its marginal revenue line unchanged
The higher price lowers MR and therefore output
The firm ignores market price once its plant is built
market_vs_firm.feedback: Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.

marginal_rule.q: How does the competitive firm’s MR = MC rule connect to the broader marginal-analysis principle?
options: Maximize output whenever average benefit is positive
Expand an activity while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost and stop near equality
Choose the activity with the largest total cost because total cost identifies the strongest marginal gain
Ignore incremental effects once fixed cost exists
marginal_rule.feedback: For the firm, marginal revenue is the marginal benefit of another unit and MC is its marginal cost.

profit_per_unit.q: How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?
options: ATC is irrelevant once output is chosen
The vertical gap P − ATC measures profit per unit when positive and loss per unit when negative
The gap P − AVC always equals total profit because fixed cost is irrelevant once the firm chooses output
profit_per_unit.feedback: Average total cost converts the firm’s chosen price and quantity into a per-unit economic-profit measure.

total_profit.q: How does total economic profit connect the revenue and cost frameworks?
options: Profit equals total revenue minus total economic cost
Profit equals total revenue minus variable cost only
Profit equals price minus marginal cost on the last unit only
Profit equals accounting revenue plus implicit cost
total_profit.feedback: The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit.

zero_economic_profit.q: Why can a firm remain in long-run competitive equilibrium when economic profit is zero?
options: The firm has no opportunity costs
Zero economic profit means total revenue is zero
Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
zero_economic_profit.feedback: Normal profit is part of economic cost, so zero economic profit can still keep resources in their current use.

break_even.q: How does break-even connect the firm’s revenue line to its average-cost curve?
options: MR equals zero at minimum ATC
At the chosen output, price equals ATC so total revenue equals total cost
Price equals AVC so fixed cost disappears
break_even.feedback: Break-even is the point where the per-unit revenue and total-cost averages match.

total_loss.q: How should a measured short-run economic loss connect to the next decision?
options: The firm should compare price with AFC instead
After measuring the loss, separately compare price with AVC to decide produce versus shut down
Any loss automatically implies exit today because a competitive firm should never operate while ATC exceeds price
A loss means the firm should maximize quantity
total_loss.feedback: Loss measurement uses ATC; the short-run operating decision uses AVC.

shutdown_rule.q: How does the shutdown rule connect to the distinction between fixed and variable costs?
options: Variable cost is sunk in the short run
Price must cover variable cost because fixed cost is unavoidable in the short run
Price must cover fixed cost before variable cost matters
shutdown_rule.feedback: The shutdown test asks whether operating revenue covers the costs that can be avoided by not producing.

produce_at_loss.q: How does producing at a loss connect to incremental decision making?
options: Use average fixed cost as the marginal benefit of output
Produce if operating adds more revenue than avoidable variable cost, even if total profit is negative
Produce only if accounting profit is positive
Ignore revenue because fixed cost is already paid
produce_at_loss.feedback: Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.

shutdown_vs_exit.q: How does the shutdown-versus-exit distinction connect to the short-run/long-run distinction in cost theory?
options: Some inputs and costs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs are adjustable in the long run
All costs are variable in the short run and fixed in the long run
Exit changes only marginal cost, not industry participation
Shutdown requires the firm to sell all fixed inputs immediately
shutdown_vs_exit.feedback: Temporary shutdown occurs with short-run fixed commitments; exit becomes possible when those commitments can be changed.

firm_short_run_supply.q: How does the firm’s short-run supply curve connect the MR = MC rule to market supply?
options: The firm supplies where ATC equals AFC
The firm’s supply is its horizontal demand curve
At each price above shutdown, P = MR identifies the quantity on rising MC that the firm supplies
Market supply is unrelated to the firm’s marginal choice
firm_short_run_supply.feedback: The output rule becomes a price-to-quantity supply schedule when repeated across possible market prices.

market_supply_aggregation.q: How does individual-firm supply become the competitive industry supply curve?
options: Use the market demand curve instead
Add firms’ quantities supplied at each common price
Add firms’ prices at each quantity
market_supply_aggregation.feedback: Horizontal aggregation connects firm-level marginal-cost decisions to the market supply schedule.

entry.q: How does entry connect firm-level profit to a market-level supply response?
options: Positive economic profit attracts firms, and additional firms increase industry supply
Positive profit shifts market demand left
Entry makes each incumbent’s MC automatically fall
entry.feedback: The profit signal changes the number of firms, linking firm outcomes to market supply.

exit.q: How does exit connect economic loss to long-run resource allocation?
options: Resources leave uses that fail to cover opportunity cost and move toward better alternatives
Exit increases the number of firms in the industry
Economic loss means variable cost is always zero
exit.feedback: Long-run exit is an opportunity-cost response: resources seek higher-valued uses.

constant_cost_industry.q: How does a constant-cost industry connect entry/exit to the long-run supply curve?
options: Entry permanently raises every firm’s ATC
The number of firms cannot change
Entry changes industry quantity without permanently shifting representative firms’ cost curves, producing horizontal long-run supply
constant_cost_industry.feedback: Stable input costs let entry absorb demand changes while long-run price returns to the original cost level.

increasing_cost_industry.q: How does an increasing-cost industry connect output-market expansion to input markets?
options: Input prices cannot matter in perfect competition
Higher input prices shift market demand rather than supply
Industry growth raises demand for scarce inputs, which can raise input prices and firm costs
Industry growth reduces input demand automatically
increasing_cost_industry.feedback: The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets.

demand_change_short_long_run.q: How does a demand increase connect short-run profit to the eventual long-run industry response?
options: Long-run price is always the short-run peak price
Higher short-run price can create profit, attracting entry; final price depends on the industry’s cost condition
Demand changes cause immediate exit before price changes
Profit has no connection to entry
demand_change_short_long_run.feedback: Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.

bridge_perfect_competition.q: Why is the competitive quantity larger than the monopoly quantity in the standard benchmark?
options: Competition uses MR=MC and monopoly uses minimum ATC
Monopoly has a horizontal demand curve
Competition expands output until P=MC, while monopoly stops where MR=MC
Competition faces stronger barriers to entry
bridge_perfect_competition.feedback: The revenue wedge causes the monopoly to stop earlier.

bridge_perfect_competition.q: Which equality holds for a competitive firm but not a single-price monopolist?
bridge_perfect_competition.feedback: A price taker sells each unit at the same price; a monopolist lowers price to expand output.

bridge_perfect_competition.q: Why can monopoly profit persist when competitive profit is eroded?
options: Barriers prevent the entry response that expands supply
Monopoly fixed cost is always zero
bridge_perfect_competition.feedback: Entry is the key long-run difference.

bridge_perfect_competition.q: At the competitive benchmark, allocative efficiency requires P=MC. What is typical under single-price monopoly?
options: P exceeds MC at the chosen output
bridge_perfect_competition.feedback: Monopoly restricts output below the P=MC quantity.

bridge_perfect_competition.q: Zero economic profit is common in long-run perfect competition. Can a monopoly also earn zero economic profit?
options: No; every monopoly earns positive profit
No; zero profit requires horizontal demand
Yes; barriers prevent entry but do not guarantee strong enough demand to cover cost
Yes only under perfect price discrimination
bridge_perfect_competition.feedback: Market structure does not guarantee the profit outcome.

bridge_costs.q: Which cost curve determines the monopolist’s output at the margin?
bridge_costs.feedback: MR is compared with MC for output choice.

bridge_costs.q: Which cost measure determines monopoly profit per unit after output and price are chosen?
A pure increase in monopoly fixed cost shifts ATC but leaves which curves unchanged?
bridge_costs.feedback: Fixed cost does not change demand or marginal and variable cost.

bridge_costs.q: Which cost threshold governs short-run monopoly shutdown?
bridge_costs.feedback: The firm must cover avoidable variable cost.

bridge_elasticity.q: Why will a single-price monopolist with nonnegative MC avoid the inelastic part of demand?
options: Reducing output there raises revenue and lowers cost
bridge_elasticity.feedback: Negative MR makes the inelastic range inconsistent with profit maximization.

bridge_elasticity.q: Under third-degree discrimination, which market generally receives the lower markup?
options: The market with more elastic demand
The market with less elastic demand
The market with higher fixed cost
The market where resale is easiest
bridge_elasticity.feedback: A responsive market requires a smaller markup.

bridge_elasticity.q: At the quantity where total revenue is maximized, demand is unit elastic and MR is:
bridge_elasticity.feedback: The derivative or marginal change in TR is zero at the maximum.

bridge_elasticity.q: Why does product differentiation sometimes soften price competition?
options: More loyal buyers make firm demand less elastic

bridge_elasticity.q: Why might a cartel be harder to sustain when close substitutes exist outside it?
options: Consumers can switch away from the cartel after price increases

bridge_surplus.q: What distinguishes monopoly profit from monopoly deadweight loss?
options: Profit is consumer surplus and DWL is fixed cost
Profit includes surplus transferred to the seller; DWL is surplus that disappears
bridge_surplus.feedback: Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not.

bridge_surplus.q: Why does reducing monopoly output below the competitive quantity create DWL?
options: Some buyers value omitted units above their marginal cost
bridge_surplus.feedback: The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade.

bridge_surplus.q: Under perfect first-degree discrimination, what happens to the competitive gains from trade in the benchmark model?
options: They are realized, but the seller captures nearly all of the surplus
They disappear because output is zero
Consumer surplus rises above total surplus
bridge_surplus.feedback: Personalized prices can restore output while changing distribution.

options: Mutually beneficial units between cartel and competitive output are not produced

bridge_surplus.q: A cartel price increase transfers some surplus from:
bridge_surplus.feedback: Higher price transfers part of consumer surplus to producers.

bridge_marginal.q: What marginal comparison determines monopoly output?
options: TR compared with fixed cost only
bridge_marginal.feedback: Produce units whose marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

bridge_marginal.q: If the next unit has MR greater than MC, what does marginal analysis imply?
options: Reject the unit because it lowers price
Produce the unit because it increases profit
bridge_marginal.feedback: The incremental benefit exceeds the incremental cost.

bridge_policy.q: A patent can create monopoly pricing while encouraging research. What tradeoff should policy evaluate?
options: Fixed cost versus sunk cost only
Static output loss versus dynamic innovation incentives
bridge_policy.feedback: Patent policy can sacrifice static efficiency to encourage innovation.

options: A concentrated structure may make coordination or unilateral market power easier
Lower costs can offset some harm if savings are real and passed through
Cost savings prove no market power
bridge_policy.feedback: Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits.

bridge_trade.q: A domestic monopolist gains access to a larger export market. Which monopoly tool still determines total output?
options: Compare marginal revenue from available markets with marginal cost
Set price equal to world price in every case
Produce where domestic demand equals MC only
bridge_trade.feedback: Market expansion changes demand opportunities, but marginal analysis remains central.

bridge_trade.q: How can foreign suppliers weaken a domestic cartel?
options: Imports provide alternative sources and can expand outside supply
bridge_trade.feedback: Outside supply can destabilize domestic coordination.

bridge_market_failure.q: Why is monopoly classified as a market-failure source in the standard model?
options: Market power can keep price above MC and block beneficial trades
Fixed cost is always socially wasteful
bridge_market_failure.feedback: The output restriction prevents allocatively efficient exchange.

barriers_to_entry.q: How do barriers to entry connect monopoly structure to persistent economic profit?
options: They make total cost independent of output
They guarantee that the monopolist chooses the efficient quantity
They prevent new rivals from entering quickly when profit appears
They force demand to become perfectly elastic
barriers_to_entry.feedback: Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets.

natural_monopoly.q: Why does natural-monopoly cost structure often lead directly to a regulation question?
options: Regulation is needed only when a patent expires
Efficient scale may favor one supplier, yet that supplier still has market power over price and output
Natural monopolies always produce where price equals marginal cost without policy
Scale economies make demand perfectly elastic
natural_monopoly.feedback: Natural monopoly can make one-firm production cost-efficient while still creating a market-power problem.

legal_barrier.q: What happens to a patent-based barrier when the patent expires, holding other barriers constant?
options: Legal protection weakens and potential entry becomes easier
The firm’s marginal revenue becomes equal to price automatically
Average total cost must rise above price
legal_barrier.feedback: Removing a legal barrier increases contestability even if the incumbent remains large.

marginal_revenue_monopoly.q: How does the monopolist’s downward-sloping demand curve create the MR curve used for output choice?
options: Demand forces MR to equal MC at every quantity
The demand curve makes ATC horizontal
MR is simply the vertical distance between demand and MC
Selling more generally requires a lower price, so MR falls below price
marginal_revenue_monopoly.feedback: The price effect from expanding sales makes marginal revenue lower than the price on demand.

elasticity_and_mr.q: What does positive marginal revenue tell you about the portion of a monopolist’s demand curve?
options: Demand is perfectly inelastic at that output
Demand must have unit elasticity at every output
Demand is elastic at that output
Demand is inelastic at that output
elasticity_and_mr.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.

competitive_monopoly_comparison.q: Why does P = MR hold for a competitive firm but not for a single-price monopolist?
options: The monopolist’s average revenue is unrelated to price
The competitive firm can sell another unit at the unchanged market price, while the monopolist generally must lower price to expand sales
The monopolist has no demand curve
The competitive firm always has zero marginal cost
competitive_monopoly_comparison.feedback: Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price.

profit_maximizing_output.q: How do monopoly revenue analysis and marginal cost combine into the output decision?
options: ATC determines quantity before revenue is considered
Price is chosen first and forces MR to equal MC
Demand generates MR, and the firm compares that MR with MC to choose quantity
Demand sets MC directly, so MR is unnecessary
profit_maximizing_output.feedback: The monopolist’s demand conditions determine MR; costs determine MC; their marginal comparison selects output.

integrated_monopoly_analysis.q: Why is monopoly price determined only after the profit-maximizing quantity is chosen?
options: Average total cost sets price before marginal analysis begins
The firm first uses MR and MC to choose output, then demand reveals the highest single price consistent with that output
Price is unrelated to demand until output is produced
The monopolist has no control over quantity
integrated_monopoly_analysis.feedback: Monopoly analysis is a two-step decision: marginal output choice first, demand-based price second.

monopoly_profit.q: How does the MR = MC output rule connect to the firm’s profit-or-loss calculation?
options: Profit is known before quantity is chosen
The shutdown rule replaces MR=MC whenever the firm has market power
MR=MC identifies the best quantity; price from demand and ATC at that quantity determine profit or loss
ATC determines output first and MR then determines price
monopoly_profit.feedback: Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis.

monopoly_deadweight_loss.q: How does the monopolist’s MR=MC output choice create the welfare result P>MC?
options: Average total cost replaces demand in setting price
Market power makes willingness to pay irrelevant
MR lies below demand, so choosing Q where MR=MC typically leaves price on demand above MC
The firm sets price equal to MC and then raises output
monopoly_deadweight_loss.feedback: The gap between demand price and MC at monopoly output is the link between firm optimization and allocative inefficiency.

natural_monopoly_cost.q: How does declining ATC connect the natural-monopoly cost story to the case for one network rather than duplicated networks?
options: Serving the market through one larger network can avoid duplicative fixed infrastructure and lower average cost
Declining ATC makes price equal MR
It guarantees one firm will choose the efficient quantity without oversight
natural_monopoly_cost.feedback: Scale economies explain why breaking the firm into many duplicative networks may raise production cost.

marginal_cost_regulation.q: How does marginal-cost regulation connect monopoly policy to the competitive efficiency benchmark?
options: Both require P=ATC at every output
Both eliminate the need for demand
Both target P=MC so the last unit’s willingness to pay matches its marginal production cost
marginal_cost_regulation.feedback: Marginal-cost pricing tries to reproduce the allocative condition associated with competitive equilibrium.

regulatory_tradeoff.q: Why might a subsidy accompany marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly?
options: A subsidy prevents all entry barriers
P=MC can leave revenue below total cost when ATC exceeds MC
A subsidy is required because MR always exceeds price
regulatory_tradeoff.feedback: The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC.

average_cost_regulation.q: How does average-cost regulation trade some allocative efficiency for financial sustainability?
options: P=ATC makes marginal revenue equal price
P=ATC covers total cost, but price can remain above MC and output below the P=MC level
P=ATC forces the firm to price below MC
average_cost_regulation.feedback: Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark.

price_cap_regulation.q: How can a well-designed price cap change a regulated monopolist’s cost incentives compared with simply reimbursing whatever costs it reports?
options: If the firm can keep some gains from lowering cost below the cap, it may have stronger cost-reduction incentives
A cap guarantees the firm will never invest
A cap automatically sets P=MC regardless of its level
A cap makes fixed costs irrelevant
price_cap_regulation.feedback: Price-cap design can affect incentives to control cost, not just the allowed price.

third_degree_price_discrimination.q: How does elasticity connect directly to third-degree discriminatory pricing?
options: Elasticity determines fixed cost rather than price
Elasticity matters only under perfect competition
Groups with less elastic demand can sustain larger markups over marginal cost
More elastic groups always pay more
third_degree_price_discrimination.feedback: Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.

resale_prevention.q: How does resale connect segmented pricing back toward a single price?
options: Arbitrage lets low-price buyers supply high-price buyers, eroding the price gap
Resale raises marginal cost only in the low-price market
resale_prevention.feedback: Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist.

price_discrimination_welfare.q: How should welfare analysis of price discrimination differ from simply asking whether some buyers pay more?
options: Track how total output and total surplus change as well as how surplus is redistributed among buyers and the seller
Any price difference is automatically deadweight loss
Only monopoly profit matters for welfare
Consumer surplus alone always equals total surplus
price_discrimination_welfare.feedback: Distribution and efficiency are separate questions; output changes can alter total surplus.

first_degree_price_discrimination.q: How does perfect first-degree discrimination connect willingness to pay to the efficient-output condition?
options: The firm must stop where one common price equals MR
The firm ignores willingness to pay and charges ATC
The firm produces only where demand is unit elastic
The firm can sell units until the next buyer’s willingness to pay falls below MC
first_degree_price_discrimination.feedback: Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.

costs_of_production.q: A differentiated firm uses MC, AVC, and ATC from cost analysis. Which curve chooses output?
Which cost measure determines short-run shutdown?
costs_of_production.feedback: The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost.

costs_of_production.q: Which cost measure determines whether long-run economic profit is zero?
costs_of_production.feedback: P=ATC means all economic cost is covered.

costs_of_production.q: Why does minimum ATC matter for excess capacity?
options: It identifies the price on demand
It identifies the output that minimizes unit cost
