costs_of_production.feedback: Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.

perfect_competition.q: Which feature does monopolistic competition share with perfect competition?
perfect_competition.feedback: Entry and exit operate in both models.

perfect_competition.q: Which long-run result occurs in both models?
perfect_competition.feedback: Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models.

perfect_competition.q: Why does monopolistic competition retain a markup unlike perfect competition?
perfect_competition.feedback: Limited market power keeps P above MC.

perfect_competition.q: Which model achieves productive efficiency in its standard long-run equilibrium?
perfect_competition.feedback: The competitive firm produces at minimum ATC.

elasticity.q: More close substitutes make a firm’s demand:
A successful loyalty program makes demand less elastic. What market-power effect follows?
options: The firm may sustain a larger markup
elasticity.feedback: Lower elasticity generally strengthens pricing power.

consumer_choice.q: Why can differentiation create consumer value?
options: It offers varieties better matched to heterogeneous preferences
It forces every buyer to pay the same willingness to pay
consumer_choice.feedback: Different buyers may prefer different attributes.

consumer_choice.q: A brand changes perceived value without changing physical quality. Which concept is central?
consumer_choice.feedback: Consumer perceptions can shape demand for a variety.

consumer_producer_surplus.q: Why can markup create lost trades?
options: Every unit becomes a fixed cost
Some units valued above MC are not sold because price exceeds MC
consumer_producer_surplus.feedback: P>MC can exclude mutually beneficial units.

advertising_information.q: How can informational advertising improve market performance?
advertising_information.feedback: Useful information helps buyers compare alternatives.

oligopoly.q: What separates monopolistic competition from oligopoly?
options: Many firms act without central strategic interdependence in the basic model
oligopoly.feedback: Strategic few-firm interaction belongs to oligopoly.

innovation.q: Why can successful product development create temporary economic profit?
options: It makes MC equal price forever
It shifts demand before imitation and entry erode the advantage
It sets accounting profit to zero immediately

short_run_output_choice.q: Cost analysis tells a differentiated firm its MC curve. Which additional curve is needed to apply the usual profit-maximizing output rule?
short_run_output_choice.feedback: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses output where MR equals MC, subject to the usual marginal condition.

short_run_shutdown.q: The shutdown rule from cost analysis carries directly into monopolistic competition. Which comparison determines whether the firm should produce in the short run?
options: Price compared with AVC at the chosen output
Price compared with AFC at the chosen output
Total revenue compared only with fixed cost
short_run_shutdown.feedback: A firm should produce in the short run when price covers average variable cost at its profit-maximizing output.

short_run_profit.q: A firm has already selected output where MR=MC. Which comparison now determines whether it earns profit or loss?
short_run_profit.feedback: At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.

advertising_elasticity.q: Elasticity analysis helps explain branding. If brand loyalty reduces the absolute value of price elasticity of demand, buyers become:
options: Perfectly responsive at one market price
Less responsive to the firm’s price
More responsive to the firm’s price
advertising_elasticity.feedback: Lower absolute elasticity means quantity demanded changes less for a given percentage price change.

selling_cost.q: Cost analysis helps separate two advertising cases. Which selling expense acts most like variable cost?
options: A fee charged on each unit sold
selling_cost.feedback: A per-unit fee varies with output and therefore enters variable and marginal cost.

innovation_product_development.q: A successful new product feature creates short-run profit in a market with easy entry. What long-run force can erode that profit?
options: A permanent legal ban on substitutes
Automatic shutdown of the innovating firm
A requirement that demand become perfectly inelastic
innovation_product_development.feedback: With relatively easy entry and close substitutes, successful differentiation can attract rivals and imitation over time.

bridge_monopoly.q: A fully effective cartel most closely imitates which market structure?
bridge_monopoly.feedback: A cartel restricts joint output like a monopolist.

bridge_monopoly.q: How does cartel price compare with the competitive benchmark?
options: It is typically higher because joint output is restricted

bridge_monopoly.q: Which monopoly rule does a cartel use for total output?
bridge_monopoly.feedback: Joint output follows monopoly marginal analysis.

bridge_monopoly.q: What prevents an oligopoly from automatically behaving like one monopolist?
options: Member incentives and rival strategic responses
bridge_monopoly.feedback: Independent firms may not sustain the joint outcome.

bridge_mcmp.q: What distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition most sharply?
options: Strategic interdependence among a few major firms
bridge_mcmp.feedback: Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive.

bridge_mcmp.q: Why can advertising matter in both structures?
options: It makes every firm a price taker
It can differentiate products and alter substitution
bridge_mcmp.feedback: Advertising can shape demand in both markets.

bridge_mcmp.q: Which behavior belongs to oligopoly rather than the basic monopolistic-competition model?
options: Choosing an action after anticipating a specific rival’s response
bridge_mcmp.feedback: The basic monopolistic-competition model abstracts from strategic interdependence.

bridge_pc.q: Compared with perfect competition, oligopolistic firms are more likely to:
options: Recognize that their own actions affect rivals and market outcomes
Have free entry eliminate market power
bridge_pc.feedback: Oligopolists possess market power and strategic influence.

bridge_pc.q: What competitive benchmark is commonly used to evaluate a cartel?
options: Price equals marginal cost at the efficient output
bridge_pc.feedback: The competitive benchmark helps identify output restriction and DWL.

bridge_cost.q: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive more output?
options: It has the highest fixed cost
It faces the least elastic demand
It is always the largest firm
Allocating production toward lower MC reduces joint cost
bridge_cost.feedback: Joint cost minimization matters for cartel allocation.

bridge_cost.q: How can excess capacity serve as a commitment?
options: Installed capacity can make a large post-entry output response more credible
bridge_cost.feedback: A sunk capacity choice can alter later incentives.

bridge_entry.q: Which basic incentive concept explains cartel cheating?
options: A member compares its private marginal gain with expected punishment
bridge_entry.feedback: Private incentives can undermine collective agreements.

bridge_entry.q: How do network effects affect oligopoly?
options: They can strengthen incumbent advantages and concentration
bridge_entry.feedback: Network effects can reinforce entry barriers.

market_classification.q: A market has four dominant firms. Which feature would most strongly distinguish oligopoly from monopoly or perfect competition?
options: Assume four dominant firms automatically mean monopolistic competition because any market with multiple sellers and differentiated products fits that model
Classify the market only by whether products are identical
Treat every concentrated market as a legal monopoly
Focus on few-firm strategic interdependence rather than requiring one firm or many tiny price takers
market_classification.feedback: Oligopoly sits between monopoly and atomistic competition because a few large firms interact strategically.

hhi.q: A student already understands market shares. What extra step turns those shares into an HHI?
options: Multiply each firm's market share by the market price and add the resulting dollar values across firms
Square each firm’s percentage share and add the squared shares
Add only the four largest shares
hhi.feedback: HHI builds on market shares by squaring each percentage share and summing across firms.

payoff_matrix_reading.q: Before trying to find a Nash equilibrium in a payoff matrix, what should a student verify first?
options: Whether the market’s concentration measure is high enough to imply that strategic behavior must be present
Whether both players earn equal payoffs
Which payoff belongs to each player and which actions define the rows and columns
Which cell has the highest combined payoff
payoff_matrix_reading.feedback: Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium.

best_response.q: A student keeps searching for one action that is always best, but the player’s preferred action changes with the rival’s move. What concept should the student use?
best_response.feedback: Best responses can vary with the rival’s action even when no dominant strategy exists.

dominant_strategy.q: A student has correctly found a player’s best response in each column. How should the student check for a dominant strategy?
options: See whether the same action is the best response in every column
Add the two players’ payoffs in each cell
Choose the action with the highest single payoff anywhere in the matrix
Look only at the rival’s payoffs
dominant_strategy.feedback: A dominant strategy must remain the player’s best response to every rival action.

nash_equilibrium.q: After marking each player’s best responses in a matrix, what identifies a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: The cell with the largest total payoff even if someone wants to deviate
Any cell where the payoffs are equal
The first cell in which one player has a dominant strategy
A cell where both players’ best-response markings coincide
nash_equilibrium.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses in the same outcome cell.

cooperative_outcome.q: A student found the cell with the largest combined payoff and calls it the Nash equilibrium. What must still be checked?
options: Whether the firms have equal market shares
Whether the cell lies on the main diagonal
Whether each player would choose to stay there given the other player’s action
Whether the two payoffs are both positive and add to more than the payoffs in every neighboring cell
cooperative_outcome.feedback: Joint-payoff maximization and Nash stability are separate questions.

noncooperative_outcome.q: How does a noncooperative game differ from an assumed cartel solution?
options: The government chooses each firm’s strategy
Each firm follows its own incentives rather than committing to maximize joint profit
The firms necessarily choose identical actions because noncooperative behavior rules out different strategies
noncooperative_outcome.feedback: Noncooperative analysis asks what individually rational strategies imply without assuming binding joint-profit coordination.

repeated_games.q: A student understands a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma. What new consideration enters when the firms expect to interact again?
options: Market concentration falls with each round
Today’s action can change future responses and future payoffs
The payoff matrix no longer matters at all
repeated_games.feedback: Repeated interaction links current choices to future rewards or punishments, which can alter incentives.

credible_commitment.q: A student knows that talk alone may not deter entry. What can make an incumbent’s announced response more believable?
options: A costly action taken in advance that changes the incumbent’s future incentives
A vague promise that entry will be punished somehow
A larger concentration ratio by itself
A public statement with no change in capacity or costs
credible_commitment.feedback: A commitment can make future behavior credible by changing what the incumbent will find profitable after entry.

nonprice_competition.q: A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes. What is the next step when firms compete through quality or advertising instead?
options: Ignore rivals because only prices create interdependence
Apply the same strategic logic to nonprice actions because rivals may respond there too
Assume nonprice choices have no effect on demand
Treat advertising as proof of collusion
nonprice_competition.feedback: Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price.
